Please find this submission as an objection to this application. In summary the site selection for this BESS is not suitable for a number of reasons, but primarily due to it's proximity to the [PLACE] and the access directly off the busy [PLACE]. The absence of a comprehensive Environmental Impact Assessment raises concerns about potential negative impacts on the nearby Site of Special Scientific Interest ([PLACE]) and local biodiversity. During peak construction, the site is expected to generate an additional 52 vehicle trips per day. It is important to note that the survey was conducted at the end of November to December 2024, a time when icy and wintry conditions likely reduced traffic flow; this road tends to be busier during the summer months. Personal Injury Accident data from 2019 to 2023 indicates that three accidents have occurred, two of which involved heavy goods vehicles (HGVs). This development is projected to result in 34 HGV visits per day at the peak of construction. The [PLACE] is known locally to have a steady flow of fast moving traffic - interrupting this with slow turning HGV vehicles as well as a multitude of smaller cars with construction workers traveling to and from site is likely to increase the accident risk. I am deeply concerned about the lack of a cumulative impact assessment, especially given that there are now six BESS sites proposed for this localized area. Despite [PLACE] Council's recommendation for an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA), one has not been conducted. My primary objections are detailed below: 1. Unsuitable Topography and Ground Conditions The site is fundamentally unsuitable due to its significant sloping topography with a 25m vertical relief. Our research has found no other site in the UK or globally, either in operation or planning, with such a degree of relief. The development plan, which includes 470 shipping containers, 4608 Solar PV Panels, and three 12m-tall transformers, will require reshaping the land through terracing to six levels. This will involve an estimated 500,000 to 1 million tonnes of groundworks. Crucially, the developer's reports contain insufficient data to support this plan, with no boreholes or geophysical surveys conducted within the project area. This absence of data on depth to bedrock, soil thickness, and groundwater movement makes it impossible to accurately assess slope stability or the potential impact on nearby private water supplies. 2. Significant and Unmitigated Visual and Acoustic Impact The scale of this development, at 16.3 hectares (the size of 23 professional football fields), coupled with its sloping nature, makes it impossible to effectively screen. Proposed mitigation, such as 8m high earth bunds, will be completely ineffective on a site that varies in elevation by 25 meters and would introduce an unnatural feature into the landscape. This development is in direct conflict with the area's landscape character, which Scottish Natural Heritage describes as having a "high degree of integrity" and being "unsuitable for turbines due to its medium scale, valley landform, quality, pattern, high value, and visual sensitivity." Furthermore, the developer's LVIA report is flawed as it omits key natural features like the wide views towards [PLACE] and [PLACE], inaccurately describing the landscape solely by its existing infrastructure. The acoustic report submitted by the developers is also lacking significant detail and fails to provide a comprehensive assessment of the cumulative noise impact. The sloping site will make noise containment very difficult, and two noise experts have advised that while it may be possible to make changes, it currently seems unlikely that sound emissions will be acceptable. 3. Incomplete and Unsafe Fire and Water Management The submitted reports contain critical deficiencies related to safety and environmental protection. The developer has not consulted with the Scottish Fire & Rescue Service ([ORGANIZATION]) on the plans, and they have not fully adhered to all National Fire Chiefs Council guidance. The Fire Assessment report lacks a contingency plan for the numerous adjacent residences, some of which have single-track access roads that would force residents to travel toward a fire to escape. Lithium-ion battery fires are very difficult to manage and almost impossible to extinguish, and having such a high density of batteries could potentially lead to a catastrophic and uncontrollable fire. Regarding firewater, the Surface Water Drainage Strategy report is incomplete. It fails to specify the capacity and location of the firewater detention tanks and states that they will be "designed by others." There is also no indication as to where water will be sourced from for the firewater. These crucial omissions leave fundamental questions unanswered. The plan's reliance on an impermeable membrane creates a high-risk scenario: if the system fails, contaminated firewater could escape into the ground, polluting the groundwater that feeds private water supplies for homes, livestock, and flows into the [PLACE] and ultimately [PLACE] River. 4. Flawed Traffic and Construction Plans The traffic report is severely flawed as it bases its traffic numbers on significantly smaller BESS sites. The document fails to account for a vast number of required vehicle movements, including those for welfare units, solar panels, the impermeable layer, and waste removal. Based on data from similar projects, it is anticipated that there will be more than 155,870 vehicle movements during the 24-month construction phase, averaging 270 journeys per day on our single-track roads. The plans do not address how the affected roads will be maintained or how the expected traffic congestion will be managed. The roads are not currently able to accommodate at least 22,232 HGV and articulated lorry deliveries, and the report makes no indication of how the three Abnormal Load deliveries will be made. The plans also make no provision for the construction area, which needs to be approximately double the final asset size for temporary offices, facilities, and parking. 5. Environmental and Community Deficiencies The developer has not conducted an Environmental Impact Assessment, meaning the effect on a known badger colony, bats, and ground-nesting birds in the adjacent Ancient Woodland has not been properly identified or mitigated. There is no consideration in the plans for the effect the disruption from construction and subsequent presence of the site will have on biodiversity, nor any planning to mitigate an ecological disaster should a fire occur and resulting contamination occur. There is also no plan or guarantees for how the site will be rehabilitated at the end of its life, including the removal of the impermeable membrane, concrete slabs, and the earth berm. The "Community Wealth Building Plan" offers no concrete commitment to local employment or community benefits. There are no guarantees of engagement with local community with respect to the development. The developer has ignored the Scottish Government's "Good Practice Principles," which promote a community benefit of £5,000 per installed megawatt per annum, equating to a significant £2.5 million annually. In conclusion, the proposed project fails to meet the requirements of the National Planning Framework 4. The planning documents contain critical omissions and are based on incomplete data, demonstrating that this development is fundamentally unsuitable for its proposed location. It will have a significant impact on the landscape; there is no commitment for local opportunities and no defined plan for community benefit. As a concerned member of the wider community, I have serious reservations about the impacts this project would have on our shared landscape, local infrastructure, and overall safety. I am particularly concerned for the well-being of those living near the development, as the developer's failure to provide a comprehensive, scientifically sound plan for fire safety, water contamination, traffic management, noise abatement, and ecological damage is unacceptable. I urge you to consider the collective well-being of all residents and to reject this application.

One of my major concerns relating to this development is the road access. - The proposed site is along a single-track narrow road with very little opportunity to create suitable passing places. - The developer themselves refer to this road as a “lane” (fig 1). This is wholly inappropriate for any large-scale development. - The road leading to the development “C1S” has been deemed inappropriate for HGV traffic by [ORGANIZATION] who are also proposing a substation in the locality. The road is so unsuitable that [ORGANIZATION] are creating their own access road which avoids using this access route and small bridge. - The small bridge over “[PLACE]” burn is not strong enough to cope with the increased HGV traffic this development will bring. I don’t see in any of the submitted documentation by the applicant that they have conducted any structural survey work to ensure this bridge is strong enough to withstand the increased HGV traffic. - The applicant refers to previous HGV traffic for the forestry operations, but they did not access the site over this small, old and fragile bridge. - Please see Fig 2, Fig 3 & Fig 4 for map and photographs of single-track road and mentioned bridge. A full structural survey is required before any large-scale developer is granted permission to use this road. Additional concern is that the developer has failed to conduct a breeding bird survey due to their rush to submit their application. - Having visited the location in June 2025 I can confirm the presence of Corn Bunting. - The Corn Bunting is a red list species, and this development will be detrimental to the species and its survival in our rural farmland habitat. 1. Location and Land Use Concerns The proposed BESS site is situated in close proximity to residential dwellings, schools, and recreational areas. The selection of this particular site raises several issues: - Proximity to Homes: The planned facility is less than 500 metres from the nearest residential properties, exposing inhabitants to potential risks associated with noise, air pollution, and possible catastrophic failures. - Impact on Community Character: BESS installations are industrial in nature. Their presence in a rural environment fundamentally alters the character of the area, undermining its aesthetic and amenity value. - Future Development Restrictions: The establishment of a large-scale, high- voltage facility may restrict future residential or commercial development in the area. 2. Safety and Fire Risk Battery energy storage systems can pose significant safety hazards, especially in the event of malfunction or fire. Lithium-ion batteries, in particular, are known for their volatility under certain conditions. - Thermal Runaway: Industry records from similar installations globally have recorded incidents of thermal runaway, leading to fires that are extremely difficult to extinguish, sometimes requiring days to fully control. - Lack of Emergency Preparedness: The application does not provide sufficient details regarding emergency response protocols, coordination with local fire services, or the provision of specialised equipment and training necessary to manage BESS incidents. - Public Health and Safety: The proximity to [PLACE] raises significant concern for the wellbeing of children. In the event of a fire or chemical release, evacuation and containment may be challenging. - The location of the fire water tank to the north of the site proposes a serious fire safety risk. In the event of any fire, any emergency vehicles will have to access this tank via the only access route which will be through burning battery compounds on either side to reach the only water source on site. Another flaw in the design which is extremely dangerous to those attending and another reason for this development to be refused planning. 3. Environmental Impact The environmental assessment presented in the application appears insufficient in several respects: - Potential for Soil and Water Contamination: In the event of battery leakage or fire, hazardous substances could seep into the soil or local waterways, posing long- term risks to ecosystems and human health. - Noise and Air Pollution: The operation of cooling fans, inverters, and other ancillary equipment may result in unacceptable noise levels, especially during periods of peak operation or emergency venting events. Chemical off-gassing and emissions during normal operation or, worse, during thermal incidents are also a concern. - Insufficient Mitigation Measures: The application does not provide robust or verifiable measures to mitigate these environmental risks, nor does it propose ongoing monitoring beyond the construction phase. - Potential disruption to private water supplies and water contamination. o [PLACE] and the [PLACE] which originate on or adjacent to [PLACE]. These feed into the [PLACE] priority catchment drinking water area. o “[PLACE]” and “[PLACE]” both run into the [PLACE] area. o Contaminants from this development have the potential to enter both [PLACE] and [PLACE]. o The developer has not referenced the potential of this or any mitigation matters, they seem to have completely ignored these watercourses and omitted any reference of them from their application in its entirety. If they have missed these obvious water courses visible on any map, what else have they omitted in their rushed application? 4. Inadequate Community Consultation A critical aspect of any major infrastructure project is meaningful engagement with the affected community. - Lack of Transparency: Many local residents became aware of the BESS proposal only after the formal application was submitted, signalling a lack of early-stage consultation. - Insufficient Information: Public information sessions, where they have occurred, have not addressed fundamental questions about risk, mitigation, or alternative siting. - 2 Public Consultations were held on 25th February and 18th March 2025. Even though the applicant has held the required 2 consultations these were held extremely close together with very little difference in the 2 sessions. This felt like a very rushed process simply to “tick the box”. 5. Alternatives and Site Selection The application does not adequately demonstrate why this specific location was chosen over others that may present fewer risks to the community. - Lack of Alternatives Analysis: No comprehensive site assessment has been shared that weighs the risks and benefits of this site versus more remote or industrial settings. - Potential for Co-location: Opportunities to co-locate the BESS with existing infrastructure or within industrial zones have not been explored in detail. This site is neighbouring the proposed [ORGANIZATION] [PLACE] 2 substation development. 6. Economic and Property Impacts Beyond the immediate health and safety risks, the presence of a BESS facility may have a profound effect on local property values and the economic well-being of current residents. - Devaluation of Property: Evidence from similar projects suggests that nearby property values may decrease due to perceived risks and reduced desirability of the area. - Lack of Compensation: The application does not identify any plan for compensating affected property owners or for contributing to community benefit funds. - A transparent and meaningful community benefit fund has not been provided by the applicant. 7. I am writing to object the Installation of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at land to North East of [PLACE], [APPLICATION_CODE]. Firstly, my objection in general terms is the further industrialisation of rural areas and the impact on an agricultural area that already has significant Energy infrastructure. Currently it is not possible to look in any direction from this area without seeing excessive amounts of windmills and pylons (both at land and at Sea). By approving this BESS within this area it will present a further huge impact on our natural countryside, wildlife, and prime agricultural land. If approved it will be adding more industrial infrastructure to an already industrially congested rural area and potentially setting precedence for even more future industrial development of a rural setting. This is wholly unacceptable to anyone who values our countryside and the well-being of its residents and inhabitants. Below I lay out more pointed reasons that I object this development. Each of these objections has merit individually and collectively. NON-ESSENTIAL INFASTRUCTURE We are already 3x above the 2045 target for net zero in the area so this is not a required facility. Within the [PLACE] catchment area there is currently 102MW of intermittent renewable energy generation online or awaiting construction, that could benefit from energy storage backup. Within the same area code, there is currently 130MW of BESS approved and awaiting construction; that leaves 28MW of excess energy storage capacity already due to come online. This local overcapacity (combined with national capacity well on the way to far exceed 2045 targets), demonstrates that no further BESS sites are necessary and should not be considered as 'essential infrastructure' within this area. As non-essential infrastructure, building this BESS will in fact be in conflict with any Green Agenda or Policy as we will be destroying natural land and expending resource and creating pollution on a scheme that provides Zero benefit due to overcapacity in supply. The environmental impact of manufacturing all items that would be installed at this site must be considered along with the destruction of agricultural land. Also, the civil engineering work utilising plant and equipment, transportation, construction of access roads, installation of foundations, and all building activities associated with the placement of these units which is not required. Where this BESS would connect to the grid, and the distance between this site and the grid connection, also has to be considered in the context of Non-Essential Infrastructure (See INADEQUATE LOCATION below) FLOOD CONCERNS The land is in a flood prone area as advised by SEPA. It has a high likelihood (10%) of annual surface flooding. Severe flooding and run off can regularly be witnessed in the area of the proposed BESS (as anyone who uses this road can confirm). The run off from [PLACE] and its natural reservoirs is significant, especially after periods of sustained rain, significant down pours, or during winter when the ground is frozen and impermeable. It is generally understood and accepted that these conditions will only get worse due to climate change and predicted weather patterns - so we can anticipate that flooding will be worse than historically experienced. When flooding does happen then any contamination will leak into the [PLACE] which will damage our wildlife, pollute the water and cause significant negative effects. Further consideration should also be made of the nearby area that these waters discharge into the sea: [PLACE] is an [ORGANIZATION] [PLACE] and any potential contamination could have a significant detrimental effect on the birdlife. Thermal runaway is a major health risk for our local community and wildlife. Current policies do not permit development in flood risk areas unless for essential infastructure. As previously noted, this is not essential due to the overcapacity of BESS. However, taking this out of the equation, there has been no valid points raised as to why this location is the most appropriate for linking to a substation that is miles away, taking up prime agricultural land, invading an area thriving with wildlife and surrounded by residential properties. There is also no clarity provided for this development on how this BESS would be connected to the substation - several miles of ditches and cabling adding to the Net Positive impact of a site that simply is not required? There are two main areas relating to my flood concerns. The first is natural flooding (which already occurs on a regular basis), and the second is flooding in a fire scenario where, as has been experienced elsewhere, substantial amounts of water have to be used over extended periods of time to control battery fires. INADEQUATE LOCATION It is understood the location of this application is a considerable distance from the substation that it is being connected to. Although nothing in the application states where this is actually being connected to? Therefore, a report should be commissioned into where this is being connected to and how they propose to do this without causing unjustifiable disruption and damage. At the initial consultation it was advised that it is due to be connected to [PLACE] and this location was carefully considered due to the close proximity to [PLACE]. The location of [PLACE] substation, which is now the presumed substation due to initial plans with [PLACE] not going ahead, is between 7.4 miles and 11 miles away depending on the route they take. Therefore, requiring major disruption to our local community during the digging to allow the cables to be placed in the ground. This road is a [PLACE] bus route and if closed is going to impact our children getting to [PLACE], along with locals getting to work and going about their daily routine. This route would need to cross the [PLACE] and would cause significant disruption to place significant quantities of cabling all this way along single track roads. It is hard to justify that this scheme and location has any logical or reasonable benefit in reaching net zero. Common sense determines that if this development is absolutely necessary, then a location near the substation is the right thing to avoid disruption to roads, noise pollution from diggers, air pollution and emissions from construction plant running in excess due to the distance required to be dug up, disruption to countryside digging up verges and therefore disturbing wildlife which may inhabit these areas. There is simply no logic that can reasonably support this as a reasonable chosen location for a BESS. I would request that a report is commissioned into why this is even considered an appropriate location, and seek clarity on the connection point to the grid which appears to be a substantial distance away? ACCESS ROAD CONCERNS Another major concern is that having the stated 21 vehicles and one HGV per day accessing the site on multiple occasions for an extended duration. Plus the cranes etc that will inevitably be involved with construction activity and loading and offloading of battery and associated units. The road is already in very poor condition (probably due to the flooding mentioned above). It has significant pot holes which get very deep very quickly due to wash out. What measures would be taken to ensure the condition of this road is not worsened by the increased volume of traffic during construction, and what will be done to ensure the road is returned to its current condition (or better) after construction There is no slip off from the [PLACE] to turn onto the single carriageway road and this is extremely dangerous for a car, having more and larger vehicles turning off is definitely going to increase the risk of a road traffic accident HGV type vehicles will need to come to an almost complete stop on the duel carriageway before turning off due to the tightness of the turn off. Knowing the behaviours of drivers on this fast stretch of road will most definitely cause accidents. Equally heading North and turning onto the [PLACE], the middle area at the intersection, that does not even fit a car comfortably, will be so dangerous for a HGV. Heading South will be HGVs turning into a Major Road without the benefit of any slip road to gain speed. CLOSE PROXIMITY TO HOMES & NATURAL RESOURCE This proposed area is encircled by properties who will all be directly impacted by the building of this BESS. The noise and light pollution emitted from it will be significant due to how open this area is. If it was to go on fire this would be a major concern for loss of property, loss of woodland, loss of protected wildlife, and health complications. Situated right next to woodland which is currently being replanted, and being in such a windy spot, this could get out of control very quickly. Recent fires of battery storage have proven that they will burn for days. The toxic chemicals leaked from this are a massive health concern for nearby residents and wildlife and these concerns also need to be considered as part of the Planning consideration. FIRE RISK As well established by media reports BESS carry significant risk of substantial fire. The fumes from a thermal runaway can be fatal to anyone present, including first responders. Via the Media we are also advised that such fires burn for at least a few days until it has burnt out. Given the proximity to houses this is not an acceptable scenario. The proposed plan states that there will be a pond, however, this only has enough to provide initial firefighting for 2 hours. The [ORGANIZATION] guidance states that there is no way to extinguish a BESS fire so it is difficult to understand how the pond is deemed adequate and simply increases the concern of local residents of an uncontrolled fire scenario. NOISE IMPACT The noise impact assessment needs to be reviewed and reconsidered as it appears to be inadequate and contains anomalies which are neither explained nor understood. Within the Report itself it states that the findings were considered unusual. It is also understood that the noise surveys were not carried out at all property locations adjacent to the site (i.e. [PLACE]). With these anomalies and omissions it is clear that a proper noise assessment has not been conducted and the proposer has not determined any level of suitability and acceptability. FLAWS IN DESIGN/LAND OWNERSHIP ERROR On the Planning application there is a proposed cut off ditch at the opposite site of the field to the access road. It is not clear what this entails? Clarity is required to determine what the intent is here. Also for your info and consideration it appears there are more than one land owners in this area, which conflicts with the proposal. The corner of the field closest to [PLACE] (approx. 0.5 acre in size) is actually not owned by the current landowner, as presented on the documentation, who is proposing to lease land for the BESS development. Therefore the proposer is misrepresenting the ownership and right to lease the land. It is likely that if this development is given the go ahead, and that area above is impacted, then legal issues could arise as ownership of lands has not been truly represented in the application? PRIME AGRICULTURAL LAND This field is currently farmed and is prime agricultural land. Once this site is changed to cater for a BESS, it is stated it will be returned to its natural farming state after use. Consideration needs to be taken as to the validity of this statement as it is not understood, or explained, how they would get this back to it's natural farming state once un-natural and harmful chemicals and construction materials had been present (especially in the aftermath of a fire scenario). VISUAL IMPACT As stated in the application the development will present a moderate to major visual impact on [PLACE]. That is not an acceptable situation for the residents, nor should it be for the decision makers within the Planning Dept. This rural area is already heavily congested with large amounts of Masts and windmills. RISK TO SPECIES The local area is home to pine marten, common toad, European water vole, and two species of owl. By allowing this BESS we would be disturbing and damaging the natural habitat of species that we should be trying to protect. OTHER SIGNIFICANT CONSIDERATION Although the following may not be wholly relevant to this particular Planning Application it cannot go un-noted that the entire concept of BESS Development is very poorly considered, fundamentally flawed, and wholly inadequate to the best interest of the country as a whole. There appears to be no consolidated Plan or consideration as to where and how many BESS are being built, and these things are becoming so numerous that they are having a detrimental impact on rural areas. I have no doubt that at a point in the future this whole topic will become a source of National shame and scandal in the way it is being handled by both National Government and Local Councils. BESS developments are not adequately controlled and are being allowed to be developed in existing agricultural areas and destroying the natural footprint of this land, industrialising rural areas. The huge and unrealistic money being paid for the BESS developers to lease this land is many many times more than the actual value of the land. The BESS sites are often located miles from the asset they will connect to, thus introducing further excessive infrastructure and destruction to achieve connection to the Network and generating significant costs that would not normally be regarded as economical. All these costs will have to be recovered and it will be the consumers who have to face the bill. Once the general public realise what is going on and are faced with large bills to pay for the excessive expenditure of these developments I imagine the roof will come off, and the decision makers such as yourselves who facilitated and approved this will be held accountable. Why can BESS units not be located at existing sites, such as within the footprint of existing windmills, where infrastructure has already been installed and exists - thus significantly reducing the cost and the damage to existing green spaces. I would appreciate these points to be put forward for objection.

I am writing to express my objection with regards to the proposals to site a Battery Energy Storage Site (BESS) on prime grade 1 arable land at [PLACE] (Refs [APPLICATION_CODE] and [APPLICATION_CODE]) both as a local resident and long serving Firefighter. -This is one of the largest active BESS in Scotland and is also much closer to residential buildings than any other existing site in the country (including a doctor's surgery and primary [PLACE]). I feel that this proposal unnecessarily risks the safety and wellbeing of the families in close proximity to the site and the community as a whole. It lowers multiple standards and protections and sets a race to the bottom. After sharing and collating our knowledge as a community, the main concerns of note are as follows: - High grade farmland will needlessly be lost with multiple brownfield sites available in similar proximity. The land in it's current state is a source of homegrown food and supports local wildlife. Current excavation in proximity of the proposed site have already correlated with instances of disrupted deer and fox activity in the area. - After meeting with my community and community council, and following multiple Q&A sessions with planning representatives (the few willing or able to speak to us), there was an alarming lack of key information relation to this development, including Emergency Plans, an Evacuation Plan, and nobody involved in the discussions could confirm the type of battery to be used in the development. It is either the current technology with all of it's documented risks or a new emerging battery technology with a reduced knowledge of real-world performance. Either way, there can be little confidence in a proposal (or the proposers) that doesn't include such a key piece of information. - The noise impact from the completed running BESS runs a high risk of being significantly, and near constantly, adverse. This is totally unacceptable to both close-living residents and the community as a whole. -The proximity to residential houses, [PLACE] and [PLACE] pose a significant risk to a great number of people in the event of a fire situation. It is widely documented that, despite fire detection and suppression systems being in place, BESS sites have suffered thermal runaway, resulting in fires, explosions and the release of toxic gases. Often over a protracted period of time. At present, and to the best of my knowledge, our policy covering BESS fires puts emphasis on defensive firefighting. Due to a number of factors including the environmental impact of contamination from water application, the dangers of explosion and sudden reignition, and where there is no immediate life risk (assuming the successful and confident evacuation of nearby houses), consideration is to be given to defensive firefighting, allowing batteries to burn themselves out. The long duration of a fire event, and given the prevailing westerly wind, could in turn lead to a large-scale evacuation of the aforementioned GP, primary [PLACE] and a significant number of houses. There is little doubt that people will be exposed to the toxic fumes, including hydrofluoric acid, and smoke to varying degrees and that this will lead to both short- and long-term health complications. - Future of the site and impact wider ecosystem Especially in the event of accident what assurances exist that the site can be returned to prime arable land? What drainage exists for emergencies other than dumping contaminated water in [PLACE]? Is there any information about the acoustic impacts on protected species such as bats? None of this is clear from the application and unless these questions are answered the longer term impact of this development on the environment of our community may be tremendous. As will be quite obvious, I do not support these applications by [ORGANIZATION] on behalf of [ORGANIZATION] and [ORGANIZATION]. Please take account of my concerns and objections in your consideration of this application.

I write to object to the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development on the following grounds: 1. Public Safety and Hazardous Materials The presence of hazardous substances in lithium-ion batteries introduces a significant risk. There is no evidence that COMAH regulations have been consulted, nor any indication of coordination with the [ORGANIZATION]. The absence of an emergency response plan, especially given the site's remote, unmanned status, raises serious safety concerns. 2. The conversion from agricultural land to an industrial facility will irreversibly change the character of the area. Its proximity to the substation does not justify such a transformation, which will be visibly and experientially intrusive to residents and visitors. 3. Unassessed Noise Impact The noise emissions from this development will be variable and dependent on load and operational conditions. Assessment should consider original baseline levels before the substation was introduced, and should evaluate cumulative noise from all adjacent infrastructure. Residents already report stress due to unresolved powerline noise - further disturbance will compound this issue. 4. Fire Risk and Emergency Preparedness Lithium-ion battery fires are notoriously difficult to manage and cannot be extinguished by conventional means. Given the site will not be permanently staffed, it is unclear how emergency services would respond, particularly in winter when roads are often impassable. Risks to nearby woodland, livestock, and rural homes have not been adequately accounted for. 5. Water Contamination and Flood Risk Fire suppression efforts would introduce contaminated water into an environment where residents rely on private wells and local watercourses. The proposed SUDS pond, situated on an elevated site, increases the risk of pollution entering aquifers and burns. With more frequent extreme weather events, overflow is a real concern. Consultation with SEPA appears absent. 6. Construction and Road Impact Significant disruption is expected during the construction phase, especially to narrow rural roads used daily by residents, walkers, and cyclists. No clear traffic impact assessments or mitigation plans have been shared for [PLACE], [PLACE], or surrounding routes. Biodiversity and Protected Species The proposed site borders sensitive ecological areas such as the [PLACE], where several badger setts and ground-nesting birds have been identified. There is no clear evidence of recent ecological assessments or consultation with relevant conservation bodies such as the Badger Trust or [ORGANIZATION]. The potential impact on bats has also been overlooked. 8. Visual Appearance and Design Control Though the developer claims the battery units will be coloured to suit the landscape, there are no binding conditions to ensure this will be upheld. Past experience with similar developments suggests this may not be enforced, leading to an eyesore in what is currently an unspoiled area. 9. Restoration and Developer Responsibility There is no plan for site rehabilitation, no soil baseline data, and no mechanism to ensure land restoration. Developers of similar projects have sold them post-approval, raising accountability concerns. An ESCROW fund for environmental recovery should be a non-negotiable requirement. 10. Cumulative Impact on Community Wellbeing The local population has already endured years of disruption from adjacent energy infrastructure. This development will only intensify noise, traffic, and stress, further diminishing the health and quality of life of residents. The area is also an important recreational space for nearby communities - its degradation will be widely felt. 11. Absence of Community Benefit It is troubling that no community benefit is proposed, particularly given the long-term impact and scale of the development. This omission highlights a lack of local engagement or responsibility toward the communities affected. Conclusion Given the risks to public safety, environmental harm, disruption to rural life, and lack of community gain, this proposal is fundamentally unsuitable for this location. I urge the Council to reject the application unless all these matters are fully addressed and resolved through meaningful consultation.

These risks are difficult to contain once initiated and would be devastating to the local area and environment. In the event of such an incident the toxic fumes to all people including a huge amount of children in the village would be catastrophic and lead to potential legal implications. Property value effects - Industrial facilities like battery storage can negatively impact nearby property prices, as well as being an eyesore for residents living nearby. This land is considered greenbelt land and as such should as per government legislation remain untouched. Noise pollution - Cooling systems and transformers can generate continuous low frequency noise that effects the quality of life of people living nearby. When [PLACE] was built there needed to be changes made to the development to ensure that noise issues would not impact the villagers and as such this goes against previous additions to mass developments. Do they have sufficient training and suitable equipment for battery specific emergencies? Would they be able to respond swiftly a would they be able to safely access the site given this is [PLACE]. The introduction of an industrial battery facility, comprised of metallic structures, high fencing, and ancillary infrastructure, would significantly disrupt the area's visual integrity. I write to object to the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development on the following grounds: 1. Public Safety and Hazardous Materials The presence of hazardous substances in lithium-ion batteries introduces a significant risk. There is no evidence that COMAH regulations have been consulted, nor any indication of coordination with the [ORGANIZATION]. The absence of an emergency response plan, especially given the site's remote, unmanned status, raises serious safety concerns. 2. Landscape and Character Degradation The area in question is part of a valued rural landscape described by the applicant's own assessment as "well settled, wooded, and attractive." The conversion from agricultural land to an industrial facility will irreversibly change the character of the area. Its proximity to the substation does not justify such a transformation, which will be visibly and experientially intrusive to residents and visitors. 3. Unassessed Noise Impact The noise emissions from this development will be variable and dependent on load and operational conditions. Assessment should consider original baseline levels before the substation was introduced, and should evaluate cumulative noise from all adjacent infrastructure. Residents already report stress due to unresolved powerline noise - further disturbance will compound this issue. 4. Fire Risk and Emergency Preparedness Lithium-ion battery fires are notoriously difficult to manage and cannot be extinguished by conventional means. Given the site will not be permanently staffed, it is unclear how emergency services would respond, particularly in winter when roads are often impassable. Risks to nearby woodland, livestock, and rural homes have not been adequately accounted for. 5. Water Contamination and Flood Risk Fire suppression efforts would introduce contaminated water into an environment where residents rely on private wells and local watercourses. The proposed SUDS pond, situated on an elevated site, increases the risk of pollution entering aquifers and burns. With more frequent extreme weather events, overflow is a real concern. Consultation with SEPA appears absent. 6. Construction and Road Impact Significant disruption is expected during the construction phase, especially to narrow rural roads used daily by residents, walkers, and cyclists. No clear traffic impact assessments or mitigation plans have been shared for [PLACE], [PLACE], or surrounding routes. The impact on domestic properties adjacent to the access point has not been addressed. 7. Biodiversity and Protected Species The proposed site borders sensitive ecological areas such as the [PLACE], where several badger setts and ground-nesting birds have been identified. There is no clear evidence of recent ecological assessments or consultation with relevant conservation bodies such as the Badger Trust or [ORGANIZATION]. The potential impact on bats has also been overlooked. 8. Visual Appearance and Design Control Though the developer claims the battery units will be coloured to suit the landscape, there are no binding conditions to ensure this will be upheld. Past experience with similar developments suggests this may not be enforced, leading to an eyesore in what is currently an unspoiled area. 9. Restoration and Developer Responsibility There is no plan for site rehabilitation, no soil baseline data, and no mechanism to ensure land restoration. Developers of similar projects have sold them post-approval, raising accountability concerns. An ESCROW fund for environmental recovery should be a non-negotiable requirement. 10. Cumulative Impact on Community Wellbeing The local population has already endured years of disruption from adjacent energy infrastructure. This development will only intensify noise, traffic, and stress, further diminishing the health and quality of life of residents. The area is also an important recreational space for nearby communities - its degradation will be widely felt. 11. Absence of Community Benefit It is troubling that no community benefit is proposed, particularly given the long-term impact and scale of the development. This omission highlights a lack of local engagement or responsibility toward the communities affected. Conclusion Given the risks to public safety, environmental harm, disruption to rural life, and lack of community gain, this proposal is fundamentally unsuitable for this location. I urge the Council to reject the application unless all these matters are fully addressed and resolved through meaningful consultation.

Hazardous operations I have seen, with frightening regularity, instances of battery plants and electric vehicles burning out of control. Given that the nature of these modern batteries means that they must be left to burn out, rather than the 'normal' fire suppression measures being successful. As the batteries contain hazardous materials, where combustion occurs the contaminants can be carried some significant distances in the air thereby potentially adversely impacting farmland and associated livelihoods of those affected. Furthermore any contamination of water courses and/or the water table could have long lasting consequences for residents and their livestock. Insufficient consideration and information is recorded in relation to emergency response planning particularly if the worst occurs during bad winter weather. Furthermore the SUDS plan does not appear to be fit for purpose in relation to adequately protecting local water courses and supplies in the event of an emergency. Industrialisation of agricultural landscape The 'Landscape Visual Impact Assessment' document in the planning application states that the location is an area of 'well settled, wooded and diverse valleys.the landscape is attractive with a high degree of integrity'. It also states that is change of use from agriculture to a BESS site would be 'apparent locally'. The justification of the location of this proposed BESS site is that it is adjacent to the substation. The visual impact and the change of use from agriculture to industry will be evident to local residents, visitors and people from the village who use the area recreationally. There is nothing in the application that relates to decommissioning and site restitution at end of life. There needs to be a decommissioning fund with security agreement (equivalent to those required for Oil & Gas) to ensure the permanent reinstatement of the land to its pre-development state prior to any site works commencing. Residential amenity impacts Noise The noise level will vary (level and type of noise e.g. whistle or a hum), depending on the configuration and set-up, as well as the time of day- e.g. if all battery sites are offloading to the gird at the same peak time. Acoustic impact needs to be measured against pre-sub-station levels, not against current levels, which have already been elevated by the sub-station, the grid stability facility. Consideration of all sites operating together (combined noise from air conditioning units = cumulative effect). There also need to be consideration of the noisy overhead power line issue that is still not resolved in [PLACE], leading to stress and anxiety issues. In much the same way as many communities and homes have been impacted by the noise from turbines, whether that be infrasound, air pressure changes due to blade rotation, wind shear or topography, there will be a change in the noise profile for local communities. Consideration needs to be given to the impact on residential amenity before rather than after the site is approved and the Council must apply the precautionary principles to protect residents first and foremost so as not to repeat the mistakes made when industrialisation by turbines was allowed. Residential amenity and recreation will also be impacted during construction due to increased traffic and site work potentially increasing the risks to local road users. Health & Safety Residents in [PLACE] and the surrounding areas have had construction noise and traffic from the substation, grid stability facility and BESS sites for the last 5 years. Development has greatly contributed to anxiety, stress and the general wellbeing of residents in the area. The impact is not just on adjacent residents; the people who live in the villages of [PLACE], [PLACE] and other areas use [PLACE] as a recreational place to walk, cycle, ride horses and generally absorb the countryside. With the loss of residential amenity, any increase in risk to the health and safety of the residents needs to be offset by an increase in General Practitioner cover and associated referral services within a reasonable distance of the projects. As noted earlier in objection, there is a risk to residents health from the water courses and supplies from contaminants from site works, construction, operation and emergency as well as from any emergency such as uncontrolled fire at the premises. Ecology It has become apparent from many developer applications over the past several years, that many of the ecological assessments are not worth the paper they're written on and that the Council does not have the resources to effectively identify and challenge false assumptions and negligent (at best)/fraudulent (at worst) claims with regard to the minimal impact on existing flora and fauna of the area. Rather than allowing the applicant to commission the ecological survey from their own choice of supplier, the Council should be commissioning an independent report at the applicant's cost. Only by doing so will all parties be able to rely on the objectivity, independence and validity of the report.

I am writing to lodge a formal objection to the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development on land near [PLACE], [PLACE]. My concerns relate specifically to the unacceptable environmental impact, noise pollution, and traffic disruption that would result from this development. 1. Environmental Harm and Ecological Risk The site lies adjacent to the ecologically sensitive [PLACE], which is home to badger setts, ground-nesting birds, and mature woodland. The planning documents provide insufficient detail about ecological surveys or consultations with relevant wildlife organisations, such as the Badger Trust or [ORGANIZATION]. No bat surveys are provided despite the woodland setting. The construction and operation of the site will cause long-term disturbance to these habitats, risking permanent loss of biodiversity. Groundworks, heavy machinery, and noise during nesting seasons could have a catastrophic impact on protected species. Additionally, the proposed SUDS pond presents a risk to local water supplies. The site's elevation means any overflow-whether due to heavy rainfall or battery fire suppression-will drain into springs and aquifers that supply private water sources to local homes. There is no clear evidence of consultation with SEPA or any guarantee that contaminated runoff will be safely managed. The impact of such runoff on local burns and downstream flooding has not been properly evaluated. 2. Noise Pollution and Impact on Wellbeing The potential for continuous low-frequency noise (hums, whines, or cooling unit buzz) from the BESS is of serious concern. The site will contribute to cumulative noise from existing infrastructure, including the substation and grid stability facility. Importantly, the acoustic baseline used for assessment is already elevated by existing development - this fails to reflect the true impact of further noise pollution on residents who once lived in a quiet rural setting. No assessment appears to have been made of peak-time noise when multiple BESS systems may discharge simultaneously. Nor is there clarity on how noise from air conditioning or battery cooling systems will be controlled. Residents have already reported stress and sleep disturbance due to existing noise. This development will worsen those conditions and erode mental wellbeing further. 3. Unsustainable Traffic Burden on Rural Infrastructure The proposed development would bring substantial construction traffic to rural, single-track roads used daily by families, dog walkers, cyclists, and horse riders. These roads are not suited to HGVs or prolonged heavy vehicle use. There has been no clear traffic impact assessment for [PLACE], [PLACE], or the roads leading to the site. No mention is made of safety measures for local residents or children walking these routes. Once operational, the site will still require maintenance access. Winter conditions often render local tracks impassable. If emergency access is needed-especially in the case of a battery fire- these limitations pose serious risks to both responders and residents. 4. Decline in Quality of Life and Loss of Amenity Local residents, including those in [PLACE] and [PLACE], rely on this area for recreation and connection with nature. The increase in noise, traffic, and industrialisation will severely reduce their enjoyment of the countryside. A development of this scale and nature simply does not belong in a peaceful rural environment. Conclusion This proposal risks serious environmental degradation, long-term health impacts from noise, and significant disruption to daily life due to traffic and access issues. The absence of meaningful mitigation strategies or ecological safeguards is unacceptable. I respectfully urge [ORGANIZATION] to reject this application on the grounds of harm to the natural environment, failure to protect public wellbeing, and lack of compatibility with rural infrastructure.

The proposed development will be visually imposing and create ongoing noise pollution during both construction and operation, negatively impacting the community and local wildlife. The noise impact assessment fails to consider all nearby homes, despite concerns raised in public consultations. Additionally, the application does not fully account for the Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) and its grid connection, which has a large footprint. It only covers the BESS site, excluding the connection route to the substation at [PLACE], leaving uncertainty about its placement and impact. This fragmented approach prevents a proper assessment of the development's overall effects. The site boundary plan is also disproportionately large, allowing the developer potential flexibility to move the BESS closer to residences or expand the project in the future. Approving this application could set a precedent for further BESS developments in the area, regardless of their suitability or impact on the CKD community.

Objection to Proposed BESS Development I object to the proposed BESS facility due to serious safety, environmental, and planning concerns. While I do not live locally, I am deeply concerned about the wellbeing of those who do live close to these developments. Fire Risk & Emergency Response Lithium-ion battery fires are difficult to control and highly toxic. This site is unmanned, rural, and prone to winter inaccessibility. No emergency plan has been provided-have fire services been consulted? Water Contamination & Flooding Toxic run-off from fire suppression poses a serious threat to private water supplies and nearby burns. The SUDS pond, on elevated ground, risks overflowing during storms or fire. Has SEPA reviewed this? Hazardous Materials Large volumes of hazardous substances will be stored on-site. Has compliance with COMAH (Control of Major Accident Hazards) been confirmed? Noise & Visual Impact Noise from cooling units and discharging batteries will add to existing stress from substation infrastructure. Visually, the site will industrialise a tranquil, rural landscape. Wildlife & Ecology There are confirmed badger setts and ground-nesting birds nearby. Have appropriate ecological and wildlife bodies been consulted? Traffic & Infrastructure Construction will mean heavy vehicles using narrow local roads frequently used by residents for walking, cycling, and horse riding. Has a traffic study been conducted? Lack of Accountability There is no robust plan to restore the land once operations cease. Developers often sell such projects on-who is responsible long-term? An escrow fund should be mandatory to guarantee site restoration. Given the risks and lack of proper national regulation, developments like this should not be approved-especially when they impact people living so close, with no meaningful protection in place.

Consideration of all sites operating together (combined noise from air conditioning units = cumulative effect). There also need to be consideration of the noisy overhead power line issue that is still not resolved in [PLACE], leading to stress and anxiety issues. Hazardous substances These sites contain hazardous substances in the batteries themselves. Are COMAH (Control of Major Accident Hazards) regulations been consulted? Fire It is not possible to extinguish a lithium-ion battery fire. Battery fires burn out over hours or days. There is no emergency plan shown for the residents who live adjacent to the site. When operational, the site will be unmanned located in a rural setting. What are the Emergency Response times? Has the fire service been consulted for an Emergency Response Plan? Tracks and roadways are regularly snowed in during winter. This site will be unmanned during the operational phase of the BESS. Who will manage the roadway and keep it clear for emergency response vehicles? If an evacuation is necessary, what happens to livestock? If a fire occurs, what is the risk to the adjacent [PLACE] and the surrounding mature trees? Fire suppression water and risk to flooding Water used to suppress a fire will be highly contaminated. If this water gets into the local water table that is not acceptable - residents all have private water supplies, and there is a burn that runs directly into [PLACE]. The planning documents indicate a SUDS pond will be built. This site is on the top of a hill, so the SUDS pond will drain into aquifers and springs that supply local residents' private water supplies. This pond is not isolated form the natural environment, in fact soak-away is part the plan. How will they ensure the pond does not overspill, adding to natural run-off during times of heavy rainfall? While citing being 'storm-proof' in the planning documents and public meetings, storms are more frequent and of higher intensity in recent years. There are documents local evidence (as recent as 2023) of flooding of resident's homes adjacent to the burn that runs towards [PLACE]. The SUDS Pond is at risk of overflow during two episodes: natural storms and if water is required to suppress a battery fire. In both cases potentially contaminated water will impact aquifers, springs and water courses. Has SEPA been consulted? Infrastructure During construction, this will cause major disruption on single track roads. There are domestic residences adjacent to the access point to the site. There is no mention of the impact on these domestic residences with increased heavy traffic. Who will maintain the roadways for potholes and damage? Is the site access clearly visible? Has a traffic impact study been done for the adjacent village of [PLACE]? What about traffic reports for the village of [PLACE] and the roads leading into the substation? If this plan goes ahead it will be impossible for residents to walk, cycle and use these normally quiet roads for access and recreation. Environment / Ecology The planning documents indicate there are 4 badger setts within the [PLACE]. Has the Badger's Trust been consulted? Has [ORGANIZATION] been consulted about the bird life? When was the ecology survey conducted? There are ground nesting birds using this landscape for nesting for generations. Has a bat survey been conducted in the woodland? Visual impact The planning documents and a condition of the application ([APPLICATION_CODE]) state that the battery units will be green or dark grey in colour to blend into the background. What assurances are there that the developer will adhere to this? Experience has shown that other BESS sites default to white units. Rehabilitation Where are the guarantees that the land will be returned to its original state at the end of project? We have seen no reports on soil sampling, microbiological content of the soil or any information relating to the current state of the soil. How can a company guarantee a return to original state when they do know, scientifically, the base line? It has already been demonstrated that the companies originally instigating the BESS planning applications have sold the projects on to other companies once planning has been achieved - how do we ensure that they remain accountable? We need to insist on an annual contribution that's put in ESCROW to protect it. Impact on the health of the community The impact on the health (physical and mental) on residents is not being considered. Residents in [PLACE] and the surrounding areas have had construction noise and traffic from the substation, grid stability facility and BESS sites for the last 5 years. Development has greatly contributed to anxiety, stress and the general wellbeing of residents in the area. The impact is not just on adjacent residents; the people who live in the villages of [PLACE], [PLACE] and other areas use [PLACE] as a recreational place to walk, cycle, ride horses and generally absorb the countryside. The heavy traffic and noise will lead to the loss of this amenity.

This proposed BESS site would significantly industrialise a currently agricultural and scenic rural landscape, directly contradicting the area's classification in the planning documents as "well-settled, wooded and attractive." The change from farmland to industrial use will be clearly visible to residents, visitors, and recreational users. The claim that visual impact will be minimal is not credible given the site's location and lack of meaningful screening. There is also no assurance that battery units will adhere to the promised green or dark grey coloring-past experience suggests white units are often used, exacerbating visual disruption. Furthermore, there is no guarantee the land will be restored after the project ends-no soil baseline data has been provided, making rehabilitation promises meaningless. The planning fails to properly assess ecological damage. Local wildlife-badgers, bats, and ground- nesting birds-are known to inhabit the area, yet it is unclear if surveys were conducted during appropriate seasons or if key conservation bodies were consulted. Finally, there is a clear and ongoing impact on community mental and physical health. For years, residents have suffered from cumulative noise, traffic, and stress due to continuous infrastructure development in the area. This site, unmanned and remote, only adds to the burden. There are no proposed community benefits-only risk, with no tangible gain for locals.

I strongly object to the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development near [PLACE] due to its likely negative effects on local ecology, disruption of long- established wildlife habitats, and the cumulative burden of ongoing energy infrastructure projects in the area. 1. Ecological Sensitivity of the Site The proposed development site borders the [PLACE], a well-established and ecologically diverse woodland. The planning documentation acknowledges the presence of at least four badger setts within the woodland, yet it is unclear whether proper consultation with relevant environmental organisations - such as the Scottish Badgers, British Trust for Ornithology, or local bat conservation groups - has taken place. Disruption during construction and operation will impact ground-nesting birds, bats, and other protected species. Seasonal use of this landscape for breeding and feeding by a wide variety of wildlife has gone largely unaddressed. 2. Inadequate Ecological Surveys and Safeguards No details have been provided on the timing, thoroughness, or methodology of the ecological surveys underpinning this proposal. Without transparent and up-to-date data, it is impossible for the public or planning authorities to assess the true scale of the threat to local biodiversity. Given the industrial nature of the proposal and the requirement for lighting, vehicle access, and continuous energy storage infrastructure, the habitat fragmentation and long-term ecological degradation may be substantial and irreversible. 3. Cumulative Pressure from Energy Developments This development is not occurring in isolation. Residents in the area have already endured years of disturbance from the substation, the grid stability facility, and other associated projects. This latest proposal adds further industrialisation to a region that is increasingly being used as a dumping ground for energy infrastructure, at the expense of its environment and people. There is no holistic environmental assessment of how all these developments - existing and proposed - combine to degrade the landscape, stress wildlife, and limit the long-term health of the local ecosystem. 4. Permanent Loss of Open, Natural Land This development would result in the permanent transformation of agricultural and semi-natural land into an industrial site. Visual mitigation measures, such as planting or paint colour, do not address the underlying loss of open space and the displacement of the ecosystems that depend on it. The long-term ecological cost is not being measured or valued in the planning process. That oversight needs to be corrected before such a development can be responsibly considered. Conclusion The proposed BESS project threatens to further erode the ecological health of the [PLACE] area and contributes to the creeping industrialisation of an already burdened rural landscape. Without robust ecological protections, independent environmental assessments, and proper cumulative impact evaluation, this application should be rejected.

I am writing as a neighbouring resident to strongly object to the proposed Battery Storage Facility in [PLACE]. My house sits at the top of [PLACE] and is mentioned in the planning document as being 220m from the proposed development. I am extremely concerned at the impact this will have on the surrounding area, and I believe the planning application severely downplays and fails to consider several key points. Whilst I'm sure everyone is in agreement that this kind of infrastructure is key to meeting climate targets, I feel this is a shortsighted lazy attempt by the applicant to situate a facility only to reap the benefits of existing (poorly situated) electrical infrastructure, instead of putting in the required investment into a suitable futureproofed site capable of housing and scaling up battery storage to meet the growing need of renewables. It is clear there will be no direct benefit to the people of [PLACE] (confirmed to me by [PERSON] staff during the consultation in May), the development will create no jobs or opportunities for business development. Presumably the only parties to financially benefit will be the applicant and the private landowner. All at the expense of local residents and the environment. I am objecting on several grounds which I will cover in detail below: Firstly the visual impact of the facility on the surrounding area. This is something I feel has not been well detailed in the submitted drawings and plans. We are talking about a field containing 53 metal containers (with dimensions of 13m x 2.5m x 2.8m) terraced down a steeply sloping incline toward the [PLACE]. Whilst I appreciate the proposed measures to shield the view of the infrastructure, there is no avoiding that this development is being placed on a hill, the bund at the bottom of the hill and trees would need to be of a great size to actually mask it's view. Drivers and pedestrians will be met with an unavoidable view of the 53 containers as you proceed along the route. The [PLACE] is a popular walking route, and the view from the currently scenic peaceful cemetery will also be blighted by the view. I also believe the development will be visible from farther up the [PLACE] beyond [PLACE], as I can often see the top of our house on the horizon as I drive toward [PLACE]. From my own point of view, from our house we will have some view of the development from upstairs and the top of our garden. Many people walk their dogs along the path at the rear of our property between [PLACE] and [PLACE] and the proposed view from this path looks nothing short of a prison camp with barb wire topping high fencing. As the environment team note in their consultation document, the proposed planting to mask the development is not fit for purpose given the exposed coastal nature of the site. My own garden and the existing landscape can attest to the fact that not much survives beyond the native gorse which does not grow high enough to mask the development. I am not confident the proposed measures can go very far in mitigating the impact of local residents from a visual perspective. During the consultation I was provided with a photo of a similar battery storage site, which were quite eye opening. I would advise the planners request some more detailed images of the proposed development, photos /3D mockups and such like, as in its current form the drawings are not very representative of the reality. Secondly what is the potential impact on nature and the environment? There is a lot of wildlife often seen in these fields, I routinely see deer, birds, rabbits, foxes and have seen badgers in the past. There is little in the way of information on safety of the battery infrastructure, these are lithium batteries - in the consultation there was notes about the risk from fire and possible pollution that I don't see considered in the application, further details should be sought on this. Next I have concerns about the construction of the site, the proposed access is via the top of [PLACE]. Can the streets of [PLACE] cope with high quantities of plant and lorries weaving along the tight roads to access the site? What will be the impact on local residents in terms of noise and pollution from this activity? Also the noise of the construction concerns me personally, we can clearly hear tractors ploughing and working in the same field. How long will the construction take and what will be the noise impact? This is not addressed in the application. My children and others also walk along the path to the primary [PLACE], what safety measures will be in place to ensure they come to no harm? Lastly the noise pollution report is not well detailed, which is also noted by the environmental health team. I was surprised to read my property is named in this section as being a closed neighbour at 220m, however is not covered in the table along with other houses of a similar distance where a predicted dB level is attributed to their position. I would kindly ask for Environmental Health to request this in addition the added information they have asked for. Lastly the area in question is already blighted by electricity infrastructure, 2 mobile phone masts and a water reservoir. I personally think this is more than enough given the proximity to residential properties and in an area of outstanding natural beauty enjoyed by many locals for walking and recreation. I am also concerned how this could potentially devalue both our own and other nearby resident's properties. Any application should weigh up the positives against the negative for the community. Here it seems there are no direct benefits to the local community but there is the potential to irreparably damage a beautiful area, impacting nearby residents significantly, with the wider community fairly unaware of the blight that could be soon built on their landscape. Whilst I appreciate my comments are quite long, I trust they are fully considered and taken on board by those considering this application.

The proposed site for this development is designated as greenbelt in the council’s approved Local Development Plan and permission to grant such a facility would be in direct contravention of an already approved plan. Not only would this facility provide an intrusion at the edge of a beautiful conservation village, it could also open the door to other industrial development in the surrounding area. Additionally, the associated ancillary infrastructure, which would include a substation, transformers, lighting and a perimeter fence would encroach on the peaceful environment to those living near the facility and would also cause an increase in traffic and disruption in an area that already has an increasing amount of traffic on local roads. This would, in turn, lead to increased traffic pollution to the local environment. There would also be glare from the lighting and noise from the substation, which would, again, cause disturbance to the environment and the tranquility of this local area. The safety of this installation is also of deep concern. There have been news items already looking at the safety of lithium batteries in general, but a recent report (April 9, 2024) of a fire in a similar battery energy storage facility in [PLACE], has provided evidence that fires can start spontaneously due to the Lithium salts in the batteries, which are self-oxidising and can’t be starved out like an ordinary fire. There is, therefore, the potential of such a fire to spread, which could be a danger to those residents living nearest to the facility. Lithium batteries also contain metals such as cobalt, nickel and manganese, which are toxic and the implications to health should also be a consideration given the possibility of such a situation. Additionally, due to its proximity to the [PLACE], there is also the danger of pollution should a fire occur. No-one, as is clear from evidence which is clearly available, can give a categorical assurance that this would not happen. The proof is already out there. People should not have to live with such a potential threat in their local area, even more so in a conservation area, which is so near to housing, farm animals and the [PLACE]. While I understand that a detrimental effect on house values is not, in itself, a valid objection for rejecting this planning application, for those of us who live in this community and are concerned for the welfare of all of our residents, this would have a devastating effect on the residents who live very near to this proposed site. In a village community where there is a great deal of community spirit and support, these issues matter. It is imperative that this planning application is rejected.

Noise Impact and Acoustic Concerns Noise emissions from the proposed site will vary based on operational conditions, configuration, and time of day-particularly during simultaneous offloading events across multiple battery units. Noise assessments must take pre-substation baseline data into account, not just current levels already elevated by nearby energy infrastructure. Cumulative noise from all operational systems (e.g., air conditioning units) must be evaluated, especially in light of ongoing complaints about the noise generated by overhead lines in [PLACE], which have been a source of considerable stress for many residents. 4. Fire Risk and Emergency Response Readiness Lithium-ion battery fires are dangerous, difficult to extinguish, and can persist for extended periods. Risk of Contaminated Runoff and Flooding Water used to suppress battery fires may become highly toxic. While the proposed SUDS pond is intended to mitigate runoff, its hilltop location poses real risks. The pond will drain into aquifers and springs, with the soakaway approach integrating it directly into the natural environment. During heavy rainfall-or if firefighting water is discharged-the pond could overflow, contaminating local watercourses. Has SEPA been properly consulted? To ensure long-term accountability, a financial mechanism-such as an annual escrow contribution-should be required for land restoration and public protection. 10. Furthermore, a comprehensive plan for the evacuation of livestock in the event of a fire is required, alongside a thorough assessment of the fire risk posed to the adjacent [PLACE] and the surrounding mature trees. The issue of Fire Suppression Water and Risk to Flooding also warrants serious consideration. The highly contaminated water used to extinguish battery fires poses a significant threat to the local water table, which serves as a source of private water for numerous residents. The proposed SUDS pond, located on a hilltop with a soak-away design, will directly drain into aquifers and springs that feed these private water supplies. Clear assurances are needed regarding how overspill from the SUDS pond will be prevented, both during natural heavy rainfall events (which are becoming more frequent and intense) and in the event of fire suppression, thereby safeguarding local water sources. The documented history of flooding in residents' homes adjacent to the burn leading to [PLACE] further highlights the inadequacy of the current drainage proposals. Confirmation of consultation with SEPA regarding these potential risks is absolutely essential. Firm guarantees and legally binding conditions are therefore required to ensure adherence to the specified colour scheme to effectively mitigate any adverse visual impact. The lack of firm commitments for the Rehabilitation of the Site at the end of its operational life is a significant concern. The absence of reports detailing baseline soil sampling and microbiological content raises serious doubts about the feasibility of such a guarantee. It is unclear how a company can ensure effective restoration without a scientific understanding of the current soil composition. Furthermore, the observed practice of initial developers selling projects after obtaining planning permission raises concerns about long-term accountability. A legally binding mechanism, such as an annual contribution held in escrow, is necessary to ensure that sufficient funds will be available for comprehensive site rehabilitation. The proposed approach to the site's end of life, which involves planting trees to mitigate the environmental changes from agricultural to industrial land use, is also concerning, as their eventual removal to return the area to farmland would represent a significant step backward for both the landscape and its biodiversity. There is no financial guarantee-such as a bond or escrow fund-that would ensure restoration takes place if the project is sold or the operator ceases trading. Given that similar BESS projects have been sold on post-approval, this is a realistic and urgent concern. Ongoing Noise Impacts: The planning application downplays the nature of the operational noise. Battery systems require continuous active cooling, which produces variable noise depending on weather, load, and system configuration. If multiple units discharge to the grid simultaneously, the aggregate noise-including fan whine, transformer hum, and inverter switching-can be significant. These impacts will be most noticeable during peak usage times, including evenings, when background noise is minimal and residential exposure is highest. The site is near homes and rural properties where residents expect quiet living conditions. Noise monitoring appears to have been done under existing substation conditions, not pre-development levels-failing to assess the full incremental impact. Planning guidance makes clear that cumulative and tonal noise should be assessed in such cases. Without enforceable limits, continuous monitoring, or mitigation conditions, granting approval would be inconsistent with noise control and environmental protection policies.
