By approving this BESS within this area it will present a further huge impact on our natural countryside, wildlife, and prime agricultural land. If approved it will be adding more industrial infrastructure to an already industrially congested rural area and potentially setting precedence for even more future industrial development of a rural setting. This is wholly unacceptable to anyone who values our countryside and the well-being of its residents and inhabitants. Below I lay out more pointed reasons that I object this development. Each of these objections has merit individually and collectively. NON-ESSENTIAL INFASTRUCTURE We are already 3x above the 2045 target for net zero in the area so this is not a required facility. Within the [PLACE] catchment area there is currently 102MW of intermittent renewable energy generation online or awaiting construction, that could benefit from energy storage backup. Within the same area code, there is currently 130MW of BESS approved and awaiting construction; that leaves 28MW of excess energy storage capacity already due to come online. This local overcapacity (combined with national capacity well on the way to far exceed 2045 targets), demonstrates that no further BESS sites are necessary and should not be considered as 'essential infrastructure' within this area. As non-essential infrastructure, building this BESS will in fact be in conflict with any Green Agenda or Policy as we will be destroying natural land and expending resource and creating pollution on a scheme that provides Zero benefit due to overcapacity in supply. The environmental impact of manufacturing all items that would be installed at this site must be considered along with the destruction of agricultural land. Also, the civil engineering work utilising plant and equipment, transportation, construction of access roads, installation of foundations, and all building activities associated with the placement of these units which is not required. Where this BESS would connect to the grid, and the distance between this site and the grid connection, also has to be considered in the context of Non-Essential Infrastructure (See INADEQUATE LOCATION below) FLOOD CONCERNS The land is in a flood prone area as advised by SEPA. It has a high likelihood (10%) of annual surface flooding. Severe flooding and run off can regularly be witnessed in the area of the proposed BESS (as anyone who uses this road can confirm). The run off from [PLACE] and its natural reservoirs is significant, especially after periods of sustained rain, significant down pours, or during winter when the ground is frozen and impermeable. It is generally understood and accepted that these conditions will only get worse due to climate change and predicted weather patterns - so we can anticipate that flooding will be worse than historically experienced. When flooding does happen then any contamination will leak into the [PLACE] which will damage our wildlife, pollute the water and cause significant negative effects. Further consideration should also be made of the nearby area that these waters discharge into the sea: [PLACE] is an [ORGANIZATION] [PLACE] and any potential contamination could have a significant detrimental effect on the birdlife. Thermal runaway is a major health risk for our local community and wildlife. Current policies do not permit development in flood risk areas unless for essential infastructure. As previously noted, this is not essential due to the overcapacity of BESS. However, taking this out of the equation, there has been no valid points raised as to why this location is the most appropriate for linking to a substation that is miles away, taking up prime agricultural land, invading an area thriving with wildlife and surrounded by residential properties. There is also no clarity provided for this development on how this BESS would be connected to the substation - several miles of ditches and cabling adding to the Net Positive impact of a site that simply is not required? There are two main areas relating to my flood concerns. The first is natural flooding (which already occurs on a regular basis), and the second is flooding in a fire scenario where, as has been experienced elsewhere, substantial amounts of water have to be used over extended periods of time to control battery fires. INADEQUATE LOCATION It is understood the location of this application is a considerable distance from the substation that it is being connected to. Although nothing in the application states where this is actually being connected to? Therefore, a report should be commissioned into where this is being connected to and how they propose to do this without causing unjustifiable disruption and damage. At the initial consultation it was advised that it is due to be connected to [PLACE] and this location was carefully considered due to the close proximity to [PLACE]. The location of [PLACE] substation, which is now the presumed substation due to initial plans with [PLACE] not going ahead, is between 7.4 miles and 11 miles away depending on the route they take. Therefore, requiring major disruption to our local community during the digging to allow the cables to be placed in the ground. This road is a [PLACE] bus route and if closed is going to impact our children getting to [PLACE], along with locals getting to work and going about their daily routine. This route would need to cross the [PLACE] and would cause significant disruption to place significant quantities of cabling all this way along single track roads. It is hard to justify that this scheme and location has any logical or reasonable benefit in reaching net zero. Common sense determines that if this development is absolutely necessary, then a location near the substation is the right thing to avoid disruption to roads, noise pollution from diggers, air pollution and emissions from construction plant running in excess due to the distance required to be dug up, disruption to countryside digging up verges and therefore disturbing wildlife which may inhabit these areas. There is simply no logic that can reasonably support this as a reasonable chosen location for a BESS. I would request that a report is commissioned into why this is even considered an appropriate location, and seek clarity on the connection point to the grid which appears to be a substantial distance away? ACCESS ROAD CONCERNS Another major concern is that having the stated 21 vehicles and one HGV per day accessing the site on multiple occasions for an extended duration. Plus the cranes etc that will inevitably be involved with construction activity and loading and offloading of battery and associated units. The road is already in very poor condition (probably due to the flooding mentioned above). It has significant pot holes which get very deep very quickly due to wash out. What measures would be taken to ensure the condition of this road is not worsened by the increased volume of traffic during construction, and what will be done to ensure the road is returned to its current condition (or better) after construction There is no slip off from the [PLACE] to turn onto the single carriageway road and this is extremely dangerous for a car, having more and larger vehicles turning off is definitely going to increase the risk of a road traffic accident HGV type vehicles will need to come to an almost complete stop on the duel carriageway before turning off due to the tightness of the turn off. Knowing the behaviours of drivers on this fast stretch of road will most definitely cause accidents. Equally heading North and turning onto the [PLACE], the middle area at the intersection, that does not even fit a car comfortably, will be so dangerous for a HGV. Heading South will be HGVs turning into a Major Road without the benefit of any slip road to gain speed. CLOSE PROXIMITY TO HOMES & NATURAL RESOURCE This proposed area is encircled by properties who will all be directly impacted by the building of this BESS. The noise and light pollution emitted from it will be significant due to how open this area is. If it was to go on fire this would be a major concern for loss of property, loss of woodland, loss of protected wildlife, and health complications. Situated right next to woodland which is currently being replanted, and being in such a windy spot, this could get out of control very quickly. Recent fires of battery storage have proven that they will burn for days. The toxic chemicals leaked from this are a massive health concern for nearby residents and wildlife and these concerns also need to be considered as part of the Planning consideration. FIRE RISK As well established by media reports BESS carry significant risk of substantial fire. The fumes from a thermal runaway can be fatal to anyone present, including first responders. Via the Media we are also advised that such fires burn for at least a few days until it has burnt out. Given the proximity to houses this is not an acceptable scenario. The proposed plan states that there will be a pond, however, this only has enough to provide initial firefighting for 2 hours. The [ORGANIZATION] guidance states that there is no way to extinguish a BESS fire so it is difficult to understand how the pond is deemed adequate and simply increases the concern of local residents of an uncontrolled fire scenario. NOISE IMPACT The noise impact assessment needs to be reviewed and reconsidered as it appears to be inadequate and contains anomalies which are neither explained nor understood. Within the Report itself it states that the findings were considered unusual. It is also understood that the noise surveys were not carried out at all property locations adjacent to the site (i.e. [PLACE]). With these anomalies and omissions it is clear that a proper noise assessment has not been conducted and the proposer has not determined any level of suitability and acceptability. FLAWS IN DESIGN/LAND OWNERSHIP ERROR On the Planning application there is a proposed cut off ditch at the opposite site of the field to the access road. It is not clear what this entails? Clarity is required to determine what the intent is here. Also for your info and consideration it appears there are more than one land owners in this area, which conflicts with the proposal. The corner of the field closest to [PLACE] (approx. 0.5 acre in size) is actually not owned by the current landowner, as presented on the documentation, who is proposing to lease land for the BESS development. Therefore the proposer is misrepresenting the ownership and right to lease the land. It is likely that if this development is given the go ahead, and that area above is impacted, then legal issues could arise as ownership of lands has not been truly represented in the application? PRIME AGRICULTURAL LAND This field is currently farmed and is prime agricultural land. Once this site is changed to cater for a BESS, it is stated it will be returned to its natural farming state after use. Consideration needs to be taken as to the validity of this statement as it is not understood, or explained, how they would get this back to it's natural farming state once un-natural and harmful chemicals and construction materials had been present (especially in the aftermath of a fire scenario). VISUAL IMPACT As stated in the application the development will present a moderate to major visual impact on [PLACE]. That is not an acceptable situation for the residents, nor should it be for the decision makers within the Planning Dept. This rural area is already heavily congested with large amounts of Masts and windmills. RISK TO SPECIES The local area is home to pine marten, common toad, European water vole, and two species of owl. By allowing this BESS we would be disturbing and damaging the natural habitat of species that we should be trying to protect. OTHER SIGNIFICANT CONSIDERATION Although the following may not be wholly relevant to this particular Planning Application it cannot go un-noted that the entire concept of BESS Development is very poorly considered, fundamentally flawed, and wholly inadequate to the best interest of the country as a whole. There appears to be no consolidated Plan or consideration as to where and how many BESS are being built, and these things are becoming so numerous that they are having a detrimental impact on rural areas. I have no doubt that at a point in the future this whole topic will become a source of National shame and scandal in the way it is being handled by both National Government and Local Councils. BESS developments are not adequately controlled and are being allowed to be developed in existing agricultural areas and destroying the natural footprint of this land, industrialising rural areas. The huge and unrealistic money being paid for the BESS developers to lease this land is many many times more than the actual value of the land. The BESS sites are often located miles from the asset they will connect to, thus introducing further excessive infrastructure and destruction to achieve connection to the Network and generating significant costs that would not normally be regarded as economical. All these costs will have to be recovered and it will be the consumers who have to face the bill. Once the general public realise what is going on and are faced with large bills to pay for the excessive expenditure of these developments I imagine the roof will come off, and the decision makers such as yourselves who facilitated and approved this will be held accountable. Why can BESS units not be located at existing sites, such as within the footprint of existing windmills, where infrastructure has already been installed and exists - thus significantly reducing the cost and the damage to existing green spaces. I would appreciate these points to be put forward for objection.

I wish to strongly object to this application, the proposal would have a significant impact to the area, especially to the homes that are well within 1km of the proposed site, my main objection points for this application are the points below - HAZARDOUS SUBSTANCE Sites contain hazardous substances in the batteries, has the appropriate regulators been consulted. NOISE The noise levels from this site, combined with current sub station/battery banks and overhead power lines will affect our area immensely CHANGE IN CHARACTER OF THE LANDSCAPE: INDUSTRIALISATION OF AGRICULTURAL LAND The 'Landscape Visual Impact Assessment' document in the planning application states that the location is an area of 'well settled, wooded and diverse valleys.the landscape is attractive with a high degree of integrity'. It also states that change of use from agriculture to a BESS site would be 'apparent locally'. The justification of the location of this proposed BESS site is that it is adjacent to the substation. The visual impact and the change of use from agriculture to industry will be evident to local residents, visitors and people from the village who use the area recreationally. FIRE It is not possible to extinguish a lithium-ion battery fire. Battery fires burn out over hours or days. There is no emergency plan shown for the residents who live adjacent to the site. When operational, the site will be unmanned located in a rural setting. Has the fire service been consulted for an Emergency Response Plan? The area is regularly snowed in during the winter months, who will manage the roadways and keep them clear for emergency response vehicles if needed. FIRE SUPPRESSION WATER AND RISK TO FLOODING Water used to suppress a fire will be highly contaminated. If this water gets into the local water table that is not acceptable - residents all have private water supplies, and there is a burn that runs directly into [PLACE]. INFRASTRUCTURE During construction, this will cause major disruption on single track roads. There is no mention of the impact on domestic residences with increased heavy traffic. The road infrastructure is not built for transporting these large vehicles/components, all roads to and from the site are narrow winding roads. Who will maintain the roadways for potholes and damage? Has traffic impact studies been done for the adjacent villages of [PLACE]/[PLACE]? These roads are used daily by people walking and cycling. ENVIRONMENT/ECOLOGY The planning documents indicate there are 4 badger setts within the [PLACE]. Has the Badger's Trust been consulted? Has [ORGANIZATION] been consulted about the bird life? When was the ecology survey conducted? There are ground nesting birds using this landscape for nesting and have done for generations. Has a bat survey been conducted in the woodland? REHABILITATION Do we have any guarantees that the land will be returned to its original state at the end of project? We have seen no reports on soil sampling, microbiological content of the soil or any information relating to the current state of the soil. How can a company guarantee a return to original state when they don't know, scientifically, the base line? IMPACT ON THE HEALTH OF THE COMMUNITY This will have a negative impact on people's health (physical and mental) this is not being considered. Residents in [PLACE] and the surrounding areas have had construction noise and traffic from the substation, grid stability facility and BESS sites for the last 5 years. Development has greatly contributed to anxiety, stress and the general wellbeing of residents in the area. The impact is not just on adjacent residents; the people who live in the surrounding villages and countryside use [PLACE] as a recreational place to walk, cycle, ride horses and generally enjoy the countryside. What will happen with heavy traffic, noise and loss of this amenity? Community Benefits There is no mention of community benefit in the planning documents. Speaking with the developers at public meetings, their representatives said there is none in their plans. Why is this the case?

Objection to Proposed BESS Development I object to the proposed BESS facility due to serious safety, environmental, and planning concerns. While I do not live locally, I am deeply concerned about the wellbeing of those who do live close to these developments. Fire Risk & Emergency Response Lithium-ion battery fires are difficult to control and highly toxic. This site is unmanned, rural, and prone to winter inaccessibility. No emergency plan has been provided-have fire services been consulted? Water Contamination & Flooding Toxic run-off from fire suppression poses a serious threat to private water supplies and nearby burns. The SUDS pond, on elevated ground, risks overflowing during storms or fire. Has SEPA reviewed this? Hazardous Materials Large volumes of hazardous substances will be stored on-site. Has compliance with COMAH (Control of Major Accident Hazards) been confirmed? Noise & Visual Impact Noise from cooling units and discharging batteries will add to existing stress from substation infrastructure. Visually, the site will industrialise a tranquil, rural landscape. Wildlife & Ecology There are confirmed badger setts and ground-nesting birds nearby. Have appropriate ecological and wildlife bodies been consulted? Traffic & Infrastructure Construction will mean heavy vehicles using narrow local roads frequently used by residents for walking, cycling, and horse riding. Has a traffic study been conducted? Lack of Accountability There is no robust plan to restore the land once operations cease. Developers often sell such projects on-who is responsible long-term? An escrow fund should be mandatory to guarantee site restoration. Given the risks and lack of proper national regulation, developments like this should not be approved-especially when they impact people living so close, with no meaningful protection in place.

target_text: The creation of this battery storage area is propelled by nothing but the greed of the landowner and the power companies. The destruction and devastation of our local countryside along with the dangers of increased traffic along quiet country lanes is untenable. The current road infrastructure is not suitable for such a huge development. The devastation of local wildlife habitats and the risk of pollution and contamination of local natural resources cannot be ignored either. There are many better suited places for this battery storage site to go. You really have picked the worst of them! Money has ruled over common sense once again.

retrieved_examples.text: I completely object to this industrialization of the countryside with such a dangerous eyesore. If you really need battery storage put it in an industrial estate where it belongs.

How can this be allowed in our beautiful countryside. I object strongly to the fact that it is unknown what health and mental issues this will cause people, especially our children, our future, in the surrounding area. Taking away valuable farmland, which has taken many generations of hard work from farmers to make a living from. I object because it will spoil the countryside. Using good agricultural land for battery' storage should not be allowed The single track roads are not build for all this heavy traffic None of the local residents will benefit from this Also worried if battery's catch fire and the water used to cool them goes into waterways and contaminates our well water and other burns

target_text: Regarding the Contents of the "Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment (LVIA)" prepared by [ORGANIZATION], I enjoyed reading this report, as much of it resonated with me and put into words how I feel about living in this part of [PLACE] and the extensive travelling by foot and bicycle that I enjoy so much. I have made some observations on the report below: 3.1.3 " A number of locations have long views towards small scale windfarms which are present in the landscape and form a backdrop in skyline views to the north east of the Site." - Whilst this may be true, it's a small part of the overall picture. Those long views include sweeping views to [PLACE], [PLACE] to the West and [PLACE] on the Morayshire border. There is so much more to this area than simply small scale wind farms. 3.2.3 Reading through the NCLA profile, is very comforting since it describes well the character of northern [PLACE]. Such a beautiful and underrated place to live in and travel through. Those quiet roads and footpaths so described certainly do provide a "sense of seclusion and allow an appreciation of the rich scenic diversity", I could not have put it better. How very ironic that the planning application associated seeks to destroy that. 3.5.1 Regarding Visual amenity; whilst there no denying the negative impact of the visual amenity for the residents that have chose to make the [PLACE] area their home, the visual impact on those travelling through the area cannot be underestimated or trivialised. As the NCLA profile describes, the sense of seclusion and appreciation of the scenic diversity is exactly the thing that draws me to this area for walking and cycling. And as I'm passing through, I see many others doing the same or folk just "oot for a run in the car". We, as travellers are very sensitive to the changes in visual amenity. 4.2.5 "Recommendations have been incorporated into the proposals which successfully mitigate potential adverse landscape and visual effects and help to integrate the proposed scheme into this location" - How can this possibly be true? It is simply not possible to successfully mitigate the adverse effects of placing an industrial feature into a natural landscape. Whatever is created will be unnatural. Please see further comments below regarding cumulative effects. 5.2.2 & 5.3.2 - Statements in this section clearly use the placement of the substation as a justification for siting more industrial equipment. This is clear evidence that rather than saying "well, its industrial now, we might as well build more" we should in-fact be saying, enough damage has been done. No more. Reading the earlier sections about the nature of the region only make it plain with hindsight that the substation should never have been built here. To now use the substation as justification for further development is a clear case of "give an inch, take a mile" It should be noted that the construction of the [PLACE], in fairness to that developer has been screened to a reasonable degree by the existing woodland and tree belt to the east and by earth berm to the south. Due to placement close to the [PLACE], it is reasonably well screened by the earth berm. Placement of the Bess plant away from the road and adjacent to the [PLACE] will not be afforded the same degree of screening. Being on top of the hill and set well away from public roads, it will have a prominent position and very visible from the east ([PLACE] -[PLACE]) No amount of fencing will make this disappear into the landscape. However, the elephant in the room is of course the 500MW BESS plant proposed by [ORGANIZATION] adjacent to this application. These developments cannot be considered in isolation. The combined and cumulative effect must be considered. Whatever considerations have to be given to individual planning applications surely must give way to common sense, when considering the overall impacts. Whilst talking about cumulative effects, the consideration of ALL the BESS plants, substation and Grid Stability Facility (GSF) must be taken into consideration in the [PLACE] and [PLACE] area. This area (like [PLACE]) is being completely transformed into an industrial zone and is carrying much more development burden than it should for the idyllic rural location that it is. [PLACE] and [PLACE] are being sacrificed and destroyed. I feel that in just one or two generations our descendants will look back and wonder why on earth we let this happen. Please stop it now.

retrieved_examples.text: Firstly – I would ask if there is a need for this particular BESS - various national reports are highlighting over-subscription of planning applications for such storage units and that the national picture for infrastructure shows that there are many more bids in the system than required. My family members attended all of the public meetings held by [ORGANIZATION] plus those with the Community Council. I feel that information was poorly presented and lack of knowledge of the area by the company undermined confidence in any appropriate approach and research for the siting. I felt that community members were not fully respected for their local knowledge and information. - Areas of specific concern Safety and fire risk Answers to questions at the open meeting around risk from fire, chemicals, smoke and ground leakage were far from detailed or clear leading those present to be very concerned. There remains lack of clarity about management of accident response at the proposed site making me feel the arrangements are not in place. no residents should be subjected to this or expected to support such a development. Impact on value of properties I have undertaken some research and expect properties in the surrounding area of the proposed BESS to suffer considerable devaluation. This is an extremely negative factor which is inescapable for many of us in the area. I assume local elected members are aware of this. Location should always be selected with minimum impact on local households. Impact on the environment The site is right next to a waterway. Local people know that this provides a haven for wildlife and could well be at risk from this development. Has this been taken into consideration adequately? Is there research to create any confidence that disturbance will be very minimal or non-existent. Inappropriate use of good agricultural land One of the arguments against the siting of the [ORGANIZATION] recent proposed large substation was the use of good agricultural land in an area of importance to farming. The same argument stands with this application even though it is smaller in scale. There is land at [PLACE] and in other places which are not designated for agriculture which should be considered before this use of good farmland. Impact on Tourism This area benefits from the tourism created around the history and culture of [PLACE] and in particular the land associated with James Leslie Mitchell – one of Scotland’s best regarded authors. This BESS will endanger the experience of tourists and affect local businesses and the wider world of tourism. This was a huge factor in the consultation with [ORGANIZATION] and many academics, historians, tourist managers and lovers of literature pointed to the danger of undermining the “Sunset Song” story. Impact on culture and heritage Following on from the issue highlighted above – this area has many sites of ancient historic interest which the University of [PLACE] are currently working with. There are neolithic sites, a stone circle and burial cairns overlooking the very area affected by this application, even if not directly. Noise and light pollution No-one from [ORGANIZATION] has been able to reassure residents about potential noise and light pollution. Research shows both of these to be factors affecting local people when such sites are up and running. The impact on wildlife is likely to be a challenge also. Danger of flooding and snow closures of roads impeding access Flooding and snow road closure is an annual issue at [PLACE], This does not seem to have been adequately allowed for. In any health and safety incident there is no mitigation against weather impeding access to the BESS. Those who live here know this. Conflicting underground cabling proposed The BESS proposal does not seem to be planned in conjunction with the likely underground cabling from the coast to [PLACE] which means local residents may be disturbed twice with considerable road closures. This lack of co-ordination does not build confidence in local people. - Final comments I would point out that the recent proposal for the substation by [ORGANIZATION] in the same area as the BESS was withdrawn and an alternative with less impact was eventually selected. I hope for the same here. If Battery Energy Storage Systems are to be agreed by planning authorities then it should be clear that the proposed sitings are appropriate – in the case of [PLACE] BESS there must be better places for such a development than in this location. Other sites should be explored – we were told that this site was not the ideal location but that the landowner concerned was the only one offering up his land. This should not be a prime aspect of any such development – it should surely be about a strategic plan and locations based on more than a single landowner being offered a sum of money. This is a very good way to destroy neighbour relations and community wellbeing. In consultation the community to be affected should be awarded the highest of status in terms of consideration and process – I definitely feel this is not the case here. I personally have felt aggrieved at the way information was shared with the public for this [PLACE] development and in particular I was offended by the declaration that the development would be going ahead as agreement was already in place with [ORGANIZATION] for access to the [PLACE] and there was no going back. This is entirely inappropriate to say at an event which is declared a consultation. This makes me feel that the information sharing and consultation was a waste of time as it was a done deal in the eyes of the developer. The impact of a sense of low status of the community in any process results in disengagement from the public and failure of the developer to build any relationship with those ultimately concerned and lessons seem not to be learned. I very much hope this development is not approved for the reasons shared above. The area is too valuable to be lost to such an inappropriately located piece of infrastructure.

Objection for the 49MW site Change in character of the landscape: industrialisation of agricultural land The LVIA in the planning documents states the location of the proposed site is an area of 'well settled, wooded and diverse valleys.the landscape is attractive with a high degree of integrity'. It is 'well settled with frequent farmsteads'. Section 3.2.7 of the LVIA report states relevant issues as the 'changing character of the agricultural landscape'. It also states that is change of use, from agriculture to a BESS site would be 'apparent locally'. One major reason given in the LVIA that the proposed BESS site could be incorporated into the landscape is that the substation is next door. This is a spurious reason; it relies only on the (fairly recent) development of the substation to validate its location. Planning applications are supposed to be judged as individual applications. Using proximity to other developments is biased reasoning and is leading to ribbon development. I completely disagree with this method of justifying this proposed BESS site. Noise The noise level will vary (level and type of noise e.g. whistle or a hum), depending on the configuration and set-up, as well as the time of day- e.g. if all battery sites are offloading to the gird at the same peak time. Acoustic impact needs to be measured against pre-sub-station levels, not against current levels, which have already been elevated by the sub-station, the grid stability facility and the BESS already in construction. Consideration of all sites operating together (combined noise from air conditioning units = cumulative effect). There also need to be consideration of the noisy overhead power line issue that is still not resolved. Fire It is not possible to extinguish a lithium-ion battery fire. Battery fires burn out over hours or days. There is no emergency plan shown for the residents who live adjacent to the site. The update planning application shows a main access track and emergency access track leading to the site from the same roadway. The emergency track is parallel to the proposed access track. How is this safe? If a fire did occur on the southern side of the proposed BESS site, the Health and Safety of the fire service personnel could be at risk as they would drive toward the fire. The site is in a rural location. What are the Emergency Response times? Tracks and roadways are regularly snowed in during winter. This site will be unmanned during the operational phase of the BESS. Who will manage the roadway and keep it clear for emergency response vehicles? Has the fire service been consulted? If an evacuation is necessary, what happens to livestock? If a fire occurs, what is the risk to the adjacent [PLACE] and the surrounding mature trees? Fire water What is their plan to prevent water used to suppress a fire from going back into the local eco- system? This water would be highly contaminated. If the water used to treat the fire gets into the local water table that is not acceptable - residents all have private water supplies, and there is a burn that runs directly into [PLACE]. The planning documents indicate a SUDS pond will be built. How will they ensure the pond does not overspill during times of heavy rainfall? There is a sensitive water course and spring-fed private water supply adjacent (within a few hundred metres) of the site. There is no hydrology report on likely impact on aquifers. Infrastructure During construction, this will cause major disruption on single track roads. There are domestic residences adjacent to the access point to the site. There is no mention of the impact on these domestic residences with increased heavy traffic. Who will maintain the roadways for potholes and damage? Is the site access clearly visible? Environment / Ecology The planning documents indicate there are 4 badger setts within the [PLACE]. There is no data mapping the routeways that the badgers take on their foraging travels. The woods will be fenced in by the BESS on its northern side. There will be trackway constructed to the east of the woodland and [PLACE] is to the west. The badgers will be trapped by industrialisation on three sides. Their environment will be greatly disturbed by construction noise and possibly at risk of fire also. The planning document on Ecology mentions bird life. The survey was not conducted in a time when ground nesting birds were observed. Residents and visitors to the area will testify to curlew, lapwings, skylarks and owls in this area. Light pollution during winter will disrupt the natural habits of nocturnal animals such as owls, bats and badgers. Light pollution impacts on residents and visitors' enjoyment of the dark skies in this area. Although the planning documents state that winter lighting will be limited; experience of other developments (the substation, grid stability facility, other BESS sites) indicate otherwise. Lighting is NOT kept to a minimum, in fact, there are lights on overnight at the substation and grid stability facility right now. Visual impact The planning documents and a condition of the application ([APPLICATION_CODE]) state that the battery units will be green or dark grey in colour to blend into the background. What assurances are there that the developer will adhere to this? Experience has shown that other BESS sites default to white units. Rehabilitation Where are the guarantees that the land will be returned to its original state at the end of project? It has already been demonstrated that the companies originally instigating the BESS planning applications have sold the projects on to other companies once planning has been achieved - how do we ensure that they remain accountable? I wish to formally object to the above planning application on the following grounds: 1. Lack of Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) The application fails to include a full Environmental Impact Assessment, despite the site's proximity to a Site of Special Scientific Interest ([PLACE]). This omission is unacceptable given the potential risks to protected habitats and local biodiversity. A development of this scale demands rigorous environmental scrutiny. 2. Cumulative Industrialisation of the Area This proposed development would be the sixth BESS installation within a 5km radius. The cumulative impact of these facilities is transforming the rural character of the [PLACE] area into an industrial zone. The planning authority must consider the broader implications of over- concentration. The visual, noise, and environmental stress on the local community. 3. Inadequate Water and Drainage Management There is no evidence of agreed drainage or discharge systems. Without established plans, the risk of uncontrolled water runoff poses a significant threat to the [PLACE] and existing local water management infrastructure. 4. Insufficient and Unsafe Road Access The proposed access point lacks detailed construction methodology and may require the removal of mature trees. Additionally, the absence of a secondary access route raises serious safety and emergency response concerns. 5. Unclear Grid Connection Proposals The application provides no detail on how the facility will connect to the grid. This uncertainty raises the possibility of unplanned, visually intrusive overhead cabling or other disruptive infrastructure. No necessary consents or agreements appear to be in place. 6. Contradictory Tree Felling Information The documentation contains conflicting information regarding tree removal, creating confusion over the true environmental and visual impact. This lack of clarity undermines trust in the application and suggests potential misrepresentation of the scheme's scope. 7. Unaddressed Noise Pollution No noise mitigation measures have been proposed. Given the operational nature of a BESS facility, the likely noise from cooling systems and inverters could significantly disturb nearby residents and local wildlife, particularly in such a rural setting. 8. Fire Safety Hazards Battery storage systems carry inherent fire risks. The proposed site's proximity to the [PLACE] increases the danger of wildfire spread, toxic smoke release, and long-term ecological damage. No detailed fire risk assessment or emergency response plan has been provided. 9. Visual Impact and Inadequate Screening The planned tree removal, coupled with unclear protections for screening vegetation, will make the facility highly visible from local viewpoints. This visual intrusion is unacceptable, especially given the rural, scenic character of the area. 10. Foundation and Structure Concerns The inclusion of solid concrete foundations for some buildings contradicts the previously stated intention to use temporary container-style units. This raises serious questions about the project's permanence and the long-term environmental implications-none of which were addressed during public consultations. 11. Absence of a Decommissioning Strategy There is no proposed decommissioning plan, which is essential for a project of this nature. Without clear commitments to dismantling, site restoration, and long-term environmental protection, the risk of leaving a derelict industrial site post-operation is high. Conclusion: In light of these unresolved issues-particularly the environmental, safety, and cumulative impacts-I urge the planning authority to reject this application until the concerns above are fully addressed through rigorous assessment, transparent documentation, and meaningful community consultation.

I personally object to the [PLACE] development ([APPLICATION_CODE]) for the following reasons: This is a rural environment with some of the best arable land in Scotland. Food security is as important as energy security. The huge majority of those living in this area are entirely invested in our rural lifestyle, our wildlife and natural habitats and our communities. The widespread industrialisation of this area will negatively change it for ever and have a devastating impact on the people who live here, including on their mental health and wellbeing. I support the transition to net zero and de-carbonisation and the role renewable energy and BESS play in that. However, I am struggling to understand why more focus is not placed on co-location with BESS and turbine and solar farms. Also, the transition to net zero needs to be balanced against an honest assessment of negative impact on communities such as ours. The lack of objection to the development of three BESS developments immediately adjacent to the sub-station at [PLACE] and the significant expansion of the [PLACE] sub-station to allow for these developments. This is not a case of "nimby-ism". The lack of objection to these developments seems to have been (somewhat erroneously) viewed as a green light for a range of prospecting developers to flood our area with further BESS developments. There is a strong feeling of a Gold Rush atmosphere with a hefty side serving of green washing. This proposed scheme is not located adjacent to the [PLACE] sub-station. It would be on prime agricultural land and extremely close to many houses. There is no specific locational need for this BESS development to be located at [PLACE] and it does not meet with the National Planning Framework guidance and ECU guidance. There appears to have been absolutely no cognisance taken of the hugely significant cumulative impact of having so many large BESS developments in what has up until now been a rural area of prime agricultural land. I operate a tourism business in this area. My guests come to stay because they enjoy the peace, beauty and tranquility of the area. They enjoy pursuits, including walking, fishing, kayaking, bird watching, photography and painting which are enjoyable because of the unspoiled landscape. I have no doubt that if the area becomes a highly industrialised one, with acre upon acre of battery storage containers, concrete and security fencing then this will have a significant negative effect not just on my business but on all tourism within the area.

Firstly I see that this planning application has been submitted prior to the 12 week notice period passing since the submission of the notice of this application, which I believe makes the application invalid. Secondly, the site of this proposal is wrong, inappropriate and unnecessary. I will note why for each reason below. Wrong The site is next door to an [PLACE] and is situated on what can be described as a nature/wildlife corridor. I do not believe that other sites were considered for this project despite this site’s complete lack of suitability. There are many other sites that would be much more suitable due to the distance from homes (physically and visually), already being shielded from view by established trees, would not require trees to be felled to gain access, would not destroy the visual impact of countryside that can be seen and enjoyed by so many. When applying for planning to build a dwelling or other building in the countryside there are so many criteria such as how the building must look to fit into the surrounding landscape, how local materials should be used etc. Why then is it OK to build an industrial site on a site right next to the main road, in the view of established and new homes and in an area of natural beauty? Why is this different to other planning applications? Inappropriate The unnecessary change to the natural landscape at this site would be wholly inappropriate. The photo examples in your application have not shown the catastrophic effect to the natural view from the houses that sit above the site, nor do they show the further disruption of the tree felling which is also proposed. In fact the photos have been taken from points where nobody will ever be viewing from. The visual impact of this proposed site will be devastating to the homes on the hill and no amount of bunding will block the visibility of the storage containers when looking from above, from these properties. Unnecessary Looking at other applications for BESS units near [PLACE] you can see that all others are in the surrounding area to the substation but this application is further away for no understandable reason other than because the land has been offered. This site is causing unnecessary disturbance and upset that could be avoided. Surely when there are so many battery storage sites in for planning applications it makes sense to proceed with the sites that are in the right locations i.e. away from homes, out of sight and in closer proximity to the substation. Surely you should only proceed with sites where these issues do not apply – these sites do exist and are available. This site is not one of them. The [PLACE] is a 60mph road and the proposed access is on a straight stretch of this road where cars have the opportunity to overtake or to sit at/exceed the speed limit. This is dangerous but so is the visibility of vehicles leaving the proposed site. Felling healthy trees to make this access visible could be avoided if another more appropriate site were chosen. Felling these trees is only going to open up the negative visual impact of the proposed site to more homes and more of the passing public. Personal Impact I live next door to my parents who built a house 3 years ago – two fields away from the proposed site, up the hill. This is a house for my mother who is housebound much of the time due to having and the quiet location and the view was why this site was chosen. The proposed BESS will not only destroy the view (see attached photos from their home) but it will bring noise and unnatural activity to their extended front garden too. Not only this but the value of their house (and neighbours’ homes) will decrease significantly because of the eye sore of an industrial site that could potentially sit below their home. This application is causing significant distress that could be avoided if an appropriate site could be chosen instead. Please reject this planning application.

target_text: I object to the proposed battery storage facility for the following reasons: 1. Road Safety Concerns The site is accessed via a road classed as an 'A' route (major road). Less than 2 miles away, an application for a new access route was refused on road safety grounds (ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]), despite that road being a 'B' route and therefore of lower classification. The rejection also states access must be a minimum of 40m from any adjacent access (includes those on opposite side of the road) this proposed layout does not meet this minimum requirement. This inconsistency raises serious concerns about the safety implications for this proposal when other applications are refused for similar access points. Drawing for site access is only uploaded to [PLACE] Planning portal on 28Jul2025 after consultee for roads has commented. This should be reviewed in full to ensure applicants plan meets minimum requirements. The application document provided - "TRANSPORT_STATEMENT_AND_CONSTRUCTION_TRAFFIC_MANAGEMENT_PLAN- 11556665" states during the peak of construction the applicants expects on average 52 vehicles per day entering and site. This is comprised of LGV and HGV which creating traffic congestion due to vehicles slowing down to turn planned from south of the site. This is a significant number leading to safety concerns from neighbouring road users with adjacent access points. 2. Inaccurate Traffic Assessment The traffic report was conducted in December, when road usage is typically reduced due to adverse winter weather. This likely underestimates normal traffic volumes and does not accurately reflect year-round conditions. 3. Distance from Substation The site is approximately 5 km from the nearest substation, with no current plans for connection. This raises concerns about the viability and necessity of the location. 4. Proximity to Protected Site ([PLACE]) The proposed site is adjacent to [PLACE], a designated Site of Special Scientific Interest ([PLACE]). The development poses potential risks to the sensitive habitat and biodiversity of this protected area. The absence of a comprehensive EIA raises concerns about potential negative impacts on the [PLACE] as no mitigation details are provided in planning application. 5. Fire Risk Assessment The proximity of the BESS to the [PLACE] poses significant fire risks, including potential fire spread, toxic emissions, and environmental contamination. Our local fire stations are not manned 24 hours and are crewed by retained (or On-Call) firefighters. This planning application does not analysis this risk. BESS fires can release hazardous gases and thermal runaway with a long burn out time as they cannot be extinguished and are often left to burn out. During this time crews would have a reduced response time & capacity to deal to attend to other nearby emergency. For these reasons, I strongly object to the application and request that it be refused.

Fire and Public Safety Risks The scale of the proposed lithium-ion battery installation presents a serious fire risk. Should thermal runaway occur, fires can release toxic gases such as hydrogen fluoride and dioxins. A fire scenario could affect nearby residents, including myself, within minutes. The proximity of local housing and lack of adequate local fire & rescue emergency response capacity within our area - combined with the difficulty of containing such fires - makes this an unacceptable risk. Our local community already has first hand experience of a large scale incident caused by fire at the [PLACE] BESS site in February 2025. There are real risks with capacity to respond to incidents of these nature as surrounding fire service facilities are operated by retained fire fighters and which may not have the experience or training to deal with large scale battery fires. 2. Environmental Contamination and Water Run-Off The risk of contaminated water run-off entering nearby burns or private boreholes is alarming. Large volumes of water may also be required in the event of a fire. If run-off containment fails, this could pollute downstream supplies, threatening wildlife and residents who like myself who rely on private water sources. 3. Noise and Amenity Impacts The facility will operate continuously and house a number of cooling units. These are expected to generate a constant humming noise, especially during energy discharge events. This will severely impact the rural tranquillity that residents currently enjoy. I am particularly concerned about the 24/7 nature of the operation and how it will affect quality of life, mental health, and sleep, especially for my children and neighbours. 4. Traffic and Road Safety The proposal would lead to a significant increase in vehicle movements - potentially hundreds per day during the construction period. This is unsuitable for our narrow rural roads. Increased heavy goods traffic poses real safety risks and would cause road degradation and disruption to our local community. 5. Landscape and impact on local Wildlife This industrial-scale development is entirely out of character with the surrounding countryside. The development risks habitat loss for local species, including badger sets, roe deer, foxes, and birdlife. No amount of screening will adequately mitigate the visual or ecological impact. 6. Planning Process and Environmental Impact Assessment It is deeply concerning that an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) was not required for this proposal, despite its scale and the clear risk to public health and the environment. This appears to contravene the precautionary principle. The local community has also not been adequately consulted or informed about the cumulative impact of all the multiple BESS sites which are progressing through planning on a project by project basis in out local area. Multiple sites are progressing in and around the [PLACE] area without any joined up thinking on how much battery storage is required within our local area. 7. Benefits to local community I note that the developer has shared no information on the benefits this scheme would bring to the local community either during construction and once operational. A multi-million pound development like is required to detail the additional social value which will be achieved and its impact on local job creation and benefits to our local economy. Once operational, there has also not been any community legacy benefits stated which would share any value of hosting battery storage with our local community. Conclusion For all the reasons above, I strongly urge you to refuse this planning application. The proposed development poses an unacceptable risk to public safety, the environment, local amenity, and the rural character of the surrounding area of [PLACE] and [PLACE]. Until a full environmental and safety assessment has been undertaken, and all risks transparently addressed, this application must not proceed.

It is submitted in line with the planning framework and public interest obligations of National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4). 1. Scale Expansion Without Re-Consultation The number of battery containers has increased from 10 (as stated during public consultation) to 22, as confirmed in application documents. This more than doubles the scale of the proposed infrastructure without updated consultation, environmental assessment, or noise and visual impact reassessment. 2. Green Belt and Landscape Character Harm The proposed site lies within the Green Belt and the Coastal Agricultural Plain (LCT 17). The area is characterised by openness, tranquility, and visual coherence. All homes in [PLACE] are single or 1.5-storey, making them more sensitive to visual intrusion. The development does not adequately assess the impact on soil stability, structure, or long-term degradation, nor does it propose mitigation. The Flood Risk and Drainage Statement claims the site is outside designated flood zones. However, SEPA maps clearly show both surface water and fluvial flood risk within 25 metres of the site boundary. No buffer analysis or exceedance modelling is provided. This contradicts the requirements of NPF4 Policy 22 (Flood Risk and Water Management). 4. Ecological Oversights: Red Squirrels and Bats Red squirrels are known to use the development site as a movement corridor between nearby woodlands. Bats are also active in the area. Despite this: - No bat activity surveys were conducted. - No mitigation for red squirrel connectivity is included in the CEMP. - Does not consider any potential impacts to nearby burns in the area. - Not clear if impacts to protecting the area of woodland have been clearly understood in terms of proximity and root protection. These omissions contradict NPF4 Policy 3 (Biodiversity) and Policy 4 (Natural Places) and protecting woodland. 5. Transport Network Misrepresentation The BESS connects onto a stretch of [PLACE] that is not a quiet rural road. It is a heavily used route with multiple nearby junctions, none of which are assessed in the Transport Statement. Further: - There is a quarry to the northeast of [PLACE], raising the likelihood of additional HGV traffic through unsuitable routes. - Local roads include single-track stretches and are not designed for increased HGV traffic. - This is an area of repeated accidents which do not appear to have been addressed in the roads officer's response despite being identified in the transport appraisal by the developer. This undermines the conclusions of the Construction Traffic Management Plan. 6. Community and Child Safety Risks The Outline Battery Safety Management Plan does not address: - Emergency planning for nearby homes (especially those with children); - Risks from toxic gas release (e.g. hydrogen fluoride); - Fire response and light/noise stress during an emergency; There is no defined evacuation plan or coordination strategy for affected residents, in breach of NPF4 Policy 1 (community wellbeing). 7. Underground Cabling - Confirmed, But Needs Conditioning Underground cabling is mentioned in application documents for both internal connections and the grid export route. However: - The grid route is not mapped; - There is no assessment of flood zones, community land, or habitat impacts along the route. This commitment should be secured as a planning condition if fully understood to have no negative impact. 8. Cumulative Impact: Adjacent Quarry Proposal ([APPLICATION_CODE]) The same landowners have submitted a parallel planning enquiry for sand and gravel extraction immediately adjacent to the BESS site. This introduces unassessed risks: - Cumulative traffic impacts from quarry and BESS construction HGVs; - Worsened landscape and visual intrusion beyond what was assessed in the LVA; - Ecological fragmentation of woodland corridors used by protected species. There is no cumulative impact assessment, despite the potential for both projects to proceed concurrently. 9. Operational Incompatibility: Excavation Next to BESS Excavation and battery storage are incompatible adjacent land uses in a community setting. Risks include: - Ground vibration affecting battery integrity and control systems; - Disruption to fire suppression and monitoring infrastructure; - Dust contamination and altered drainage stability; - Increased likelihood of thermal runaway, equipment failure, or hazardous emissions. None of these risks are assessed in the safety documentation, breaching NPF4 Policy 11 (resilient energy infrastructure). 10. Regulatory Threshold Concerns: [PLACE] Limit This proposal is deliberately set at [PLACE] - just below the 50MW threshold that would trigger enhanced regulatory scrutiny under the Electricity Act and National Infrastructure planning regime. Given the scale of infrastructure (22 battery containers and 11 inverters), it is not clear how the operators will ensure the site remains permanently under this threshold. Each battery container model referenced in the documents (e.g. Sungrow PowerTitan 2.0) is capable of delivering between 1.5MW and 2.5MW of power. With 22 containers and 11 inverters, it is technically feasible for the installation to exceed 50MW if not deliberately limited. The application does not provide sufficient technical detail or verifiable mechanisms (such as fixed output capping or regulator oversight) to demonstrate long-term compliance with the sub-50MW capacity claim. This raises concerns of future expansion, cumulative risk, and a potential attempt to avoid more robust oversight. Given the sensitive setting - including residential proximity, flood zones, and ecological corridors - the proposal should be subject to higher regulatory scrutiny regardless of nominal capacity, and any permission granted should include strict monitoring and output enforcement conditions. Requested Actions Given the above, I respectfully request that this application be refused.
