target_text: I would like to provide an overview of the relevant NPF4 policies concerning the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) scheme. Policy 1: This policy emphasises the need for support in addressing the climate and nature crisis. While energy infrastructure, as outlined in Policy 11, is a potential response, the applicant must demonstrate how this development contributes to reducing greenhouse gas emissions to claim strong support for Policy 1. Since the development does not exceed 50MW, it is classified as major development and does not receive in-principle support under NPF4. Policy 2: This policy focuses on climate mitigation and adaptation. Developers are required to assess the carbon contributions of their proposed developments. Recent guidance from the Scottish Government reinforces that the applicant must provide an assessment of greenhouse gas emissions, applicable to all development types, including renewable energy. The applicant has not included this necessary information, which means the application does not comply with Policy 2. The policy states that development proposals should be designed to minimize lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions. For battery storage schemes, proximity to the sub-station is crucial, as greater distances lead to increased electricity losses. Additionally, minimising infrastructure such as access roads and earthworks is essential. There is no evidence that the applicant has adequately considered Policy 2 in their proposals. Policy 3: This section is for proposals which contribute to enhance biodiversity including restoring and strengthening nature networks so they are in a better position without intervention. The policy encourages the consideration of alternative solutions that may have less environmental impact. If a BESS project does not adequately assess or present alternatives that could achieve similar energy storage goals with less environmental disruption it does not align with the policy. During consultation no other site has been considered with in the area thus not aligning with the policy. Policy 6: This policy addresses the loss of trees, stating that adverse impacts on trees of higher biodiversity value are not supported unless appropriate mitigation measures are identified. In this case, the removal of trees north of the [PLACE] is necessary for access and visibility, and no mitigation can be provided. Therefore, the current design proposed by the applicant does not align with the anticipated outcomes of Policy 6, as it fails to protect existing trees. Policy 11: This policy supports various technologies, including battery storage. It requires consideration of several factors, particularly the project's contribution to renewable energy generation and greenhouse gas emission reduction targets. Since this development does not involve renewable energy generation, the only supportive weight lies in its potential for greenhouse gas emissions reductions. However, the applicant has not quantified these reductions, resulting in no supportive weight being attributed to the application. Furthermore, sub-paragraph (e) of Policy 11 highlights the importance of project design and mitigation measures. It is my assessment that the current application has not adopted an appropriate design. The choice of access through a tree line is unsuitable, and selecting a site in open rural countryside without existing infrastructure is questionable. The application lacks for point IX for biodiversity including impacts on birds. Point XXI of the relevant guidelines emphasises the need to assess cumulative impacts. However, it appears that the application does not adequately consider the cumulative effects of the six BESS sites that have either been approved or are currently in the planning stages within the area. This oversight is concerning, as the combined impact of these developments could significantly affect the local environment, community, and infrastructure. I urge [ORGANIZATION] to take into account the cumulative impacts of all BESS sites when evaluating this application. A comprehensive assessment will ensure that the potential effects on the landscape, biodiversity, and local communities are fully understood and addressed.

retrieved_examples.text: [PLACE], [PLACE] 12 August 2025 Dear Sirs, APPLICATION AT FAIRFIELD, INVERURIE [PLACE] [APPLICATION_CODE] INSTALLATION OF BATTERY ENERGY STORAGE SYSTEM (BESS) WITH AN INSTALLED CAPACITY OF [PLACE] AND ASSOCIATED INFRASTRUCTURE Key Issues Landscape and Visual Impacts The landscape and visual impacts have been understated in the landscape appraisal. The choice of photomontage locations has not fully represented the receptors. Photomontage 5 is not reflective of the visibility of the BESS development and associated access infrastructure from the north. The viewpoint is at an oblique angle. Another key point in relation to the images is that these have been produced at 90 degrees and therefore they tend to over play the wider context in which the viewpoint sits and that is reflective of the horizontal scale of the photomontages. In real life, the infrastructure will look larger and will not be seen in as broad a context. This is a matter that needs to be carefully evaluated in placing weight on the visualisations. It is important that any value judgements are made from using the material at the locations. Furthermore, in respect of viewpoint 1, it is anticipated that some of the trees shown in the photomontage may not be actually retained after the access arrangements have been implemented. There are a number of mature tree removals which are required to facilitate the access. Another key aspect in considering the landscape and visual impact is the impression given with the application papers is that in order to produce an impact that may be unacceptable, it would have to be a significant one in Environmental Impact Assessment terms. That is simply not the threshold which is applied in the context of planning. In particular, the vast majority of planning applications that are refused for landscape and visual reasons are not development which would give rise to significant environmental impact. That is an important consideration when it comes to applying policy. In terms of landscape character, the application sits within two landscape character types within [PLACE]. The start of the access and the [PLACE] is located within the LCT 23 which is the farmed basin. The battery element of the development sits just north of the boundary in LCT 19 which is the farmed rolling ridges and hills. It is this landscape character type in which the greatest visibility of the proposed development is to be found and in particular, this is to be found to the north. The landscape and visual appraisal also makes reference to landscape character LCT 32 which extends further north beyond LCT 19 and is the LCT 32, farmed and woodland river valleys. The first point to note is that this is character references. All landscape character types reference farming. It is clear that this part of [PLACE] represents open countryside which is primarily characterised by farmland and some elements of woodland. In terms of the access, it requires the removal of a significant number of mature trees from a line of mainly beech trees located to the north of the [PLACE]. LCT 23 specifically references policy woodlands and shelter in the landscape appraisal notes. Part of the character of LCT 23 are the numerous groups/line of trees. The trees to the north of the [PLACE] therefore form part of the landscape fabric of this LCT. The proposed development will require a material break in the tree line and the loss of mature/semi-mature trees. This is a partial loss of landscape fabric and increases the local impact on landscape character. In most circumstances, if an Applicant were proposing to remove such trees for development it would have to be last resort and having considered all the alternatives. The choice of access has increased the adverse effects of this development and proposes to lead to a loss of landscape fabric. The photomontage from viewpoint 1 is not an accurate depiction of the localised impact that this development will have on the landscape character at this location. The description of LCT 19 is of a rural agricultural landscape with rolling topography and hill slopes being characteristic. The location of the BESS development on lower ground immediately below sloping ground to the north means it will be overlooked from the higher ground. The loss of landscape character from views from the north will be particularly prominent. This reflects the fact that there will be a visible linear access road from the [PLACE] to the BESS. The BESS landscape treatment with bunds and planting will, by its very nature, inevitably look like an intrusion into the landscape. It is almost impossible to mitigate effects from looking down onto the development. The development is entirely alien to the LCT 19. The Planning Design and Access Statement summarises the development as approximately 22 BESS containers with the dimensions set out in paragraph 3.2. These dimensions are slightly larger than a standard container. How would a proposed storage depot for 22 containers be considered in landscape and visual terms? The simple answer to that question is that it would not be permitted. Furthermore, the decision to locate such a proposal in open agricultural land would be considered wholly unacceptable. There is no difference in looking at the BESS development in the same location. Even if you were choosing to locate such a development in this general vicinity, it would make far more sense to locate it closer to the [PLACE] where it would not be overlooked and the bunding would effectively potentially mitigate views into the development itself. This is important as at times when considering such matters, basic planning principles are not properly considered. Simply put, this is an inappropriate location for such a development. There is no existing infrastructure which it relates to. It is simply a location in open countryside. This does in fact contrast with many other of the BESS proposals which propose to access [PLACE]. Most of these are located in close proximity to existing electrical overhead and ground-based infrastructure. This is relevant when coming to consider the overall suitability of this site for this type of development. There is an inherent conflict in promoting this type of development in this location. In terms of the visual impact, it is understated in the appraisal and particularly the choice of viewpoints has been poor. There is no viewpoint due north of the proposed development. This would reveal the true impact that the development would have on the visual amenity to the north of the proposed development. In essence, this would disclose an obvious man-made track running southwards for a considerable length and thereafter culminating in an obvious artificial man-made structure with battery storage infrastructure visible. It is this type of viewpoint which would illustrate the true incongruous nature of the development location. It is simply not understood why viewpoint 5 has been selected when, in terms of the ZTV heat map with Screening Effect of Woodland (figure3), the full development is not visible. Why was a location with a "deeper red to the north" not shown. Policy Analysis The key policies relative to the Application Before going on to consider the policy matters, it is perhaps important to also set out the cumulative context to this Application. The [PLACE] area has seen considerable development pressure. Planning Application [APPLICATION_CODE] for the installation of a BESS of [PLACE] has been granted Planning Permission. It is understood that amendments to this Planning Permission have been sought and a new submission is currently under consideration under Application Ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]. Furthermore, a Planning Application for a further BESS scheme of [PLACE] under reference [APPLICATION_CODE] is now under construction and a further Application was granted for a BESS under reference [APPLICATION_CODE]. In addition, a further Section 36 Application for a BESS of 500MW has been submitted to the Energy Consents Unit, described as "land west of [PLACE]". These sites are located in much closer proximity to the sub-station. These developments are all located in closer proximity to the sub-station and that reflects the nature and character of existing infrastructure in and around the sub-station. This includes the sub-station itself and substantive overhead electrical infrastructure as well. This reflects that this Application is an outlier both in terms of its distance to the sub-station, but also in terms of its proposal to locate it in a rural agricultural setting with more limited infrastructure context. NPF4 Policy 1 - in terms of NPF4, key policies that are potentially applicable in the context of a BESS scheme in broad terms are policies 1, 2 and 11. In terms of Policy 1, there is general support responding to the climate and nature crisis. One of the ways of responding is through energy infrastructure associated with Policy 11. However, to claim strong support for Policy 1, the Applicant would have to be able to demonstrate how this particular development contributes to the reduction in greenhouse gas emissions. The development does not exceed 50MW and is therefore not national development. It is therefore major development. In terms of NPF4, this does not have in-principle support. Policy 2 - Policy 2 deals with climate mitigation and adaption. In terms of climate mitigation, developers are required to assess the carbon contributions that the proposed development would give rise to. Policy 2 has recently been supported by further guidance issued by the Scottish Government in relation to its application. It is suggested that, on any reading, the onus is on the Applicant to set out an assessment of greenhouse gas emissions. It is clear from the guidance that this applies to all forms of development and also includes, for example, renewable energy development. If there were existing methodologies for demonstrating the issue, then they should be used. Alternatively, it is recommended that general methodologies be applied. The Applicant has not included this information and, as a consequence, the Application cannot be said to be in accordance with Policy 2. Policy 2 stated in the following terms: "Development proposals will be sited and designed to minimise lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions as far as possible". In the context of battery storage schemes, proximity to the sub-station will be a measure of this. The longer the distance from the sub-station, the greater the losses of electricity through the cables. This policy therefore strongly supports a location in as close a proximity to the sub-station as possible. In addition, it would also seek to minimise other infrastructure such as the extent and length of access road and the need to carry out earth works such as bunding. There is no evidence that the Applicant has not had regard to Policy 2 in formulating the relevant proposals. Policy 11 - general policy Energy Policy 11 is also clearly relevant to the consideration of a battery scheme. The policy provides general support for a range of technologies which also includes battery storage. Sub-paragraph (e) provides a range of topic matters that have to be considered. Finally, in terms of the overall decision making, significant weight is to attach to the contribution that the development will make either to renewable energy generation targets, or greenhouse gas emission reduction targets. The development is not renewable energy generation and therefore the only weight that can be in support of a BESS scheme is the greenhouse gas emissions reductions. At no point has the Applicant sought to quantify these and therefore no weight can be attributed in the balance to that. In addition, in terms of the design of the scheme, sub-paragraph (e) identifies that there are a range of factors that parties should take into account in formulating such projects and, in particular, project design and mitigation have to demonstrate how impacts are addressed. In terms of sub-paragraph (2), it is considered that this Application has not adopted an appropriate design. The choice of access location through a tree line is wholly inappropriate and should not have occurred. Furthermore, the choice of location which is a design consideration. It should not have selected a site in the open rural countryside which has no equivalent infrastructure in place already. Furthermore, the impact on trees also specifically has to be considered in the context of the Application. Policy 6 - the loss of trees is addressed in NPF4 by Policy 6. Sub-paragraph 3 of Policy 6 states that adverse impacts on individual trees of higher biodiversity value would not be supported unless appropriate mitigation measures are identified. In the context of the current Application, there can be no mitigation for the removal of the trees to the north of the [PLACE] because they are required to facilitate the access and also maintain the visibility for the access. Against that background, it is clear that the current design, as promoted by the Applicant, is not consistent with the policy outcomes anticipated by Policy 6. In particular, the existing trees are not being protected and this design choice is contrary to policy. [PLACE] Local Development Plan In addition to NPF4, the [PLACE] Local Development Plan also incorporates policies which are relevant. In terms of Policy P1, the LDP promotes high quality places and recognises the importance of good design. The choices made by the Applicant in respect of the design of this Application do not accord with those principles and, in particular, the access arrangements run entirely contrary to the concept of good design and would be contrary to Policy P1. In terms of Policy E1 on natural heritage, the removal of the trees associated with the access do not accord with policy. In particular it will fragment habitats and have adverse impacts upon the site's environmental quality. In terms of Policy E2 on landscape, the access arrangements are clearly contrary to the thrust of the objectives. In particular, the trees will be lost are part of the landscape fabric. It was the choice of the Applicant to select an access through these trees and the loss would have an adverse impact on landscape fabric. It therefore could not be said that the development in terms of the location, scale and design is of a high standard. Policy E3 - forestry woodland - the woodland loss is not consistent with the aims and objectives of the policy. Higher quality trees would be lost to the access. Providing planting around the BESS does not compensate for this loss of landscape fabric, nor the quality of the existing trees. RD1 - Policy RD1 states that the Councill will only allow development "if it is located and designed to take advantage of, or incorporate the services, facilities and infrastructure necessary to support it". Such matters may include "sustainable transport linkages and supporting infrastructure, facilities for alternatively field vehicles, road access, waste management provision or to supply waste water connections and treatment and other elements as may be appropriate in the circumstances". In the context of this BESS, it is not well located relative to the sub-station. It is critical infrastructure to which it requires to connect into. The alternative Applications which have come forward are far better located and would not require such extensive connection works. Policy C2 - Policy C2 provides the relevant policy in relation to battery storage. It supports developments which are "in appropriate sites and of appropriate design". As identified in the above, it is submitted that this Application Site is wrong in that it is in open rural countryside and, in addition, the design is wholly inappropriate in that the access has chosen to go through a mature line of trees which form part of the landscape fabric of the area. It then lists the range of factors which can be taken into account. This includes the adverse environmental ones and also the positive ones regarding greenhouse gas emissions. As stated above, the Applicant has not set out in any meaningful way how the Application proposals will contribute. Finally - Is there really a need for this development? The Applicant's justification for the project is contained in paragraph 2.2.2 of the Planning Design & Access Statement. This just states that the Applicant has studied the information provided by DNOs for this type of project. [PLACE] is one of these locations, therefore suggesting demand for the proposed development. That is the only site-specific policy that is referenced. The Planning Design & Access Statement goes on to analyse general policy support in Section 5 and references in support the Clean Power 2030 Action Plan at paragraph 5.4.9. It references positive comments about the general need for storage across the whole of the UK. What the Applicant fails to do is to point out that within the Action Plan the requirement for battery storage is not a general one and is one which is tied to grid location. In terms of the 2030 Action Plan, it was also accompanied by a connections reform annex "which has been updated". This provides estimates of generation required for particular technologies. The Applicant quotes from the general figures but does not drill into the subsequent information which gives information on breakdowns of technologies required by 2030. This Application is a distribution connected scale of development. This identifies that for 2030 across the whole of the distribution networks of [ORGANIZATION] and Scottish Hydro Electric Power Distribution (SHEPD) some 900MW is required. [PLACE] alone has received connection requests for over 700MW to date. [ORGANIZATION] and SHEPD have received applications for over 8GW in total so there is only a demand for around 10% of applications. Only the most suitable sites should be selected. [PLACE] is certainly not in this category as the points raised in this letter demonstrate. I earnestly request that this planning application is refused. [PERSON]

As a frequent visitor to this lovely area I want to object to this battery storage application: The application for the [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) and associated infrastructure, presents critical issues that make it wholly unsuitable for approval. Although positioned as a renewable energy storage solution, the project introduces significant risks to public safety, the environment, and community well-being that far outweigh its potential benefits. These concerns are further exacerbated by the proposal's failure to comply with Scotland's National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4) and other relevant legislative requirements. 1. Fire Safety and Emergency Preparedness The application's failure to provide an adequate emergency response plan is a major concern, particularly given the inherent risks of lithium-ion battery fires. Such incidents are notoriously difficult to manage, producing toxic contaminants and requiring significant water resources. In addition, this site only has one main access for emergency services which further amplifies these dangers, placing both local residents and the environment at unacceptable risk. This omission directly conflicts with NPF4's prioritisation of public safety and environmental protection. 2. Environmental and Biodiversity Risks The development threatens local ecosystems through habitat loss, pollution, and operational disturbances such as noise and light pollution conflicting with NPF4 policies on biodiversity and natural places. 3. Community and Infrastructure Impacts The proposal imposes significant burdens on the local community and infrastructure. Increased traffic during construction and limited access routes would disrupt daily life and strain rural roads. Residents face anxiety over safety risks, property devaluation, and potential impacts on their quality of life from noise, light pollution, and industrialisation of the landscape. These effects undermine NPF4's vision of fostering resilient, inclusive, and thriving communities. 4. Cumulative and Landscape Impacts When considered alongside other energy developments in [PLACE], the [PLACE] BESS contributes to cumulative environmental degradation and the industrialisation of a predominantly rural and scenic area. There have been 2 BESS developments ALREADY approved in this area so there is NO NEED for another! The facility's visual intrusion, and its impact on tourism detract from the region's natural heritage, reducing its appeal to visitors and harming the local economy. These cumulative effects are inconsistent with NPF4's emphasis on protecting Scotland's landscapes and cultural integrity. 5. Non-Compliance with Policies and Legislation The proposal fails to comply with key NPF4 policies, including: - Policy 3: Biodiversity, requiring developments to enhance biodiversity and avoid harm to ecosystems. - Policy 4: Natural Places, mandating the protection of designated sites and landscapes. - Policy 22: Flood Risk and Water Management, necessitating robust water management to prevent contamination. - Policy 16: Quality Homes, focusing on safeguarding community well-being and quality of life. Additionally, the application does not adequately address requirements under the Town and Country Planning (Scotland) Act 1997 or the Electricity Act 1989. 6. An industrial development on this scale should be built on a more appropriate brownfield site and not within a small rural community. Conclusion and Recommendations The [PLACE] BESS application fails to meet the essential requirements of Scotland's planning policies and legislative framework. Its numerous deficiencies in fire safety, environmental protection, biodiversity conservation, and community impact render it incompatible with the principles of sustainable development outlined in NPF4. The potential risks associated with this development far exceed its purported benefits. Rejecting this proposal is necessary to protect the [PLACE] region's natural, cultural, and social integrity and to uphold Scotland's commitment to responsible and sustainable development. Approving this project in its current form would set a dangerous precedent, undermining Scotland's environmental and community-focused planning objectives. For these reasons, it is strongly recommended that this application be rejected in its entirety.

I write to formally object to the proposed [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development, and I wish to outline the key reasons for my objection: 1. Fire Safety Concerns The significant anxiety surrounding the potential risks of living near such a hazardous facility is very real. The developer has indicated that they will create an emergency response plan prior to construction. This is deeply concerning, as this plan has not been provided to date, which should be grounds for rejecting the application outright. There is no mains water supply at the site, no pressurised hydrants, and the nearest fire stations are far away ([PLACE] is 16 miles away, [PLACE] 30 miles). With one main access point for emergency services, and no clear plans for managing contaminated water that may spill into local rivers, these deficiencies cannot be ignored. Furthermore, the applicant has suggested that fires will be left to burn out, but extensive cooling measures are needed to prevent thermal runaway and explosions, and to protect against toxic fumes that may travel with the prevailing westerly winds. A comprehensive and detailed fire safety plan must be available before any consideration of this application. To this end, when considering NPF4 - Community Wellbeing Policy 5 and Environmental Risk Policy 22 The absence of a fire safety plan raises significant concerns for community wellbeing, local ecosystems, and the potential spread of contamination in the event of an incident. Without detailed risk mitigation plans, this project poses unacceptable risks to public health, safety, and the surrounding natural environment. 2. Impact on Protected Wildlife The developer's statement that "pre-construction surveys will be carried out" indicates these have not yet been conducted, and no Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) has been carried out either – this should have been required for a development of this scale. Previous surveys for other nearby projects confirmed the presence of protected species such as otters, badgers, pine martens, red squirrels, mountain hare, and potentially bats. Additionally, the area is home to various bird species, including osprey, golden eagles, red kites, and more. It is completely unacceptable that the developer intends to investigate these issues only after the project is approved, rather than before. This approach contradicts NPF4 policy, particularly Policy 1 on tackling the nature crisis and Policy 4 on protecting natural places. 3. Deforestation and Tree Protection The Scottish Government opposes the permanent removal of woodland unless there are significant public benefits. This project does not offer such benefits. Furthermore, the site contains ancient Scots pine woodland – who will ensure its protection? NPF4 policy supports the enhancement and preservation of woodlands, and the developer's approach to tree removal and replanting should be scrutinised accordingly. 4. Poor Consultation and Community Engagement The local consultation events were poorly conducted. The developer provided low-quality maps and struggled to answer basic questions. They failed to properly advertise the consultation, leading to many residents being unaware of it. Their lack of local knowledge, as well as their minimal engagement with the community, shows a lack of interest in receiving genuine feedback. Their promotional materials and online resources were also subpar. 5. Unnecessary Development This tiny community already has approved: [PLACE] Battery Storage ref: [APPLICATION_CODE], [PLACE] Wind Farm Extension 11 including battery storage ref: [APPLICATION_CODE], and [PLACE] including battery storage ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]. These are all within a few miles of this proposed development. We do not require yet another 200MW facility in such a small, rural community. Scotland's energy storage capacity is already three times the required amount by 2050, according to a recent FOI request via EIA Scotland, no. [APPLICATION_CODE]. 6. Cumulative Impact of Energy Infrastructure The surrounding area already contains extensive energy-related infrastructure, including several wind farms, substations, hydro sites and associated power lines. The cumulative effect of these developments is significant, and this area has already contributed heavily to renewable energy generation. The sheer number of developments here raises concerns about overdevelopment and democratic fairness, especially given the small population. Therefore, when focusing on NPF4 Cumulative Impacts Policy 11.3 The cumulative impact of energy infrastructure in this area already exceeds what is reasonable for a rural community, as detailed above. This development does not provide significant additional benefit and fails to meet NPF4’s requirement for projects to align with local needs and priorities. 7. Inappropriate Scale for the Area A 200MW battery storage facility covering 18.3 hectares with 66 x 20ft battery containers is entirely disproportionate to the size of the surrounding rural area. This industrial facility would be highly visible from nearby hills. The scale of this development in such a rural community is inappropriate, and it represents the wrong type of development for the area. 8. Precedent for Future Expansion If this facility is approved, it sets a dangerous precedent for further expansion, such as the potential need for an extended substation or additional power lines. Our community already hosts a large amount of infrastructure, and there is no need for further development of this kind. Given the already disproportionate concentration of energy infrastructure in the area, exacerbating cumulative impacts on local landscapes and ecosystems. Future expansions or associated developments would only amplify these negative effects. 9. Proximity to Residential Properties When considering NPF4 Policy 5 - Health and Wellbeing - The proposed development is located within 300 meters of a private residence, raising concerns about the impact of noise, light pollution, and potential toxic fumes. Locating such facilities near homes contradicts NPF4’s emphasis on ensuring developments enhance community wellbeing and minimise harm. Facilities like this should be located on brownfield sites, closer to the areas where energy is most needed. 10. Negative Impact on Community Wellbeing While rural communities are often targeted for such developments due to their low population density, the mental and emotional strain on local residents is severe. The lights, noise, and potential health impacts are significant concerns, particularly when combined with the extensive industrial developments already planned or approved in the area. 11. Traffic and Construction Disturbance The construction phase of this project will generate a substantial amount of traffic, noise, and disruption, particularly along the [PLACE], which has become busier with the [PLACE] route. The developer's claim that this access has been used for prior developments is inaccurate, as the [ORGANIZATION] required alternative access routes during the construction of the [PLACE]. 12. Lack of Local Socio-Economic Benefits NPF4 policy mandates that renewable energy projects provide local economic benefits. This project offers no such benefits. While the developer mentions working with local schools to promote STEM careers, this is a public relations exercise with no real impact on the community. There are no plans for community benefit funds, local employment opportunities, or any positive economic contribution to the area. 13. **Questionable Contribution to Climate Goals** Contrary to public perception, the energy stored by these batteries is not exclusively from renewable sources. Instead, it is typically charged during off-peak hours when fossil-fuel-powered electricity generation is at its highest. This development is primarily a profit-driven venture and not an initiative aimed at contributing to net-zero goals. To this end, while in consideration of NPF4 Policy 2 Climate Emergency energy storage is an essential part of the transition to net-zero, this project does not demonstrate how it will maximize renewable energy use or align with Scotland’s climate goals. The lifecycle emissions of battery production and the lack of clear benefits for renewable energy integration undermine its contribution to a sustainable future. 14. Misalignment with Planning Policy NPF4 supports energy storage, but only where there is a clear, tangible benefit to the local community and where biodiversity is enhanced. This development fails to meet these criteria, as it provides no direct benefit to the community and does not demonstrate any meaningful enhancement of local biodiversity. 15. Environmental and Ecological Damage The environmental consequences of this project, including tree removal, destruction of peatland, and harm to wildlife habitats, are serious. The stored energy will only last for a short duration, and the long-term ecological and social costs far outweigh the limited benefit. 16. Mitigation Measures and Landscape Impact The developer proposes using existing trees for screening and additional planting, but the adequacy of this mitigation is questionable. The destruction of significant parts of the local landscape will have a lasting effect, especially on tourism, which is a vital local industry. 17. Flooding and Environmental Risks Considering NPF4 Policy 22 - Flood Risk Management - the flooding risks associated with this site, particularly in light of the 2017 flooding events, have not been adequately addressed. NPF4 mandates that developments must demonstrate resilience to climate risks, and this proposal fails to provide sufficient assurances regarding flood prevention and water management thus poses an ongoing risk to the project's viability. 18. Environmental Impact of Battery Production While the development is framed as a step toward sustainability, the environmental impact of manufacturing lithium-ion batteries, including the mining of rare metals, significant carbon emissions, and human rights concerns, should not be overlooked. These issues contribute to the very climate crisis we are trying to solve. 19. Developer's Background Finally, the background of the developer raises concerns. [PERSON], a former energy trader and co-founder of Bulb, which collapsed in 2021, does not have a strong track record in battery storage or renewable energy expertise. This calls into question the developer's suitability to carry out such a large-scale project. Focusing solely on deliverability and transparency this means - Concerns arise regarding the developer’s track record and ability to deliver a project of this scale especially as clear, transparent plans for long-term maintenance, fire safety, and decommissioning are essential and have not been provided to date. In conclusion, this area has already made significant contributions to Scotland’s renewable energy targets, bearing more than its fair share of infrastructure. This proposal fails to align with NPF4’s emphasis on delivering local benefits, enhancing biodiversity, and safeguarding community wellbeing. I urge the rejection of this application, as it is incompatible with the local environment, disproportionate in scale, and inconsistent with Scotland’s planning framework.

Our objection to the proposed BESS is explained below with the concerns listed in relation to policies in NPF4. We understand that NPF4 is to be read and interpreted as a whole and that as stated in policy 1 in considering all development proposals significant weight will be given to the global climate and nature crises. Whilst the case for any renewable energy generation scheme or battery storage facility can be made to some extent based on contribution to address net zero targets we would argue that they still have to be in appropriate locations, where the benefits clearly outweigh the negative impacts. In this case we feel the impacts on the local area are too great to justify approving the scheme. Woodland The intent of NPF4 policy 6 is to protect and expand forests, woodlands and trees. From the proposals seen and Scottish Forestry’s consultation response it is identified that areas of native woodland are going to be adversely affected (see policy 6 b) ii). It is also not clear that mitigation measures will be identified and implemented in line with the mitigation hierarchy (see policy 6 b) iii). Historic Assets and Places Part of the policy intent of NPF4 Policy 7 is to protect and enhance historic environment assets and places and one of the identified policy outcomes is to recognise the social, environmental and economic value of the historic environment to our economy and cultural identity. The historic environment report supplied by the developer seems to have seriously underplayed the extent and importance of the neolithic landscape and assets in the area. We note that the applicant’s HE desk based report is also rather vague as to what the impact will be on prehistoric/neolithic assets. From our research and site visits we note that there are 7 cup and ring marked rocks, (which form part of the wider setting of the [PLACE] which is a scheduled ancient monument), along the boundary of the site and 9 more within 250m of the boundary. The [PLACE] (also known as the Whitehill stone), which is one of the most important and most extensive pieces of prehistoric rock art in Britain (K, Brophy (2018) “The finest set of cup and ring marks in existence’: the story of the [PLACE], [PLACE]. Scottish Archaeological Journal, 40(1),pp1-23. (doi:10.3366/saj.2018.0092)) lies only 500m from the boundary of the development. There appear to be around 24 identified stones with neolithic markings in the wider setting (possibly more if linked stones are counted separately). You can see from the map below that the proposal site (marked red) dominates the Neolithic landscape of [PLACE] and would significantly impact on the setting of the stones. Map of locations of cup and ring marked rocks from Canmore (search on cup and ring marked rocks and go to 'map view') The stones and their setting have a huge cultural and significance locally and are a major part of the attraction of the area for locals and walkers taking access. Policy 7 a) and 7 o) therefore need to be carefully considered. It does not appear that the cultural significance of the stones and their setting has been properly assessed - or how the setting and wider historic landscape will be impacted. Green Belts and Brownfield Land Two of the the policy outcomes of NPF4 Policy 8 are that the character, landscape, natural setting and identity of settlements is protected and enhances and also that development is directed to the right locations. Whilst policy 8 a) includes renewable energy developments in the list of potentially supported development proposals, no specific mention is made there of battery storage. If we assume that the battery storage is for renewable energy, then the five requirements set out at Policy 8 ii) must be met for support to be given to the proposal and this is clearly not the case. Specifically the proposal could be located on an alternative site outwith the green belt; it also undermines the purpose of the green belt at that location destroying the natural setting, and landscape around the settlement and will have significant impacts on recreation and access rights in the area, including impacting on long distance walking routes and core paths. There will be significant visual impact given the proposal is essentially an industrial development with associated fencing and floodlighting. There will clearly be significant long-term impacts on the environmental quality of the green belt with an industrial use of the site for at least one or two generations, and wider impacts including light pollution. This kind of development is clearly not compatible with the surrounding established countryside and landscape character. Such a proposal could potentially be accommodated in an appropriate site within designated green belt but only where the pollution and visual impact could be mitigated such as within an old quarry. NPF4 Policy 9 clearly steers such development to brownfield or derelict land to reduce the need for Greenfield development. Policy 9 b) says that proposals on Greenfield sites will not be supported unless the site has been allocated for development or the proposal is explicitly supported by policies in the LDP. This does not seem to be the case. Energy NPF4 Policy 11 gives support for renewable, low-carbon and zero-emissions technology and includes battery storage at policy 11 a) iii). However, it is not clear if policy 11 c) is being met and we are very concerned that the list of impacts at Policy 11 e) have not been addressed by the project design and mitigation. Many have been ignored or vaguely alluded to rather than fully addressed. These include Policy 11 e) i), ii), iii), vii), viii), ix), xi), xii) and xiii). Community Wealth Building The proposed development does not seem to be designed to achieve either of the policy outcomes in NPF4 Policy 25. Blue and Green Infrastructure The proposal appears to impact on the local communities accessible green space. It also seems to cover an area where there are real access demands and it is not clear that the overall integrity of the network will be maintained given the impact on Core Paths and long distance walking routes as well as the negative consequences it will have for local access - the site being popular for open air recreation and walking with local people. The site is a place of significant walking interest with the site bounded on three sides by core paths and with many other routes of access to and around the surrounding countryside and the [PLACE]. The long distance route - the Clyde Coastal route passes through the middle of the site (according to their website ) but this may have subsequently shifted eastward to where the current core paths are marked. Policy 11 Energy in NPF4 says that impacts on "public access, including impact on long distance walking and cycling routes and scenic routes" must be addressed. Diagram showing proposal site (red) superimposed on screen shot of core paths from NatureScot website Business and Industry NPF4 policy 26 would give support for this development if it was proposed for a site allocated for industrial use in the LDP. However, the site is not allocated for business or industrial use - it is designated as green belt and is a greenfield site. Policy 26 d) says that development proposals to business, general industrial and storage and distribution uses outwith areas identified for those used in the LDP will only be supported where there are no suitable alternatives and ii) the nature and scale of the activity will be compatible with the surrounding area. The nature and scale of the activity are clearly not compatible with the countryside setting, the historic landscape and the public access and recreation usage of the area.

Landscape and Visual Impacts The proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) would be situated on open, elevated farmland within Landscape Character Type (LCT) 143: Farmed Lowland Plain, a landscape highly regarded for its expansive skies, peaceful ambiance, and agricultural heritage. The visual impact of the project is expected to be substantial, given its large industrial scale featuring more than 200 battery units, fencing, transformers, and the introduction of stark, metallic security infrastructure. This development would be prominently visible from nearby residences, public roads, and popular tourist routes, such as the [PLACE]. Superficial landscaping efforts are unlikely to adequately offset the lasting visual disruption to the landscape. The applicant's assessment significantly underplays both the immediate and cumulative visual detriments of the project. In contravention of NPF4 Policy 11(e)(ii), the proposal overlooks the necessity to thoroughly evaluate and mitigate the combined impacts alongside existing infrastructure like the [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], and [PLACE] facilities, all located within close proximity to each other. Community Consultation and Planning Process The proposal was directly submitted to the Energy Consents Unit of the Scottish Government, bypassing the local democratic planning oversight process. There has been a lack of substantial public consultation with the residents of [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], or [PLACE]. In communities where the consequences will be enduring and daily, this approach undermines environmental justice and contravenes the place-based policy ethos of NPF4. Consultations for the [ORGANIZATION] BESS were conducted independently of related developments in the area. The community affected by this proposal should have a fair opportunity to voice their opinions on whether industrial energy infrastructure is suitable for their surroundings. Decisions regarding developments with significant local implications should involve meaningful local engagement, rather than being treated as peripheral aspects of energy infrastructure planning. Cumulative Impact The [ORGANIZATION] BESS does not exist in isolation but is part of a larger network of energy projects in the vicinity. These include the [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], and the extensive [PLACE] marine energy infrastructure. Together, these initiatives create a concentrated industrial cluster that is significantly reshaping the visual, ecological, and social landscape of the area. Despite the requirements outlined in NPF4 Policy 11(e), a comprehensive Cumulative Impact Assessment (CIA) has not been submitted. Instead, there are fragmented and piecemeal applications that obscure the full scope of the regional transformation currently unfolding. This absence of a cumulative assessment not only misguides decision-makers and the public but also poses a risk of allowing extensive landscape alterations to occur without proper oversight, evaluation, or mitigation measures in place. Industrialisation of Prime Agricultural Land The proposed development would result in the permanent sterilisation of 5.5 hectares of productive farmland, which has long served as the foundation of rural livelihoods and land stewardship in the area. The installation of hardstanding, impermeable surfaces, high-voltage equipment, and fencing would make the land unsuitable for agriculture, grazing, or supporting biodiversity. This goes against NPF4 Policy 5, which aims to protect prime agricultural land for resilient food systems and sustainable land management. By replacing fertile farmland with speculative energy infrastructure, the project threatens local resilience and undermines Scotland's objectives for food security. Industrialising rural areas in this manner represents a myopic and irreversible decision that fails to strike a balance between national infrastructure requirements and local sustainability. Summary This proposal is of an industrial scale, lacking justification, and fundamentally incompatible with the setting of a protected royal heritage site, local land use, and the planning principles outlined in NPF4 and HEPS. There is no demonstrated national need for this facility at this specific location. The proposal would have significant negative impacts visually, ecologically, and socially. Approving this development would jeopardize a cherished rural community to uncontrolled infrastructure expansion. It would harm the integrity of one of Scotland's most iconic landscapes and undermine national policies on heritage, nature, and rural sustainability. This large-scale project offers no discernible community benefits, such as local employment, infrastructure improvements, or revenue sharing. There is no community vote, referendum, or substantial community support in favor of this development. A project that impacts daily life, health, heritage, and land should not be imposed without active, positive, and locally driven consent, which this development lacks. It is inconsistent with NPF4's fundamental values of sustainability, place-based decision-making, heritage protection, and rural fairness. When considered alongside other projects like the [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], and the [PLACE], this development would transform the iconic [PLACE] landscape into an extensive industrialized area. It would permanently change the local landscape and the historic rural setting of [PLACE], a site of national and symbolic significance. Approving an industrial battery installation in such proximity to a Royal heritage site based on speculation, incomplete evidence, and flawed policy application is not acceptable. The development conflicts with the core objectives of the National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4), which prioritize rural protection, nature restoration, climate resilience, and community well-being. It also goes against the [PLACE] Council's goal of conserving the cultural and environmental quality of [PLACE]. Introducing a large-scale battery compound in a rural landscape directly undermines these planning goals. This industrial facility is being imposed in a sparsely populated, minimally consulted area, contributing to a broader trend of designating rural areas as sacrifice zones for national energy infrastructure. Rather than attempting to address or rectify deficiencies in the application, I respectfully urge the Reporter and Scottish Ministers to DENY CONSENT for the [ORGANIZATION] BESS entirely and to uphold the long-term public interest in safeguarding the [PLACE] landscape and cultural environment.

am writing to formally object to the proposed large-scale battery storage development at [PLACE]. While I recognise the importance of renewable energy and grid resilience, I believe this particular proposal raises serious concerns that have not been adequately addressed and would result in unacceptable harm to the local area and its residents. 1. Fire and Safety Risks Large battery storage facilities carry a well-documented risk of thermal runaway, fire, and toxic smoke. Given the scale of the proposed installation, any incident could pose a significant danger to nearby homes, businesses, emergency responders, and the wider environment. It is unclear whether sufficient fire suppression measures, emergency response plans, and access routes have been fully assessed or agreed with local fire authorities. 2. Proximity to Residential Properties The proposed development is in close proximity to residential areas. This raises concerns regarding public safety, constant industrial presence, visual dominance, and long-term health impacts. Residents should not be exposed to increased risk or anxiety due to the siting of a high- risk industrial facility near their homes. 3. Noise and Disturbance Battery storage sites operate continuously and rely on cooling systems, transformers, and inverters that generate noise both day and night. This would adversely affect residential amenity, particularly during night-time hours, and may exceed acceptable background noise levels. 4. Visual Impact and Character of the Area The scale, height, and industrial nature of the development would significantly harm the visual character of the area. The site would be out of keeping with its surroundings and would negatively affect landscape quality, local views, and potentially property values. 5. Environmental and Ecological Concerns The development may result in habitat loss, increased surface water runoff, and pollution risks from battery chemicals in the event of leakage or fire. The long-term environmental consequences, including decommissioning and disposal of batteries, have not been convincingly addressed. 6. Lack of Demonstrated Local Benefit There appears to be limited direct benefit to the local community, while the risks and negative impacts are borne almost entirely by nearby residents. This imbalance weighs heavily against the proposal. For the reasons outlined above, I respectfully request that this application be refused or, at the very least, subject to significantly more rigorous scrutiny, including independent safety assessments, greater separation distances from housing, and meaningful community consultation. Thank you for considering my objection.

Unlike such as grain driers in the countryside these operate 24/7/365. It should be noted that the [PLACE] residents have experienced noise from the ‘[PLACE] Buzz’ from SSEN’s transmission hub for over six years. [ORGANIZATION] have spent £millions on mitigation and have still only partly succeeded. Would a small developer and local farmer have the resources to address new noise issues. - Connectivity: No plans for connection to the substation are included and we would point out that the development of [PLACE] was mitigated by the undergrounding of most overhead cables in the Braes. If the developer’s option is an overhead cable that is directly in conflict with the ethos and practice adopted by [ORGANIZATION], [ORGANIZATION] and the Community over the last few years. Lithium fires are difficult to extinguish, often lasting four days or more and give off toxic gases such as Hydrogen Flouride, potentially lethal even in relatively small doses. At [PLACE], the local [PERSON] recommends should a fire occur it would be left to burn itself out. Considering the limited water resources in the Braes that is a disaster waiting to happen. With the proximity of local residents that is unacceptable. The system is reliant on keeping batteries cool which means 24/7/365 air-conditioning units which are in themselves a fire risk. The limited water resources of the Braes would make fighting fires of this magnitude a challenge for the local Fire Services. These concerns are well documented in a report to the [ORGANIZATION] by Prof Wade Allinson, emeritus professor of physics at Oxford University, Dr. Edmund Fordham, fellow of the Institute of Physics and Prof. Sir David Melville, former vice- chancellor of the University of Kent. If ever there was a case for the Precautionary Principle this is surely it! - Environmental impact: In essence it is not unreasonable to suggest that a green field site would have little negative environment impact beyond the serious consideration of taking arable land out of food production. Their mitigation based on feedback from their last attempt is inadequate. 5. Cumulative impact - visual. Ironically, [PLACE] (meaning 'beautiful place') is home to: a. a power station and dam b. a large quarry currently being extended c. probably the largest electricity substation in [PLACE] d. a plethora of pylons, to the extent that [ORGANIZATION] agreed a few years ago to mitigate the cumulative effect and underground some of them. e. Possibly another, larger substation and more, larger pylons. This new proposal effectively for 36 shipping containers in a field is only adding to a significant set of eyesores. The cumulative impact is totally unacceptable. Where is the 'just transition'? 6. Cumulative impact - noise. There is significant disturbance from the quarry. [ORGANIZATION] planning department are only too aware of the '[PLACE] buzz'. Whilst noise mitigation in this proposal allegedly helps the closest buildings on a similar level, noise will be projected up the hill to overlooking properties and others enjoying the amenity. Also, how can the proposal provide calculations about noise when the type of battery is not known? 7. All 3 access roads are single track, with steep sections and sharp bends. These I suggest are totally unsuitable for the thousands of tons of kit to be transported there on large lorries. 8. It is disingenuous of the proposer to say that there will be little ongoing traffic. Batteries of all technologies have a limited lifespan, therefore there will be periodic disruption from traffic to replace failing units. With no commitment to type of battery, the proposer cannot comment meaningfully on ongoing traffic. 9. Access roads are not a priority for gritting and there are accidents every year on the steep sections under present traffic loads, never mind heavy lorries. Can be difficult too for emergency services eg fire engines. 10. Decreased amenity value. More so since Covid, this area is popular with walkers, cyclists and horse-riders. An industrial site has no place amidst the peaceful landscape that local people come to enjoy. 11. There is no information on additional infrastructure needed to connect the farm to the grid and the proposer denies any responsibility for this. A suggestion of undergrounding but no details or feasibility study. There are no guarantees that [ORGANIZATION] would underground any connection. These details need to be added into the cumulative visual impact analysis. 12. Lithium battery technology is still very much under development (mostly for cars, which makes very different demands on energy storage) and it seems unclear as to whether it will emerge as the dominant technology for large scale energy storage, especially to deliver power over periods of days (such as happens with high pressure weather systems in the UK). I do not wish to have the environment round here trashed by an experiment. 13. Lithium together with cobalt and other minerals potentially used are limited and environmentally damaging resources to mine. What are the plans for ensuring its recycling? A more general point: battery farms are a solution to a problem of the Scottish Government's making - an over-reliance on unreliable and unpredictable energy sources such as wind. A more balanced energy generation policy together with energy conservation measures would mitigate the need for additional developments such as this. Small battery farms like this would be depleted in hours if not minutes when there's no wind. I hope [ORGANIZATION] will make the point through the appropriate channels that some of us in [PLACE] resent paying the price in the quality of our environment for the government's narrow-minded dogma.

Given the close proximity between our property with no buƯer zone separating the main access route to and from the BESS facility, the safety concerns for us are extremely heightened with potential for property damage and or incidents to ourselves, our young children, neighbours and pets with the proposed level of passing construction vehicles This Proposed route 2.5-3m in width that passes our property with 700mm separation between the proposed HGV, LGV, and associated traƯic, with no pavements for pedestrians, the likelihood for an incident will increase. No consideration has been given to properties within a 500m radius to be notified of the proposed BESS development. Residents located 1.5km away from the proposed development received [ORGANIZATION] planning notifications, however residents located in [PLACE] 200m south of the BESS proposed development did not receive any notification. This is certainly NOTa good example of the applicant's commitment to thorough community engagement and transparency throughout the planning process. Site Development is in the Green Belt, but there are other more appropriate sites available. Development is highly inappropriate in this location. Environmental argument invalidated by site choice. Development would be located to close to residential properties. Land is currently used for farming (prime agricultural land). Industrial site would be more appropriate. Brownfield site would be more appropriate. Development would be best located at the site of energy generation for maximum eƯiciency. I assume that if granted [ORGANIZATION] would carry out noise monitoring to establish background noise measurements at key locations prior to the development and to set strict noise levels with the developers and to also measure the noise afterwards to confirm those levels have been meet and to take appropriate enforcement action if they have not, this was not done at [PLACE] but a lot has been learned since the [PLACE] - Denny upgrade. As we have seen from the [PLACE] very little time attention and cost has been spent on the visual impact of this development, it has been designed for convenience and cheapest cost of implementation. I did take part on the first virtual meeting and asked whether there were going to be 25 containers or 50 containers on site as the initial planning notification mentioned 25 and subsequently was changed to 50, I was told it depended on the battery suppliers they use, potentially they could get 2MW of storage in one container rather than 1MW, no doubt this is a more expensive options but would reduce the footprint and impact of the development. Another grave concern is the stability of lithium batteries as you will no doubt have seen in numerous newspaper articles there have been several occasions where these batteries have exploded and water cannot be used to put these fires out and with the toxic gases that are released.

Planning Application: [APPLICATION_CODE] Construction and operation of an energy storage facility with capacity of up to 49.9mw comprising up to 36 energy storage modules, control building, electrical equipment, access, landscaping, fencing, land 410m south west of [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE]. The application to construct and operate a containerised energy storage facility on farmland at [PLACE], a registered croft. "An area of improved pasture consisting of several large fields." We wish to register a strong objection to this planning application for the following reasons: - The application for a battery storage facility was rejected almost a year ago as it was considered an unsuitable location. The location is still unsuitable and the application must be rejected once more. - The road infrastructure - single track road - is inadequate for the size and number of vehicles required to transport containers and plant to create this site. This would create a 'high risk' situation for drivers and pedestrians. - This development would significantly reduce the amount of land currently used for pasture of sheep and cattle. Agricultural land is needed for the benefit of the nation and should not be forfeited for industrial use. Namely, 36 steel shipping containers, plus ancillary structures. THIS IS NOT A LOW IMPACT PROPOSAL. - This development is invasive in a rural residential area. Thirty-six 40ft long containers creates an industrial site. The developer acknowledges that landscaping is required to "reduce and soften" the potential visual effects of the acoustic fencing. For many, and from my elevated location, nothing would reduce the visual impact. It will completely destroy our visual amenity. THIS IS NOT A DISCRETE PROPOSAL. - Noise - If the developer intends to use acoustic fencing, then 'attractiveness' should not be part of the justification. The residents of this area have already suffered from the '[PLACE] Buzz' at [PLACE]. It is to be hoped that history will not repeat itself with this proposal. - "There is to be no permanent lighting". This statement is misleading as motion sensitive lighting in the countryside will produce interrupted lighting as birds fly past. The beauty of darkness in a rural setting will be destroyed. Cumulatively, there will be a negative impact for local residents from noise and light pollution. Suggested measures to address this will be totally ineffectual. - Need for the Project - Industrial scale development of the countryside is not farming diversification. It is a loss of available farmland. No evidence has been provided to justify the need for this development. THIS PROPOSAL DOES NOT CONTRIBUTE TO OR ENHANCE THE RURAL LOCATION. It is necessary to repeat what was stated in a previous objection: This is an inappropriate development as it is the industrialisation of the countryside. If this type of development is required in the future, to quote: Roadnight Taylor, Independent Power and Energy Consultancy - "Brown field sites are preferred. Landscape designations need to be considered and the site's visibility from dwellings." This particular proposal destroys the visual amenity for local residents and should, once again, be refused. Submitted by: [PERSON] and [PERSON]

I am writing to formally object to the proposed development of an industrial-scale battery storage facility in the [PLACE] area. My primary concern is the serious risk posed by lithium-ion battery fires. These types of fires are notoriously difficult to extinguish, highly volatile, and capable of producing large volumes of toxic fumes and potentially hazardous waste. In the event of such a fire, both human and animal life in the surrounding area would be placed at significant risk due to the release of harmful gases and contaminants into the environment. In addition, the infrastructure in this rural area is wholly unsuitable for supporting a rapid emergency response. The narrow access roads are not designed for large emergency vehicles travelling at speed, particularly in high-pressure situations. This, combined with the area's distance from the nearest emergency service hubs, means that any response to an incident would likely fall well outside recommended guideline times. Can this please be investigated? A delayed response in the event of a fire could lead to widespread exposure to toxic fumes and a potentially catastrophic outcome for the local community. For these reasons-specifically the heightened fire risk, environmental hazard, and inadequate emergency access-I strongly urge the planning authority to reject the proposal. The safety of residents, the protection of the environment, and the practical limitations of emergency services in this area must take precedence.

I wish to formally object to the above planning application on the following grounds: 1. Lack of Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) The application fails to include a full Environmental Impact Assessment, despite the site's proximity to a Site of Special Scientific Interest ([PLACE]). This omission is unacceptable given the potential risks to protected habitats and local biodiversity. A development of this scale demands rigorous environmental scrutiny. 2. Cumulative Industrialisation of the Area This proposed development would be the sixth BESS installation within a 5km radius. The cumulative impact of these facilities is transforming the rural character of the [PLACE] area into an industrial zone. The planning authority must consider the broader implications of over- concentration. The visual, noise, and environmental stress on the local community. 3. Inadequate Water and Drainage Management There is no evidence of agreed drainage or discharge systems. Without established plans, the risk of uncontrolled water runoff poses a significant threat to the [PLACE] and existing local water management infrastructure. 4. Insufficient and Unsafe Road Access The proposed access point lacks detailed construction methodology and may require the removal of mature trees. Additionally, the absence of a secondary access route raises serious safety and emergency response concerns. 5. Unclear Grid Connection Proposals The application provides no detail on how the facility will connect to the grid. This uncertainty raises the possibility of unplanned, visually intrusive overhead cabling or other disruptive infrastructure. No necessary consents or agreements appear to be in place. 6. Contradictory Tree Felling Information The documentation contains conflicting information regarding tree removal, creating confusion over the true environmental and visual impact. This lack of clarity undermines trust in the application and suggests potential misrepresentation of the scheme's scope. 7. Unaddressed Noise Pollution No noise mitigation measures have been proposed. Given the operational nature of a BESS facility, the likely noise from cooling systems and inverters could significantly disturb nearby residents and local wildlife, particularly in such a rural setting. 8. Fire Safety Hazards Battery storage systems carry inherent fire risks. The proposed site's proximity to the [PLACE] increases the danger of wildfire spread, toxic smoke release, and long-term ecological damage. No detailed fire risk assessment or emergency response plan has been provided. 9. Including this application, there are now six proposed BESS sites in this local area, along with multiple renewable projects around [PLACE]. Yet no consideration has been given to the cumulative effects of these developments. Despite [PLACE] Council’s recommendation, no Environmental Impact Assessment has been undertaken to address these impacts. My principal objections are as follows: Landscape and Visual Impact The site covers 16.3 hectares (equivalent to 23 football pitches) with a 25m gradient. The developers propose six terraces to address the slope. The project includes 470 shipping containers (332 battery containers and 138 power converters), 4,608 solar PV panels, three 12m-high Super Grid Transformers, and other associated infrastructure. Even with the proposed 4m fences and 8m earth bunds, this scale of development will remain highly visible on the sloping site. This would create a significant and permanent industrial intrusion into the rural landscape, contrary to National Planning Framework 4 (Policy 11). Noise The noise assessment submitted is inadequate, omitting key details on sound sources, site layout and receptors. Experts have concluded that the development could raise background noise levels to three times their current levels. The sloping nature of the site makes effective noise mitigation unlikely, both during construction and operation. With insufficient detail on equipment specifications and cumulative impact, there is a high risk of significant noise pollution affecting the locality. Fire Risk Lithium-ion battery fires cannot be extinguished by conventional means. Scottish Fire & Rescue have not been consulted, and National Fire Chiefs Council guidance has not been fully followed. A robust emergency response plan is essential, including evacuation procedures for residents and livestock. Alarmingly, some households currently have no evacuation route that avoids the site. Water for Fire Suppression Large volumes of water would be required on site for fire containment. It is unclear where this supply would come from, whether it would be trucked in (increasing traffic), and what chemicals would be added to prevent stagnation or freezing. Drainage, Water Supply and Contamination The terracing of the slope and installation of an impermeable membrane have not been properly modelled in relation to drainage, infiltration, SuDS performance, or the risk of contaminating private water supplies and watercourses. There has been no peer-reviewed assessment of the potential impact on groundwater. Infrastructure and Traffic Construction will cause severe disruption on narrow single-track roads. Over 100 workers will travel to and from the site daily, in addition to heavy goods deliveries of equipment and materials. The developer’s Construction Management and Traffic Plan significantly underestimates vehicle movements, excluding welfare units, fencing, solar infrastructure, water tanks, landscaping, and waste removal. Biodiversity Without an Environmental Impact Assessment, there has been no proper evaluation of the effects on habitats for badgers, bats, ground-nesting birds and other protected species in the adjoining Ancient Woodland. Construction disturbance, extensive earthworks, and kilometres of 4m-high fencing will cause major disruption. In the event of a fire, contaminated run-off could pollute the [PLACE] and the [PLACE] with devastating consequences for local ecology. Decommissioning and Land Restoration There are no clear or enforceable guarantees regarding how the site will be restored after the 25-year lifespan of the project. The removal of impermeable membranes, extensive concrete foundations and 8m-high berms, once matured with trees and shrubs, is not addressed. Community Benefit The “Community Wealth Building Plan” offers no firm commitment to employing a local workforce and provides no direct community benefit. Scottish Government guidance recommends community benefits equivalent to £5,000 per installed megawatt per annum – for this project, £2.5 million annually. The developer has ignored this entirely. Planning Policy National Planning Framework 4 (Policy 11) supports renewable energy projects only where landscape and visual impacts are minimised and where there are demonstrable local and community benefits. This proposal fails on both counts and therefore does not meet the requirements of national policy. Conclusion In summary, the proposed development poses unacceptable risks to the environment, local amenity, and community wellbeing. It does not comply with planning policy and should therefore be refused.

It will have a significant impact on the important historic agricultural landscape and rural ambience that so characterises the [PLACE] in the area between [PLACE] and [PLACE].
