Negative effects on wildlife and nature Hidden away in the vast amount of material that accompanies this proposal are details of the dimensions of the new additional turbines. They have a swept diameter of 136m and a ground clearance of 14m. This is a massive threat to species that inhabit that airspace and a significant disturbance to ground nesting birds and other species. A simple calculation of the total area swept by the turbines illustrates what this application is seeking. It seems incredible that the Ornithology report for the proposal essentially says that “Yes, two species that are ‘red-listed’ with regard to survival will be affected, but never mind, these birds exist elsewhere”. Similarly it seeks to dismiss concerns regarding the populations that inhabit the important protected wet lands to the north on the basis that the turbines are 300m outside the designated protection zone. All of this in the context of a more than 5.5 times increase in the turbine-blade swept area for the installation. The statements 8.1.6 and 8.1.7 are self serving interpretations of analysis based on limited evidence or theoretical models. Were they to, for example, consider some more recent studies from independent sources such as work in Finland on the effects of energy developments on wildlife populations ([LINK]) they would find that “.many bird and mammal groups avoid wind power. The full or partial displacement of individuals from the wind turbine area may reduce population sizes which will especially have an adverse impact on rare and threatened species”. The cumulative impact of such a laissez-faire approach to nature conservation is what leads to total population collapse of endangered species. The ornithology report goes to great lengths to attempt to minimise the effect on collision risk to species but does so on the basis of data derived from theoretical models and lack of evidence arising from occasional inspections around the existing four turbines. There has been no attempt at automated collection of data through photographic or radar based monitoring and a distinct lack of candour regarding the more than 5.5 times increase in the turbine-blade swept area for the installation. Statements are repeatedly made for the different species along the lines of The four turbines of the operational [PLACE] are situated less than 500 m from the proposed new turbine locations, searches were carried out in both winter periods for any evidence that there had been any collisions with the turbines by any goose or swan species and none was found. This would indicate that birds are habituated to turbines in this area. This seems to be somewhat equivalent to someone claiming that they had seen no evidence of road traffic accidents on the [PLACE] or A99 in [PLACE] and using it as the basis that all was well with road safety in [PLACE]! It is inevitable that wildlife and nature will be affected, both during and after development. Curlews, once very common throughout [PLACE], are a species now in serious decline. They are 'red listed' which is a category that recognises them as in danger of extinction. It is claimed that populations have declined by around 65% since 1970. Would curlews in this area survive? Doubtful. They are up against effects that include direct habitat loss through construction and displacement through indirect loss of habitat and disturbance that causes birds to avoid the development and surrounds. See for example, the following reference for further information on the Wetland Restoration Charity’s efforts in support of the serious predicament of the curlew ([LINK]). Furthermore, the curlew is at particular risk during the breeding season. It is not a colonial species and pairs live independently, but it exhibits a nest collaborative behaviour when danger threatens. It will take to the air with its alarm call and overfly any other nests in the neighbourhood, making it at particular risk if there are turbines in the vicinity. There is clear evidence that bee populations are adversely affected by electromagnetic fields such as those that will arise out of electrical charge sources such as battery storage - see for example [LINK]. Harming bee populations has very severe consequential effects. With eye-watering inducements to land owners to forsake agricultural production in favour of income derived from energy companies for doing nothing other than lease land, means that the cumulative effect will be to change the agricultural landscape forever. If this trend continues, the entire county will become an energy production desert with little meaningful employment within the rural community that remains. It is vitally important to preserve agricultural land if the very essence of the [PLACE] is to be preserved. Construction impact During the construction there will be a significant impact. As well as noise and dust there will be huge impacts associated with the construction traffic and significant impacts on the users of the road. Wind and the open aspect of the area will contribute to exacerbating the effects of noise and dust in particular. Similarly the evidence emerging from the covid period when wildlife flourished, clearly indicates that there will be a serious effect on the natural environment and its inhabitants. Noise As well as noise during the construction phase noise will be generated from the proposed installation. Further independent evidence is required to establish that the nature of the type of noise generated by battery storage systems does not have deleterious effects on others including human, animal, bird and insect populations. The evidence on the effect on bee populations has already been referred to. Light pollution There will be considerable light pollution disturbance during construction but also likely afterwards. This will make a major change to the natural environment with consequent effects on human and natural populations. Risk of serious incident A full assessment of the risk associated with this proposal should include risks identified with the post construction phase as well as risks during construction. This has not been done in its entirety and there is ample evidence of issues relating to fire, toxic fumes and consequent residue from battery related fires elsewhere. There is no specialist service available to deal with such incidents and even if there were, the problems of maintaining such a service that could quickly deploy to incidents across a large area served in general by poor quality roads, are considerable, particularly during times when roads may be busy. Question of need There is no independent evidence that this development is needed for the future of energy provision to [PLACE] or indeed the UK. It arises out of the view of the various governments that there is a need to make money out of energy production by generating more than is required and deriving an income from the surplus. Permitting a multitude of developments that are not required generates other demands that are not required such as the upgrade of the transmission network from [PLACE] to the south. target_text: While the Local Planning Authority is responsible for the approval of the majority of BESS installations through the planning process, we find no evidence that the Applicant has engaged in any dialogue with [ORGANIZATION] ([PLACE] is served by a volunteer service) with regard to a comprehensive risk management assessment of the site and adjoining sensitive receptors and area, i.e. residential homes, farms, ancient woodlands, protected species within a 1 km radius together with the major [PLACE] road which is 1.2 km from the site. We do not consider it appropriate to consider consenting this application until such a Risk Management Assessment as described above is carried out. This would enable appropriate emergency planning, something which was raised at the time of the PAN event. The Group seek assurances that the principles set out in the [ORGANIZATION] guidance will form the basis for discussion/dialogue between the [ORGANIZATION]/Owners/Operators – 1. Effective identification and management of hazards and risks specific to the siting, infrastructure, layout and operations at the facility. 2. Siting of renewable energy infrastructure so as to eliminate or reduce hazards to emergency responders. 3. Safe access for emergency responders in and around the facility, including safe and effective emergency response. 4. Provision of adequate water supply and firefighting infrastructure to allow safe and effective emergency response. 5. Vegetation site and managed so as to avoid increased bushfire and grassfire risk. 6. Prevention of fire ignition on site. 7. Prevention of fire spread between site infrastructure (solar panel banks, wind turbines, battery containers/enclosures). 8. Prevention of external fire impacting and igniting site infrastructure. 9. Provision of accurate and current information for emergency responders during emergencies. 10. Effective emergency planning and management, specific to the site infrastructure and operations. Objection 2 - Risks of co-location with renewable generation and other storage. Co-locating energy storage with energy generation is becoming increasingly common. Energy storage could be co-located with solar panels, wind turbines, hydroelectric generators, hydrogen production facilities or storage or different battery technologies. Where there is the potential for co-location, additional risk assessments need to be undertaken for the combination of technologies at a given site and the potential propagation of hazards. Where multiple generation, storage or industrial facilities are located in close proximity (but not necessarily co-located in such a way as to pose a direct risk to one another), consideration should also be given to the local capacity to deal with multiple concurrent issues and the implications for emergency response. This site is approximately 1+km distant from three other BESS sites, 1 of which is already consented, 1 currently being progressed through the development process, and 1 application still to be submitted making a potential total of 4 BESS within a 1 KM radius of each other, all connecting along [PLACE] which currently contains the [PLACE] comprising numerous businesses including Sawmill, Civil Engineering, Crane Hire and construction equipment amongst many others. We note that the [ORGANIZATION] is not a statutory consultee to the planning process but in the light of clear guidance from the [ORGANIZATION] and the Health and Safety Guidance for Grid Scale Electrical Energy Storage Systems and the impact of the proliferation of BESS in local communities, there is clearly an identified need prior to consenting this application for the Developer to engage with the [ORGANIZATION] to determine and set out the local capacity to deal with multiple concurrent issues and the implications for emergency response. Objection 3 – The Group are concerned that with 2 BESS (already consented) and another 3 proposed developments (5 BESS developments in total) being located within an appx 2 km radius or less i.e. up to >200 containers and >220 MW electricity storage. The cumulative impacts on local communities and businesses will be significant in many ways and will not “maximise net economic impact, including local and community socio-economic benefits such as employment, associated business and supply chain opportunities”. Objection 4 – No mention is made in any Developer documentation to the high pressure gas line which is situated within this site and the adjacent local road network. This is a matter for Scottish Gas Networks to clarify and pursue. Objection 5 – Local businesses along [PLACE], together with nearby housing areas will be impacted as all 5 BESS intend to connect to the [ORGANIZATION] substation- located on this road and therefore for each development underground cables and connection to the substation will be required. This will entail significant ground works on a single track road used by log lorries, cranes/earth moving equipment, a substantial fleet of HGV vehicles, and delivery and other service vehicles. Notwithstanding the impact on businesses there is also the impact on local residents, workers, and support services. Already businesses are being advised of disruption to service by [ORGANIZATION] and this is just the start. Over the next 2/3 years disruption in the form of power outages and probably many more unforeseen issues are going to occur. This all comes at a cost to local businesses and the local economy. Objection 6 – The siting of this development is within the 1+ km of sensitive receptors. Should a fire event occur or a potential thermal run down occur, there would be significant health and safety impacts for local residents and workers from any smoke and/or vapour cloud because of the proximity of this development to homes, farms and businesses. Consultation/discussions between [ORGANIZATION]/local businesses/home owners/Applicant need to be undertaken prior to any consent in order to reassure the community and businesses at large that they will be given sufficient warning and be protected from such an event. Objection 7 - The close proximity of the [PLACE] which is the main arterial route from [PLACE] and [PLACE] and also the new [PLACE] (yet to be built but already planned) will be adversely impacted by smoke/vapour cloud threatening not only the [PLACE]/[PLACE] Communities and their economies but the whole [PLACE] corridor to Elgin and beyond. In the past 9 months there has been 3 major fires caused by exploding lithium batteries, all of which severely impacted the trunk and local road network, local businesses and residents i.e. April 2024 – [PLACE] ([PLACE]), June 2024 – [PLACE] ([PLACE]) and most recently January 2025 – [PLACE] (nr Perth) [PLACE]. Objection 8 – The Applicant stated at the PAN event that the site will be monitored remotely from Madrid, Spain but does not provide evidence of how this will be done. An effective and appropriate method of early detection of a fault within the batteries should be in place, with the ability to disconnect the affected battery/batteries remotely. This should be achieved automatically through the provision of an effective Battery Management System. Should thermal runaway conditions be detected then there should be the facility in place for the early alerting of emergency services and of nearby businesses and homes. External audible and visual warning devices, as well as addressable identification at control and indicating equipment, should be linked to (a) the Battery Management System and (b) Detection and suppression system activation. We can find no maintenance plan for the batteries and other electrical equipment. We consider this is essential to protect public safety. The [ORGANIZATION] seek assurance that all maintenance work required for the batteries and other electrical equipment is undertaken by a local contractor as part of the benefits to the community. Additionally we seek clarification if the CCTV network at the development site will be automatically linked in to Police and Fire and Rescue Services. Objection 9 – The site plan sets out the layout of the containers. However, it is difficult from this drawing to determine the space between each container. A standard minimum spacing between units of 6 metres is recommended and any reduction in spacing requires a clear, evidence based, case for the reduction should be shown. Clarification should be sought on this safety issue. Objection 10 – The Transport Statement and Construction Traffic Management Plan supporting the application states at – (a) Para 3.6. “Construction vehicles should not approach the site from the southeast along [PLACE]. (ie the rural lane which is 3.8 m wide – 375 long). (b) Para 6.12. “Construction vehicles must, at all times, only approach the site from the northwest via the [PLACE] and the approximately 375m long section of [PLACE].” (c) Para 6.13. “Given that [PLACE] is singletrack in nature, a call up procedure must be utilised for construction traffic travelling and to and from the site. Any incoming drivers will be told to wait in an informed appropriate safe location, from where they can then be instructed on when it is safe to approach the site.” (d) Para 6.14.”There is a lay-by on the [PLACE], approximately 900m to the northeast of the site access location. There are also lay-bys on the [PLACE] in both directions in the vicinity of the [PLACE] / [PLACE] ghost-island junction. Hauliers must be made aware of any safe spaces to wait.” (e) Para 6.15.”Authorised ‘Banks people’ will be located on site to assist with manoeuvring of large vehicles along [PLACE] as necessary and to assist with the safe movement of vehicles within the site” (f) Para 6.16. “Subject to agreement with the Local Highway Authority (LHA), temporary signage advising road users of construction vehicle movements and large vehicles turning will be provided along [PLACE] in the vicinity of the site access.” The [ORGANIZATION] would make the following comments – (i) The CMP must consider a one way flow of traffic onto the site i.e. from [PLACE] entrance exiting onto [PLACE] rather than as indicated that construction traffic can access the site via [PLACE] and [PLACE]. A one way flow of traffic would make for better public and pedestrian safety and facilitate a better traffic flow within the site. (ii) A one way flow system should operate permanently within the site even after the construction phase has been completed and apply to all traffic. (iii) The CMP should not be reliant on the use of laybys on the [PLACE], [PLACE] /[PLACE] ghost island junction. The Applicant should ensure proper programming and co-ordination of construction HGVs etc. on a day to day basis. (iv) [PLACE] is used by local people regularly cutting across from [PLACE] to [PLACE]. If a one way traffic flow is operated within the site, then local people will not have to deal with HGVs turning off the [PLACE] or [PLACE] into [PLACE]. All traffic will flow from [PLACE] in a westerly direction. (v) The CMP states that ‘Banks people’ will be located on the site to assist with manoeuvring of large vehicles along [PLACE] and within the site. We note that [PLACE] is only 3.8 m wide with no pavement on any side for pedestrians or cyclists. We consider this to be a public safety hazard and would therefore request that if the Applicant intends to use this [PLACE] (which to all intents and purposes is little more than a rural lane) a suitable pavement should be constructed up to the junction with the [PLACE] in the interests of public safety. If the applicant is not prepared to construct this pavement, the applicant should consider the construction of an alternative exit point within the site. (vi) [ORGANIZATION] guidance requires the undernoted access for fire and rescue service vehicles. We note from ACCESS_LAYOUT-3519620.pdf shown below that the site gravel track will be 4 m wide with 4 m gate access at the entrance and exit to the site. On examining SITE LAYOUT PLAN 3508349 dated 29/01/25 shown below we note the track has too many turns in its layout with 4/5 x 90 degree angular turns which could prove problematical dependent on the type of vehicle. No turning circle provision is shown but this should be compliant with [ORGANIZATION] guidance shown below. The track appears to run down the inside of the fencing barrier which means vehicles must have appropriate gate access. Additionally the track abuts the inside fencing barrier with little if any space available for FRS staff to get round to the other side of their vehicle. Please refer to SITE LAYOUT PLAN 3508349 shown above. If a traffic flow from north to south is to be adopted, any gateways within the combined sites will require to meet the attached criteria set out by the [ORGANIZATION] in the above table. We also note from ROAD_LONG_SECTIONS_PLAN-3498462 that 63mm is the depth of the gravel laid over the 4 metre track with a tapered slope showing the drainage channel. The [ORGANIZATION] seek clarification if this proposed gravel pathway construction will comply with [ORGANIZATION] guidance of 17 tonnes minimum carrying weight for fire and rescue service vehicles and also fully laden HGVs, heavy lifting equipment etc. of up to 45 tonnes. Objection 11 – Fire Management Plan states. (a) “The proposed strategy to manage / control 2,145m3 of firewater runoff generated is for Full Containment within the proposed SuDS Attenuation Basin. The storage capacity is equivalent to approximately 19 hours of firewater storage without intervention.” (b) “The Hydrobrake chamber at the attenuation basin outlet is to be fitted with a penstock valve and appropriately signposted as the Firewater Isolation Valve. As the attenuation basin shall be lined, the piped outlet is the only viable pathway for contaminated firewater to enter the water environment.” (c ) “The Client will sign into an agreement with a local emergency waste disposal service who can provide a sealed mobile tanker to the site in a timely manner.” (d) “Access for a mobile tanker would be achieved via the proposed site access tracks. A mobile tanker shall be able to empty the attenuation basin with an extended suction hose able to extend up to 10m from the site access track. If required, a piped route from the base of the SuDS basin can be installed to provide pumping access (via a manhole chamber) from a preferred location.” From the above statements, [ORGANIZATION] take this to mean that all contaminated runoff will be removed by a mobile tanker and that no contaminated runoff will drain to adjoining fields or watercourses. Assurance is requested. The [ORGANIZATION] would also seek assurance that the SUDs basin is located a minimum of 10 metres away from the Battery Storage containers. (e) Firefighting water supply – the FWMP states (i) “A 150mm water mains runs parallel to the [PLACE] to the north of the site and may be able to provide the required minimum flow rate of 1900l/min stipulated in the [ORGANIZATION] guidance. Available flow rates within the water mains would be confirmed with Scottish Water at detailed design stage and a final new water mains layout would be agreed (indicatively shown on Drawing FWMP-001). (ii) “ As a backup option, the firefighting water supply can be provided by buried firewater supply tanks within the development area providing a minimum total volume of 228m3. This volume ensures the minimum flow rate required by [ORGANIZATION] guidance can be provided for the stated 2 hours”. Firstly, It would appear that no discussions have taken place with Scottish Water regarding either of the above two scenarios. This is concerning as the [ORGANIZATION] guidance requires access to a water supply. The [ORGANIZATION] are aware from the current SWIA that there are significant problems with water supply in the [PLACE] catchment area and therefore we seek clarification, before any consent is considered, that the FRS and Scottish Water are consulted as to the most appropriate solution and that any solution agreed can be constructed and implemented before the battery containers and other electrical infrastructure is located to the site. Secondly, if buried firewater supply tanks is the chosen option, how will these tanks be replenished/topped up? Clarification is required. Objection 12 - Flood Risk and Drainage Assessment supporting the application shows the following table - The [ORGANIZATION] note that the SUDS pond is to serve a dual purpose as firewater runoff storage and that it is not considered a suitable method for the BESS development. Surface water runoff from the development is to be discharged to the adjacent field drain to the west. Firstly, the [ORGANIZATION] seek clarification if the SUDs pond is to serve a dual purpose, will the Fire Isolation Valve require to be left open to drain the SUDs pond into the neighbouring watercourse as shown below until there is a fire incident when the Fire Isolation Valve will be ‘manually’ closed to prevent any contaminated runoff entering the water environment. Who will have responsibility for this? Secondly, we note that the surface water runoff from the development is to be discharged to the adjacent field drain to the west. However as can be seen from the Hydrology overview the vast majority of surface water from the development site flows naturally from west to east. We seek clarification that when the land is cleared for the battery containers compound, the natural flow of surface water will be changed and forced into the west field through drainage channels. Objection 13 – The Outline Drainage Strategy paras 4.4.1-4.4.4 show an extensive set of maintenance requirements. The [ORGANIZATION] seek to ensure that any such maintenance work is undertaken by a local contractor as part of the benefits to the community. Objection 14 - No Emergency Response Plan (ERP) has been submitted with this application (which should indicate the prevailing wind direction and if possible should include an analysis of fire gas plume modelling and Explosion / deflagration strategies particularly in this case of the number of ancient woodlands in the immediate vicinity. Such an ERP should be drawn up in collaboration with the [ORGANIZATION] and comply with the recommendations of the [ORGANIZATION] which should cover Local residents and businesses are anxious about BESS storage facilities and would wish to scrutinise the ERP before consent is considered. Objection 15 – Fire Safety is a significant concern to the community at large. Albeit the focus of the local planning authority is from a land use perspective to ensure that risks to the environment are considered and mitigated, fire safety, in itself, is not a material planning consideration and therefore, we understand it is not for the Council to regulate safety in regard to fire. In the light of a further 3 proposals for BESS development in this area, and as previously mentioned the 3 lithium battery fires which occurred in Scotland within the last 9 months, the [ORGANIZATION] would urge the Council to ensure that a planning development template/framework is instigated immediately with the involvement of the [ORGANIZATION] as a statutory consultee on all BESS applications to ensure the health and wellbeing of the community are protected and any negative impacts on local businesses and local economy are minimised. Objection 16 – The development site is not included as an allocated site for business and industry within the current IMFLDP2. Objection 17 – The [ORGANIZATION] expect to see tangible and long lasting benefits from net zero developments like BESS. The Applicant has not included a Community Benefit statement which draws on the projects/opportunities set out in the area’s Local Place Plan nor does it detail, for example, the economic benefits to the area such as Job creation: Development of renewable energy projects can create new jobs in construction, maintenance, and related industries, providing employment opportunities for local residents. Supply chain development: Local businesses can benefit from supplying goods and services to the project, stimulating the local economy. Investment in community infrastructure: Developers may contribute funding for upgrades to local infrastructure like roads, public transportation, and community centres. While we understand ‘community benefits sit independently of the planning and consenting system’, the Scottish Government is keen to see local communities benefit from net zero energy developments like BESS which are located within their local community area. In the light of what could be 5 BESS sites with over 200 containers and over 200 mw of capacity, within a stone’s throw of homes, businesses, ancient woods, protected species, major road infrastructure, farms etc., the communities of [PLACE] and [PLACE] must see some tangible and long lasting benefits. General comments The local community wish to see local businesses expand and develop and to create more well paid jobs for local people. Attracting new businesses and creating more local employment was by far the top outcome identified in the community- led Local Place Plan. However, the ever increasing number of BESS sites in this area and the disruption to businesses and their workforce will act as a barrier to potential new businesses wanting to locate to [PLACE] and make forward investment and planning more difficult when looking to the future. Additionally, Tourism is a major economic driver for the local economy, and visiting an area which is covered in battery storage containers across the eastern entrance to [PLACE] is not inviting or conducive to promoting [PLACE] as a tourist destination with great beaches, country and riverside walks, open green spaces, and a wonderful array of wildlife, sealife and birds. It would be a complete disaster for [PLACE] if visitors had to bring their own mask in case there is a fire/explosion/thermal rundown!

retrieved_examples.text: I am writing to formally object to the proposed development of a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) facility in [PLACE]. I am very concerned that The Scottish Government has set out a “proportionality of planning assessments”. It states. "The costs associated with preparing and supporting information and assessment and particularly where this involves appointing consultants some developers may be unable to secure finance for their proposal until they've received planning permission. In such circumstances where they have a cash flow it may be helpful for the planning authority and the applicant developers to discuss the timing of certain information requirements and whether, in some cases, these could be appropriately back-loaded through conditions suspensive or otherwise attached to retrospective permissions." Does the above statement mean that I can now apply to build a very large extension on my home, but due to the costs involved and the timing of certain information requirements, and my cash flow problems, I can suspend certain of your planning requirements or attach them to retrospective permission once I have built the bowling alley in my extension? Not to be frivolous but this directive makes a mockery of Planning regulations and casts severe doubts on the democracy of fair and equal assessments in Planning for all applications and not just those in which huge amounts of money/profits are involved. We have a Powerwall 2 which we can charge overnight at a cheap rate (8.5p per kWh) and which provides us with 13.5kWh the following day, every day, regardless of the weather. When combined with solar panels, it is possible to be off grid most days, particularly in the summer. At one of the ‘Public consultations’ I attended for this application I asked why this system (even a Powerwall per household alone) could not be provided for everyone. I was told, “There’s no money in it.” This is a shocking and unacceptable statement, but I suspect, true. I have serious concerns regarding the overwhelming cumulative totality of what is being proposed for this area, the pylon lines, the running of corridors of underground cabling, the substations, the battery storage systems of which we now know there are at least three in this area at the time of writing, the workers camps and all the ancillary infrastructure, the massively increased traffic, both lorries and cars, we also have a large landfill within a mile and a major power station in [PLACE]. Where does the responsibility for this totality actually lie? Who is calculating the cumulative effect of all these developments? We are bearing the brunt of Westminster’s headlong rush to meet Net Zero without seeing any benefit from it in our energy costs, where we are paying far higher costs for our electricity than in south east England where all the electricity stored in these facilities is going whilst the destruction of Scotland’s green arable land continues. So called ‘Community Benefits’ are tiny. For example, the west coast wind farm, Ben Aketil has paid out over 16 years, £700,000 to the local community, whilst paying £51million to shareholders. This is clearly all about money. National energy operators predict we are going to need 11GW of power in Scotland by 2050, we already have 20GW of renewable power built or online in Scotland. Double what is needed! Now. All these Planning Applications are to meet the power needs of the south of England, not Scotland, but we have to bear the blight literally on our landscape, and pay twice what they are paying for it. The UK only emits 2% of the world’s CO2. Scotland about 0.3% so nothing we do is really going to benefit the world and yet we are destroying our countryside and landscapes. How much concrete is being used to cover acres of current farmland? 30 acres on this one site alone. What is the calculation of CO2 to produce this amount of concrete? We now have a number of existing and prospective huge industrial developments in this area ie a major landfill currently taking waste from all over the east of Scotland due to the closure of the Incinerator in [PLACE] at the time of writing; at least three, possibly more to be proposed Battery storage facilities covering a minimum of 30 acres each of currently green arable land used for farming for generations; a new pylon line cutting across the area; major gas lines; and underground cabling the route of which is yet to be determined. The totality of these planning applications is overwhelming and clearly undemocratic. The cumulative impact of all major renewable energy infrastructure developments including transmission, storage, and generation, with all ancillary infrastructure should be looked at in a holistic way rather than the current wild west Klondyke of applications by trail blazing speculators who openly admit there is no money in domestic systems, that would actually work far more efficiently by not paying out millions to shareholders at the expense of Scotlands heritage. What systems have been put in place too mitigate the risk from fire and explosions at such sites? On 15th September 2020, calls were received by [ORGANIZATION] Fire Control reporting an explosion with smoke and flames visible from the small Battery storage facility in [PLACE]. Two appliances responded to the incident. They arrived within 5 minutes of the first call at a secure, double gated site, that had four 12m long shipping containers within the inner compound; one of these was alight and had signs of an explosion. Parts of this container were blown across the compound the furthest of which had travelled 23m. The explosion was a result of a failure within Battery Zone 3-Rack 7 Module 6 (BZ3-R7M6) which led to a thermal runaway, which, in turn produced gases within the container culminating in a deflagration. The resulting investigation was unable to identify the root cause of the failure within module 6. fitted with a NOVEC 1230 fire suppression system. I am not reassured at all that systems 5 years on will not suffer the same fate. It was stated in the fire report that there is no Industry standard for what is considered “adequate” maintenance but conduct maintenance in conjunction with the warranty agreement and what is recommended by the provider. Light weight parts of the HVAC system had been thrown up to 23m from the container towards the control room within the fence line. The container walls and roof had bowed outwards. All four HVACs had come detached from their fittings and landed in a row alongside the container. The door closest to The Fisheries had been blown off its hinges and had ripped through the yellow safety rails before landing in the compound. These doors are of substantial weight and it would have taken great internal pressure and force to eject them to the distance. Work conducted by [ORGANIZATION] showed that cells can give off the following toxic vapours: Hydrogen Fluoride, Hydrogen Sulphide, Hydrogen Chloride, Hydrogen Cyanide, Hydrogen, Propylene, Methane, Carbon Monoxide, Sulphur Dioxide, Ethylene, Ethane. Despite being told by a representative at the recent Public Consultation that technology and fire prevention had developed since the [PLACE] fire there continue to be numerous reports of these storage facilities catching fire; Following a massive lithium-ion BESS battery fire at the [PLACE] on January 16, 2025, residents have filed a lawsuit against multiple energy companies, accusing them of failing to maintain adequate fire safety measures. The fire, which began after a fire suppression system failed, smouldered for four days and led to the temporary evacuation of over 1,200 residents. The blaze released toxic gases and scattered heavy metals over the surrounding area. The [PLACE] Power Plant fire may serve as a wake-up call for the energy storage industry, highlighting the importance of stringent safety measures to protect these large stores of lithium batteries from thermal runaway. On January 16, 2025, the storage building’s suppression system failed to suppress, and its containment system failed to contain. The suppression system either did not exist, did not rapidly initiate, was inadequate for the number of batteries exposed to thermal runaway heat, or it failed to operate. Large lithium battery storage fires are common in [PLACE]; they have occurred annually since April 2022. The link is to the 120 page report into the [PLACE] fire; [LINK] A fire broke out at the Fenix Battery Recycling plant in [PLACE], for the second time in a year. The blaze, which occurred on April 9, 2025, led to the evacuation of nearby homes. The fire was not deemed to be suspicious after an investigation. On 15 May 2024, a fire broke out at LS Power’s 250MW Gateway energy storage facility. While firefighters quickly responded, the fire flared up multiple times until 28 May. The root cause of the fire is not known. In February this year a fire broke out at a battery storage facility near [PLACE] at the facility at [PLACE]. At the time of writing, I contacted [ORGANIZATION]. They stated they had no knowledge of any proposal to build battery storage in this area. There is no single piece of legislation that sets specific requirements for BESS sites. Lithium-ion batteries pose significant fire hazards when stored improperly. They contain flammable electrolytes that can ignite and create a fire that can quickly spread, leading to property damage, injuries, and even fatalities. When lithium-ion batteries are stored together, there is a risk of a chain reaction where a single battery’s thermal runaway can cause other batteries to catch fire. This application is in direct conflict with the Guiding Principle and ‘overarching aim’ of the Local Development Plan which is to be ‘people centred’ and to ‘protect and enhance our environment’. ‘We live in communities that are inclusive, empowered and safe’. The key expectations of the Plan is ‘People Centred’, ‘Putting people and communities at the heart.’ The LDP states quite clearly that ‘Local Development Plans should set out opportunities for the sustainable reuse of brownfield land, including vacant and derelict land and empty buildings’. Further, ‘Potential redevelopment uses of brownfield land could include renewable energy, green infrastructure.’ The LDP makes no mention at all of the totality of, and huge industrialization, of rural farm land in north east Scotland. The proposal would introduce large-scale and complex infrastructure diminishing the simplicity of the landscape and its uncluttered character. Effects on character would be significant and adverse, extending to around 3km from the site. In Scotland, a cumulative effects objection to a planning application refers to the concern that the combined impact of a proposed development, along with existing or planned developments, will negatively affect the area. This could involve impacts on the environment, infrastructure, or local character. This would certainly be the case with this and other developments. Key aspects of a cumulative effects objection in Scotland: Combined Impacts: The core of the objection is that the development, considered alongside other existing or proposed developments, will create a greater negative impact than the sum of the individual impacts. Relevant Considerations: This can include issues like: 1. Environmental Degradation: Increased pollution, habitat loss, or strain on natural resources. 2. Infrastructure Strain: Overburdened roads, inadequate parking, or strain on utilities. 3. Impact on Local Character: Changes to the visual landscape, loss of green space, or alteration of the area's identity. 4. Loss of Amenity: Increased noise, traffic, or other disruptions to residents' quality of life. Importance of Cumulative Effects Assessment (CEA): Scottish planning policy increasingly emphasizes the need for CEA to assess the combined impacts of multiple developments. This helps ensure that planning decisions consider the overall effects of development, not just individual projects. The nature and extent of this site are not in keeping with the surrounding environment. This is partly due to the type of infrastructure, or lack thereof, found in this area. However, above all this is a farming community and the type of development in question would disrupt the operation of surrounding farms and other businesses in this area. This is a vast proposal to be located in several agricultural fields. This open countryside is a very important part of the [PLACE] landscape, and consists of agricultural land providing an important country side buffer between settlements. The battery proposals will urbanise this agricultural area, blighting the visual amenity for nearby residents and walkers with the industrialised nature of the units, the substation equipment and containerised support accommodation makes no effort to address this rural location. Noise and light pollution associated with both its construction and future operation risk affecting farm animals grazing in surrounding fields, especially during winter months when this type of pollution is prolonged. Moreover, the visual blight would impact properties beyond the site’s immediate surroundings. In addition to my previous comments, the impact on the local road network from construction would be too much in itself. The safety risk from HGVs delivering materials to construction sites; this extends to HGVs and LGVs leaving as well, specifically the risk of mud and dust emanating from these vehicles. This development would also exacerbate existing pressures on local water courses and would likely worsen the impact of flooding. During periods of heavy rainfall this area often experiences severe flooding which the site’s impermeable surface area would worsen through increased runoff into nearby fields and watercourses, in turn heightening the risk of severe flooding for nearby farms and properties. This would also limit access for emergency services reaching the site by road. In the event of fire the response from fire crews would be hampered by the single-track roads that surround the perimeter of the site and indeed this whole area. The process of firefighting is also noteworthy with regard to the resources involved. The volume of water required is extremely large. The explosion and fire of a small battery storage site in Belgium in 2017 required 1.4 million litres of water to contain. The planning guidance on battery storage proposal specifically highlights the need for applicants to liaise with the fire and rescue service. This has NOT been done. Other similar applications estimate that production of materials plus construction and replacement of the batteries over a period of 40 years will generate up to 1,083,320 tonnes of CO2. By contrast, it is impossible to know definitely what if any savings are achievable during operations, varying from positive to negative. Therefore the scheme cannot be considered to be a major contributor to net zero regardless of its size and scope. Indeed, in the short to medium term it will cause an increase in greenhouse gas emissions due to the fact that all material, equipment and personnel required for both construction and operation of the site must arrive by road. Furthermore, the applicant’s calculations do not account for emissions associated with the shipping and import of key component parts from overseas sources, including from China where such components receive far less scrutiny from a safety perspective. I would challenge the representations made by [ORGANIZATION] regarding their proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at [PLACE]. After reviewing their submitted materials particularly those produced by [ORGANIZATION]. I must highlight serious and deeply troubling concerns around the accuracy, impartiality, and transparency of the entire application process. Scotland’s environmental future should be based on responsible, well-managed development not unregulated industrialisation of rural land. There is a significant risk of contamination to private water sources in the area, including springs, burns, wells, and aquifers. I formally request that a comprehensive hydrogeological assessment be undertaken by an independent body at the expense of [ORGANIZATION] to ensure that not only my private water supply, but also those of neighbouring properties, are fully protected even in the event of a catastrophic incident. It is deeply concerning that part of the proposed infrastructure is planned to be constructed directly above a live underground gas pipeline. This appears to be in direct contravention of established safety guidance, including the Health and Safety Executive’s publication HSG47: Avoiding Danger from Underground Services, which outlines strict precautions for any construction or excavation near such critical infrastructure. While the Pipelines Safety Regulations 1996 do not specify a fixed exclusion zone, industry best practice and [ORGANIZATION] guidance strongly discourage any construction directly over or within close proximity to high-pressure gas pipelines without thorough risk assessment, stakeholder consultation, and mitigation measures. In many cases, a minimum clearance distance of up to 100 metres is observed, depending on the pipeline’s pressure and classification. I note that [ORGANIZATION] consulted with a minor player in this area, the conclusion being that there were no major gas pipes under pressure on the proposed site. THIS IS TOTALLY INCORRECT. Allowing this proposal to go ahead would fundamentally contradict the risk assessments, safety protocols, and development exclusion zones that have been enforced for years to protect critical infrastructure, the environment, and public health. Moreover, in an era of increased global and domestic security concerns, it is reckless to permit high-risk battery infrastructure directly above or adjacent to strategic energy assets. A situation that could become a target in times of geopolitical tension or conflict. I would remind everyone that this country has been and is regularly threatened by a major power. The proposed development raises serious concerns regarding emergency response capabilities and fire safety, particularly in relation to lithium-ion battery fires. These types of fires are highly complex and hazardous, often involving thermal runaway, toxic gas emissions, and the potential for rapid escalation. They require specialist firefighting techniques, including prolonged cooling with large volumes of water and the use of specific suppression agents. It is well known that [ORGANIZATION] currently lacks the specialist training, equipment, and resources necessary to manage lithium-ion battery fires effectively. These incidents are not comparable to conventional fires and demand a coordinated response involving hazardous materials, teams and continuous access to a high-capacity water supply - something that is not available on-site, regardless of the size of the proposed BESS water storage system. As above I contacted [ORGANIZATION] regarding this application, and they reported that they were not aware of any such application and that such an application would present them with serious challenges. Furthermore, the proposed catchment pond is inadequate for managing runoff from a major fire event. Of even greater concern is its proposed location, on the side of a hilltop (skyline), which would significantly increase the velocity of water runoff during an emergency, reducing the effectiveness of containment and increasing the risk of uncontrolled discharge. In the event of overflow, the runoff could carry contaminated water containing heavy metals, electrolytes, and toxic combustion by-products into nearby watercourses. This poses a serious threat to groundwater quality, local ecosystems, and marine environments. The presence of a burn on the opposite side of the road provides a direct hydrological pathway for these pollutants to reach the sea, thereby compounding the environmental risk. Given the topography and the nature of potential contaminants, a comprehensive hydrological (as mentioned above) and environmental risk assessment must be conducted. This should include detailed modelling of runoff scenarios, containment capacity, and mitigation measures to prevent pollution of surrounding land and water bodies. Given these factors, it is imperative that a comprehensive Fire Safety and Emergency Response Plan be developed in consultation with local fire services, environmental agencies, and hazardous materials experts and shared with local residents. This plan must include: 1. A full risk assessment of fire scenarios. 2. Specialist training and equipment for local responders. 3. On-site infrastructure capable of supporting extended firefighting operations. 4. Containment systems to prevent environmental contamination. Without these critical safeguards, the proposed development poses an unacceptable risk to public safety and the environment. Flexpower’s repeated claims that “BESS-related fires are rare” and that “fire suppression technology has advanced” do not replace or negate the need for independent, site-specific safety and environmental risk assessments particularly for a high-risk industrial project of this scale, sited within close proximity to homes, livestock, private water supplies, and live pipelines. Flexpower’s reliance on static water tanks, a catchment pond, and a sluice gate may sound technically adequate on paper, but again, these are generic, template-driven features applied without any genuine engagement with: In addition, no information has been provided as to whether the firefighting water supply is winterised or heated to prevent freezing during colder months. In rural [PLACE], where freezing temperatures are common, this is not a minor detail, it is a life-safety issue. If the static tanks are frozen during a fire event, then the stated water availability becomes meaningless. Has this been considered, and has the fire service even verified its viability in winter conditions? Let me be clear: the statement “we do not have an environmental risk assessment” is not a minor oversight, it is a major regulatory failure. Without this, the planning authority, emergency services, environmental agencies, and the public have no verifiable way to assess the cumulative and long-term risks of this proposal. To date, no plans have been presented for: 1. Road upgrades to accommodate heavy goods vehicles (HGVs) 2. Ongoing maintenance during the construction phase 3. Post-construction repairs to address damage caused by construction traffic According to the UK Highway Code and the Road Vehicles (Construction and Use) Regulations 1986, there are strict limits on the maximum permissible weights for vehicles using public roads. Many B-roads are not rated for the maximum axle loads of construction lorries, which can exceed 32 to 44 tonnes depending on configuration. Using such vehicles on unsuitable roads can lead to structural damage, increased safety risks, and long-term degradation of the local transport network. This lack of planning and foresight is unacceptable, particularly given the potential for disruption to local residents, emergency access, and agricultural operations. A comprehensive transport and logistics plan must be submitted, including: 1. A full road condition survey before and after construction 2. Traffic impact assessments 3. Mitigation measures such as designated haul routes, vehicle weight restrictions, and scheduled maintenance. It is completely unacceptable to withhold critical safety information from the public under the guise of confidentiality, particularly when it relates to the serious risks associated with a proposed BESS (Battery Energy Storage System) site. If this project is to progress, the public must be informed without delay about how emergency notifications will be issued, what immediate actions residents are expected to take in the event of a system failure, and how local impacts will be managed. Are we to receive evacuation orders in the middle of the night without prior warning or preparation? What provisions exist for farmers managing livestock, and is it acceptable that local wildlife be treated as collateral damage? These questions cannot be ignored. I therefore demand a formal, face-to-face consultation with Scottish Parliament ministers to directly address these critical issues and to strongly oppose and shut down this project. Furthermore, the confidentiality of the ERP, with only essential information shared with those potentially impacted, limits the ability of residents to have confidence that emergency procedures are comprehensive, appropriate, and communicated effectively. Given the nature of the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) site and potential risks involved, it is vital that a clear, accessible summary or draft of the ERP be made available for public review prior to granting permission. This would demonstrate a commitment to transparency and community safety. I would also like to request clarification on emergency preparedness during the construction phase, which carries its own set of risks and requires robust planning and communication with the local community.
