I am writing to formally raise objections to the Section 36 planning application put forward by [ORGANIZATION] ([ORGANIZATION]) for the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development located to the north of [PLACE], near [PLACE]. The development aims to establish a 100 MW lithium-ion battery facility on presently undeveloped agricultural land, along with associated transformers, fencing, lighting, fire infrastructure, and drainage. My objection is centred on the significant risks that the development poses to public safety, the local environment, and community well-being. These risks include fire and contamination hazards, potential damage to biodiversity, landscape deterioration, traffic disruption, and inadequate emergency planning. The planning documents submitted by the developer lack the necessary technical detail, safety strategy, and adherence to policies required for responsible energy development of this magnitude. Each section of this objection highlights specific reasons why the application does not meet the criteria set out in the National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4) and the [PLACE] Local Development Plan. These reasons include shortcomings in consultation, the absence of ecological safeguards, failure to conduct a cumulative impact assessment, and neglect in addressing the complete lifecycle of hazardous infrastructure. I strongly urge the planning authority to reject this application in its entirety. Deficiencies in the Consultation Process The applicant's engagement with the local community was deemed as limited and insufficient. Only two public drop-in sessions were conducted, with notably low attendance and minimal feedback. Many residents did not receive adequate notice or subsequent communication. Crucial design details, such as fire safety systems, access routes, and layout alterations, were not disclosed during the consultation period. There is no documentation of substantial interaction with emergency services or public health authorities, and no further consultation took place once major aspects of the proposal were finalised. Essential safety and environmental issues highlighted by the community remain unaddressed. This approach falls short of meeting the requirements set out in National Planning Framework 4 Policy 12, which stipulates early and effective community engagement in significant infrastructure projects. It also does not comply with the UK's commitments under the Aarhus Convention, which ensures public access to environmental information and involvement in decision-making processes. The consultation procedure failed to ensure transparency, neglected to engage affected stakeholders adequately, and prevented the public from fully assessing or responding to the development's risks. As a result, it is considered a significant deficiency in the application. Environmental and Ecological Impact The development site is located in a rural farmland area surrounded by hedgerows, marshy grassland, and drainage features that provide support to wildlife and contribute to the local ecological network. It is positioned near the [PLACE] and encompasses habitats recognised for their biodiversity value, such as waterlogged ground and species-rich grass margins. However, the ecological assessments that have been submitted are incomplete and do not include essential seasonal survey data. No assessments have been carried out for bat roosts, dusk or dawn emergence surveys, monitoring of badger activity, or studies on amphibians during the appropriate seasons. These are standard requirements outlined in the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 and the Nature Conservation (Scotland) Act 2004 when development impacts potential habitats. The absence of this data means the developer cannot accurately claim to comprehend or mitigate the ecological risks associated with the proposal. The site is set to be significantly covered with containerised battery units, impermeable roads, fencing, firewater tanks, and related infrastructure, leading to the permanent loss of semi-natural grassland and the fragmentation of hedgerow corridors. This will eliminate foraging and commuting routes for protected species like bats and birds. While the planting of replacement hedgerows is presented as a biodiversity benefit, no Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG) calculation has been provided, and there is no proposed habitat management or monitoring plan. According to National Planning Framework 4 Policy 3, developments must enhance biodiversity and prevent harm to existing natural assets. Similarly, [PLACE] Local Development Plan Policy PV7 mandates protection and mitigation for priority habitats and species. Unfortunately, this proposal fails to meet either standard. The lack of survey efforts, habitat loss, and speculative mitigation render it environmentally unsound and pose a risk of long-term ecological degradation in an area that supports farmland species and local biodiversity. Risk of Battery Failures and Fire Hazards The proposed Battery Energy Storage System would utilise lithium-ion technology, known for its significant and well-documented fire and explosion risks stemming from the potential of thermal runaway. These fires are intense, self-sustaining, and emit highly toxic smoke and contaminated firewater. Past incidents at similar BESS sites worldwide have led to prolonged fires, public health advisories, and emergency evacuations. Despite these recognised hazards, the application lacks a formal Fire Safety Management Plan. While the site plans include a firewater pump house and tank, there is no indication of capacity modelling, hazard containment design, or coordination with the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service ([ORGANIZATION]). The Pre-Application Consultation report reveals that [ORGANIZATION] did not respond to the applicant’s email inquiry, with no subsequent follow-up or evidence of collaborative emergency planning. Moreover, the application overlooks crucial aspects such as fire scenario modelling, toxic plume dispersion assessments, emergency access planning for responders, community evacuation protocols, and firewater containment and pollution control measures. In the event of a fire, suppression water could become contaminated with lithium salts, acid gases, heavy metals, and fine particulates. Without engineered containment systems like bunds, spill basins, or diversion channels, this runoff could endanger the surrounding land, drains, and the [PLACE], particularly given the sloping terrain of the site and its proximity to surface water features. This absence of fire safety and environmental protection planning violates NPF4 Policy 23, which mandates development to protect human health and manage risks. It also disregards national guidance from the National Fire Chiefs Council ([ORGANIZATION]), which categorises BESS sites as high-hazard and calls for site-specific risk management. Without robust fire planning, this development poses an unacceptable risk to local residents, first responders, and the environment. Proximity to [PLACE] – Water Contamination Risk The development site is situated next to the [PLACE], a small yet ecologically significant watercourse running along the southern boundary of the proposed Battery Energy Storage System. The land slopes downwards towards the burn, which raises concerns about the potential for surface runoff, pollutants, or firewater from the development to enter the waterway. During regular operations, the site is expected to generate runoff from paved areas and electrical infrastructure, carrying oils, chemicals, and particulate matter. Of greater concern is the risk of a battery fire, which could lead to the production of large quantities of contaminated firewater. This firewater typically contains hazardous compounds like lithium, cobalt, nickel, and hydrogen fluoride, posing acute dangers to aquatic life and downstream land users. While the application includes a firewater tank and a basic drainage plan, it lacks a specific strategy for containing firewater or spills. There are no bunds, interceptor tanks, or environmental protection measures outlined to prevent polluted water from reaching the [PLACE]. The Flood Risk Assessment also notes that parts of the site are within or close to a surface water flood zone, heightening the risk of off-site contamination during heavy rainfall or fire incidents. No hydrological modelling or pollution pathway assessment has been provided to show how the burn would be safeguarded in case of a fire, chemical spill, or drainage system failure. This absence of preventative infrastructure goes against environmental protection obligations set out in national planning policy and Scottish water regulations. Considering the potential irreversible harm that a single contamination incident could cause, coupled with the lack of credible protective measures from the applicant, the proposal poses an unacceptable risk to the local water environment. Failure to Collaborate with Emergency Services Despite the high-risk nature of the proposed development, there is no evidence of meaningful consultation or joint planning with emergency services. The Pre-Application Consultation Report confirms that the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service ([ORGANIZATION]) was contacted once via email but did not respond. No further action was taken to engage them, and no formal agreement or operational plan has been submitted. Battery energy storage systems require specialised emergency response procedures, as fires involving lithium-ion technology cannot be extinguished with standard methods and may reignite repeatedly. Responders need site-specific information, including containment strategies, ventilation risks, access protocols, and toxic gas exposure plans, none of which has been developed or shared. There is no evidence of collaboration with [ORGANIZATION], the [ORGANIZATION], or any local emergency planning authorities. The application includes no evacuation plan for nearby residents, no identification of exclusion zones, and no assessment of how local emergency services would safely access or control a major incident on site. This lack of preparation not only places the public and responders at risk but also contradicts key principles of safe infrastructure planning. It breaches NPF4 Policy 23, which demands that public safety be at the core of energy infrastructure decisions, and it fails to meet expectations set out in national emergency preparedness guidance for hazardous facilities. In the absence of any coordinated emergency response plan, the proposal is incomplete and cannot be responsibly approved. Landscape and Visual Impact The proposed Battery Energy Storage System is set to significantly transform the rural landscape to the north of [PLACE]. Currently an open farmland with extensive views across the surrounding countryside, the development plans include the installation of rows of metal battery containers, security fencing, lighting columns, and industrial infrastructure, resulting in a permanent and visually intrusive presence. The Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment submitted by the applicant recognises that the project would have a substantial visual impact within a 250-metre radius, remaining visible from nearby residential areas, roads, and public rights of way, including [PLACE]. Photomontages illustrate that the site would continue to be highly visible to nearby receptors, particularly to the north and northwest, even five years after completion. Furthermore, the project would introduce new sources of light pollution to an area known for its dark night skies. The proposed security lighting and motion-activated CCTV systems would operate continuously, affecting neighbouring residences and nocturnal wildlife. The absence of a lighting impact assessment and a control strategy to minimise glare, sky glow, or light spill is noted. The proposed development would alter the visual and sensory characteristics of the area from rural to industrial, impacting landscape quality, recreational value, and local identity in a lasting manner, as the changes are expected to endure for 40 years. This proposal is in conflict with National Planning Framework 4 Policy 4 and Policy 6, which emphasise the importance of developments respecting landscape character and maintaining high-quality environments. The developer has not presented sufficient evidence on how these adverse effects would be mitigated or justified. Given the unacceptable scale and permanence of the visual impact in this rural setting, it is recommended that consent for the project be withheld on this basis. Cumulative Impact The [PLACE] area has emerged as a significant hub for energy infrastructure projects, encompassing large substations, overhead transmission lines, solar developments, and numerous Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) proposals. The addition of a 17-acre BESS to the existing cluster of industrial energy assets would intensify the physical, environmental, and psychological strains on the local community. Despite the proximity of other approved or pending developments within a 1 km radius, the current application lacks a cumulative impact assessment. There is no consideration of how concurrent construction activities, noise levels, lighting, fire hazards, or traffic flow will be coordinated. This fragmented approach to development overlooks the overall implications of infrastructure saturation on the land, wildlife, and residents of [PLACE]. Local residents have expressed significant apprehensions regarding the industrialisation of the area and the combined effects of these proposals on mental well-being, safety, and environmental standards. It is imperative for the planning authority to evaluate not only the repercussions of this individual project but also its contribution to a broader trend of encroachment and disturbance. Policy 29 of the National Planning Framework 4 clearly stipulates the necessity of accounting for cumulative effects in decision-making processes. The absence of such an assessment represents a crucial oversight. Sanctioning this development without strategic supervision would reinforce an inequitable and unsustainable strain on this rural community. Noise Pollution Battery Energy Storage Systems produce continuous operational noise from inverters, transformers, and cooling equipment. This noise, which is low-frequency, can easily travel in open rural areas, particularly at night when ambient noise levels are low. Over a 40-year period, nearby homes could be subjected to a constant mechanical hum. The Noise Impact Assessment provided with the application is deemed inadequate as it lacks a comprehensive baseline survey of current background noise, detailed modelling of low- frequency sound, and an assessment of nighttime impacts on residents and wildlife. These shortcomings are worrying, especially in light of previous noise complaints linked to the neighbouring [PLACE]. Furthermore, there is no operational noise management plan, post-consent monitoring strategy, or commitment to taking corrective action if noise levels exceed acceptable limits. This deficiency leaves nearby residents vulnerable to potential disturbances. Noise pollution can have serious health consequences, including sleep disturbances, heightened stress levels, and long-term cardiovascular effects. It can also disrupt foraging and breeding behaviours in nocturnal species like bats and owls, which are found in the vicinity. The Alpacas at [PLACE] could also be significantly impacted as they communicate through humming. According to National Planning Framework 4 Policy 23, developments must safeguard health and wellbeing by implementing effective noise management practices. This proposal falls short of meeting this standard. The absence of reliable noise data, coupled with the likelihood of substantial disturbances, constitutes a key reason for rejecting the proposal. Increased Traffic and Infrastructure Strain The development of the BESS will necessitate approximately 900 Heavy Goods Vehicle (HGV) movements over a span of 12 months, with peak daily traffic reaching up to 15 large vehicles. These vehicles will traverse narrow, rural roads not originally intended for heavy industrial traffic, including [PLACE] and the surrounding local road network, which are currently shared by [PLACE] transport, agricultural vehicles, cyclists, and pedestrians. Despite the presence of multiple other energy projects either proposed or already in progress in the vicinity, there has been no comprehensive assessment of the cumulative traffic impact. The planning application lacks any proposed mitigation measures, such as road reinforcement, visibility enhancements, or traffic diversion plans. Furthermore, there is no outlined construction delivery schedule or strategy to avoid peak traffic hours, and no road safety assessment has been provided. The proposed development also exerts strain on [PLACE], a cherished walking and cycling route that runs near the site. The construction compound and associated access roads are anticipated to cause disruptions, visual obstructions, and potential safety risks for users. There is no provision for temporary diversions or safeguarding strategies for the path. In accordance with NPF4 Policy 13, infrastructure should be designed to minimise impacts on local networks and ensure safety for all users. Regrettably, this application falls short of meeting these standards. Without adequate transport planning, this project poses risks of road damage, heightened collision probabilities, and sustained disruptions to the community and local access rights. Waste Management and Decommissioning The planning application does not outline a clear strategy for the long-term management of hazardous waste or the safe decommissioning of the site following its 40-year operational lifespan. Throughout this period, the BESS facility will amass a significant volume of materials necessitating specialist disposal, such as lithium-ion battery modules, electronics, fire suppression systems, and contaminated infrastructure. There is no mention of waste tracking or handling procedures in the application. The applicant has not specified licensed disposal facilities capable of handling lithium-ion components, nor have they provided a plan for monitoring the chemical stability of batteries at the end of their life. This omission raises serious concerns about the safe treatment and removal of hazardous materials that could remain reactive or flammable long after deactivation. Moreover, the proposal lacks a decommissioning plan. There is no commitment to remove foundations, cabling, or underground infrastructure, nor has there been an assessment of potential soil contamination or the need for remediation. The absence of a restoration scheme or financial bond to ensure decommissioning places the responsibility for future clean-up on the landowner or the public. According to NPF4 Policy 22, energy developments must demonstrate full lifecycle responsibility, including sustainable decommissioning. This application falls short of that standard. Without a robust waste and end-of-life strategy, the risk of environmental damage and long-term neglect is unacceptably high. Security and Terrorism Risk The proposed development is situated in a small area that already accommodates a growing cluster of nationally significant energy infrastructure, such as substations, overhead lines, and other Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) projects, all linked to the wider transmission network. The concentration of these assets in one location raises serious concerns regarding national security and vulnerability to physical or cyber threats. BESS facilities are known targets for sabotage due to their ability to disrupt electricity supply and their use of flammable, reactive materials. However, the application lacks a security risk assessment, threat modelling, and evidence of consultation with Police Scotland’s Counter Terrorism Security Advisors or other relevant agencies. Although drawings show perimeter fencing and CCTV, these measures are deemed insufficient deterrents and not commensurate with the strategic importance of the site. There is no cybersecurity plan for remote monitoring systems, intrusion detection network, or emergency response procedure for malicious incidents. Given the growing national focus on infrastructure resilience, the absence of a threat analysis is a significant shortcoming. Approving this application without a comprehensive security and risk mitigation plan would introduce an unnecessary vulnerability into Scotland’s energy system and place nearby communities at an unacceptable level of risk. Community Wellbeing, Mental Health, and EMF Concerns The proposed development near [PLACE] raises significant concerns beyond physical risks and environmental impacts, particularly regarding community wellbeing and mental health. The area is already facing pressure from multiple energy projects, and the introduction of another large-scale, high-risk facility is causing stress and anxiety among residents. Real concerns about battery fires, pollution, explosions, and toxic smoke have been observed at similar sites globally, heightening fears among locals. Living near such infrastructure, which is poorly understood and regulated, can lead to persistent fear, sleep disturbances, and a loss of trust in public decision-making processes. The absence of a Health Impact Assessment with the application is worrying, as it fails to acknowledge the psychological impact of long-term proximity to a high-risk site, especially in rural areas where quality of life depends on peace, safety, and environmental stability. This omission is particularly concerning for families, elderly residents, and individuals with existing mental health conditions. Additionally, worries about potential exposure to electromagnetic fields (EMFs) from the site's electrical infrastructure, without transparent monitoring or public information, add to local unease. National Planning Framework 4 Policy 23 mandates that developments safeguard health, wellbeing, and safety, including mental health and quality of life considerations, not just physical risks. The lack of a wellbeing assessment or mitigation strategy further highlights the applicant's disregard for the local population. Summary The application in question is significantly flawed as it does not adequately address or mitigate the substantial risks associated with large-scale lithium-ion battery storage. The planning documents lack essential details concerning fire safety, pollution control, waste management, biodiversity, and community health. The consultation process was deemed inadequate, and the proposal does not adhere to the standards set by the National Planning Framework 4 or the [PLACE] Local Development Plan. If this development is approved, it would industrialise a rural landscape, compromise local wellbeing, strain emergency services, and create enduring environmental liabilities. It fails to represent responsible energy infrastructure and does not align with the public interest. Therefore, it should be rejected. Personal Comments We request a moratorium on this and all other renewables infrastructure proposals in Scotland's highlands. A pause in developments will allow time to assess and address the cumulative impact of this, and similar proposals. These are damaging communities and their environments in an unsustainable way. The human toll also involves the developing socioeconomic disaster which is witnessed in our excessively high energy bills and excessive tax hikes: this developing Scottish community-poverty scandal is due to the nationally significant government actions subsidising power companies at public expense. We are forced to pay government back for this folly of theirs. We cannot afford any further renewables developments. Stop and reassess these damaging issues. Then start to plan a way forward. Government is forgetting, in their rush, to properly devise a real workable plan for this industry. It should not be based on, and led by, power company revenue and profits.

1. Safety Concerns: Battery energy storage systems, particularly large-scale installations, have been known to present serious safety risks. In recent years, incidents involving battery fires and chemical leaks have raised concerns about the safety of these facilities. The proximity to [PLACE] would place students, staff, and the surrounding residential area at unnecessary risk in the event of an accident. The risk of fire, explosion, or hazardous material release is a major concern that cannot be overlooked. In the event of a fire involving lithium-ion batteries, such as those used in BESS, the combustion process can generate a range of toxic gases, with hydrogen fluoride being the most significant in terms of toxicity. Hydrogen fluoride is a highly toxic and corrosive substance. Exposure to concentrations as low as 1.16 milligrams per cubic meter (mg/m3) can cause irritation of the eyes and nose, with sore throat, cough, chest tightness, headache, ataxia, and confusion. Acute exposure to higher concentrations can be fatal, often due to pulmonary edema. The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) has established an Immediately Dangerous to Life or Health (IDLH) concentration for hydrogen fluoride at 30 ppm. This level is considered the maximum concentration from which one can escape within 30 minutes without experiencing irreversible health effects. The Atkins report published on the UK planning inspectorate website indicates that under standard wind conditions, HF concentrations of 30 ppm could be detected up to 240 meters from the source of a BESS fire. This suggests that in the event of a release, individuals within this radius could be exposed to life-threatening levels of HF gas. The potential for hydrogen fluoride exposure at concentrations that are immediately dangerous to life and health presents an unacceptable risk to public safety. 2. Environmental Impact: The proposed site is situated on Greenbelt land, which is designated to protect open spaces, prevent urban sprawl, and preserve biodiversity. The development of a battery storage facility would result in the loss of valuable Greenbelt land and disrupt local wildlife habitats. The environmental impact of such a facility, including potential pollution and disruption to the natural landscape, would be detrimental to the area`s ecological balance. 3. Health and Well-Being of Children, School Staff and Residents: The proximity of this facility to a [PLACE] and residential area raises significant concerns regarding the health and well-being of students and staff. The potential for exposure to electromagnetic fields (EMFs) and the associated long-term health risks is not fully understood, but it is a factor that should be carefully considered before approving the development. Children are particularly vulnerable to environmental stressors, and the potential risks posed by this facility are too great to ignore. 4. Traffic and Noise Pollution: The construction and ongoing operation of a large battery storage facility would likely generate significant traffic, leading to congestion in the area and potential safety hazards for students and pedestrians. Additionally, the noise associated with the facility`s operation and the movement of large vehicles would disrupt the learning environment and overall quality of life for those living nearby. National Planning Framework 4 underscores the need to protect residential amenity by ensuring that do not adversely affect the living conditions of nearby communities. The proposed BESS installation appears to conflict with NPF4`s commitment to protecting residential amenities. The potential negative impacts on visual amenity, noise levels, and local traffic conditions suggest that the development may not contribute to creating a sustainable and liveable environment for existing residents. 5. Alternative Locations: There are alternative sites that do not pose such risks to vulnerable populations and are not in close proximity to schools or residential areas. A more suitable location for the battery storage facility should be explored. 6. BESS Unnecessary: This BESS is totally unnecessary given that Scotland will have surpassed its Net-Zero target for battery storage by 2026 (FESV4/TEC Register), close to two years before this facility would be operational. Given this progress, the urgent need for additional energy storage systems to further reduce emissions appears redundant. The demand for grid connections for battery storage projects has surged, with proposed capacities exceeding the government’s targets. By 2030, the queue of proposed BESS projects seeking grid connections in the UK has expanded to 61 gigawatts, far surpassing the target of 27 gigawatts. This oversubscription has led to policy measures by [ORGANIZATION] and the National Energy System Operator ([ORGANIZATION]) to prioritize necessary and ready projects, potentially excluding non-viable ones. Granting consent to this development could potentially hamper a development that is actually required. A critical initiative by the National Grid called National Pathfinder 2 Project, aimed at identifying locations in Scotland that require infrastructure improvements for system stability, balancing, and resilience. This project utilised extensive data and modelling to determine where energy storage solutions, such as BESS, are necessary for maintaining grid stability and supporting renewable energy integration. As part of this process, specific regions or sites are flagged for interventions where a demonstrated need exists. However, upon reviewing the Pathfinder 2 findings, it is evident that the location proposed for this BESS development is not among the areas identified as having grid stability challenges. This omission raises concerns regarding the necessity and justification of the proposed installation at this particular site. If the National Grid has not identified this area as a priority for stability improvements, it calls into question the validity of implementing a BESS system here without any evidence of grid vulnerability. In addition to the lack of identification in the Pathfinder 2 report, I urge the ECU to consider alternative sites where there is a proven need for grid stabilization measures. It is essential that developments of this scale be carefully aligned with the national infrastructure planning objectives and based on robust data analysis that supports the deployment of energy storage systems in locations where they are truly required. 7. Nation Fire Chief Council Guidelines: The proposed development at [PLACE] only has one access route and therefore does not comply with the guidelines set out by the National Fire Chiefs Council ([ORGANIZATION]). The [ORGANIZATION] guidance specifies that developments of this scale should have at least two separate access routes for fire appliances and emergency services and a compass rose showing north and the prevailing wind direction, to ensure the safety of occupants and to allow for effective firefighting operations. It is particularly crucial to maintain an alternative route in the event one access becomes compromised due to fire or other obstructions. The lack of a secondary access could hinder the timely arrival of fire appliances and reduce the effectiveness of firefighting and evacuation efforts. This non-compliance with the NFCC's guidelines poses an unacceptable risk to [PLACE] students, staff and the wider community. As a result of feedback from the consultation events the applicants have altered the location of the access to the proposed development to minimise the impact of construction and operational traffic. In addition the applicant has increased the height of bunding around the site and increased planting of native trees. The proposed development is consistent with the National Planning Framework's (NPF4) policies on tackling climate change (Policy1), implementing net zero (Policy 2), tackling biodiversity (Policy 3), impact on local landscape (Policy 4), impact on historic assets or places (Policy 7), promotion of renewable energy development (Policy 11), mitigation of flood risk (Policy 22) as well health and safety (Policy 23) and rural development (Policy 29). In addition the development appears to be consistent with the relevant policies of the [PLACE] Local Development Plan - development in the countryside (Policy R2), Layout, Sitting and Design (Policy P1), hazardous, potential polluting developments and contaminated land (Policy P4), impact on natural heritage (Policy E1) and on landscape (Policy E2), renewable energy (policy C2) and flood risk (Policy C4). Although the application appears to be consistent with the policy framework. The Community Council has a number of concerns: 1. The applicants state that they will sign up to a decommissioning and restoration programme when the facility reaches the end of its operation life of around 40 years. This would be achieved through a suitably worded planning condition. Given the various uncertainties in business it perhaps would be better if the applicant were required to post a financial bond equivalent to the anticipated decommissioning and restoration costs.This could be used if for any reason e.g. the applicants were to sell the site or become insolvent. 2. There are 6 proposed developments of this nature in the wider [PLACE] area. We appreciate that the reasons for this is the nearby junction of two High Voltage power lines and a major electricity substation. However the [ORGANIZATION] is concerned that we are seeing the creeping industrialisation of an attractive rural area and this is occurring without any strategic policy framework being developed by the local planning authority. Perhaps [ORGANIZATION] should be looking at the cumulative impact of these (and potentially other additional) developments and setting limits on what the area can accommodate. In our view the applicant has provided all the information required to enable the Community Council to reach a view, they have also shown themselves willing to alter their plans to address the concerns of local people - increasing the height of the bund and increased tree planting to screen the development and altering the access road to alleviate local traffic. The development may bring local construction jobs but there are unlikely to be many permanent jobs created. On balance the [ORGANIZATION] recommendation is not to object to this application but to ask [PLACE] County, if they approve this application, to pursue an appropriate financial bond from the projects developers to ensure that the funding for decommissioning and restoration are available when the project reaches the end of its lifespan. The application is not competent. The application is a major application in terms of the hierarchy and, as a consequence, the requirements of Section 36B of the Town and Country Planning (Scotland) Act 1997 apply. We note from the Pre-Application Consultation Report submitted by the Applicant with the application that a number of Pre-Application Notices have been submitted to [ORGANIZATION]. This is consistent with the Applicant altering the proposals and, as a consequence, further notifications of the Council being required. There is no provision within the legislation for amendment and therefore each Notice needs to be treated on its own merits. It is understood that the third notification to the Council arose from a change in the site proposed for development. This in effect constitutes a new notification to the Council and a new requirement to carry out consultation. Appendix C of the Pre-Application Consultation Report contains the further Pre-Application Notice from the representatives on behalf of the Applicant and is dated 07/04/2025. Appendix F of the Pre-Application Consultation Report includes the Council’s response which is dated 8 April 2025. The 8 April response by the Council confirms that 12 weeks must elapse from the submission of the proposal application notice and the submission of the application. The planning application was submitted on 20 June 2025. This means that the planning application was submitted before the 12 week period had expired in terms of the response to notice of 7 April 2025. In terms of Section 39(1A) of the 1997 Act, a planning authority “must decline to determine an application for planning permission for the development of any land” if, in their opinion, there was a requirement for compliance with Section 35B and there has not been such compliance. The terms of the legislation are absolute and in those circumstances it would not be competent for the planning authority to determine this planning application.

I am writing to vehemently oppose the proposed battery energy storage facility. While acknowledging the imperative shift towards renewable energy, the selected site for this project raises profound environmental concerns that cannot be overlooked. First and foremost, the construction and operation of the facility would disrupt delicate ecosystems and wildlife habitats in our area. Our village is surrounded by pristine natural landscapes, home to diverse flora and fauna. Introducing a large-scale industrial facility threatens to fragment these habitats, disturb migratory patterns, and potentially endanger local wildlife populations. Moreover, the increased traffic and industrial activity associated with the facility's construction and ongoing operation would exacerbate air and noise pollution in our already serene environment. The idyllic atmosphere that draws residents and visitors alike would be compromised, impacting not only our quality of life but also our physical and mental well-being. Additionally, the visual intrusion of such a facility contradicts the principles of conservation that our village holds dear. Our community has worked tirelessly to preserve its historic charm and rural character, and the presence of towering battery storage units would starkly contrast with our scenic surroundings, detracting from the beauty that defines our village. Furthermore, the long-term implications of the facility on our local environment are deeply troubling. The disposal of battery components, potential leaks or spills, and the risk of fire pose significant environmental hazards that could irreversibly damage our ecosystem and compromise the health of our residents. In light of these profound environmental concerns, I urge the Planning Committee to reconsider the proposed location of the battery energy storage facility and explore alternative sites that minimize harm to our natural surroundings

The site of the proposed Battery Storage Facility shares a boundary with one of my farm Fields. The site is Grade 3.1 Prime arable agricultural land and is cropped annually and has been for many decades. The development would be visible from my farm. I wish to lodge my objection to this proposal. The proposed development is a sizeable industrial unit which would remove prime agricultural land from crop production for the next generation and more. In these uncertain times it makes no sense to sacrifice such a scarce resource in favour of an industrial unit more suited to an industrial estate or ‘brown field’ site– claimed to be ‘stand-alone’ yet also said to be Phase 1 of a 2 Phase development involving up to 300 acres of solar arrays – an inefficient form of green energy - which would gobble up more Prime arable land for the foreseeable future. This is a small rural community and the ‘wrong’ place for such venture. The Environmental Impact Assessment prepared by [ORGANIZATION] with respect to the effects of this development on the area is a copy and paste of the EIA prepared for an application that went before [ORGANIZATION] in respect of Solar Arrays on agricultural ground at [PLACE] ([APPLICATION_CODE]) as can be seen by the failure to fully ‘tweak’ the EIA to relate to [PLACE]. It is also out of date as it does not factor in the effects on this environment of the upheaval of the Seagreen Project. The applicant has not clarified how this site might be accessed. The access road is not owned or controlled by either the applicant or the site landowner and the transport plan lodged with this application is based on their assumptions that access will be permitted, as opposed to stating credible facts. Access is CRUCIAL and it is difficult to see how any such application can be granted permission to proceed without first establishing whether or not the site can actually be lawfully accessed for the purposes of this proposal. The main roads approaching the proposed site are used extensively by residents, leisure users and ‘vulnerable road users’ as specified in the updated Highway Code. In particular, [PLACE] is a single track road with poor visibility along much of it and the volume of traffic proposed during any construction of this development would endanger and severely inconvenience many of these other road users in addition to causing significant damage to the road surface and embankments. [PLACE] would not afford access from the public road to the ‘party’ access road without adjustments being permitted and carried out. The site of the proposed battery facility is located between 2 electricity transformers, both of which were struck by lightning in 2021 causing emergency situations with danger of explosion. In the event of such an incident at the proposed facility, the fact that it is to be unmanned, the remote location and the poor roads and lack of water hydrant/water pressure would impede the emergency services in tackling the incident and preventing any spread to the adjoining properties (my arable crops and the adjacent woodland). There are a number of businesses located nearby who rely on the natural state of the countryside, horse livery yards, natural burial ground etc for their business. This would impact detrimentally on them. This area is part of a ‘leisure and recreational corridor’ on the outskirts of [PLACE] that is heavily used throughout the year by residents and recreational users. The recent grant of permission for a [PLACE] and Spa with golf course, at nearby [PLACE] demonstrates this. This will, of course remove more arable land from crop production. The solar array that is proposed as Stage 2 makes a nonsense of the applicants claim that Phase 1, the battery Storage Facility is a ‘stand-alone’ development. It is a clear attempt to gain a ‘foot in the door’ by the applicant in respect of subsequently seeking permission in respect of phase 2. Solar arrays are ‘the poor relative’ in terms of energy production in Scotland given it’s climate and terrain and technology in terms of production of green energy is evolving rapidly. What a shame it would be if prime agricultural land and our community, is sacrificed for up to 40 years, to a technology that is overtaken and surpassed and becomes nothing more than a lesson to those in authority to look at the bigger picture. The decommissioning provision states that the land would be returned to agriculture as the batteries and solar arrays and their supportive structures would be removed. Would this also include the removal of all of the trees and hedges planted to screen this from public view, bearing in mind that, doubtless, wildlife will have settled in them by this time? It is hard to see how the land could be returned to agriculture and I would be very interested to know if there are any sites that have been subject to decommissioning. I respectfully request that Scottish ministers take note of the impact that such a development would have on the community and area in which I live and reject this application.

The project's inconsistency with NPF4's fundamental principles of sustainability, locally-driven decision-making, heritage preservation, and equitable rural development is evident. When considered alongside other nearby developments, such as the [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], and the [PLACE], the cumulative impact would transform the iconic [PLACE] landscape into an extensive industrialized area, irreversibly altering the local environment and the historical backdrop of [PLACE], a site of national significance. The decision to approve an industrial battery installation in such close proximity to a royal heritage site based on speculative grounds, insufficient evidence, and flawed policy interpretation is not justifiable. It also contradicts the [PLACE] Council's commitment to safeguarding the cultural and environmental richness of [PLACE]. Introducing a large-scale battery compound into a rural landscape directly undermines these planning goals and contributes to the creation of rural sacrifice zones for national energy infrastructure. Rather than attempting to address the shortcomings in the application, I urge the Reporter and Scottish Ministers to reject the [ORGANIZATION] BESS proposal entirely, in the interest of long-term public welfare and the preservation of the [PLACE] landscape and cultural heritage.

This formal objection is hereby lodged in response to planning application [APPLICATION_CODE] (Council Ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]) submitted by [ORGANIZATION] for the establishment of a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at [PLACE] within the jurisdiction of the [ORGANIZATION]. The proposed industrial development poses a threat to the historic landscape and rural character of the area. Despite the applicant's claim of "limited visibility," the BESS's location on a ridge would make it clearly visible from various vantage points, including roads frequented by locals and visitors. The peaceful, agricultural, and tourism-oriented character of the current area would be permanently altered. The lack of a clear local or national strategic framework for the placement of such developments raises concerns about why this specific rural location was chosen over brownfield or industrial alternatives. The absence of strategic siting criteria leaves rural communities in Scotland vulnerable to unplanned industrial projects that erode landscape quality and cohesion. Additionally, the potential risks to local residents and the broader community from incidents such as fires at the site have been downplayed. Of utmost concern is the impact on the setting and ambiance of [PLACE], a significant and symbolic heritage asset in Scotland. The [PLACE], a cherished retreat of the late Queen Mother, holds a special place in the Commonwealth's history. Its carefully preserved setting is integral to its historical significance. Allowing a BESS facility in close proximity risks commercializing and devaluing the legacy of this royal site. This decision carries international visibility and could have lasting repercussions on Scotland's planning credibility and tourism appeal. Landscape and Visual Impacts The location of the proposed site is situated in a vast, open landscape with expansive views over [PLACE]. Even with the addition of vegetation, this area is not conducive to accommodating large-scale energy infrastructure without significantly altering its natural character. The project would bring in elements such as rigid boundaries, metal fencing, and 6-metre structures to a tranquil rural environment, where numerous residents live just a short distance from the entrance. The adverse effects of this development are not justified or adequately mitigated in any substantial manner. Fire and Safety Risks From Battery Infrastructure Large lithium-ion battery storage systems pose well-documented fire risks. Although rare, these incidents can be severe, challenging to extinguish, and pose a threat to nearby individuals, animals, and emergency services. The developer has not provided a comprehensive emergency response plan or addressed how rural firefighting resources would handle a battery fire. Given the close proximity to woodland and peat, a fire in a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) could potentially lead to a catastrophic rural wildfire. The rural location also means that there would be a delayed emergency response time and insufficient firefighting capability. BESS installations come with specific emergency hazards, including thermal runaway, toxic gas emissions, and prolonged electrical fires. The applicant has not demonstrated how local emergency services, already under strain in remote areas, could effectively manage such incidents. With no dedicated fire station nearby, the responsibility would fall on general rural response teams that lack the necessary expertise for dealing with specialized battery-related emergencies. The risks to life, property, and the natural environment should not be overlooked for the sake of convenience. Threat to Local Wildlife and Habitats The area forms a mosaic of pasture, hedgerow, and woodland habitats that provide a home for various bird species, small mammals, and invertebrates. A comprehensive ecological evaluation for the BESS proposal has not been made available, only a rudimentary checklist likely influenced by the developer's perspective. The introduction of concrete surfacing, fencing, artificial lighting, and vegetation removal would result in an ecological void within the immediate environment. This goes against the nature-positive planning principle outlined in NPF4. No Long Term Decommissioning or Restoration Plan The applicant has not presented a definitive long-term plan for the decommissioning, restoration, or safety measures to be implemented at the conclusion of the BESS's operational lifespan. In the absence of enforceable restoration requirements and secured financial guarantees, there is a potential risk of the site being abandoned with deteriorating infrastructure, environmental contamination, or ongoing maintenance responsibilities persisting well beyond the cessation of any energy generation benefits. Summary This development is being proposed in close proximity to a small rural village without clear public benefits, contravening the principles of environmental justice and democratic planning. The Council's own guidance acknowledges "particular sensitivities in this area" that remain unresolved. The large-scale industrial project offers no discernible community advantages, such as local employment opportunities, infrastructure enhancements, or revenue sharing, thus falling short of the standards outlined in the Scottish Planning Policy (SPP) and the [PLACE] Council's Community Benefit Policy for Renewables. There has been no community referendum, vote, or significant public support for this development. Consultation efforts have been minimal and largely ineffective, disregarding clear local opposition. A project with significant implications for daily life, health, heritage, and land should not be imposed without active, genuine, and locally driven consent. This development is incongruent with the core principles of sustainability, place-based decision-making, heritage preservation, and rural fairness outlined in the National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4). It is glaringly disproportionate and unsuitable for the area. The proposed development would irrevocably change the local landscape and disrupt the historic rural setting of [PLACE], a site of national significance and symbolic value. Approving an industrial battery installation in such close proximity to a Royal heritage site based on speculation, incomplete evidence, and flawed policy application is unacceptable.

target_text: We are writing to raise our concerns and state that we formally OBJECT to the development of the above facility in the area identified. We would like to state that we are not against BESS development in general and are aware of the proposed facility at [PLACE]. Firstly, much is made in your documentation about the use of the woodlands and forestry for cover to reduce the visual impact to residents on the west side of your facility. However, residents in this area were notified a few years ago, that this woodland would be due for deforestation/reforestation shortly, and therefore unless you have updated information on this, ie who owns the wooded area and has the deforestation been cancelled, then we will have no barrier between our properties and the development. Any attempt to conceal the facility with hedges and woodland would be many years in the making (far more than ten) and for those on the East side including [PLACE], it is doubtful that the visual impact would ever be negated [We note in your documents that you state hedging would only be allowed to grow to a maximum of 3m]. In general terms it will always remain an eyesore. This will significantly alter the landscape of the area in a negative way and we feel it is unnecessary. We know the [PLACE] is a minor road but it has been getting busier with both tourists (due to the [PLACE]) and locals – some of this due to ‘Annie’s Bakery’ which is just along the road in [PLACE]. You state that there will be a minimal increase in traffic during the construction phase but then go on to say that work will generate approximately 144 vehicle movements per day. This will put a huge strain on the road network and seriously hinder traffic flow. Something like this should be sited well away from a busy road. My father part owns the road beside our homes (from the [PLACE]) which connects us to the [PLACE]. We are responsible for the upkeep which is expensive and time consuming. Even though you state that your workers will be expected to use the [PLACE] in all circumstances, we would be concerned about an increase in the use of our road even by locals who want to avoid the disruption you will cause, particularly throughout the construction phase. This will be a financial burden for us. We note efforts to reassure us that the noise pollution will be minimal. This is a very quiet area and I think it would be naive to think that residents within close proximity won’t be affected by the noise, regardless of when charging cycles occur during normal operation. The noise levels during construction are likely to be considerable when you look at the length of the construction period and working hours. There would also be disturbance due to onsite security lighting which will be a concern to anyone living in close proximity. Residents in this area are appreciative of the dark skies associated with living in a quiet and relatively undisturbed landscape. Due to the low lying nature of the site with higher ground all around this compound will be seen for miles. There are of course other risks to us as individuals and property owners as far as fire is concerned. We note the placement of water tanks, but do wonder if this would be enough when you consider the emergency services are at least 30 – 40 minutes away. In the planning application ([APPLICATION_CODE]) you state that this is “Land 700m East of Woodlands, [PLACE]. It is in fact around 450m from Woodlands and probably about 500m from [PLACE] (my father’s property) and again 550m from our own. We will be looking directly onto the development and so will our neighbours. We are at a loss to understand why an alternative site has not been chosen. This development is huge with over 350 batteries covering a stretch of several hundred metres along the road side on agricultural land. As you state the area itself is relatively flat so there is no way that a development of this size can be hidden or made to look acceptable, particularly for those on the East side who will be looking down on the plant. [We note a new house being planned beside [PLACE] which would be about 300m from your site.] Although we do not believe this second development should be anywhere near the first, if being close to the [PLACE] plant is desirable, why is this facility not being developed there, sharing access, and lessening the impact on residents? What alternatives have been looked at, and why have they been discounted? Finally, and I suspect this is of no concern to those involved, but we could be looking at a devaluation of our properties with not one but two BESS plants within walking distance. In view of the above, we believe the siting of this second BESS is misjudged and would dispute entirely your point number 7.1.3 in the Design and Access Statement, which states that this development is “sensibly located” or that it is in any way sensitive to the local landscape or its residents. As we have said above, this development will completely alter the landscape in this area and impact its residents in a negative way.

retrieved_examples.text: I am writing to object the Installation of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at land to North East of [PLACE], [APPLICATION_CODE]. Firstly, my objection in general terms is the further industrialisation of rural areas and the impact on an agricultural area that already has significant Energy infrastructure. Currently it is not possible to look in any direction from this area without seeing excessive amounts of windmills and pylons (both at land and at Sea). By approving this BESS within this area it will present a further huge impact on our natural countryside, wildlife, and prime agricultural land. If approved it will be adding more industrial infrastructure to an already industrially congested rural area and potentially setting precedence for even more future industrial development of a rural setting. This is wholly unacceptable to anyone who values our countryside and the well-being of its residents and inhabitants. Below I lay out more pointed reasons that I object this development. Each of these objections has merit individually and collectively. NON-ESSENTIAL INFASTRUCTURE We are already 3x above the 2045 target for net zero in the area so this is not a required facility. Within the [PLACE] catchment area there is currently 102MW of intermittent renewable energy generation online or awaiting construction, that could benefit from energy storage backup. Within the same area code, there is currently 130MW of BESS approved and awaiting construction; that leaves 28MW of excess energy storage capacity already due to come online. This local overcapacity (combined with national capacity well on the way to far exceed 2045 targets), demonstrates that no further BESS sites are necessary and should not be considered as 'essential infrastructure' within this area. As non-essential infrastructure, building this BESS will in fact be in conflict with any Green Agenda or Policy as we will be destroying natural land and expending resource and creating pollution on a scheme that provides Zero benefit due to overcapacity in supply. The environmental impact of manufacturing all items that would be installed at this site must be considered along with the destruction of agricultural land. Also, the civil engineering work utilising plant and equipment, transportation, construction of access roads, installation of foundations, and all building activities associated with the placement of these units which is not required. Where this BESS would connect to the grid, and the distance between this site and the grid connection, also has to be considered in the context of Non-Essential Infrastructure (See INADEQUATE LOCATION below) FLOOD CONCERNS The land is in a flood prone area as advised by SEPA. It has a high likelihood (10%) of annual surface flooding. Severe flooding and run off can regularly be witnessed in the area of the proposed BESS (as anyone who uses this road can confirm). The run off from [PLACE] and its natural reservoirs is significant, especially after periods of sustained rain, significant down pours, or during winter when the ground is frozen and impermeable. It is generally understood and accepted that these conditions will only get worse due to climate change and predicted weather patterns - so we can anticipate that flooding will be worse than historically experienced. When flooding does happen then any contamination will leak into the [PLACE] which will damage our wildlife, pollute the water and cause significant negative effects. Further consideration should also be made of the nearby area that these waters discharge into the sea: [PLACE] is an [ORGANIZATION] [PLACE] and any potential contamination could have a significant detrimental effect on the birdlife. Thermal runaway is a major health risk for our local community and wildlife. Current policies do not permit development in flood risk areas unless for essential infastructure. As previously noted, this is not essential due to the overcapacity of BESS. However, taking this out of the equation, there has been no valid points raised as to why this location is the most appropriate for linking to a substation that is miles away, taking up prime agricultural land, invading an area thriving with wildlife and surrounded by residential properties. There is also no clarity provided for this development on how this BESS would be connected to the substation - several miles of ditches and cabling adding to the Net Positive impact of a site that simply is not required? There are two main areas relating to my flood concerns. The first is natural flooding (which already occurs on a regular basis), and the second is flooding in a fire scenario where, as has been experienced elsewhere, substantial amounts of water have to be used over extended periods of time to control battery fires. INADEQUATE LOCATION It is understood the location of this application is a considerable distance from the substation that it is being connected to. Although nothing in the application states where this is actually being connected to? Therefore, a report should be commissioned into where this is being connected to and how they propose to do this without causing unjustifiable disruption and damage. At the initial consultation it was advised that it is due to be connected to [PLACE] and this location was carefully considered due to the close proximity to [PLACE]. The location of [PLACE] substation, which is now the presumed substation due to initial plans with [PLACE] not going ahead, is between 7.4 miles and 11 miles away depending on the route they take. Therefore, requiring major disruption to our local community during the digging to allow the cables to be placed in the ground. This road is a [PLACE] bus route and if closed is going to impact our children getting to [PLACE], along with locals getting to work and going about their daily routine. This route would need to cross the [PLACE] and would cause significant disruption to place significant quantities of cabling all this way along single track roads. It is hard to justify that this scheme and location has any logical or reasonable benefit in reaching net zero. Common sense determines that if this development is absolutely necessary, then a location near the substation is the right thing to avoid disruption to roads, noise pollution from diggers, air pollution and emissions from construction plant running in excess due to the distance required to be dug up, disruption to countryside digging up verges and therefore disturbing wildlife which may inhabit these areas. There is simply no logic that can reasonably support this as a reasonable chosen location for a BESS. I would request that a report is commissioned into why this is even considered an appropriate location, and seek clarity on the connection point to the grid which appears to be a substantial distance away? ACCESS ROAD CONCERNS Another major concern is that having the stated 21 vehicles and one HGV per day accessing the site on multiple occasions for an extended duration. Plus the cranes etc that will inevitably be involved with construction activity and loading and offloading of battery and associated units. The road is already in very poor condition (probably due to the flooding mentioned above). It has significant pot holes which get very deep very quickly due to wash out. What measures would be taken to ensure the condition of this road is not worsened by the increased volume of traffic during construction, and what will be done to ensure the road is returned to its current condition (or better) after construction There is no slip off from the [PLACE] to turn onto the single carriageway road and this is extremely dangerous for a car, having more and larger vehicles turning off is definitely going to increase the risk of a road traffic accident HGV type vehicles will need to come to an almost complete stop on the duel carriageway before turning off due to the tightness of the turn off. Knowing the behaviours of drivers on this fast stretch of road will most definitely cause accidents. Equally heading North and turning onto the [PLACE], the middle area at the intersection, that does not even fit a car comfortably, will be so dangerous for a HGV. Heading South will be HGVs turning into a Major Road without the benefit of any slip road to gain speed. CLOSE PROXIMITY TO HOMES & NATURAL RESOURCE This proposed area is encircled by properties who will all be directly impacted by the building of this BESS. The noise and light pollution emitted from it will be significant due to how open this area is. If it was to go on fire this would be a major concern for loss of property, loss of woodland, loss of protected wildlife, and health complications. Situated right next to woodland which is currently being replanted, and being in such a windy spot, this could get out of control very quickly. Recent fires of battery storage have proven that they will burn for days. The toxic chemicals leaked from this are a massive health concern for nearby residents and wildlife and these concerns also need to be considered as part of the Planning consideration. FIRE RISK As well established by media reports BESS carry significant risk of substantial fire. The fumes from a thermal runaway can be fatal to anyone present, including first responders. Via the Media we are also advised that such fires burn for at least a few days until it has burnt out. Given the proximity to houses this is not an acceptable scenario. The proposed plan states that there will be a pond, however, this only has enough to provide initial firefighting for 2 hours. The [ORGANIZATION] guidance states that there is no way to extinguish a BESS fire so it is difficult to understand how the pond is deemed adequate and simply increases the concern of local residents of an uncontrolled fire scenario. NOISE IMPACT The noise impact assessment needs to be reviewed and reconsidered as it appears to be inadequate and contains anomalies which are neither explained nor understood. Within the Report itself it states that the findings were considered unusual. It is also understood that the noise surveys were not carried out at all property locations adjacent to the site (i.e. [PLACE]). With these anomalies and omissions it is clear that a proper noise assessment has not been conducted and the proposer has not determined any level of suitability and acceptability. FLAWS IN DESIGN/LAND OWNERSHIP ERROR On the Planning application there is a proposed cut off ditch at the opposite site of the field to the access road. It is not clear what this entails? Clarity is required to determine what the intent is here. Also for your info and consideration it appears there are more than one land owners in this area, which conflicts with the proposal. The corner of the field closest to [PLACE] (approx. 0.5 acre in size) is actually not owned by the current landowner, as presented on the documentation, who is proposing to lease land for the BESS development. Therefore the proposer is misrepresenting the ownership and right to lease the land. It is likely that if this development is given the go ahead, and that area above is impacted, then legal issues could arise as ownership of lands has not been truly represented in the application? PRIME AGRICULTURAL LAND This field is currently farmed and is prime agricultural land. Once this site is changed to cater for a BESS, it is stated it will be returned to its natural farming state after use. Consideration needs to be taken as to the validity of this statement as it is not understood, or explained, how they would get this back to it's natural farming state once un-natural and harmful chemicals and construction materials had been present (especially in the aftermath of a fire scenario). VISUAL IMPACT As stated in the application the development will present a moderate to major visual impact on [PLACE]. That is not an acceptable situation for the residents, nor should it be for the decision makers within the Planning Dept. This rural area is already heavily congested with large amounts of Masts and windmills. RISK TO SPECIES The local area is home to pine marten, common toad, European water vole, and two species of owl. By allowing this BESS we would be disturbing and damaging the natural habitat of species that we should be trying to protect. OTHER SIGNIFICANT CONSIDERATION Although the following may not be wholly relevant to this particular Planning Application it cannot go un-noted that the entire concept of BESS Development is very poorly considered, fundamentally flawed, and wholly inadequate to the best interest of the country as a whole. There appears to be no consolidated Plan or consideration as to where and how many BESS are being built, and these things are becoming so numerous that they are having a detrimental impact on rural areas. I have no doubt that at a point in the future this whole topic will become a source of National shame and scandal in the way it is being handled by both National Government and Local Councils. BESS developments are not adequately controlled and are being allowed to be developed in existing agricultural areas and destroying the natural footprint of this land, industrialising rural areas. The huge and unrealistic money being paid for the BESS developers to lease this land is many many times more than the actual value of the land. The BESS sites are often located miles from the asset they will connect to, thus introducing further excessive infrastructure and destruction to achieve connection to the Network and generating significant costs that would not normally be regarded as economical. All these costs will have to be recovered and it will be the consumers who have to face the bill. Once the general public realise what is going on and are faced with large bills to pay for the excessive expenditure of these developments I imagine the roof will come off, and the decision makers such as yourselves who facilitated and approved this will be held accountable. Why can BESS units not be located at existing sites, such as within the footprint of existing windmills, where infrastructure has already been installed and exists - thus significantly reducing the cost and the damage to existing green spaces. I would appreciate these points to be put forward for objection.

It also states that change of use from agriculture to a BESS site would be 'apparent locally'. The justification of the location of this proposed BESS site is that it is adjacent to the substation. The visual impact and the change of use from agriculture to industry will be evident to local residents, visitors and people from the village who use the area recreationally. FIRE It is not possible to extinguish a lithium-ion battery fire. Battery fires burn out over hours or days. There is no emergency plan shown for the residents who live adjacent to the site. When operational, the site will be unmanned located in a rural setting. Has the fire service been consulted for an Emergency Response Plan? The area is regularly snowed in during the winter months, who will manage the roadways and keep them clear for emergency response vehicles if needed. FIRE SUPPRESSION WATER AND RISK TO FLOODING Water used to suppress a fire will be highly contaminated. If this water gets into the local water table that is not acceptable - residents all have private water supplies, and there is a burn that runs directly into [PLACE]. INFRASTRUCTURE During construction, this will cause major disruption on single track roads. There is no mention of the impact on domestic residences with increased heavy traffic. The road infrastructure is not built for transporting these large vehicles/components, all roads to and from the site are narrow winding roads. Who will maintain the roadways for potholes and damage? Has traffic impact studies been done for the adjacent villages of [PLACE]/[PLACE]? These roads are used daily by people walking and cycling. ENVIRONMENT/ECOLOGY The planning documents indicate there are 4 badger setts within the [PLACE]. Has the Badger's Trust been consulted? Has [ORGANIZATION] been consulted about the bird life? REHABILITATION Do we have any guarantees that the land will be returned to its original state at the end of project? We have seen no reports on soil sampling, microbiological content of the soil or any information relating to the current state of the soil.
