IMPACT ON THE HEALTH OF THE COMMUNITY This will have a negative impact on people's health (physical and mental) this is not being considered. Residents in [PLACE] and the surrounding areas have had construction noise and traffic from the substation, grid stability facility and BESS sites for the last 5 years. Development has greatly contributed to anxiety, stress and the general wellbeing of residents in the area. The impact is not just on adjacent residents; the people who live in the surrounding villages and countryside use [PLACE] as a recreational place to walk, cycle, ride horses and generally enjoy the countryside. What will happen with heavy traffic, noise and loss of this amenity? Community Benefits There is no mention of community benefit in the planning documents. Speaking with the developers at public meetings, their representatives said there is none in their plans. Why is this the case?

I would like to lodge objections to the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) Development at [PLACE] for the following reasons: 1. Increased risk of traffic accidents due to access to the proposed site being from the [PLACE] which has a 50mph speed limit and is on a blind bend. 2. Location is next to [PLACE] which is often subject to fire raising. High risk of any fire raising at the Scrap Yard adversely affecting the BESS Development and increasing the risk of it going on fire. 3. BESS is relatively new technology and statistics to date prove that there is a high risk of such developments going on fire. This will become more prevalent as the batteries get older. There is not enough proof that siting a BESS near residential housing will not cause any adverse effects to residents in the future. 4. Containment of any fire would require significant amounts of water. It would also be dependent on the availability and response time of the fire brigade getting to site as systems in place at the BESS would not contain a fire for long. Water used to extinguish such a fire would be contaminated and would most likely run downhill and into the [PLACE]. This would impact the wildlife in the area and contaminate the River thus affecting wildlife etc downstream and into the mouth of the North Sea. 5. The proposed development is less than 50 meters from residential housing. Any thermal runaway would cause an unacceptable risk to people living in the [PLACE] area. Toxic fumes and hydrofluoric acid in the air would be life threatening. What are the proposals for evacuating the surrounding area in the event of this happening? 6. Disposal of the batteries are a concern as they will land up in landfill with leakage causing detrimental damage to the earth which in turn will affect wildlife, livestock and crops. This negates the very idea of battery storge being "green" and good for the environment. 7. A further application has been made for another company to build a bigger BESS less than 500m from this site. There must be a lot of money to be made from this type of business! What philanthropic initiatives do the companies proposing building a BESS have to help the local community?

We wish to object to the erection of the BESS development on land at [PLACE] for the following reasons: 1. Increased risk of road traffic collisions for vehicles entering and leaving the proposed development (50 mph road). NOTE: Many vehicles drive at speeds far in excess of this. 2. The development will be very close to housing - particularly houses in [PLACE] at approx 50m range - which, in the event of an explosion and fire and subsequent release of toxic fumes, is far too close. The most hazardous gases released from lithium-ion batteries to air is Hydrofluoric acid. Inhalation of a just a few ppm of HF can have serious toxic effects. It readily penetrates the skin and accidental dermal exposure has caused death in humans. This risk is unacceptable. 3. Disruption to surrounding area during hook-up to the national grid. 4. Environment disruption to local area: Lithium-ion batteries have a limited life-span and their disposal is a serious problem. The toxic metals contained in them can contaminate water supplies and ecosystems if they leach out of landfill sites. 5. Fire raising and vandalism is a fairly common occurrence at the [PLACE] which is in very close proximity to [PLACE] - clearly, this behaviour creates further risk to the BESS. 6. There are many hazards associated with lithium-ion battery storage: Inadequate temperature control within the containers can lead to thermal runaway; a chain reaction resulting from a damaged battery releasing heat with risk of fire, explosion and release of highly toxic gases. Clearly, this presents risk to the safety and health of nearby residents. 7. Risk associated with failure of remotely operated control system, slowing down emergency response. 8. Scientific papers state repeatedly that the research area of lithium-ion battery toxic gas emissions needs considerable more attention to mitigate the associated risks. Until these risks have been robustly mitigated, the location of BESS facilities should be restricted to areas far from dwellings and other highly populated areas, thus reducing the risk to as low as reasonably practical. 9. There are serious difficulties associated with extinguishing lithium-ion battery fires. The 2020 BESS fire in [PLACE] took over 30hrs to extinguish. Fires can re-start hours or even days after they have initially been extinguished. There have been over 65 BESS fires worldwide since 2017 ([LINK]) - this does not include fires that occurred in transit. 10. Noise level: We understand that the developer intends to erect a noise suppression (acoustic) fence as there will be a level of background noise from the air conditioning system within the BESS containers. However, sound is omnidirectional so unless the whole storage facility was enclosed the noise level will not be adequately reduced. The tonal buzzing and humming resulting from the high voltage electrical equipment onsite will be offensive to people living nearby. 11. Re-sale of housing in [PLACE] would be adversely affected. Many people would not entertain the thought of buying a house beside a 49 MW BESS for all the reasons listed above.

I am writing to formally object to the [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage Project No. [APPLICATION_CODE]. As a community we have accepted the need for some development in our area as part of the transition to renewable energy. We did not object to the extension of [PLACE], nor to the first three applications for BESS development namely [ORGANIZATION], [ORGANIZATION] and [ORGANIZATION]. These three applications have now been granted whereby over 80 acres of our prime agricultural land will be lost and the environment around [PLACE] industrialised from rural countryside. My understanding is that National Planning Framework 4 addresses the need for Cumulative Impact to be considered. This development, if approved, would be in a field adjacent to the [ORGANIZATION] development which has already been approved and close to the other developments mentioned above. Further development in this area will change our environment out of all recognition. I object to the development on the basis that it would not be for essential infrastructure and as such would not be permitted by NPF4 on prime agricultural land. [ORGANIZATION] has identified the total requirement for battery storage across the UK and divided this into regions. The region concerned in this development is [PLACE] where the quota is 3.9GW. At this time there is 1.6GW in operation with a further 7.6GW with planning consent. There is therefore no justification for further planning permissions to be granted for BESS in our area. Our community has provided a clear mandate to our Community Council to oppose all further BESS development in our area. That mandate is reflected in our Place Plan which has been registered with [ORGANIZATION]. I have lived and worked in this area for over 24 years and during that time I have enjoyed the peace, tranquility and unspoilt countryside in this beautiful part of the Scottish Borders. I have no wish to live near to an industrial site and this development will totally destroy my lifestyle, cause my family and I much stress, worry and anxiety for not only our future health, wellbeing and safety but also for that of our community. The light and noise level of the development is also of major concern. I am extremely concerned about the environmental impact as well as the risks due to fire pollution. Having this development within our local community will detract from the future marketability of our properties. There are already three BESS developments that have been approved within the local community so to accept more BESS sites will change the character and demeanour of this area. Our community should not be paying a higher price in terms of local amenity than other communities across Scotland. There should be no further developments within this locality other than the three BESS developments that have already been approved immediately adjacent to [PLACE] Sub-Station.

target_text: This formal objection is hereby lodged in response to planning application [APPLICATION_CODE] (Council Ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]) submitted by [ORGANIZATION] for the establishment of a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at [PLACE] within the jurisdiction of the [ORGANIZATION]. This proposed industrial development poses a threat to the historic landscape and rural character of the area. Despite claims of "limited visibility," the BESS's location on a ridge would make it clearly visible from various vantage points, including roads frequented by locals and visitors. The current tranquil, agricultural, and tourist-oriented character of the area would be irreversibly altered by this development. Furthermore, the BESS is being proposed without a clear local or national strategic framework dictating suitable locations for such installations. The lack of rationale for choosing this rural site over brownfield or industrial alternatives raises concerns about the potential for ad hoc industrial proposals to compromise landscape quality and community cohesion across rural Scotland. Additionally, the potential risks to local residents and the wider community from incidents such as fires at the site have been downplayed. Of utmost concern is the impact of this development on the setting and experience of [PLACE], a significant and symbolic heritage asset in Scotland. The Castle, once a cherished retreat of the late Queen Mother, holds landmark status within the Commonwealth and has had its setting carefully preserved for decades. Allowing a BESS facility in close proximity risks commercializing and devaluing the legacy of this royal site. The decision regarding this development carries international visibility and could have long-term reputational implications for Scotland's planning integrity and tourism image. Landscape and Visual Impacts The proposed site is situated in a vast, open landscape with expansive views across [PLACE]. Even with the addition of vegetation, this area is not conducive to accommodating large-scale energy infrastructure without significantly altering its natural character. The project would introduce stark elements such as metal fencing and 6-metre structures into a tranquil rural environment, where many residents reside just a short distance from the entrance. The resulting impact is neither justified nor adequately mitigated. Community Consultation and Consent Process Residents and community groups in the local area were not adequately engaged in the decision-making process concerning the BESS proposal prior to it reaching the consent stage. The consultations were limited in scope, poorly publicised, and not integrated with other relevant developments in the vicinity. The community directly affected by the proposal should have a genuine opportunity to voice their opinions on whether industrial energy infrastructure is suitable for their surroundings. The application for the BESS project has circumvented the local planning procedures by directly approaching the Scottish Government’s Energy Consents Unit. This approach undermines the ability of communities to influence the outcome of a project that will directly impact their lives. It is essential that developments of such significance to the local area involve meaningful engagement with the community, rather than being treated as mere addendums to energy infrastructure projects. Cultural Heritage - The [PLACE] The [PLACE] stands as a Category A Listed Building, a significant royal residence, and a beloved tourist destination. It holds a central position in Caithness’s cultural heritage. The proposed introduction of a high-security, fenced industrial site near the Castle is concerning as it could detract from the historical importance of this royal location. The developer's assurances of no negative impact are speculative rather than based on concrete evidence. The Castle's views, serenity, and symbolic value are integral to its national importance, and these would be compromised by the proximity of an industrial battery site just 1.5km away. Such an unsuitable neighbour would diminish the stature of one of Scotland's most iconic heritage sites. The industrial development would be visible from various vantage points around [PLACE], including upper windows and approach paths. The developer's claim that trees and hedgerows will shield the site remains unsubstantiated. Given the flat, open, coastal landscape, the battery compound with its fencing and transformers would disrupt the rural expanse and historic vistas that define the essence of the area. The Heritage Impact Assessment (HIA) was carried out by the developer and lacks independence. It acknowledges the inability to access the Castle and its grounds for a thorough evaluation during the 2023 assessment. Consequently, conclusions regarding visibility and impact rely on outdated information from 2022 and general assumptions. Crucial viewpoints, such as those from the Castle's upper levels and gardens, have not been adequately considered. Any development affecting a royal heritage site should not be based on conjecture. The [PLACE] project is not an isolated venture but part of a cluster of energy initiatives in the vicinity, including the [PLACE], the [PLACE], the [PLACE], [PLACE], and the proposed [PLACE]. Together, these projects contribute to the encroaching industrialization of the Castle of Mey's rural environs. The developer has neglected to address how these combined projects erode the historical setting and character of the broader landscape, contravening NPF4 Policy 7(a). The developer's proposed mitigation of tree planting falls short of what is required for such a nationally significant location. No alternative sites have been explored, and no design adjustments have been suggested to lessen the development's visual or cultural impact. This disregard for both national planning policy and [ORGANIZATION] guidance, which emphasize the avoidance rather than concealment of harm, is unacceptable. This development fails to adhere to key policies outlined in the National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4) and the Historic Environment Policy for Scotland (HEPS). These policies mandate developers to safeguard the character and surroundings of listed buildings, preserve the cultural importance of designed landscapes, minimize harm to historic assets, and consider cumulative effects with neighboring developments. In this instance, none of these obligations have been met. The project is evidently non-compliant and should not be approved. Harm to Tourism and Rural Economy [PLACE] is renowned for its expansive horizons, tranquillity, and untouched rural charm, qualities that are becoming increasingly scarce and precious. These picturesque landscapes are a magnet for hikers, cyclists, artists, and eco-tourists. The large-scale energy industrialization plans, such as the construction of battery storage facilities, threaten to erode the region's unique appeal and jeopardize the prospects of the local economy in sustainable, countryside-based tourism. Precedent For Cumulative Industrial Development Approving the [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in this location could establish a precedent for a series of energy-related projects in a historically undeveloped rural area. The proposal is situated near the [PLACE] and planned developments at [PLACE] and [PLACE]. Despite sharing the same local road access and grid infrastructure, these projects are being evaluated separately, potentially overlooking their combined impact on the rural landscape. This fragmented approach to planning compromises transparency and the long-term preservation of the landscape. The lack of a comprehensive assessment may indicate a failure to adhere to National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4), particularly in relation to Policies 1, 2, and 6, which address climate resilience, nature conservation, and cultural heritage. Fire and Safety Risks From Battery Infrastructure Large lithium-ion battery storage systems pose well-documented fire hazards. Although rare, these incidents can be severe, challenging to extinguish, and pose risks to nearby individuals, animals, and emergency responders. The developer has not provided a comprehensive emergency response plan or addressed how rural firefighting resources would handle a battery fire. Given the proximity to woodlands and peat, a fire in a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) could lead to a rural wildfire crisis. The rural location implies a delayed emergency response time and insufficient firefighting capabilities. Battery Energy Storage Systems introduce specific emergency risks like thermal runaway, toxic gas emissions, and prolonged electrical fires. The applicant has not demonstrated how local emergency services, already stretched thin in remote areas, could effectively manage such incidents. With no dedicated fire station nearby, general rural response teams would bear the responsibility, despite being ill-prepared for specialized battery-related emergencies. The potential threats to life, property, and the environment must not be overlooked for the sake of convenience. Impacts from Noise: Flooding and Site Hazards Serious concerns have been raised regarding the adequacy of the noise impact assessment presented for the proposed [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS). The assessment lacks transparency, is not tailored to the specific site conditions, and has not undergone the necessary level of independent scrutiny suitable for a development of this magnitude in a rural and heritage-sensitive location. As it stands, the assessment is deemed insufficient, and the proposal is deemed unsuitable for the site due to the inevitable acoustic impacts it would bring about. BESS facilities are known to produce continuous operational noise from various equipment components including cooling fans, HVAC systems, transformers, inverters, and fire suppression systems. Experts in the industry have pointed out that such systems can emit tonal noise and persistent background hums that are notably more intrusive than their decibel ratings would imply—especially in tranquil, rural settings where ambient noise levels are low. Tonal noise is recognised as a "penalised" noise type under BS4142:2014 ([PLACE]:2019) due to its heightened impact on residential quality of life. In serene environments like [PLACE], even moderate industrial noise can prove to be highly disruptive. The submitted report seems to disregard the importance of preserving the area's acoustic tranquillity alongside its visual charm. Furthermore, the application fails to adequately address historical surface flooding concerns. The construction of impermeable infrastructure such as container bases and access roads is likely to increase surface runoff, potentially posing a greater risk to nearby properties. This gives rise to significant worries regarding local water management and flood resilience. Road Network and Inadequate Access Infrastructure The location is accessed via narrow, unclassified rural roads that are currently under pressure due to agricultural and residential activities. The introduction of construction traffic, heavy machinery, and ongoing maintenance vehicles would likely lead to congestion, road surface deterioration, and potential risks to local residents and livestock. The applicant has not provided sufficient evidence of their plans to effectively handle the heightened traffic levels on roads that were not originally intended for industrial purposes. Threat to Local Wildlife and Habitats The area forms a mosaic of pasture, hedgerows, and woodland edges that provide a habitat for various bird species, small mammals, and invertebrates. A comprehensive ecological evaluation of the BESS project has not been made available, with only a superficial assessment conducted to meet developer requirements. The introduction of concrete surfacing, fencing, artificial lighting, and vegetation removal would result in an ecological void within the immediate environment. This goes against the nature-positive planning principle outlined in NPF4. Grid Expansion and Landscape Fragmentation The planned Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) would solidify the presence of high- voltage energy infrastructure in this area of [PLACE]. With the establishment of a battery installation, switching station, and turbines, it establishes a precedent that simplifies the case for more pylons, substations, and transmission lines. This gradual industrialization process gradually breaks up the previously cohesive rural landscape, undermining its distinctive features, compromising its environmental and cultural significance, and reducing its worth for generations to come. Absence of Environmental Impact Assessment Despite the size and characteristics of the proposed BESS, a comprehensive Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) has not been conducted. Considering the potential for substantial effects on the landscape, cultural heritage, biodiversity, noise pollution, and overall infrastructure, an EIA would typically be required for a project of this nature. The lack of a mandated EIA highlights a significant gap in environmental assessment and compromises the transparency and effectiveness of the planning procedures. No Long Term Decommissioning or Restoration Plan The applicant has not presented a definitive long-term plan for the decommissioning, restoration, or safety measures to be implemented at the conclusion of the BESS's operational lifespan. In the absence of legally binding restoration requirements and financial guarantees, there is a potential for the site to be abandoned with deteriorating infrastructure, environmental contamination, or enduring maintenance responsibilities once the energy generation ceases. Industrialisation of Prime Agricultural Land The planned BESS would be constructed on land that has been used for productive agriculture, cultivating crops such as oats for an extended period. The project's footprint, which includes transformers, fencing, road access, and associated infrastructure, would result in the irreversible loss of valuable farmland. This contravenes national planning objectives aimed at promoting sustainable land use in rural areas. Once the development is completed, the land cannot be restored for agricultural purposes or to enhance food security in the future. NPF4 Policy 1 emphasizes the importance of sustainable land use and climate resilience. Therefore, converting prime agricultural land for industrial infrastructure conflicts with this objective and jeopardizes local food security. Summary This development is being situated on the doorstep of a small rural village without a clear public benefit, contravening the principles of environmental justice and democratic planning. The Council's own guidance acknowledges "particular sensitivities in this location" that remain unresolved and unaddressed. This large-scale industrial project offers no discernible community advantages, such as local employment guarantees, infrastructure enhancements, or revenue sharing, thus falling short of the requirements outlined in the SPP (Scottish Planning Policy) and [PLACE] Council's Community Benefit Policy for Renewables. There has been no community vote, referendum, or significant public support for this development. Consultation has been merely procedural, minimal, and ineffective, with local opposition consistently disregarded. A project that impacts daily life, health, heritage, and land should not be imposed without active, positive, and locally driven consent. This development lacks such consent. It contradicts NPF4's fundamental values of sustainability, place-based decision-making, heritage preservation, and rural fairness. The project is fundamentally disproportionate and unsuitable for the area. It would irrevocably change the local landscape and the historic rural backdrop of [PLACE], a site of national and symbolic significance. Approving an industrial battery installation in such close proximity to a Royal heritage site based on speculation, incomplete evidence, and flawed policy implementation is unacceptable. Personal Comments The whole of [PLACE] and Sutherland is becoming one big industrial site, with very little benefit to the local community. Landscape, farmland and wildlife is being destroyed. Wind turbines and battery storage units are anything but "green!" Scotland already produces way more electricity than it requires, for what benefit other than having the highest electricity prices in the country! A halt needs to be called now to any more Turbines/storage units or extensions to existing sites. It is no longer about being "green" or "saving the planet", merely a money making exercise for the Power companies, who are on a win win situation and cannot lose., as they are paid to produce electricity and also paid not to produce it. Plus they know that if planning permission is refused by the [ORGANIZATION], all they have to do is appeal to the Scottish government who in 99% of cases will grant planning permission.

This cluster of projects is significantly reshaping the visual, ecological, and social landscape of the region. Despite the requirements set out in NPF4 Policy 11(e), a comprehensive Cumulative Impact Assessment (CIA) has not been submitted. The current approach of fragmented and piecemeal applications fails to provide a full picture of the combined impact of these developments. This lack of cumulative assessment is misleading decision-makers and the public, potentially allowing significant landscape changes to occur without adequate oversight, evaluation, or mitigation measures in place. Tourism and the Rural Economy The economy of [PLACE] is closely tied to its pristine landscapes, serene natural environment, and rich cultural heritage. Tourism plays a vital role in driving the economy, supporting local businesses, accommodation providers, artisanal industries, and historic sites. The region's allure stems from its rugged beauty, stunning coastal vistas, and historical landmarks, notably [PLACE], a popular destination for thousands of visitors each year. The presence of industrial energy infrastructure, like large-scale battery compounds, poses a threat to this unique charm by introducing visual clutter, noise pollution, and an industrial character that clashes with the rural tourism experience. The close proximity of the [ORGANIZATION] BESS to [PLACE] and the [PLACE] tourist route raises concerns about diminishing the quality of visitor experiences, potentially discouraging future tourism growth, and negatively impacting the delicate rural economy. This development proposal directly contradicts Scotland's objectives for sustainable tourism and the localized aspirations outlined in NPF4. Cumulative Impact The [ORGANIZATION] BESS is part of a larger complex of energy projects in the area that includes the [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], and the extensive [PLACE] marine energy infrastructure. This cluster of projects is significantly reshaping the visual, ecological, and social landscape of the region. Despite the requirements set out in NPF4 Policy 11(e), a comprehensive Cumulative Impact Assessment (CIA) has not been submitted. The current approach of fragmented and piecemeal applications fails to provide a full picture of the combined impact of these developments. This lack of cumulative assessment is misleading decision-makers and the public, potentially allowing significant landscape changes to occur without adequate oversight, evaluation, or mitigation measures in place. Environmental Impact The lack of an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) for a development of this magnitude, complexity, and sensitivity is a matter of great concern. Given the project's proximity to protected habitats, its potential interactions with existing infrastructure, and the possible impacts on water, biodiversity, heritage, landscape, and community well-being, an EIA should have been a mandatory requirement under the Town and Country Planning (Environmental Impact Assessment) (Scotland) Regulations 2017. Battery Energy Storage Systems are known to generate continuous operational noise, particularly from cooling fans, HVAC systems, transformers, inverters, and emergency fire suppression systems. Industry experts highlight that these systems can also produce constant background noise and tonal disturbances that can be more disruptive than their measured decibel levels, especially in quiet rural settings. The BS4142:2014([PLACE]:2019) standard acknowledges the increased nuisance of tonal noise in peaceful environments, a factor that has not been adequately addressed in the assessment. Additionally, there is a lack of effective measures to mitigate issues such as nighttime security lighting, disruptions during the construction phase (including dust, traffic, and noise), and the long-term impact on residential quality of life. In [PLACE], this leads to the gradual transformation of open rural landscapes into zones for energy production and storage. These developments cut through and break apart cohesive landscape character areas, disturb natural views, and diminish the unique identity that defines rural communities. The applicant has not provided a comprehensive traffic management plan, nor have they assessed the structural risks to road verges and bridges, or considered the cumulative impact of increased road use due to other local energy developments. The presence of construction traffic, heavy equipment, and future maintenance vehicles poses a risk of congestion, surface damage, and potential danger to local residents and livestock. The Drainage Impact Assessment (DIA) falls short of meeting the requirements set out in NPF4 Policy 22 (f) and [PLACE] LDP Policy 66 concerning sustainable drainage and water quality protection. While rare, these incidents can be severe, challenging to extinguish, and pose a threat to nearby individuals, animals, and emergency responders. Firstly, it lacks a clear strategy for how emergency services would handle a thermal runaway event or toxic gas release. The plan also lacks evidence of consultation with the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service, a crucial stakeholder in ensuring effective emergency response. Without specific requirements and sufficient financial resources for site restoration, there is a significant risk of prolonged neglect. Once the infrastructure is established and profitability decreases, developers may lack motivation to carry out comprehensive site cleanup, landscape rehabilitation, or environmental remediation. This situation could result in the community being left with abandoned infrastructure, potential hazards of toxic contamination, and irreversible loss of land. NPF4 emphasises the importance of circular economy principles and obligations for post-operational restoration. However, the applicant has not even met the basic criteria for ensuring decommissioning security. Summary This proposal is of an industrial scale, lacking in justification, and fundamentally incompatible with the setting of a protected royal heritage site, local land use, and the planning principles outlined in NPF4 and HEPS. There is no proven national need for this facility at this particular location. The proposal would have significant negative impacts visually, ecologically, and socially. Approving this development would essentially sacrifice a valued rural community to unplanned infrastructure expansion, damaging the integrity of one of Scotland’s most iconic landscapes and undermining national policies on heritage, nature, and rural sustainability. This large-scale project offers no tangible community benefits, such as local employment guarantees, infrastructure improvements, or revenue sharing. There is no community vote, referendum, or meaningful community support in favor of this development. A project that has such a profound impact on daily life, health, heritage, and land should not be imposed without active, positive, and locally driven consent, which this development lacks. It goes against the core values of sustainability, place-based decision-making, heritage protection, and rural equity as outlined in NPF4. Furthermore, in conjunction with other developments in the area, this project would transform the iconic [PLACE] landscape into an extensive industrialized zone, permanently altering the local landscape and the historic rural setting of [PLACE], a site of national and symbolic importance. It is unacceptable to approve an industrial battery installation in such close proximity to a Royal heritage site based on speculation, incomplete evidence, and flawed policy application. This development directly contradicts the key objectives of NPF4, which prioritize rural protection, nature restoration, climate resilience, and community well-being. It also goes against the [PLACE] Council’s goal of preserving the cultural and environmental quality of [PLACE]. Introducing a large-scale battery compound in a rural landscape undermines these planning objectives and contributes to a pattern of rural sacrifice zones for national energy infrastructure. Rather than attempting to address or rectify the shortcomings in the application, I respectfully urge the Reporter and Scottish Ministers to reject consent for the [ORGANIZATION] BESS entirely, in order to uphold the long-term public interest in safeguarding the [PLACE] landscape and cultural environment.

Considering the potential for notable effects on the environment, such as landscape, heritage, biodiversity, noise levels, and overall infrastructure impact, an EIA would typically be required for a project of this nature. The lack of a legally mandated EIA indicates a significant gap in environmental scrutiny and weakens the transparency and effectiveness of the planning process. Summary This new project is being introduced near a small rural village without any evident public benefit, going against the principles of environmental justice and democratic planning. The Council's own guidance acknowledges the "particular sensitivities in this location," which remain unaddressed. This large-scale industrial project offers no clear community advantages, such as local job opportunities, infrastructure improvements, or revenue sharing, failing to meet the criteria set out in the Scottish Planning Policy and [PLACE] Council's Community Benefit Policy for Renewables. There has been no community input through a vote, referendum, or petition supporting this development. Consultation has been minimal and unproductive, disregarding clear local opposition. Any project that impacts daily life, health, heritage, and land should not be enforced without genuine, positive, and locally-driven consent. This development lacks such consent. It goes against the core principles of sustainability, place-based decision-making, heritage preservation, and rural fairness outlined in NPF4. The project is disproportionate and unsuitable for the area, threatening to permanently change the local landscape and the historic rural surroundings of [PLACE], a site of national significance. Approving an industrial battery installation in such close proximity to a Royal heritage site based on speculation, insufficient evidence, and flawed policy implementation is unacceptable.

This formal objection is hereby lodged in response to planning application [APPLICATION_CODE] (Council Ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]) submitted by [ORGANIZATION] for the establishment of a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at [PLACE] within the jurisdiction of the [ORGANIZATION]. The proposed industrial development poses a threat to the historic landscape and rural character of the area. Despite the applicant's claim of "limited visibility," the BESS's location on a ridge would make it clearly visible from various vantage points, including roads frequented by locals and visitors. The peaceful, agricultural, and tourism-oriented character of the current area would be permanently altered. The lack of a clear local or national strategic framework for the placement of such developments raises concerns about why this specific rural location was chosen over brownfield or industrial alternatives. The absence of strategic siting criteria leaves rural communities in Scotland vulnerable to unplanned industrial projects that erode landscape quality and cohesion. Additionally, the potential risks to local residents and the broader community from incidents such as fires at the site have been downplayed. Of utmost concern is the impact on the setting and ambiance of [PLACE], a significant and symbolic heritage asset in Scotland. The [PLACE], a cherished retreat of the late Queen Mother, holds a special place in the Commonwealth's history. Its carefully preserved setting is integral to its historical significance. Allowing a BESS facility in close proximity risks commercializing and devaluing the legacy of this royal site. This decision carries international visibility and could have lasting repercussions on Scotland's planning credibility and tourism appeal. Landscape and Visual Impacts The location of the proposed site is situated in a vast, open landscape with expansive views over [PLACE]. Even with the addition of vegetation, this area is not conducive to accommodating large-scale energy infrastructure without significantly altering its natural character. The project would bring in elements such as rigid boundaries, metal fencing, and 6-metre structures to a tranquil rural environment, where numerous residents live just a short distance from the entrance. The adverse effects of this development are not justified or adequately mitigated in any substantial manner. Fire and Safety Risks From Battery Infrastructure Large lithium-ion battery storage systems pose well-documented fire risks. Although rare, these incidents can be severe, challenging to extinguish, and pose a threat to nearby individuals, animals, and emergency services. The developer has not provided a comprehensive emergency response plan or addressed how rural firefighting resources would handle a battery fire. Given the close proximity to woodland and peat, a fire in a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) could potentially lead to a catastrophic rural wildfire. The rural location also means that there would be a delayed emergency response time and insufficient firefighting capability. BESS installations come with specific emergency hazards, including thermal runaway, toxic gas emissions, and prolonged electrical fires. The applicant has not demonstrated how local emergency services, already under strain in remote areas, could effectively manage such incidents. With no dedicated fire station nearby, the responsibility would fall on general rural response teams that lack the necessary expertise for dealing with specialized battery-related emergencies. The risks to life, property, and the natural environment should not be overlooked for the sake of convenience. Threat to Local Wildlife and Habitats The area forms a mosaic of pasture, hedgerow, and woodland habitats that provide a home for various bird species, small mammals, and invertebrates. A comprehensive ecological evaluation for the BESS proposal has not been made available, only a rudimentary checklist likely influenced by the developer's perspective. The introduction of concrete surfacing, fencing, artificial lighting, and vegetation removal would result in an ecological void within the immediate environment. This goes against the nature-positive planning principle outlined in NPF4. No Long Term Decommissioning or Restoration Plan The applicant has not presented a definitive long-term plan for the decommissioning, restoration, or safety measures to be implemented at the conclusion of the BESS's operational lifespan. In the absence of enforceable restoration requirements and secured financial guarantees, there is a potential risk of the site being abandoned with deteriorating infrastructure, environmental contamination, or ongoing maintenance responsibilities persisting well beyond the cessation of any energy generation benefits. Summary This development is being proposed in close proximity to a small rural village without clear public benefits, contravening the principles of environmental justice and democratic planning. The Council's own guidance acknowledges "particular sensitivities in this area" that remain unresolved. The large-scale industrial project offers no discernible community advantages, such as local employment opportunities, infrastructure enhancements, or revenue sharing, thus falling short of the standards outlined in the Scottish Planning Policy (SPP) and the [PLACE] Council's Community Benefit Policy for Renewables. There has been no community referendum, vote, or significant public support for this development. Consultation efforts have been minimal and largely ineffective, disregarding clear local opposition. A project with significant implications for daily life, health, heritage, and land should not be imposed without active, genuine, and locally driven consent. This development is incongruent with the core principles of sustainability, place-based decision-making, heritage preservation, and rural fairness outlined in the National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4). It is glaringly disproportionate and unsuitable for the area. The proposed development would irrevocably change the local landscape and disrupt the historic rural setting of [PLACE], a site of national significance and symbolic value. Approving an industrial battery installation in such close proximity to a Royal heritage site based on speculation, incomplete evidence, and flawed policy application is unacceptable.

target_text: Cumulative impacts of [PLACE] Windfarms and Battery Energy Storage Systems on a protected bird Introduction [PLACE] is an important area for wildlife, and this is reflected in the designation of Special Protection Areas for our wintering geese and swans, and of course now incorporating a World Heritage Site. Key site for birds have been consented for industrialisation. There is no evidence of a joined-up approach that takes account of cumulative impact, both on our local human population and on our environment. There is a lack of understanding of the impacts of the developments already in place, and a paucity of monitoring, analysis and review of those site impacts cumulatively that would inform changes to planning processes and perhaps to energy policy. A key species for our county is the Greenland White-Fronted Goose, a species in alarming decline, and now globally rarer than a Polar Bear. As it happens, our two remnant flocks at [PLACE] and [PLACE] now have their feeding and roosting sites threatened by the current development at [PLACE] and a proposed one at [PLACE]. The disturbing thing is not just that local opinion (and science) has been, and continues to be, ignored – that is nothing new for remote geographical areas – but that there is no real oversight over what is going on. This is a Wind Rush, with lots of rush, and of course a Gold rush too, with little ongoing benefit for the local population. We would urge the powers-that-be to bring in a moratorium on future windfarm and battery developments in [PLACE]. This would allow time to assess the story so far rather than let the feeding frenzy to continue unabated until it is too late for [PLACE] and its environment. A family group of ‘[PLACE] white-fronted geese’ at [PLACE], [PLACE]. This field was recently drained, ploughed and re-seeded. The geese have not been seen feeding at the site since. [PERSON] [PLACE] Bird Club was founded in 1963, and has championed Greenland white-fronted geese, for many decades - what follows is a detailed exposé by CBC, of the threats to this protected species and the environment, based on robust data and over 60 years of local experience. But our objections have so far been vindicated by the subsequent evidence. This document presents a compelling case for the government to re-think its strategy. [PLACE] Bird Club would like to bring to the attention of ministers, councillors, developers and power providers, the stark issues which face the Greenland white-fronted goose in [PLACE] - for the next 40-50 years. The SPA was last designated on 13 October 2000. It consists of a suite of six lochs and a mire ([PLACE]) in [PLACE] supporting a wide diversity of aquatic and wetland vegetation. The SPA is designated for winter populations of: - Greenland white-fronted Geese (non-breeding): - Greylag Geese (non-breeding): and - Whooper Swan (non-breeding). This ‘endangered’ taxon of goose is at a crucial pinch-point in its recent history, and as custodians of the populations in northern Scotland, it is imperative that our government and its agency take full responsibility for the birds’ protection as expressed in their mission statements’ and thereby “raise the bar of global leadership”. Landscape and Visual Impacts The proposed [PLACE] Wind Farm is anticipated to have a significant and unacceptable visual and landscape impact. The project is expected to lead to the direct loss of valuable deep peat soils categorised as Class 1 and 2, which are recognised nationally for their importance in carbon storage, biodiversity, and hydrological functions. In addition to the disturbance of peatlands, the grid connection required for the wind farm would traverse through delicate habitats, including ancient woodlands and blanket bog, and in proximity to internationally designated sites such as the [PLACE] (SPA), Special Area of Conservation ([PLACE]), and National [PLACE] (NNR). Notably, colonies of pipistrelle bats within 3 kilometres of the proposed site face a heightened risk of collisions with turbine blades and pressure changes caused by rotating blades. Even the Scottish Ministers, in their screening response, have acknowledged that the project would lead to the loss and degradation of carbon-rich soils and woodlands, with adverse climate consequences. They have also identified the potential for substantial negative impacts on ancient woodlands, core paths, habitat integrity, and landscape value. In summary, the [PLACE] Wind Farm development does not represent an environmentally sustainable solution. It would compromise critical environmental resources, biodiversity, and ecosystem services in the pursuit of energy generation that could be more suitably located elsewhere. The overwhelming evidence suggests that the environmental impact of the proposed wind farm is not only significant but also untenable. Wild Land Protection The proposed [PLACE] Wind Farm is situated on the periphery of one of Scotland's most treasured and delicate wild landscapes, [PLACE]: [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE]. These areas hold national and international significance, providing a rare sense of remoteness, natural beauty, and sanctuary. Scotland's wild land is a non-renewable asset; once compromised, its original character cannot be restored. Located on a section of [PLACE], forming part of the broader [PLACE] massif, the site is known for its expansive, unspoilt vistas, absence of built structures, and profound sense of seclusion and peace. These characteristics underpin its designation as wild land and its protection under Scottish planning regulations. The erection of turbines reaching 200 metres above the landscape, coupled with permanent access routes and associated facilities, would disrupt the integrity of the area and transform its essence, affecting how future generations perceive and experience it. It does not represent essential infrastructure in this location and lacks the requisite public interest to justify the loss it would entail. Consequently, the development must be deemed fundamentally incompatible with the principles of wild land protection and rejected accordingly. Birds and Wildlife The proposed [PLACE] Wind Farm presents a significant and concerning risk to birds and wildlife, many of which are safeguarded under national and international laws. The Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) provided by the applicant, in conjunction with SSEN's evaluation for the associated grid connection, clearly highlights the presence of numerous vulnerable and red-listed species whose habitats or flight paths intersect directly with the proposed development site. These birds, several of which are already experiencing population declines, face significant risks such as turbine collisions, displacement, and habitat fragmentation. Additionally, the anticipated presence of Schedule 1 breeding species in the vicinity, including red kite, goshawk, honey buzzard, and merlin, would be further disrupted by the noise, movement, and scale of the planned infrastructure. The regular sightings of white-tailed eagles and ospreys fishing at [PLACE] and traversing the [PLACE] Wild Land Area underscore the critical importance of this location as a key raptor corridor. Furthermore, the site is situated between two significant designated areas: the [PLACE] (NNR), Special Protection Area (SPA), and Site of Special Scientific Interest ([PLACE]), and the [PLACE] to [PLACE] SPA. The proposed turbine placement falls within essential foraging and commuting zones for these species. The resulting habitat fragmentation and danger posed by rotating blades present an unmitigable level of risk that cannot be addressed through conditions or design alterations. Mammal species that inhabit the area are equally at risk, including badgers, pine martens, wildcats, and various bat species, with a significant colony of 300–400 pipistrelle bats located within 3 kilometres of the site. Pipistrelles are known to travel considerable distances to feed and are highly vulnerable to barometric pressure changes and collision hazards associated with turbine operations. The combined disturbances from construction, operation, and lighting would lead to habitat degradation and diminished reproductive success for these protected species. Of particular concern is the confirmation from SSEN's grid connection screening that the proposed route traverses irreplaceable habitats like ancient woodland and peatland. It also highlights the threat to European Protected Species (EPS) and the presence of UK Biodiversity Action Plan species such as red squirrel, pine marten, badger, and adder. The prospect of irreversible harm to protected species and the ecological balance of this delicate region is not solely a matter of planning consideration but a moral obligation. The risks posed to birds and wildlife further reinforce the argument for rejecting the proposal. Need and Justification The rationale behind the [PLACE] Wind Farm is fundamentally flawed and does not withstand scrutiny when evaluated against national energy statistics, local context, and the principles of equitable development. The [PLACE] of Scotland already make a disproportionate contribution to the nation's renewable energy generation. Electricity production in this region significantly surpasses local demand, yet residents experience some of the highest energy prices in the UK and Europe. This disparity raises significant questions about who stands to benefit from further projects like [PLACE]. The Scottish Government's target for onshore wind generation has not only been achieved but has been surpassed by a considerable margin. Current data shows that 10.3 GW is already operational, with an additional 8.1 GW in the planning stage, 5.4 GW awaiting construction, and 1.4 GW under construction. At this juncture, any new developments are not driven by local or national demand but are geared towards export, profit, and shareholder returns. This reality undermines any argument that [PLACE] is a necessary or strategically essential endeavour. While the National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4) endorses renewable energy, it does so with conditions that safeguard irreplaceable natural assets, local communities, and protected environments. The appropriate development must occur in suitable locations, and [PLACE] is not deemed as such. Permitting another industrial development here under the guise of national necessity would prioritise private developer interests over public and environmental well-being. Future energy strategies should prioritise locating generation facilities closer to areas of demand, thereby reducing the necessity for extensive and ecologically harmful transmission infrastructure. The outdated, inefficient, and environmentally damaging long-distance export model underpinning this proposal is detrimental to rural Scotland. The purported benefits, such as limited temporary employment opportunities and vague community contributions, do not outweigh the adverse impacts on local residents, wildlife, and the landscape. There is no compelling rationale for this project. The policy backing for renewables should not supersede the fundamental requirement that developments be environmentally sustainable, socially equitable, and geographically appropriate. [PLACE] fails to meet any of these criteria. Its approval would signify a significant lapse in planning integrity and policy coherence. The evidence unequivocally shows that there is neither current nor future need for this development in this location. Summary The proposal for the [PLACE] Wind Farm is deemed an unwarranted and indefensible intervention in a treasured and sensitive landscape of Scotland. It fails to adhere to both the [PLACE]-wide Local Development Plan and the National Planning Framework 4, contravening numerous policies aimed at environmental protection, community welfare, and sustainable development. From its adverse effects on the [PLACE] Special Landscape Area and [PLACE] to its potential harm to biodiversity, peatlands, tourism, and residential quality of life, this application is fundamentally incompatible with the principles and objectives that guide responsible planning practices in Scotland. Despite having been previously rejected at the same location due to its landscape impacts, this revised proposal is even more detrimental, featuring notably taller turbines and additional aviation lighting that intensify its visual impact. The existing and proposed energy infrastructure in this region already exceeds a sustainable threshold, disregarding the saturation point that has been reached and the concerns of the communities expected to bear the consequences. The rationale behind the site selection and scale of this project lacks substantive justification. The [PLACE] have played a significant role in the renewable energy transition, and any future developments must be equitable, reasonable, and situated where they will cause minimal harm. [PLACE] does not meet these criteria. It offers limited local advantages, poses considerable and lasting harm to protected landscapes and ecosystems, and exacerbates the feeling of powerlessness experienced by rural residents in the face of continuous large-scale development proposals. Given the substantial and unacceptable non-compliance with planning policies, the irreversible impact on peatlands and protected species, the adverse economic and social effects on local communities, and the significant environmental degradation involved, this application should be rejected in its entirety. The future of Scotland's [PLACE] should not be characterised by uncontrolled industrialisation, but rather by thoughtful stewardship, reverence for the environment, and planning decisions that prioritise the well-being of both people and nature.

We object for the following reasons: - We object as we do not agree that it can be concluded that there would be no adverse effects on the site integrity of the [PLACE], due to potential impacts on Greenland White-fronted Goose and Whooper Swan. These impacts include loss of feeding habitat and displacement of feeding birds, barrier effects and collision risk. Further to this, a cumulative/ in combination assessment has not been conducted for [PLACE] species. Considering all this, we are of the opinion that there is insufficient information to inform an Appropriate Assessment under the Habitat Regulations. We are concerned that the proposed development could adversely effect the Conservation Objectives of the [PLACE] and a conclusion of ‘no adverse effect on the site integrity’ of the SPA cannot be reached. The EIAR concludes that it is considered highly unlikely that roosting or feeding Whooper Swan would be displaced and effects on the conservation status of their regional population are deemed to be negligible and not significant under the EIA Regulations. For Greenland White-fronted Geese (GWFG) it is concluded (in section 8.8.30 of the EIAR) that with bird protection plan (BPP) protocols in place to avoid disturbance through the construction phase, it is considered unlikely that roosting or feeding GWFG would be displaced and effects on the conservation status of the regional population are deemed to be negligible and not significant under the EIA Regulations. However, it is important to remember that an assessment must also be made by the determining authority under the Habitat Regulations as both are SPA features. The Conservation Objectives of the SPA are: to avoid deterioration of the habitats of the qualifying species (Greenland White- fronted Goose, Greylag Goose and Whooper Swan) or significant disturbance to the qualifying species, thus ensuring that the integrity of the site is maintained; and to ensure for the qualifying species that the following are maintained in the long term: 1- Population of the species as a viable component of the site. 2- Distribution of the species within site. 3- Distribution and extent of habitats supporting the species. 4- Structure, function and supporting processes of habitats supporting the species. 5- No significant disturbance of the species. We are of the opinion that the proposed development could compromise the Conservation Objectives for the [PLACE]. This includes: - Turbine construction and operation may displace feeding Greenland White- fronted Geese and Whooper Swan as habitat which they currently use to feed would be lost to the species, Objective 4 compromised. - Turbines may create a barrier between roost sites at [PLACE] and [PLACE] to GWFG and Whooper Swan. Survey and Assessment In our scoping response, we requested that dusk and dawn focal goose roost watches were undertaken on the [PLACE] to fully inform the EIA and appreciate that the Focal Vantage Point and Nocturnal Audio Recordings have been carried out. However, we have concerns that the surveys are not adequate in informing assessment. Our concerns are: - Flight activity surveys (VPs) used a pre-design freeze site boundary, which differs from the final proposed development. - Despite [PLACE] being a component part of the SPA, and is known as a roost for Greylag Goose, Whooper Swan and historically, Greenland White-fronted Goose, no focal vantage point surveys were conducted at this location. The results of the Goose and Swan feeding distribution and winter walkover survey show how important [PLACE] is for these species. - NatureScot2 guidance states that for non-breeding wildfowl, especially geese and swans, birds should be counted “as required twice per month at roosts and/or feeding areas depending on site between August-May.” And “Two years’ survey is required unless shorter survey period has been justified.” The first year of surveys (October 2020 to March 2021) were insufficient in informing a proper assessment as both the winter walk overs and goose and swan distribution surveys were only conducted twice per month in November and February. October, December and March were only surveyed once, and January was not surveyed at all. - In 2020/2021 three of the Goose and Swan distribution surveys occurred directly after the Winter Walkover surveys, the disturbance caused by this may have impacted results. - This first year of surveys, as well as being insufficient in scope is now also out of date. A second year of robust survey effort would be required to fully understand risk to this SPA. Greenland White-fronted Geese Greenland White-fronted Goose (GWFG) are a red-listed Bird of Conservation Concern and an Annex 1 species of international conservation importance. The entire world population of the GWFG breeds in Greenland and winters in Ireland and the United Kingdom with over-wintering GWFG are a qualifying feature of the [PLACE]. The infrastructure of the proposed development would be approximately 1.1km from the SPA, within connectivity distance for GWFG3 (i.e., within the 5- 8km foraging range from night roosts during the winter season), therefore GWFG roosting or feeding in or around the application site can be assumed to part of the SPA population. The GWFG has shown significant declines in its small wintering population since the 1990s and during recent years the loss of some local populations have caused a retraction of its traditional range. The GWFG returns to the same areas to winter each year and population of birds in the area local to the proposed development is known as the [PLACE] flock. The [PLACE] flock is extremely small with a 2021/2022 census maximum count of 155 birds4. The maximum winter count in 2022 was recorded as only 130 birds5. As surveys undertaken for this application recorded a flock count of 131 in December 2022 (Section 8.6.12 of EIAR) at [PLACE], this can be assumed to be most of the population that year. This estimated 155 birds is a decline from 180 birds in 2020. This population if particularly vulnerable to disturbance and change of land use due to its small size and site faithfulness. A population viability modelling study commissioned 2 [LINK] 3 [LINK] 4 REPORT OF THE 2021/22 INTERNATIONAL CENSUS OF GREENLAND WHITE-FRONTED GEESE 5 [LINK] by NatureScot6 found that any additional mortality within the [PLACE] population could have a catastrophic effect on the future of this species in [PLACE]. Collision with turbines is also a potential significant impact, as the tendency for geese to fly in groups means that if a collision does occur, the event is likely to kill more than one bird, which could have a devastating impact on such a small population. Habitat loss, disturbance and displacement We do not have confidence in the conclusion in Section 8.8.30 of the EIAR which states that, “it is considered unlikely that roosting or feeding Greenland White-fronted Geese would be displaced and effects on the conservation status of the regional population are deemed to be negligible and not significant under the EIA Regulations.” We are concerned that permanent displacement could occur due to the loss of foraging habitat resulting from the location of infrastructure within areas the species use for feeding. Due to the highly threatened nature of GWFG, a precautionary approach should be taken. The results of the surveys carried out for the application show that GWFG use the Application Site. It is stated in Section 8.6.12 of the EIAR that in November 2022 up to 77 birds were recorded feeding on site at Toftranald. This was approximately 50% of the [PLACE] population in 2022 (155 birds). We disagree with Sections 8.8.24 and 8.8.27 in which it is stated that this was an unusual event. The area in which the site is situated is known to be important for GWFG, with the Greenland White-fronted Goose Small Sites Report7 shows the field containing proposed Turbine 2 to be frequently used by GWFG. This is further confirmed in wintering distribution maps in the [PLACE] Bird Atlas8. There are also records from the [PLACE] Bird Club and from local [ORGANIZATION] staff sightings. The loss of traditional foraging fields would result in loss of suitable habitat and could lead to further restriction of range for the [PLACE] flock. Collision Risk Analysis We are concerned that collision risk has not been adequately assessed in this EIA. Although we acknowledge that vantage point (VPs) to monitor flight activity covered a 500m buffer of the site boundary (Appendix 8.1, Section 1.10), the boundary used differs from the final proposed development (Section 8.5.1) including missing Turbine 1 and some infrastructure. Further it is not clear why a 200m buffer is used (Section 8.8.84 of EIAR) in relation to the collision risk assessment when the Band Model, used to model collision risk, requires a 500m buffer. The paper explaining the model advises, “The survey area should include an envelope extending at least 500m beyond the outermost proposed turbines to reduce the risk of failing to record birds that use the wind farm area only occasionally”9. We are therefore concerned that all collision risk is underestimated at this site. We are further concerned by the choice of Band CRM methods for Curlew and Whooper swan (discussed in relevant sections) and by the lack of CRA for Pink-footed Goose, Herring Gull and Lapwing (discussed in Annex 2). We suggest appropriate CRA is conducted for all listed species. CRA has only been conducted at the NHZ level, we recommend that this is also conducted at SPA level for the relevant species to inform the Habitat Regulations Appraisal by the competent authority. We object due to inadequate collision risk modelling. We recommend that collision risk analysis is conducted using the appropriate 500m buffer, for all relevant species, at the appropriate population level and uses appropriate methods for Curlew and Whooper Swan. OBJECTION TO CORRIEMOILLIE BATTERY ENERGY STORAGE SYSTEM UP TO 200MW The application for the [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), proposing a capacity of up to 200MW and associated infrastructure, has been lodged under [ORGANIZATION] Planning Reference: [APPLICATION_CODE] and ECU Reference: [APPLICATION_CODE]. Despite the intention behind the proposal to support Scotland's renewable energy objectives, it raises significant concerns warranting its rejection. Located in the [PLACE] region, this development presents notable risks to the local environment, public safety, and community welfare. It fundamentally contradicts the principles and priorities outlined in Scotland's National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4), which underscore sustainable development, community resilience, and environmental safeguarding. target_text: As a countryman and a member of the [PLACE] community for 56 years I think I am certainly entitled to make my point regarding these Bess applications. I have worked in agriculture and my hobby is wildlife photography and the idea of our beautiful countryside being turned into industrial areas is absurd. I have been watching the site at [PLACE] being developed and it is obvious already that that land will never be returned to agricultural use especially once it is covered in concrete and metal containers. Technology, as always, moves on and these BESS will probably end up obsolete fairly quickly. As far as I am aware a further 2 sites beside the [PLACE] have received consent to go ahead and I think that is more than enough for our area. Also there are dangers associated with these BESS which I am sure you will be aware of and they can’t be ignored. National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4),Policy5 (Soils) makes it clear that development proposals will only be supported if they are designed and constructed in accordance with the mitigation hierarchy by first avoiding and then minimising the amount of disturbance to soils on undeveloped land. It also clearly states that development proposals on prime agricultural land will only be supported where it is for essential infrastructure AND there is a specific locational need and no other suitable site. All are being built on Prime Agricultural Land (BMV) alongside or opposite the Substation. This fourth application from [PLACE] BESS for 340MW storage is also on land classed as ‘Arable Agriculture’ by the LCA Scotland as capable of producing a wide range of crops. The NPF4 Policy 5, SOILS, states that prime agricultural land will only be supported in limited circumstances including for energy generation from renewable sources. “This application does NOT represent a form of electrical generation infrastructure rather it draws power from the grid stores this and releases it back as required”. (Quote from application for [PLACE] BESS by Energy Workshops) The NPF4 Policy 5 SOILS, also makes it clear that development proposals will only be supported if they are designed and constructed in accordance with mitigation hierarchy by first avoiding and then minimising the amount of disturbance to soils on undeveloped land. It also clearly states that development proposals WILL ONLY be supported where it is for essential infrastructure AND there is a specific location need and NO other suitable site. This Application by [PLACE] BESS is, over 2 miles from the Substation. This indicates there is NO “specific location need” for the BESS to be on this site. If A BESS can be 2 miles distant, it can be 5 miles or further distant or better still built to utilise ‘Brown Field’ sites close to the Wind or Solar energy generators.
