Any wildlife within the nearby small Wood of [PLACE] (also within our ownership), was undisturbed by the construction of the large [ORGANIZATION] [PLACE] sub station in recent years, which is over the fence from the Wood. 2 - the site is already very effectively screened from sight in three directions, from the north, south and west, due to the adjacent substation, the topography of the land (small rolling hills in all directions). and current mature woodland and tree belts which are prevalent in all directions. There will be mimimal view of the site, even before the landscaping involved with the project. There are also multiple pylons and overhead lines in close proximity so the landscape already has energy infrastructure, as well as the [ORGANIZATION] substation itself. 3 - the site is directly adjacent to the [ORGANIZATION] substation so there is no requirement for expensive, disruptive ground cables to be laid across farmland or roads. 4 - several mature trees within the site are being landscaped into the design, and are not being cut down or removed. 5 - the nearest property, [PLACE], is already fully screened from view due to their own existing trees. Most of the nearly residential properties are also already fully or partially screened due to trees or being below the site due to land topography. 6 - many of the objections to this site (in common with other BESS applications), arise due to the misleading information and scaremongering that is so prevalent on social media. Many falsehoods about these sites are then pedalled on the likes of Facebook as being "facts" without any objectivity or investigation of the information to establish what is the reality. 7 - there is no "cummulative effect" with the other 2 small [PLACE] BESS sites currently under construction, due to distance and land topography and they are far apart in opposite directions. The site at [PLACE] (to the west) is on the other side of the [ORGANIZATION] substation, and the site at [PLACE] (to the north east) is more than a mile away and over a hill. At no point on this proposal site, can either of these other BESS sites be seen or heard. 8 - there will be a huge financial contribution to the local economy with a construction project of this size - local food vans, village shops, local petrol station, tradesmen, B&B's, hotels, etc. will all benefit significantly from this project. 9 - the current national Grid is not fit for purpose and urgently needs BESS sites in order to operate efficiently due to the proliferation of wind farms and other energy sources. The need for electricity will only increase with the push for EVs, data centres etc and a BESS of this size will be hugely advantageous to the entire Scottish energy system. The need for this project is evidenced by the already agreed connection to the [ORGANIZATION] substation. 10 - it is a welcome and much needed farm diversification income stream for us, as small farmers, but will only use approx 12% of our land (32 acres of 250 acres). Plus the project is sited such that we will be enabled to continue our sheep and arable enterprises. The developer has consulted us throughout the design phase to ensure that our farming ability will be unhindered. 11 - the project is supported by the Scottish Govt National Planning Framework 4 which specifically refers to battery storage to assist in the drive to net zero carbon targets. We ask that the ECU consents to the planning application for this 500 MW BESS, reference [APPLICATION_CODE].

I am writing to formally object to the [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage Project No. [APPLICATION_CODE]. As a community we have accepted the need for some development in our area as part of the transition to renewable energy. We did not object to the extension of [PLACE], nor to the first three applications for BESS development namely [ORGANIZATION], [ORGANIZATION] and [ORGANIZATION]. These three applications have now been granted whereby over 80 acres of our prime agricultural land will be lost and the environment around [PLACE] industrialised from rural countryside. My understanding is that National Planning Framework 4 addresses the need for Cumulative Impact to be considered. This development, if approved, would be in a field adjacent to the [ORGANIZATION] development which has already been approved and close to the other developments mentioned above. Further development in this area will change our environment out of all recognition. I object to the development on the basis that it would not be for essential infrastructure and as such would not be permitted by NPF4 on prime agricultural land. [ORGANIZATION] has identified the total requirement for battery storage across the UK and divided this into regions. The region concerned in this development is [PLACE] where the quota is 3.9GW. At this time there is 1.6GW in operation with a further 7.6GW with planning consent. There is therefore no justification for further planning permissions to be granted for BESS in our area. Our community has provided a clear mandate to our Community Council to oppose all further BESS development in our area. That mandate is reflected in our Place Plan which has been registered with [ORGANIZATION]. I have lived and worked in this area for over 24 years and during that time I have enjoyed the peace, tranquility and unspoilt countryside in this beautiful part of the Scottish Borders. I have no wish to live near to an industrial site and this development will totally destroy my lifestyle, cause my family and I much stress, worry and anxiety for not only our future health, wellbeing and safety but also for that of our community. The light and noise level of the development is also of major concern. I am extremely concerned about the environmental impact as well as the risks due to fire pollution. Having this development within our local community will detract from the future marketability of our properties. There are already three BESS developments that have been approved within the local community so to accept more BESS sites will change the character and demeanour of this area. Our community should not be paying a higher price in terms of local amenity than other communities across Scotland. There should be no further developments within this locality other than the three BESS developments that have already been approved immediately adjacent to [PLACE] Sub-Station.

I support the above application. I welcome this development due to the increase in our energy security and ongoing sustainability it will help along with other projects to provide lower cost future energy requirements and help the energy network which is under strain with ever increasing demand. The project is out of main view and a site that can be returned to land use after the period has finished. The technology is latest generating and lesser risk to the local community and like many other projects will help support local community by generating income for the area as opposed to going to another district.

I have lived and worked in this area for nearly 20 years and during that time I have enjoyed the peace, tranquillity and unspoilt countryside in this beautiful part of the Scottish Borders. I have no wish to live next to an industrial site and this development will totally destroy my lifestyle, cause my family and I much stress, worry and anxiety for not only our future health, wellbeing and safety but also for that of our community. National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4), Policy 5 (Soils) makes it clear that development proposals will only be supported if they are designed and constructed in accordance with the mitigation hierarchy by first avoiding and then minimising the amount of disturbance to soils on undeveloped land. It also clearly states that development proposals on prime agricultural land will only be supported where it is for essential infrastructure and there is a specific locational need and no other suitable site. The site at [PLACE] is located on prime agricultural land and as such, specifically goes against the mitigation hierarchy. Its location over 2 miles from the [PLACE] means there is no “specific locational need” for the BESS to be on this site. Location at this site is purely based on landowner speculation for financial gain, and as far away as possible from his own residence and land he owns nearer the [PLACE]. Granting it permission would set a hugely dangerous precedent and would open up the potential for BESS developments outside the immediate vicinity of substations right across Scotland, unnecessarily threatening swathes of prime agricultural land and deeming the guidance within NPF4 Policy 5 to be virtually meaningless. Using the fields in this way will be damaging food production; this is a rural area where the fields are required for food production not BESS sites. This site is prime arable land and should remain so, the applicant states it will be reinstated once the site is not longer required, due to the proposed length of time the site is to operate, and that it will most likely fall to the applicants descendants or subsequent landowner to clear the site, the current landowner should be required to lodge with the Scottish Government a sum of not less than 1 million pounds to enable the site to be reinstated once it is redundant, this should be a condition applied to all applications of this nature by the ECU, so that future generations do not have to pay for any reinstatement costs for these projects. BESS sites should not be sited on prime arable land, but on brownfield sites away from homes. FIRE*** Fire-fighting issues is another great concern. Is the infrastructure for the water supply to the sites adequate for this purpose. Scottish Water should also be consulted as to whether their infrastructure is resilient enough. The lithium batteries have a concerning reputation for combusting into flames and creating uncontrollable fires. The local [PERSON] are not equipped to cope with such fires. There will always be a threat and risk of fire/explosion and vapour cloud within these sites which I find totally unacceptable. I am extremely concerned about the environmental impact as well as the risks due to fire pollution. The applicant has not read the guidance from the fire service stating that there should two points of access to the site, in the application there is only one very restricted access which would make fighting any fire almost impossible. The prevailing wind direction from the site puts properties at risk from the toxic cloud created by any fire including the village of [PLACE], the applicant does not provide any evacuation plan and also accommodation plan for residents during a fire at the site. The light and noise level of the development is also of major concern. Having this development within our local community will detract from the future marketability of our properties. There are already three BESS developments that have been approved within the local community so to accept more BESS sites will change the character and demeanour of this area. With three other BESS developments within the local community having been approved, the generation of construction traffic and associated noise will be vastly increased. This has already been proven with current works to the [PLACE]. I work with in the construction industry and having read the proposed number of vehicle movements stated, it is quite apparent that this vastly understated. Our community should not be paying a higher price in terms of local amenity than other communities across Scotland. There should be no further developments within this locality other than the three BESS developments that have already been approved immediately adjacent to [PLACE] Sub-Station.

Fire Safety - We have already seen the impact caused by thermal runaway and explosion at the BESS facility on [PLACE] in Sept 2020 which took a total 59hrs to extinguish. I am writing to formally object to the proposed installation of a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) near my residence in [PLACE]. While I support the advancement of renewable energy and sustainable infrastructure, I have serious concerns about the siting of this project so close to a [PLACE], playpark, doctors surgery and residential area. First and foremost, BESS facilities pose well-documented safety risks, including the potential for thermal runaway events, fires, and even explosions. Incidents involving large lithium-ion battery installations in other communities have resulted in hazardous conditions, evacuations, and long-term health and environmental consequences. Locating such a facility near homes, schools, or community centers increases the potential danger to public safety. Additionally, there are concerns about the environmental and health impacts of such a facility. Potential noise pollution, electromagnetic fields, and chemical leakage during operation or in the event of an accident are all issues that must be carefully considered. These factors could significantly degrade the quality of life for residents and potentially impact property values in the area. Furthermore, there appears to be a lack of transparency and community consultation regarding this project. Decisions of this magnitude should involve meaningful input from those most affected, and many residents were either unaware of the proposal or not given an adequate opportunity to voice their concerns. In light of these issues, I strongly urge the relevant authorities and project developers to reconsider the location of the BESS facility. A more appropriate site — at a safe distance from residential neighbourhoods — should be identified to minimize the risks to human health and property.

We object very strongly to the planning proposal for erection and operation of battery energy storage system (BESS), substations, switchgear and control buildings, landscaping, fencing and ancillary infrastructure- land 340M SW of [PLACE], [PLACE]. Our reasons are: Firstly the battery storage scheme is extremely dangerous. There have been reports in the news regarding battery fires and the difficulties associated with extinguishing enormous fires. Our local fire stations do not have the capacity to deal with such a blaze. The potential fumes and affluent from a possible fire will be hazardous to health and put many in the area at risk. This proposed site is close to a productive salmon river. We are concerned a rise in the water table could cause leachate to enter the river system and cause environmental devastation. We are also concerned about access to this site, we feel that the local roads will not be able to cope with the volume of traffic. There are also further plans to build at [PLACE], this combined with the movement of people and kit to site will cause disruption to the local roads. Finally, we do not feel that there is a need for such a scheme here and there are far too many projects of this scale or larger that are vying for planning consent at the moment and in the future. As residents and custodians of this land, living here for many generations, we object to the plans and feel that there is no benefit of having this project in the area. This is not something that we want our children, grandchildren, and greatgrandchildren to inherit.

Location is next to [PLACE] which is often subject to fire raising. Containment of any fire would require significant amounts of water. Water used to extinguish such a fire would be contaminated and would most likely run downhill and into the [PLACE]. The proposed development is less than 50 meters from residential housing. Any thermal runaway would cause an unacceptable risk to people living in the [PLACE] area. Toxic fumes and hydrofluoric acid in the air would be life threatening. What are the proposals for evacuating the surrounding area in the event of this happening? 6. Disposal of the batteries are a concern as they will land up in landfill with leakage causing detrimental damage to the earth which in turn will affect wildlife, livestock and crops. This negates the very idea of battery storge being "green" and good for the environment. 7. A further application has been made for another company to build a bigger BESS less than 500m from this site. There must be a lot of money to be made from this type of business! What philanthropic initiatives do the companies proposing building a BESS have to help the local community?

The [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) proposal presents significant risks to public safety, the environment, and local communities. Concerns persist regarding the fire hazards associated with lithium-ion batteries, for which no comprehensive emergency response plan has been provided, nor assurances that the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service is adequately prepared to manage a thermal runaway incident. Furthermore, the potential release of toxic gases and the generation of contaminated firefighting runoff pose a threat to public health and the protected ecosystem of the [PLACE]. The site's proximity to designated conservation areas generates additional environmental concerns, including the risks of pollution, habitat destruction, and loss of biodiversity, all of which are at odds with both national and local planning policies. Moreover, anticipated increases in noise, traffic, and visual intrusion could adversely affect local residents, tourism, and road safety. A critical issue is the lack of transparency throughout the consultation process. Essential information, such as detailed fire safety strategies, emergency response plans, and specifics of the battery technology, has not been disclosed, thereby rendering any thorough assessment of the proposal unfeasible. Furthermore, there has been no substantive engagement with emergency services or local authorities. Given that existing energy developments are already placing considerable strain on the area’s infrastructure and local services, this project would only exacerbate these issues. The cumulative impact of multiple large-scale energy projects in [PLACE] has already strained rural infrastructure, including narrow roads, emergency services, and public health resources beyond sustainable levels. Introducing another industrial project would only amplify these pressures, making it increasingly challenging for residents to uphold their quality of life. This is yet another blow for our much cherished community. How much more is our beautiful landscape going to be ruined, our beloved homes and businesses de-valued, our health—both mental and physical—detrimentally impacted, and our way of life changed forever? We are fortunate to live in an area of world-renowned beauty, surrounded by hills, river, and woodland, immersed in nature and peace. Would YOU choose to live anywhere near a monstrous Battery Energy Storage System? Or for that matter, a gigantic Converter Station? Or indeed, the already vast [PLACE]! Or all 3 of them!! We have already fought the giant pylons. How much more are we going to have to put up with? What about the next and future generations? Will there be anything left of our much loved and cherished land? I live, as the crow flies, within 1/2 mile of the proposed converter station, within 1 mile of the [PLACE] and proposed BESS. The future seems frightening indeed.

At a recent residents meeting (July 12th) we were made aware that the proposal submitted to the Scottish Government Energy Consents Unit (ECU) in respect of [ORGANIZATION] is still under consideration. The communication with residents on this project has been woeful with many unaware that there was a deadline to provide comment to [ORGANIZATION] ([ORGANIZATION]) by 30th June. We understand that ELC's deadline to provide comment to the ECU is the end of July and we are therefore writing now to raise concerns that we trust can be incorporated into the Council's response and taken on board directly by the ECU. At the outset, we wish to make clear that our concerns are not in relation to the adoption of renewable energy but to the lack of consultation and lack of oversight and management of a number of projects which will all impact significantly on a very small rural area for a number of years. With particular reference to the [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage Facility [APPLICATION_CODE], much of the below is very similar to the representation made by [PLACE] (ELCC) objecting to the proposals. It is disappointing to note that the submission, suggestions and offer to assist do not appear to have been addressed. Indeed the offer to facilitate a coordinated approach between [ORGANIZATION], the Scottish Government and the developers by ELCC for the various projects seems a sensible approach and one which we would urge be actioned. Key issues are: the negative impact on the environment and the community during the construction phase the unsuitability of the transport plan the lack of meaningful consultation the number of projects taking place concurrently or with some overlap which negatively impact the area yet without any oversight or requirement for the responsible delivery organisations to collaborate A few comments with particular relation to the proposed transport plan, the lack of collaboration and the negative impact: There has been no meaningful consultation with those of us who live on the proposed route. Surely there are procedures to ensure communities are apprised of plans and informed on how to provide comments with any deadline dates highlighted? See the comment above regarding the offer from ELCC to facilitate meaningful engagement. Based on the experience of residents who have already experienced similar transport routes in the development of the onshore wind farm at [PLACE] there are ongoing concerns about the safety of pedestrians, cyclists, equestrians, wildlife and other road users. As far as we can see the only nod to this being raised previously is the proposed 30mph speed limit. Access issues for emergency vehicles have not been addressed nor has the management of traffic should the [PLACE] close (the chaos this generates on the local 'back' roads is immense). Lack of joined-up thinking and collaboration to the benefit of all around the multiple projects which are planned. E.g. the traffic plan for the haul road, which actually undermines the planned one-way system for a small stretch and the total amount of traffic that these projects will bring not just in the transport of goods and materials but also the workforce. Desk research has been carried out (Transport Statement [ORGANIZATION] | B5728- 948 | Version 4 P4) but there is no indication that detailed consideration has been given to transport means and the suitability of the roads proposed in the route. Could the planned haul road for the substation not also be used for the battery storage facility, with an extension if necessary or indeed could the storage facility also build a haul road and new slip road off the [PLACE] at [PLACE], providing for two-way construction traffic and a much shorter and safer route to the battery storage facility? This would negate the need for the use of the proposed [PLACE] roundabout, [PLACE], [PLACE] and [PLACE] route and the one-way system that this entails. While there will be potential issues for residents and other road users with the proposed haul road traffic for the substation exiting the [PLACE] at the [PLACE]/[PLACE]/[PLACE] junction and over the railway bridge to the haul road, even with a new slip road, this does at least greatly reduce, if not remove, the need for all the construction traffic on our local roads. Network Rail has raised concerns about the use of the bridges at [PLACE] and at [PLACE] junction heightening concerns for residents about the capacity of these bridges to cope with the traffic. The low bridge on the [PLACE] which is part of the proposed one-way system is just under 14ft. This bridge is not suitable for some of the existing agricultural traffic that uses the roads. These vehicles would not be able to use the one-way system and there are no alternative routes to the [PLACE]. Could the abnormal loads designated access over the disused [PLACE], not also use the haul road? This would avoid the need to implement the swept path analysis on the full stretch of our local roads. The following statement appears in the Transport Statement [ORGANIZATION] B5728- 948 Version 4 P9 Below are general measures which will be followed when developing the detailed transport plan which will be included in the final CTMP. This will incorporate consultation and advice from two other important sources: - First, local residents and community groups to benefit from their local knowledge and to minimise disruption to their environment and activities and to maximise safety; - Secondly, there are several other electricity infrastructure projects which are likely to be in various stages of development/construction in the local area. [PLACE] BESS will work together with them to coordinate transport plans again to minimise disruption to their local communities and to maximise safety. It would be extremely helpful if both of these could be implemented now.

This submission draws on our submission, dated 09 March 2024 and appended as Appendix A, to the original, pre-amended, [APPLICATION_CODE] consultation. In the interests of avoiding repetition this response will focus on areas where new information has come to light in the intervening months. The absence of any points in this submission that are present in Appendix A should not be taken as a withdrawal of those comments. We stand by them entirely, except where new information unavailable to us in March has come to light, detailed below. As a Community Council we also have concerns that [ORGANIZATION] (which is, we understand, the parent company of [ORGANIZATION] and [ORGANIZATION], based on comments by [PERSON] of [ORGANIZATION]) and [ORGANIZATION] have not provided responses to our questions in a timely fashion which has limited our ability to respond to this consultation. Fundamentally we remain of the firm opinion that the proposal in its current form is deficient in four main areas and should not be granted consent on that basis: 1. Proposed Location National Planning Framework 4 clearly sets out its policy intent “To encourage, promote and facilitate the reuse of brownfield, vacant and derelict land and empty buildings, and to help reduce the need for greenfield development.” And desired policy outcome that “Development is directed to the right locations, maximising the use of existing assets and minimising additional land take.”1 The proposed site is greenfield grade 1 arable land,2 sitting as the only such site (approx. 5ha) within a much larger site of approx. 100ha the vast majority of which is brownfield and requiring redevelopment with, as yet, no other applications for its final use. As set out in our response of 09 March 2024 we do not believe this site to be the optimal location in the vicinity for such infrastructure, even allowing for possible need (see 4. National policy, below) and that approx. 95ha of alternatively suitable land exists within the vicinity.3 We can now demonstrate that the proposal additionally diverges from standard industry practice in regards to the development of these sites. Shortly after our 09 March response, [ORGANIZATION], the world’s largest independent renewable energy company, sent a representative to present at a meeting of the Association of [PLACE] Community Councils on 21 March 2024. There, they reported that among their usual guidelines for site selection [ORGANIZATION] considers: 1. Any site within 200m of residential properties unsuitable. 2. Any site within 500m of a substation to be optimal (i.e. no greater preference is given to a site 499m from a substation over one 200m from a substation). 3. Any site within 2-3km of a substation as viable. In an email to the Community Council on 23 December 2024, [ORGANIZATION] again referenced the site’s selection under [PLACE] Council’s 2018 Local Development Plan, however this policy requires that “Any redevelopment proposal will be expected to make best use of the location’s assets and bring significant economic benefits.” As we have previously detailed, there are as yet no identified economic benefits to the community from this development, let alone significant ones. Additionally, the 2018 Local Development Plan was written with reference to National Planning Framework 3 and, due to the widening of possible uses of the former [PLACE] site by National Planning Framework 4, which came into effect prior to this application being brought originally, the requirement for economic benefit on the site has been further strengthened. [ORGANIZATION] claim that the Planning Design and Access Statement addresses this, however the only discussion of Alternative Site Selection notes that no other land was considered due to the Levelling Up application and that “A convenient point of connection negates the need to lay lengthy cable routes and/or install additional overhead power lines and pylons. Thus, reducing the disruption to local residents and road users during construction. This then became the nearest land for the point of connection away from a built-up area.”4 This statement could not be further from the truth: first, we must assume the primary desire to avoid additional cable run is due to cost, and secondly the Community has not been consulted over disruption during construction for any other site and, based on the community’s views expressed at Community Council meetings, there is an overwhelming desire to ensure safety concerns are mitigated as a primary consideration and that temporary disruption during construction on an alternative site is overwhelmingly preferable to ongoing loss of amenity, green space, agricultural land, and increased safety concerns for residents. In relation to the Levelling Up application: it was successful work on the coal store site will be complete during 2025, but no final plans have yet been submitted for any further use. The site has lain unused for almost a decade. Why would an unused brownfield site not be preferable to a productive arable field? The issue with the proposed location is at the crux of our objection as the decision to site the BESS in this location exacerbates the issues with loss of amenity and safety. The decision to site in that location cannot be understood or accepted by the community as the location is unsuitable. The community has proposed alternatives which may be more suitable. 3 Hectare amount for overall site taken from [PLACE] Technical Appraisal, page 20: [LINK] former cockenzie power station site technical appraisal, accessed 18 December. 4 6.79, Planning Design and Access Statement (Page 45), [ORGANIZATION], January 2023. 2. Safety This remains the community’s primary concern. Despite our multiple requests for further assurances since August 2023, and the concerns raised in our original response, [ORGANIZATION] have provided no further information in these new applications to reassure the community. An email sent on 23 December 2024 to the Community Council finally provided confirmation that [ORGANIZATION] proposes to use Lithium-Ion batteries on the site (this information has been requested since August 2023). Lithium-Ion batteries are different to Lithium Iron Phosphate batteries (a specific type) and behave differently in relation to the risk of thermal runaway and in the emergency response. The Battery Storage Safety Management Plan prepared by National Fire Safety Services (Ltd) on two occasions states the presence of Lithium-ion Phosphate batteries on the site.5 Lithium-ion Phosphate is not a recognised technology. It was previously assumed that this was a typographical error for Lithium Iron Phosphate batteries, noted within the report as “relatively safer than other types of batteries”. The report must be discarded as deficient as it does not mention the possibility of the production of Hydrofluoric Acid from Hydrogen Fluoride which is possible in the event of a fire. Without this consideration no other safety information contained in the report can be trusted. Where hydrofluoric acid production during an emergency is possible, a Plume Assessment, Evacuation Plan, and Emergency procedures must be considered. Due to the prevailing winds, in the event of a large accident, [PLACE] and the [PLACE] (the community’s primary emergency shelter) would both be downwind, as would the main evacuation routes out of the village. The National Fire Chiefs Council guidance specifically identifies battery chemistry alongside various other measures which should be contained in an application, allowing Fire and Rescue Services to appropriately respond.6 This guidance is due to be updated in early 2025 and the community must ask that the new guidance is taken into account at the earliest possible moment to allow a proper response from the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service. A member of the community, a more than 15-year fire service veteran, has confirmed that locally there is insufficient equipment for the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service to respond to a fire of this type with anything other than defensive firefighting and their only viable course of action would be to allow a fire to burn out over a course of hours or days. They also note that the application of water as an extinguant would not be used due to the risk of environmental contamination from water application. With all of these points considered, we consider the current design of the site to be unsuitable for the proposed location. Further work should be carried out such as a Plume Assessment, Evacuation Plan, and Emergency Response, involving Community Resilience and the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service, should also be undertaken Until such time there can be no true consideration of the absolute safety of the site, but the risks of this particular site are clearly higher than other possible sites due to their proximity to houses and core amenities of the community. Even were changes such as a safer technology (e.g. Lithium Iron Phosphate, or a nascent technology like a Sodium Battery, or noble gas suppression systems in hermetic sealed systems), the overwhelming conclusion must be drawn that this site is not suitable. 5 Battery Storage Safety Management Plan (Page 4, Page 6), National Fire Safety Services Ltd. 6 National Fire Chiefs Council “Grid Scale Battery Energy Storage System Planning”: [LINK] accessed 23 December 2024. 3. Loss of amenity [ORGANIZATION] still maintain in an email dated 23 December 2024, that the site will have “no significant adverse impact” to the neighbouring residents, this appears to be a reference to the Acoustic Design Specification. However, the Acoustic Design Specification notes that an increase over background noise of +5dB (the rating level reported for the site based on modelling) may be considered an adverse impact (i.e. their statement is not incorrect but is, in isolation, misleading), with +10dB over background being a significant impact.7 The report also notes a margin of error in their modelling of +/-3dB, therefore meaning the true impact may be much closer to the threshold for ‘significant adverse impact’.8 According to [PERSON] (spoken to via phone on 18 December), who prepared the report, all modelling is based on information provided by the manufacturers of the systems. We must therefore assume these measurements to be taken in controlled (and, therefore we must presume optimised) conditions with equipment in pristine condition. rather than any independent testing in real world conditions. As the cooling systems’ performance may be impacted by a wide variety of environmental factors, including, air temperature, humidity, air salinity, wind speed. The equipment’s efficacy and performance may also be affected by build-up of dust, leaves, salt, and any other materials on intakes. In a real world setting, cooling equipment regularly produces more noise than encountered under manufacturer tests. Therefore there should be some scepticism as to the conclusions of the modelling. As previously noted, the New Link Road’s construction has still not been taken into account in terms of visual impact despite the fact that work has already begun. Additionally, there are major concerns about the wider loss of amenity due to the fencing off of the site meaning loss of use of the area for leisure activities and exercise. The importance of green space was highlighted during the COVID lockdowns. Due to the fencing off of this site and path only being available to the north edge, the loss of green space for the community is major. 4. National policy It has been stated in the Scottish Parliament that, according to a BESS developer, “there is a gold rush to get applications for battery sites into the planning process before the Scottish. Government puts controls in place”.9 The UK Government’s CP30 document, released in December 2024, outlines that the UK as a whole requires 23-27GW of Battery Storage.10 Morag Watson of Scottish Renewables has stated that Scotland requires 10GW of Battery Storage, but that this includes domestic installations, e.g. connected to solar, and use of Electric Vehicles (EVs) plugged into the grid.11 There is already a vast amount of BESS consented within the UK, including in Scotland. While there is clearly a need, surely there should be a national process to evaluate suitable sites to ensure appropriate distribution and planning of such key national infrastructure. Such a process is important and sites like [PLACE] must be evaluated against each other to ensure that sites are placed suitably both for the grid and for the communities around them. Given the issues raised above, the community of [PLACE] and 7 5.5.4 Acoustic Design Specification (Page 13), [ORGANIZATION]. 8 7.1 Acoustic Design Specification (Page 19), [ORGANIZATION]. 9 Douglas Lumsden MSP, Scottish Parliament, 05 December 2024: [LINK] M2641E383P719C2637183 accessed 23 December 2024. 10 Clean Power 30, UK Government (Pages 10-11) [LINK] accessed 23 December 2024. 11 Morag Watson, Director of Onshore at Scottish Renewables, Edinburgh Climate Change Institute Community of Practice, September 2024 [PLACE] deserves better than being the victim of a speculative prospector’s application, especially when other BESS operators like [ORGANIZATION] have described that they would not select the site. We have concerns that a site like this could form a precedent for national developments of BESS in proximity to residential and important local assets such as schools and to permit development on greenfield sites even where suitable brownfield sites exist. This cannot be allowed to happen. SUMMARY The Community Council and members of the community have engaged with this process at every stage and the very first response made at the 01 June 2023 consultation was that the proposed site was unsuitable and that better alternative sites existed in the vicinity. That the developers and [ORGANIZATION] have ignored these concerns is unfortunate. The [PLACE] development on the former Power Station site demonstrates that landowner permission is not required before an application is submitted to the ECU and a compromise was later found. That the same process has not taken place in this instance and instead a proposal so deficient (and against the wishes of the community when alternatives have been suggested) now awaits a final decision from the ECU is a sad state of affairs. We hope the Energy Consents Unit take our objections into account and deny permission for this project. If any further information is required we would be happy to provide it We would welcome the opportunity to meet with all parties involved in this application, including the Energy Consent Unit to discuss this in more detail.

target_text: As a retired employee of [ORGANIZATION] who served the Council as a primary [PLACE] teacher for nearly forty years and always had the safety and duty of care as my prime objective for my pupils, I write to express my concern and formal objection at the proposals to site a Battery Energy Storage Site (BESS) at [PLACE] (Refs [APPLICATION_CODE] and [APPLICATION_CODE]) so close to our local primary and nursery schools. The proposal would be one of the largest BESS in Scotland and the UK at 342MW in total, more than three times the size of the largest active BESS site. My concerns are summarised below. 1. The location of this proposed site is close by to a large Secondary School, a [PLACE] and housing on the North, South and Western Borders (Circa 200-400 meters). 2. I believe there are health and safety issues linked to such sites as there is the potential Hydrogen Floride exposures that are immediately dangerous and therefore cannot believe that a proposal of at least 100MW would be sited in a location so close to the aforementiomed in point one. 3. It is also my understanding that to date Scotland already has enough storage capacity to meet its 2045 Net Zero Target. It appears that Companies such as [ORGANIZATION] are just looking for land opportunities and hoping that enough applications will succeed and they can then sell on to energy companies for a healthy profit for themselves and shareholders. I have four grandchildren who visit regularly and have major concerns over the safety of such a site. 4. I would also ask the question as to how ready the [PERSON] are should one of these storage facilities catch fire which we have seen recently. 5. I am told that these sites are very quiet. As we live approx. 250 metres from the proposed site I refuse to believe this is true and we will be affected by noise. 6. I believe the storage is to be linked to the [PLACE] and cables will run from the site down [PLACE], up [PLACE] to the [PLACE] and up [PLACE] to the Substation (Circa just under 2 miles). Anyone familiar with this road will know that at peak times the traffic can be chaotic, and any disruption will cause major issues. You only have to look at last week, when a burst water pipe at [PLACE] caused mayhem and was reported on Radio Clyde on a daily basis. I am led to believe road disruption could last for two years which is very unfair on residents and businesses in the area which will suffer. 7. Given the amount of Sink Holes in the area, one of which can only be circa 100 metres from the site, is this really a well-structured and thought-out plan for what will be heavy equipment. 8. If the Scottish Government push this through how the site will be accessed is currently an issue as there is no viable option that I can see. 9. Our Local MP (Labour), MSP (SNP) and Councillor (Labour) are all to the best of my knowledge against the proposal which must surely tell you how ill thought out the location of this site is.

I am writing to express my objection with regards to the proposals to site a Battery Energy Storage Site (BESS) on prime grade 1 arable land at [PLACE] (Refs [APPLICATION_CODE] and [APPLICATION_CODE]) both as a local resident and long serving Firefighter. -This is one of the largest active BESS in Scotland and is also much closer to residential buildings than any other existing site in the country (including a doctor's surgery and primary [PLACE]). I feel that this proposal unnecessarily risks the safety and wellbeing of the families in close proximity to the site and the community as a whole. It lowers multiple standards and protections and sets a race to the bottom. After sharing and collating our knowledge as a community, the main concerns of note are as follows: - High grade farmland will needlessly be lost with multiple brownfield sites available in similar proximity. The land in it's current state is a source of homegrown food and supports local wildlife. Current excavation in proximity of the proposed site have already correlated with instances of disrupted deer and fox activity in the area. - After meeting with my community and community council, and following multiple Q&A sessions with planning representatives (the few willing or able to speak to us), there was an alarming lack of key information relation to this development, including Emergency Plans, an Evacuation Plan, and nobody involved in the discussions could confirm the type of battery to be used in the development. It is either the current technology with all of it's documented risks or a new emerging battery technology with a reduced knowledge of real-world performance. Either way, there can be little confidence in a proposal (or the proposers) that doesn't include such a key piece of information. - The noise impact from the completed running BESS runs a high risk of being significantly, and near constantly, adverse. This is totally unacceptable to both close-living residents and the community as a whole. -The proximity to residential houses, [PLACE] and [PLACE] pose a significant risk to a great number of people in the event of a fire situation. It is widely documented that, despite fire detection and suppression systems being in place, BESS sites have suffered thermal runaway, resulting in fires, explosions and the release of toxic gases. Often over a protracted period of time. At present, and to the best of my knowledge, our policy covering BESS fires puts emphasis on defensive firefighting. Due to a number of factors including the environmental impact of contamination from water application, the dangers of explosion and sudden reignition, and where there is no immediate life risk (assuming the successful and confident evacuation of nearby houses), consideration is to be given to defensive firefighting, allowing batteries to burn themselves out. The long duration of a fire event, and given the prevailing westerly wind, could in turn lead to a large-scale evacuation of the aforementioned GP, primary [PLACE] and a significant number of houses. There is little doubt that people will be exposed to the toxic fumes, including hydrofluoric acid, and smoke to varying degrees and that this will lead to both short- and long-term health complications. - Future of the site and impact wider ecosystem Especially in the event of accident what assurances exist that the site can be returned to prime arable land? What drainage exists for emergencies other than dumping contaminated water in [PLACE]? Is there any information about the acoustic impacts on protected species such as bats? None of this is clear from the application and unless these questions are answered the longer term impact of this development on the environment of our community may be tremendous. As will be quite obvious, I do not support these applications by [ORGANIZATION] on behalf of [ORGANIZATION] and [ORGANIZATION]. Please take account of my concerns and objections in your consideration of this application.

I am writing to lodge an objection to the proposed installation of a Battery Energy Storage Site (BESS) at [PLACE], [PLACE] under the above reference number. My concerns are summarised below: DISRUPTION: The proposed BESS will be connected to [PLACE]. In order to achieve a connection, cables must be laid from the BESS along [PLACE] and [PLACE], [PLACE] for approximately 1.5 -2 miles to the substation. Undoubtedly this will result in traffic control measures (traffic lights). Both of these roads are already very busy and there are traffic jams at peak times. The resulting roadworks will disrupt the local community and be detrimental to local businesses for up to 2 years. The local community will see all of the disruption but receive no benefit. Unnecessary: I do not believe that there is any specific requirement for the development to be in my local area as there are no grid stability issues here. This facility is not needed to meet the 2045 Net Zero target. Scotland will already exceed the 2045 best case scenario target for battery storage by 2030. breach OF Scottish government strategy The developer has indicated that the project will be handed over to private investors / hedge funds. This project will bring no benefit to the local community which breaches the Scottish Government Energy Strategy guidelines. Proximity to residents and local [PLACE]: Residential housing and the local secondary [PLACE] are in close proximity to the planned site with the nearest resident only 150 m away. Lithium BESS is hazardous heavy industry and produce toxic smoke plumes when they explode. Research published on the UK government planning inspectorate website into smoke plume analysis confirms that 30ppm of Hydrogen Fluoride can be detected 240m away in standard wind conditions. 30ppm of Hydrogen Fluoride is deemed a threat to life. There has been countless reported incidents globally involving BESS sites where fires and vapour clouds have been experienced. I believe this BESS is a high risk to the local community and any incident at this proposed site will have a detrimental impact on our children’s lives, health and education. ACCESS TO THE SITE: The developers consultation report states that “the site is approached from the existing access which serves [PLACE], off [PLACE]”. There is only one way to get to [PLACE] and that is via [PLACE]. I would suggest that this access is utterly unsuitable as it is a residential street and a ‘no through road’ where children often play, indeed access to [PLACE] from [PLACE] was closed permanently by [PLACE] council in the 1990’s. Current access to [PLACE] is via [PLACE] off [PLACE]. The junction of [PLACE] and [PLACE] is on a blind bend and in my opinion is unsuitable for lorries and heavy machinery. COURT RULINGS BESS INVERNESS: ILI appeal refusal notes:- "The appellant says that the safety aspects of battery storage are not a material planning consideration." I believe that these comments by ILI who are the proposers for the [PLACE] BESS show that they have little consideration for the local communities health, safety and well-being. DEVELOPERS CONSULTATION REPORT. I believe the developers consultation report conclusion is disingenuous and misleading. It suggests that the wider local community are in favour of the BESS site. I firmly believe this to be untrue. The report suggests that the minority that attended their consultation events who were against the project do not represent the wider community who are in favour. Surely the developer can only report the feelings of those who attended and they can not infer the feelings of the wider local community. I would be grateful if you would acknowledge my correspondence and confirm that my objections to the BESS site at [PLACE], [PLACE] have been formally lodged.

I write to strongly object to the above application. I am co-owner of the adjacent fields to the East of this proposed Battery Storage Site - land known as [PLACE]. I have never at any point received neighbour notification regarding this project and was not aware of the public consultations held back in 2024. The first I knew about it, was reading about the planning application in our local newspaper! My grave concerns are that, as there are reports almost on a daily basis of fires breaking out from BESS installations, though the industry wants to play this down, the poisonous smoke and fumes will seriously affect those living close by and depending on the direction and speed of the wind, could be carried for miles! The toxic particles in the smoke will most definably, be detrimental to human health and these particles will also contaminate waterways and fields for miles around. Who will compensate us if we can no longer grow crops in our fields or graze livestock? If these Battery units catch fire, is there provision to contain run off? I can see no mention of this in their website. How can this be classed as environmentally friendly and green energy? Minerals used to construct the batteries is mined in foreign countries, with no regard to pollution caused by their extraction, then shipped half way round the world to get here. A huge carbon footprint has already been created getting the materials into this country! It is of little benefit to our community, as it will not create local jobs. The workforce employed for the construction will be from other parts of the country. I find it very hard to believe, that [ORGANIZATION] have not had to complete an environmental risk assessment given the wildlife that reside in the gully between our land and [PLACE]! How many hours will the BESS hold power for? Is the environmental impact and carbon footprint caused by this project going to be offset by the benefits? There is no mention of any of this on their website! There is also no mention of how the site will be maintained, secured or what measures will be in place to prevent unauthorised access. There is no mention of how long this BESS will be in place. Surely these are all points that should be stated before any planning application is considered! It is criminal what the Scottish Government is allowing to happen to Scotland - desecrating the beautiful countryside with Wind Turbines, BESS, Solar Panels and Power Stations. The one thing we can't make any more of on this island is land. If you continue allowing permission for all of these projects to develop, and all of the tree planting that is taking place on good agricultural land, there will be a food shortage! I find it particularly concerning that the area around [PLACE] has been picked on for so much infrastructure and the above application is just the first of many that are in the pipeline for our area. [ORGANIZATION] want to construct 3 rows of Pylons through our farm, which is going to totally devalue our land not to mention the privately owned houses in close proximity, but no-one seems to care as long as it's not in their backyard! Scotland is responsible for just 0.3% of the Global Emissions yet you are going to allow the destruction of our beautiful country to meet Net Zero, when all of the biggest polluting countries in the world don't care!

Say NO! to the [PLACE] Battery Storage System (BESS) For the attention of the ECU I am a resident of [PLACE] in [PLACE]. You will be aware of plans to site a large Battery Electricity Storage System at [PLACE] on prime agricultural land adjacent to [PLACE]. The proposed site is totally unsuitable, being too close to large residential areas, a Primary School and a Medical Centre. A fire at this facility could contaminate anywhere in [PLACE] and beyond. As more of the residents become aware of these proposals and the risks associated with Lithium Battery Storage, opposition to this project is growing. Whilst planning applications for BESS sites are multiplying, the need for so many BESS is doubtful. Scotland already exports power. The initial application for the BESS at [PLACE] was originally to be one of the largest in the UK. It has since been divided into 2 smaller sites (perhaps to hide the true size of the development?) Both sites are owned by the same company. See - [LINK]. [ORGANIZATION] declined to object to the applications. They own the land the BESS(s) would occupy, and would benefit significantly financially if the land was leased to a developer. The purchase of this land was supposed to promote local employment. Thus far there are no indications of long term job creation. Indeed, once installed, it is proposed that the BESS will be remotely monitored. There is no indication of who will provide onsite security or first response to emergencies. The local Fire and Rescue service have not been formally consulted but have indicated they have no specialised equipment or procedures to fight Lithium Battery fires. The nearest permanently manned Fire Station is at [PLACE], 4.5 miles from the proposed site. Other adjacent Fire Stations are “On Call” only. Water will not extinguish a Lithium battery fire. If water is used in an attempt to contain the fire it will become contaminated with toxic chemicals and will need to be contained and not simply allowed to run off. Fire crews attending recent Lithium Fires have worn breathing apparatus and have allowed the fire to burn itself out. This may take several days. Meantime the TOXIC SMOKE PLUME formed will spread downwind. This may require the evacuation of large numbers of the population. How will residents be told of an emergency and the need to evacuate? Has anyone considered procedures for evacuation of all staff and pupils from the Primary School? Would you be happy to send your child to a [PLACE] so close to a BESS? Would you choose to live within one mile? The smoke plume from a Lithium fire in the USA was detected 40 miles down wind and caused breathing problems for residents. It is too early to know if their health is permanently damaged. A 40 mile radius from [PLACE] could affect [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], or [PLACE] depending on wind direction. In summary 1. The need for large numbers of BESS developments is doubtful. If there is need, they should be sited well away from large residential areas and not where they affect the lives of established centres of population. 2. The proposed site is totally unsuitable due to the extreme proximity of large residential areas, a Primary School and Medical Centre. The site was chosen because of its closeness to already existing electrical grid infrastructure, thereby reducing the cost of the development. 3. The size of each BESS should be limited, and designed to minimize the likelihood of a major fire or leak of toxic materials. BESS site should be permanently manned 24/7 to ensure safety and security 4. Consideration must be given to the effects of the creation of toxic materials and potential damage caused to wider areas. 5. Plans need to be formed for dissemination of information, and emergency evacuation if required. (Including all the staff and pupils of the Primary School). The plans should be available to the public and they should be made aware of the dangers that come with a Lithium fires, 6. If the construction of a BESS site affects wild life or habitat this must be given due consideration before development commences. The loss of public recreation facilities should be avoided. 7. If the BESS is allowed. Homes will be devalued and families will move away from danger.

target_text: Installations of this type, posing a well documented fire and explosion risk, should not be situated at the proposed site, close to residential areas as well as to a local [PLACE] ([PLACE]) and [PLACE] ([PLACE]) all of which are situated in a northerly / easterly direction from the planned facility / facilities and as such are in direct exposure to all evolved toxic fumes resulting from any operational malfunction of the BESS faciiity(ies) as carried via the regular I prevailing strong / stormy southerly and south westerly winds. The Acoustic Design Specification report (ADS; Section 4.6*) details distances to 4 main residential areas, one of which is our residential street, and also to the buildings associated with [PLACE] (which incorporates a nursery; Section 4.7) but ignores the playing / sports fields associated with the [PLACE] campus and which are much closer to the proposed facility than the buildings themselves. The proposed BESS must be constructed on a site which is significantly more distant from all residential areas and significantly greater than all of those distances cited in the aforementined sections of the ADS report and most certainly not in an up-wind (wrt prevwling wind directions) position relative to residential areas. An expert report prepared following a major fire at a relatively small (20MW), remotely monitored, BESS facility at [PLACE] in [PLACE] in 2A20 highlighted issues with its closeness to residential properties. In 2024, [ORGANIZATION], the worlds' largest independent renewable energy company stated, at a meeting of the Association of [PLACE] Community Councils, that in accordance with their policies any BESS facility should not be constructed within 200m of residential properties and this distance relates from the nearest boundary of the facility and not the centre as detailed in the current ADS repoft. In the Pre-Application Consultation Report (PACR), [ORGANIZATION] avoided residents' questions regarding the close proximity of the proposed installation to residences and play parks despite both these being very close to the installation i.e. ca80m from the centre of the planned facility ([PLACE] has a large play park at its western end, ref Appendix A of NFSS report); this park, r,rtric is part of the nearest residential estate, is adjacent (ca 40m) to the sites' northern boundary and in the main is not protected by the "indicative bund". [ORGANIZATION] responded to the residents' questions using the single, less specific term "leisure amenity" to cover both residences and leisure facilities. This is unacceptable and demonstrates a lack of concern for residents as well as unfamiliarity with the site location which is clearly much too close to the communities as a whole and as such the current application should not be approved. [ORGANIZATION] also stated that locating a BESS very close to a substation is not necessary and up to 500m in this respect is optimal and 2-3 km is viable with minimal loss of transferred energy. Therefore the currently proposed location is unnecessary and the Applicant / Agent is placing convenience and cost over public safety. Based on safety, geographic and climatic (prevailing winds) considerations, alternative sites of 2 - 3 km from the current substation can and should be considered. The installation will emit substantial and continual noise of varying frequencies from the "24 / 7" cooling systems, battery units and higher frequency noise from the substations / transformers (magnetostriction). The ADS report leaves the reader in no doubt that there will be an increase in noise disturbance (both day and nighQ resulting from the operation of the installation (now both Farcels A and B). The report states that there is a significant margin of error of +/-3dB in the emitted noise estimations / modelling. The noise modelling is based on system manufacturers' information but such information will be clearly dependent on battery type which at the time that the modelling was undertaken was "unknown" and only very recently has been "confirmed" (refer next paragraph) changing &om the newer and safer type, lithium iron phospahte (LFP), as considered eafly 2A24, to an older technology Lithium-ion (Li-ion). Of great concern is Section 4.5 of the ADS report whereby a "4m high bund will be installed to the northern boundary of the compound (now [PLACE]) to provide further attenuation to houses of.[PLACE]" since [PLACE] also extends along the eastern boundary of the compound so this attenuation will be ineffective with a resultant detrimental acoustic effect on our day to day living. Clearly increased attenuation towards our home is critical and any increase in constant background noise in particular humming I brghff frequency is unacceptable. Of particular concern to us is the ADS report Summary Point 1.9 which statos that the facility ". would not have a significant adverse impact on the neighbouring properties" so this implies that with the +l- 3dB error in modelling estimations the impact will fall between adverse impact (+ 5dB above background) and significant adverse impact (+10dB) and outside the limits set by [ORGANIZATION]. Totally unaccptable and one of the main reasons, along with battery safety (refer ensuing text) for our overall objection to this planning application, Of key importance is the "final?" choice of battery which has only recently been communicated to CPSCC in answer to questions raised at a recent CPSCC meeting which [ORGANIZATION] joined remotely. [ORGANIZATION] have stated in their response that the batteries used for this propos al are ta be "lithium-ion batteries which have been widely used for the last 50 years and are a praven and safe technologt.althouglt the type used in grid-scale batteries although using a slightly dffirent type of lithium-ian chemistry "; lithium-ion batteries are not proven safe technology and pose a greater safety risk than the alternative LFP batteries. Even so the definitive cathode chemistry still has not been specified so it can be assumed that this is the "different type"? The statement from [ORGANIZATION] is at odds with the e.mail copied at the end of this objection** (and previously submitted to the ECU) as received from [ORGANIZATION] on 21 February 2024 which implies that LFP batteries are proposed, and that the Jinal choice will be determined on the best option available on the market at the time and that the final battery chemistry choice is driven by thermal runoway temperature. Battery technologies are developing allthe time and it is therefore difficult to rationalise how batteries with a "50 year" history constitutes the "best option available on the market at the time" especially as the e.mail goes on to state "the expectation is that the technologl,t will have moved farward tn the intervening period.up to 5-10 years transmisson connection timeline". Lithium-ion batteries are an older technology and have a range of thermal nrnaway tempertures and based on available information it is assumed that the closest design to LFP batteries in respect of thermal runaway is the Li-NMC111 battery which, if this is the one being considered, has the additional safety concern (both human and environmental) of producing the toxic metals nickel and cobalt in the event of thermal runaway. Even with the safer LFP batteries it is important to note that thermal runaway occurs at much lower temperatures when the batteries are maintained in a fully charged state as is the case in a functional BESS (as low as 100oC) and even lower if overcharged (NFSS report). Indecision regarding the battery type is clear and coupled with conflicting statements at this stage of the application is of great concern and the definitive tlpe of battery needs to be made known, accompanied by a fulI safety review, to all concemed parties (i.e. local communities) for further evaluation and comment. Compared with the newer and safer LFP batteries lithium-ion batteries have a greater energy density so it appears that the Agent / Applicant is prioritising power storage over newer and safer technologies. In relation to the choice of lithium-ion batteries, the previously cited PACR and recent feedback from [ORGANIZATION] to CPSCC state that in the event of fire, hydrogen fluoride (HF) will be produced as one of the numerous toxic gases. However great emphasis is also placed, in the various documents / communications, on the use of a water mist system to cool overheating batteries but no mention is made of the fact that should overheating occur and a fire break out then the HF will dissolve in the water mist to produce the highly dangerous and corrosive hydrofluoric acid (HFA); such a mist if released into the atmosphere and carried in prevailing winds will be highly dangerous to residents especially their lungs and eyes. Furthermore the HF originates primarily from the electrolyte lithium hexafluorophosphate and the associated chemical reaction which produces HF is enhanced in the presence of water (i.e. the proposed heat I fre suppression system). Although it is stated in the NFSS report th"t th" procedure of Off-Gas Detection is to be employed in the early stages of thermal runaway of the batteries in order to prevent explosion and fire, nevertheless the possibility of the latter occurring still exists. In the case of the [PLACE] BESS, the large number of battery units increases the statistical chance of failure. There is always a risk which can never be removed, "No Risk" can ever be stated in any professional context. Even with Off-Gas Detection the NFSS report states that volatile products (including HF) will be released in trace (unspecified) amounts but that this will occur at lower temperatures than thermal runaway. Even trace amounts of HFA are unacceptable and stand a chance of being released (e.g. via the air conditioning units, maybe even attacking seals) into the atmosphere in very close proximitry to residential areas and agunthe large number of units increases the risk (and magnitude) of this happening. Should the worst happen and thermal nrnaway occur with resultant fire and explosion, then toxic fumes containing HFA, and toxic organic volatiles will be released into the atmosphere putting local residents, [PLACE] primary / nursery [PLACE], the [PLACE], road users and first responders at severe risk. The toxic products will constitute a significant plume which will likely be carried on the prevailing winds towards surrounding communities and to date no plume assessment has been undertaken and there appears to be no clear emergency plan within this application. Throughout this objection letter, numerous references have been made to the NFSS report. However Section 2.2, Lrmitations, of the this report is too vague using terms such as "good faith" and "assumed" which are unacceptable and of gteat concem. Similarly Section 3.2,Emergency Response Procedures, appears to be written as if the site is manned 2417 but the site will be remotely monitored and not staffed on a continual basis, again grounds for our objection. Once operational the proposed installation does not offer any employment or economic benefit to local communities. The stored power will be released into the National Grid and there is no 2417 on-site personnel either monitoring engineers nor security, which we believe to be unacceptable especially when over-heating resulting in thermal runaway could result from "wilful damage"; hands on personnel are essential under such circumstances, again grounds for our objection. In summary the proposed installation poses a real and unacceptable risk of severe fire and explosion culminating in the release of extremely toxic fumes incorporating the highly corrosive hydrofluoric acid and which will be caried on prevailing winds towards the very close surrounding residences, communal establishments (e.g. [PLACE] and [PLACE]) and general communities of Cockeruie and, [PLACE]. For these reasons, and as detailed previously, there is no justification for the choice of the proposed site so close to populated areas and up-wind thereof or for any other local up-wind location. The installation will also generate an unacceptable level, i.e. adverse impact, of continuous noise at our home, on other close I nearby residential areas and communal / areas. We are retired so this will cause us anxiety and continual distrurbance and will undoubtedly cause both acute and chronic health risks within the local communities especially to susceptible individuals.
