retrieved_examples.text: Installation of a grid battery energy storage facility (up to 70MW) with associated development at land north of [PLACE], [PLACE], is objected to on the following grounds: Location issues - The Application states the site is within the administrative boundary of [ORGANIZATION], but it is actually within the boundary of [ORGANIZATION]. This mistake raises questions over the accuracy of the information in the rest of the Application. - The Application states a BESS cannot be located within a built-up area. However, there is a population of around 4,000 in [PLACE], 19,000 in the [PLACE], and planning for thousands of more homes just north of the proposed site has already been granted by [ORGANIZATION]. The [PLACE] was once the fastest growing [PLACE] in Europe. The proposed facility is immediately next to a long-standing quiet housing area on [PLACE]. The proposed site is also just across the [PLACE] from the [PLACE] and [PLACE] developments, and not far from parts of [PLACE]. This is a residential/built-up area, soon to be vastly increased in size, and is therefore unsuitable for a BESS facility. - The Application states a BESS cannot be located within a heavily industrial area. Within an extremely short walking distance of the proposed site is a Waste Water Treatment Works which serves the local community and beyond, there is also a scrapyard, a [PLACE] with a filling station, a Health Club, 3 Nursing Homes, as well as other commercial businesses. This also makes this an industrial and commercial area which is unsuitable for a BESS facility. An installation on this site could prevent any future expansion of the Waste Water Treatment Works to accommodate the large number of houses for which planning permission has already been granted. - The Application states many types of wildlife which live in and around the location of this proposed facility - bats, badgers, hedgehogs, otters, deer, foxes, rabbits, squirrels, kingfishers, swans, pink-footed goose, swifts, golden eye, black-headed gulls, herring gulls, song thrush and many more. Disturbing their habitat when the location is unsuitable anyway is wrong. Many of these animals are having their habitats shrunk due to ongoing house building nearby, this facility would further limit their habitat options. - There are also plans submitted to [ORGANIZATION] for another BESS facility only 0.2 miles away. Surely 2 BESS facilities within less than 1⁄4 mile of each other is too much risk for 1 area? Any fire at one location could potentially affect the other. Connectivity issues - The Application states the site is located within suitable proximity of a Substation with an active grid connection offer from a DNO. However, no information is given on how this facility is to be connected to the grid. No answers could be given at the public consultation, and it appears that no information is available yet either. Traffic issues - The proposed access route to the site is almost 5 miles longer than simply turning towards the site off [PLACE], which adds in many extra miles and exhaust fumes beside residential areas. The route involves very narrow country roads, B classification at best, with very tight spots, and no passing places. There is also a narrow bridge to navigate with no traffic control, in the middle of a blind corner with a narrow road on both approaches. There is simply no way for HGVs and cars to pass safely. Construction vehicles travelling along these roads which are used daily by local residents will cause traffic issues and greatly increase the possibility of collisions with motorised vehicles, including motorbikes, as well as bicycles and pedestrians who all use these roads, as well as deer which live in the countryside surrounding the road. - The Application states the access track will be surfaced by crushed stone/aggregate, ensuring the access road is permeable, and also minimising visual impact of the access route. There is no information given as to how this "crushed stone/aggregate" will be stopped from leaving the facility in the tread of vehicle tyres and becoming a hazard on the road. This seems like an accident waiting to happen. - The Application states all HGV deliveries will be coordinated to be "Just in Time" to control traffic flow. They will be asked to pull up away from the site. No information is given as to where these vehicles will be pulling up, and there is nowhere on the proposed route from Persely roundabout to the site which is appropriate for this use. - No explanation is given as to why a right-hand turn, therefore across oncoming vehicles, is being suggested as the only means of entry to the site. HGVs already ignore entry instructions to a local housing development where there is no means to monitor it, so are likely to do the same at this proposed installation too. - Further questions are raised as to how the waste management vehicles are to access the proposed facility. No information is given in the Application as to where the person checking on the facility will be travelling from. What is the carbon footprint of their journeys? How far will the person who attends to alert the Fire Brigade if there is an issue be travelling? No information is given on this. Safety issues - Worldwide, there have been many issues with fires at these kinds of installations - eg 23 fires at BESS units in South Korea in 2018 alone, and a fire at a BESS installation, with half the capacity of this proposed one, in [PLACE] in 2020 which burned in excess for over 11 hours. This proposed installation would bring these risks into our community. - The Application states the risk of a fire is relatively low from the types of battery used (lithium iron phosphate), which are intended to reduce the risk of thermal runaway, but should it occur the ignition will be detected, any gas that could cause an explosive risk will be exhausted, the fire will be extinguished and has very limited ability should failure to control a fire occur to spread to other parts of the site until such time as fire service intervention occurs. If this Application gets the go ahead, this is to be an unmanned facility. How will the ignition be detected? How will gas be exhausted? How will the fire be extinguished? - As a Church we strongly object to the comment: "if a fire occurs with no one on site there is no life safety risk". What about the local community? If there is an incident, there appears to be no information of how the wider area will be alerted so they can either be evacuated, or know to go inside and close all doors and windows to avoid the chemicals which could be in the air. Is there an emergency plan? Where will people be evacuated to? What plans have been developed and put in place to protect the local community should a fire arise? - In the case of any fire, hazardous fumes can travel in a variety of directions and can affect a much larger area than the proposed facility itself. This is an expanding neighbourhood area with many families, young children, and elderly residents, including in Nursing Homes. It is unacceptable to bring this potential risk into such a highly populated residential community. - The [PLACE] used to almost come to a standstill at morning and evening rush hour due to only having 2 bridges for access in and out of the city. The [PLACE], and the [PLACE], have helped ease those traffic congestions. However, if there was to be a fire at the proposed site it could affect the [PLACE], the nearby [PLACE], and depending on wind direction also the [PLACE]. Not only would this impact on the traffic flow in the [PLACE] and [PLACE], but it also raises the question of how quickly the emergency services would be able to respond to any call. The Police no longer have a presence this side of the [PLACE] ([PLACE] has been closed) and using alternative routes will increase the response time. There are no emergency services based in our community to deal with any issues arising from this installation. - Worrying, the Application states in the event of a large-scale fire, it is not envisaged that the fire service will fight the fire and the equipment will be subject to a controlled burn. This statement is of great concern to us, as reading between the lines, it shows that it is not possible to put out any fire. Any fire at this facility could result in a lengthy burn period, bringing traffic in the [PLACE] and [PLACE] to a standstill as well as bring unknown hazardous fumes to the area, with unknown health concerns, for an unknown length of time. - How far will the person who attends to alert the Fire Brigade if there is an issue be travelling? No information is given on this. - The Application mentions an underground gas pipe to the east of the Site which planting should be appropriately offset from the pipe and easement. However, no information is given about how the gas pipe will be protected against any potential fire, or construction works. The only mention of the gas pipe comes with regards to being careful when planting trees. Surely a gas pipe underneath a battery storage facility is not recommended? This is a massive explosion risk. - The Application states both no storage of materials or fuel and fuels are to be stored within the fuelling area/diesel bowser where they must be stored in double skinned bunded tanks with drip trays and spill kits. Fuelling is prohibited elsewhere on site. These contradictory statements raise serious safety concerns. Fuel being stored on this site also raises safety concerns. - The location of this installation near a scrapyard and close to a petrol station seems unwise bearing in mind the fire risk associated with lithium. The location of this installation near a Waste Water Treatment Works seems unwise bearing in mind the media interest in sewage release into the waterways in UK. The location of this installation near the [PLACE] seems unwise bearing in mind the potential damage which would result from any fire. This is a location which flooded in 2002. How would a flood affect the facility? - We are concerned that there does not appear to have been an independent fire test carried out, rather the tests were carried out in a Sungrow lab, the manufacturer. Acoustic issue - The Application states the NIA has modelled the expected noise impact of the proposed development with this barrier in place, and found that noise levels at the nearest Noise Sensitive Receptors only slightly exceed the recommended standards set out in the [ORGANIZATION] guidance on noise. 3.21 It is not considered that this exceedance is of significant enough magnitude to outweigh the positive benefits of the proposed development in terms of benefitting renewable energy and tackling the Climate Crisis. It should also be noted that the noise modelling is based on a ‘worst Supporting Statement [PLACE] Section 36 BESS case’ scenario, involving all equipment running at maximum volume simultaneously and constantly, which would be rare if ever at all. Noise limits are there for a reason. No application should be approved if it exceeds a noise limit. The statement that this would be a rare if ever occurrence is not satisfactory. Once permission to this facility is given who will be monitoring the noise levels to ensure this is not a constant event, which could cause a disturbance to local residents including those in nearby Nursing Homes. This is also at least the third time the Application appears to go against safety limits/regulations, which in our opinion does not bode well for the future development of this potential installation. We do not see any evidence of what the noise levels of rain hitting the cabinets would be. Job opportunities - The Application states the proposed development would be beneficial to the local area, in terms of potential for temporary and longer-term job opportunities, for instance in the construction and supply chain. While we appreciate that perhaps more people could be employed during the construction phase, we believe it to be more likely that existing firms, with existing workforce, would be appointed to do the construction work. Nor is it guaranteed that local businesses would benefit from the constriction work or the supply chain. As for longer term job opportunities, we fail to see how an unmanned facility can be said to provide longer term job opportunities for the local area. Maintenance - The Application states this is to be an unmanned facility. There is no information given about how the facility will be monitored with regards to graffiti, vandalism or fly tipping to prevent it being abused like the [PLACE] BESS facility also run by the Applicant. There is no information given about how the facility will be maintained or who will undertake the work eg ensuring fences and cabinets are secure. - The Application states in terms of recycling the batteries the applicant notes that the battery recycling process is still in its infancy stage and we are unable to provide exact details of how these units will be recycled in 40 years time. We appreciate that recycling processes might develop over the next 40 years, but to give no idea of how the recycling might happen is unacceptable and sounds a little like "it won't be my problem, so doesn't matter". Not enough information is given on this subject. Consultation issues - Despite 2 Public Consultations being held in our building we do not feel that adequate information has been made available to the local communities which will be affected. There are many people in [PLACE], and in the wider [PLACE], who were not informed of this Application by the Applicant and have no idea of the plans being spoken of. The Applicant states they sent out leaflets to "877 properties". This low level is unacceptable. When we used to help run the [PLACE] Gala pre-Covid we used to send out 10,000 leaflets and still didn't cover the whole area, further indicating the significant population of the area, which is currently being expanded. This installation could affect the property values, and the health and wellbeing of those in a much larger area than has been consulted by the Applicant. The Church members of [ORGANIZATION] find all of the above very concerning, and on the above grounds we strongly object to this Application. We therefore urge those with the power to grant planning permission to refuse this particular application.

This correspondence serves as a formal objection to the planning application for the [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), as detailed under Energy Consents Unit Ref: [APPLICATION_CODE] and [ORGANIZATION] Ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]. The proposal entails the establishment of a lithium-ion battery storage facility, along with its associated infrastructure, in close proximity to residential areas, agricultural land, and environmentally sensitive locations. The objection is rooted in verifiable and legally applicable concerns, with a specific focus on matters related to public safety, environmental hazards, adherence to planning regulations, and procedural deficiencies within the consultation process. In light of the inherent risks associated with large-scale battery storage projects and their potential implications, it is imperative that this application undergoes rigorous scrutiny. Deficiencies in the Consultation Process The public consultation events were found to lack substantial engagement, as representatives were unable to provide satisfactory responses to important inquiries concerning fire safety, emergency response plans, and environmental impact. Requests for detailed site layout drawings were either disregarded or provided in a heavily redacted format. Furthermore, the applicant indicated that the specific battery technology to be utilised had not been finalised, hindering residents' ability to thoroughly evaluate potential risks. Email correspondences directed to [ORGANIZATION], the applicant, have gone unanswered, prompting apprehensions regarding the developer's level of transparency. The apparent lack of interaction implies that legitimate concerns raised by the public may not be adequately addressed following approval. Environmental and Ecological Impact The proposed [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development poses significant environmental risks, particularly in relation to air and water contamination, biodiversity loss, and landscape disruption. Located near the [PLACE], a Special Area of Conservation ([PLACE]) for Atlantic salmon, the site falls within an ecologically sensitive area that encompasses multiple Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs) and the [PLACE], renowned for its internationally significant wetland habitats. Any potential contamination or disruption to this fragile ecosystem could have widespread and enduring repercussions. In the event of a thermal runaway incident in a lithium-ion battery storage system, a variety of toxic gases and airborne pollutants would be released, posing a serious hazard to public health and the environment. Such incidents could result in the emission of hydrogen fluoride (HF), carbon monoxide (CO), and sulfur dioxide (SO2) in significant quantities. HF is particularly hazardous due to its highly corrosive nature, capable of causing severe respiratory damage and chemical burns. CO, an odourless gas, can be fatal in high concentrations, while SO2 is a known trigger for asthma and lung diseases. Additionally, particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) would be released, further deteriorating air quality and heightening the risk of long-term cardiovascular and respiratory complications. Given the prevailing wind patterns in the [PLACE] region, these toxic emissions could easily spread into residential areas, agricultural land, and water sources, directly endangering the health of local communities. The potential threat to water quality is equally concerning, particularly in the event of a BESS fire and subsequent firefighting activities. Lithium-ion battery fires necessitate substantial amounts of water for suppression, resulting in toxic runoff contaminated with heavy metals, lithium, and acidic compounds. This contaminated water could infiltrate the [PLACE], jeopardising its [PLACE]-designated Atlantic salmon population and other aquatic species. Furthermore, SEPA flood risk mapping indicates that the proposed site is situated within or near a floodplain, heightening the risk of pollutants dispersing over a wider area during periods of heavy rainfall or flooding. Despite these risks, the application lacks a comprehensive containment strategy to prevent such contamination. The development also poses a threat to local biodiversity, which includes protected species such as ospreys, buzzards, curlews, red squirrels, pine martens, otters, and great crested newts. Construction activities, noise, and artificial lighting could disrupt migration patterns, breeding cycles, and natural behaviours, while habitat destruction and potential chemical contamination pose enduring risks to wildlife. The proposal fails to adhere to crucial planning policies aimed at safeguarding the environment. NPF4 Policy 3 (Biodiversity Enhancement) stipulates that new developments should deliver net environmental benefits, rather than just avoiding harm; however, this application lacks a clear mitigation strategy for habitat loss. NPF4 Policies 22 and 23 require developments to steer clear of negative impacts on protected conservation areas, while HWLDP Policies 28, 36, 58, 59, 61, 63, 72, and 73 focus on preserving the landscape and natural environment, all of which are evidently compromised by this proposal. In the absence of robust environmental safeguards, effective mitigation measures, and a well-defined risk management plan, the [PLACE] BESS development poses an unacceptable environmental risk. The potential for airborne and waterborne contamination, destruction of protected habitats, and non-compliance with planning policies render this proposal fundamentally flawed and incompatible with its environmentally sensitive location. Cumulative Impact The [PLACE] area has already experienced significant industrialisation as a result of multiple energy infrastructure projects. The potential addition of a large-scale Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) could further impact local communities, landscapes, and public services. It is essential to evaluate the combined effects of these developments rather than considering them in isolation to fully understand the extent of disruption they may cause. The region has seen a rapid growth in energy-related infrastructure, such as substations, battery storage facilities, wind farms, and high-voltage power lines. These developments have had negative repercussions on residents. For instance, SSEN's [PLACE] Expansion has led to ongoing noise complaints. The proposed [PLACE] BESS would introduce another industrial-scale energy storage site, increasing the risks associated with lithium-ion battery storage. The replacement of [PLACE] and [PLACE] Substations, along with the planned [PLACE] development on an 868-acre site, will further concentrate energy infrastructure in the area. The construction of multiple 400kV overhead power lines and pylons, some as tall as 70 metres, is already altering the rural landscape significantly. The cumulative impact of wind farm developments, such as the [PLACE] with 36 turbines at 230 metres each and the [PLACE] adding 14 turbines at 200 metres, contributes to the industrialisation of the area. These projects, combined with the proposed [PLACE] BESS, could have irreversible effects on the natural environment and visual appeal of the region. Additionally, the planned closure of [PLACE] for up to a year will divert all traffic, including heavy goods vehicles carrying construction materials, through [PLACE], leading to congestion and safety concerns for residents, schoolchildren, and local businesses. The proliferation of energy developments in [PLACE] has placed an unsustainable burden on rural infrastructure, including narrow country roads, emergency services, and public health resources. Introducing another industrial project would exacerbate these challenges, making it harder for residents to maintain their quality of life. National and local planning policies mandate the consideration of cumulative effects when evaluating new applications. NPF4 Policy 29 requires energy infrastructure projects to demonstrate that they will not have unacceptable combined impacts on local communities or the environment. Given the existing industrialisation in [PLACE], the continual expansion of large-scale energy developments is no longer viable. NPF4 Policy 3 stipulates that developments should enhance biodiversity, yet the cumulative loss of natural landscapes and habitats goes against this principle. Similarly, HWLDP Policy 36 states that developments should not disproportionately burden rural communities, a standard that is not being met given the current strain on local infrastructure and services. Public Safety and Risk Awareness The [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) proposal raises significant concerns regarding fire safety, primarily due to the well-documented hazard of thermal runaway in lithium-ion battery storage systems. Such incidents can lead to unmanageable fires, explosions, and the release of harmful substances, such as hydrofluoric acid, dioxins, and heavy metals. Notable incidents, like those at the [PLACE] in the USA, have underscored the associated risks, with contamination levels in the surrounding environment found to be significantly elevated. Addressing such emergencies demands substantial resources, as per the guidance from the National Fire Chiefs Council ([ORGANIZATION]), where even minor BESS fires necessitate 1,900 litres of water per minute for a minimum of two hours, with actual cases requiring over one million gallons. Despite this, the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service ([ORGANIZATION]) has not disclosed its readiness for such scenarios. The lack of response to a Freedom of Information (FOI) request made in January 2025 regarding emergency plans raises doubts about local response capabilities. The risks are not confined to fire incidents, as the runoff from firefighting activities could potentially contaminate the [PLACE], a designated Special Area of Conservation ([PLACE]) for Atlantic salmon, posing a threat to biodiversity and water quality. The absence of a specified containment strategy in the proposal to mitigate this risk is concerning. The [ORGANIZATION] strongly advises against siting BESS facilities in close proximity to populated areas. The current proposal falls short of meeting the requirements outlined in NPF4 Policies 2, 4, 22, and 29, which emphasise prioritising health, safety, and environmental protection in energy developments. Given the inadequate fire safety measures, the absence of a resolved emergency response plan, and the environmental hazards associated with toxic contamination, the viability of this application is questionable in terms of safety and suitability. Summary The [PLACE] BESS proposal presents considerable hazards to public safety, the environment, and local communities. The inherent fire risks linked to lithium-ion batteries are not adequately addressed; there is neither a definitive emergency response strategy nor any assurance that the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service would be capable of managing a thermal runaway scenario. Furthermore, the potential emission of toxic gases and the risk of contaminated firefighting runoff pose serious threats to public health and the integrity of the protected [PLACE] ecosystem. Concerns are equally pronounced regarding the project's close proximity to conservation areas. The anticipated environmental impacts—including pollution, habitat degradation, and a decline in biodiversity—are in direct conflict with both national and local planning policies. Additionally, the probable increase in noise, traffic congestion, and visual disruption is likely to adversely affect local residents, tourism, and road safety. The consultation process has been marked by a significant lack of transparency; crucial information such as fire safety measures, emergency response plans, and detailed battery technology specifications has been absent, rendering a comprehensive assessment unfeasible. Moreover, there has been a noticeable absence of meaningful engagement with emergency services and local authorities. With the area's infrastructure and local services already under strain from existing energy developments, the further addition of this project would intensify these pressures. In light of the above, I urge the [ORGANIZATION] to reject this application and consider alternative, less risky options that align with the principles of sustainable development and public safety.

target_text: I am writing to formally object to the proposals for a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) on prime grade 1 arable land at [PLACE] (Refs [APPLICATION_CODE] and [APPLICATION_CODE]). My mother resides in close proximity to the proposed site, which amplifies my concerns about its location and the risks it poses to the surrounding community. While I acknowledge the importance of energy storage within the grid, I feel this particular location is unsuitable for the proposed development. My concerns are outlined below: 1. Loss of Prime Grade 1 Arable Land National Planning Framework 4 stipulates that greenfield land should only be developed if no suitable brownfield sites are available. This is not the case here, and the use of brownfield land should be prioritized. 2. Incomplete Documentation Key information required for proper assessment, such as an Emergency Plan, Evacuation Plan, and clear specifications of battery types, is missing. Without this, it is impossible to fully assess the risks, including the potential release of hydrofluoric acid during a fire. Proceeding without complete and accurate information is unacceptable. 3. Noise and Amenity Impact The proximity of the site to homes, including where my mother resides, raises serious concerns about noise pollution. The proposed site is projected to produce noise levels of up to 33dB(A), which could cause adverse effects for residents. This does not account for potential uncertainties, and no clear mitigations have been proposed. 4. Safety Risks The proposed site poses significant safety concerns. Fires in BESS facilities are notoriously difficult to manage, with local firefighters confirming that current protocol involves allowing such fires to burn. This could necessitate large-scale evacuations, affecting homes, businesses, [PLACE], [PLACE] (just 38m from the site), and critical community facilities. Given these risks, the site’s proximity to residences and essential infrastructure is unacceptable. 5. Long-Term Environmental Impact There is insufficient information about how the site will be managed in emergencies or returned to its original state if decommissioned. Issues such as contamination, drainage management, and potential harm to local wildlife, including protected species, remain unresolved. 6. Alternative Locations There are more suitable brownfield sites in the vicinity that could support this development without compromising safety, community well-being, or environmental integrity. In conclusion, this proposal is fundamentally flawed due to its location, incomplete documentation, and failure to address key safety and environmental concerns. I urge you to reject these applications and instead encourage the developers to explore more appropriate sites.

retrieved_examples.text: Battery Energy Storage Site (BESS) proposal on prime grade 1 arable land at [PLACE] (Refs [APPLICATION_CODE] and [APPLICATION_CODE]) While I understand the need for energy storage, I am writing to: note my objections to the above proposal; raise concerns about the handling of the case so far, as well as the gaps in policy it has exposed; and to ask that you take supportive action. My concerns are particularly: 1. Safety Government guidance and well-documented global incidents confirm that BESS facilities pose a risk of thermal runaway events, which can lead to uncontrollable fires, explosions and toxic gas releases. The current location is the worst possible from a safety perspective in the event of a fire. It is just too close to people, including housing, a playpark, a [PLACE], a [PLACE] and the primary routes into and out of our community. I understand that no other sites in the UK are located so near to residences and local amenities. Local firefighters have confirmed that current policy with BESS fires is to leave it to burn. A prevailing wind fire at this site would mean a huge evacuation of most of the community, including the main shelter at the Community Centre. I understand that there would be a possibility of the production of a range of harmful and toxic fumes. All of this means huge risks to the local area, including the [PLACE] and the primary [PLACE]. This is simply unacceptable - exposing the community to needless risk while better options exist elsewhere. An incident would also pose unacceptable risks to wildlife habitats and farmland, because there would be no way to prevent harmful liquid or gases entering [PLACE] or wider local environment. 2. Lack of key information in the application The documentation relating to this site is worryingly lacking in adequate safety procedures. For example, there is no Emergency Plan and no Evacuation Plan, as recommended in Fire UK National Fire Chief’s guidance. Also, it refers to different types of batteries which require differing solutions and management. We have to assume the worst scenario which would be that an accident would trigger a plume of Hydrofluoric acid. Therefore, the ECU is being asked to give consent to a half- complete plan whose underlying assumptions may be incorrect by the time of construction. I do not find this acceptable. 3. Ongoing impact on community, locals, health, local environment and amenities The proximity of the site will lead to constant noise for nearby residents. The application’s Acoustic Design Specification notes this will be at least an ‘adverse impact’ at night – and potentially worse. Long-term exposure to this would undoubtedly cause sleep and mental/emotional health problems. I am aware that developers such as [ORGANIZATION] recommend no closer than 200m to residences – almost three times further than this proposal. The likely negative impact on house values, and on the ability to obtain insurance, would also have knock-on effects on mental and emotional health. 4. Community distrust and developer transparency The beneficiary of this development is London-based [ORGANIZATION] financial investment company. Meanwhile [ORGANIZATION] has several roles: as a landowner, with opportunity to profit from land-leasing, and as a planning authority, with responsibilities to the local community (in addition a statutory role in monitoring of noise and air pollution). These are unacceptable conflicts of interest, and I am aware that the Council has recently refused a Freedom of Information request for the expected annual profit from the leasing arrangement. This land was purchased to create economic development opportunities and create local jobs, but it is my understanding that the BESS will create no jobs. 5. Loss of prime grade 1 arable greenfield land National Planning Framework 4 sets out that greenfield land should only be considered for development where brownfield land is unavailable. That is not the case here, therefore the nearby brownfield site should be preferred. Action requested I request urgent consideration of the following: · There must be clear national guidance developed around the proximity of BESS to residences; no communities should be faced with the risks being proposed at [PLACE]. · There should be a properly independent body to oversee the planning process. The fact that local authorities to act as both landowners and planning authorities is a conflict of interest which needs to be addressed urgently. · BESS sites should never be sited on greenfield land where appropriate brownfield sites exist, and careful consideration must be given to permanent loss of prime agricultural land for a BESS site which may supply the grid only infrequently and at great benefit to its owners. · Communities’ interests and benefits for land next to residences, amenity and community space must be prioritised over financial gain for landowners. I specifically request that you: · raise my concerns directly with [PERSON] MSP, Acting Cabinet Secretary for Net Zero and Energy; · identify opportunities in parliament (such as questions and debates) to raise the case of the proposed BESS at [PLACE] and the concerns of our communities; · work with other MSPs, including through Committees and Cross-Party Groups, to explore how regulation in relation BESS sites could be tightened, and the interests of communities could be better represented, as suggested above.

I am writing to express my objection with regards to the proposals to site a Battery Energy Storage Site (BESS) on prime grade 1 arable land at [PLACE] (Refs [APPLICATION_CODE] and [APPLICATION_CODE]) both as a local resident and long serving Firefighter. -This is one of the largest active BESS in Scotland and is also much closer to residential buildings than any other existing site in the country (including a doctor's surgery and primary [PLACE]). I feel that this proposal unnecessarily risks the safety and wellbeing of the families in close proximity to the site and the community as a whole. It lowers multiple standards and protections and sets a race to the bottom. After sharing and collating our knowledge as a community, the main concerns of note are as follows: - High grade farmland will needlessly be lost with multiple brownfield sites available in similar proximity. The land in it's current state is a source of homegrown food and supports local wildlife. Current excavation in proximity of the proposed site have already correlated with instances of disrupted deer and fox activity in the area. - After meeting with my community and community council, and following multiple Q&A sessions with planning representatives (the few willing or able to speak to us), there was an alarming lack of key information relation to this development, including Emergency Plans, an Evacuation Plan, and nobody involved in the discussions could confirm the type of battery to be used in the development. It is either the current technology with all of it's documented risks or a new emerging battery technology with a reduced knowledge of real-world performance. Either way, there can be little confidence in a proposal (or the proposers) that doesn't include such a key piece of information. - The noise impact from the completed running BESS runs a high risk of being significantly, and near constantly, adverse. This is totally unacceptable to both close-living residents and the community as a whole. -The proximity to residential houses, [PLACE] and [PLACE] pose a significant risk to a great number of people in the event of a fire situation. It is widely documented that, despite fire detection and suppression systems being in place, BESS sites have suffered thermal runaway, resulting in fires, explosions and the release of toxic gases. Often over a protracted period of time. At present, and to the best of my knowledge, our policy covering BESS fires puts emphasis on defensive firefighting. Due to a number of factors including the environmental impact of contamination from water application, the dangers of explosion and sudden reignition, and where there is no immediate life risk (assuming the successful and confident evacuation of nearby houses), consideration is to be given to defensive firefighting, allowing batteries to burn themselves out. The long duration of a fire event, and given the prevailing westerly wind, could in turn lead to a large-scale evacuation of the aforementioned GP, primary [PLACE] and a significant number of houses. There is little doubt that people will be exposed to the toxic fumes, including hydrofluoric acid, and smoke to varying degrees and that this will lead to both short- and long-term health complications. - Future of the site and impact wider ecosystem Especially in the event of accident what assurances exist that the site can be returned to prime arable land? What drainage exists for emergencies other than dumping contaminated water in [PLACE]? Is there any information about the acoustic impacts on protected species such as bats? None of this is clear from the application and unless these questions are answered the longer term impact of this development on the environment of our community may be tremendous. retrieved_examples.text: I am writing to formally object to the proposed installation of a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) near my residence in [PLACE]. While I support the advancement of renewable energy and sustainable infrastructure, I have serious concerns about the siting of this project so close to a [PLACE], playpark, doctors surgery and residential area. First and foremost, BESS facilities pose well-documented safety risks, including the potential for thermal runaway events, fires, and even explosions. Incidents involving large lithium-ion battery installations in other communities have resulted in hazardous conditions, evacuations, and long-term health and environmental consequences. Locating such a facility near homes, schools, or community centers increases the potential danger to public safety. Additionally, there are concerns about the environmental and health impacts of such a facility. Potential noise pollution, electromagnetic fields, and chemical leakage during operation or in the event of an accident are all issues that must be carefully considered. These factors could significantly degrade the quality of life for residents and potentially impact property values in the area. Furthermore, there appears to be a lack of transparency and community consultation regarding this project. Decisions of this magnitude should involve meaningful input from those most affected, and many residents were either unaware of the proposal or not given an adequate opportunity to voice their concerns. In light of these issues, I strongly urge the relevant authorities and project developers to reconsider the location of the BESS facility. A more appropriate site — at a safe distance from residential neighbourhoods — should be identified to minimize the risks to human health and property.

Battery Energy Storage Site (BESS) proposal on prime grade 1 arable land at [PLACE] (Refs [APPLICATION_CODE] and [APPLICATION_CODE]) While I understand the need for energy storage, I am writing to: note my objections to the above proposal; raise concerns about the handling of the case so far, as well as the gaps in policy it has exposed; and to ask that you take supportive action. My concerns are particularly: 1. Safety Government guidance and well-documented global incidents confirm that BESS facilities pose a risk of thermal runaway events, which can lead to uncontrollable fires, explosions and toxic gas releases. The current location is the worst possible from a safety perspective in the event of a fire. It is just too close to people, including housing, a playpark, a [PLACE], a [PLACE] and the primary routes into and out of our community. I understand that no other sites in the UK are located so near to residences and local amenities. Local firefighters have confirmed that current policy with BESS fires is to leave it to burn. A prevailing wind fire at this site would mean a huge evacuation of most of the community, including the main shelter at the Community Centre. I understand that there would be a possibility of the production of a range of harmful and toxic fumes. All of this means huge risks to the local area, including the [PLACE] and the primary [PLACE]. This is simply unacceptable - exposing the community to needless risk while better options exist elsewhere. An incident would also pose unacceptable risks to wildlife habitats and farmland, because there would be no way to prevent harmful liquid or gases entering [PLACE] or wider local environment. 2. Lack of key information in the application The documentation relating to this site is worryingly lacking in adequate safety procedures. For example, there is no Emergency Plan and no Evacuation Plan, as recommended in Fire UK National Fire Chief’s guidance. Also, it refers to different types of batteries which require differing solutions and management. We have to assume the worst scenario which would be that an accident would trigger a plume of Hydrofluoric acid. Therefore, the ECU is being asked to give consent to a half- complete plan whose underlying assumptions may be incorrect by the time of construction. I do not find this acceptable. 3. Ongoing impact on community, locals, health, local environment and amenities The proximity of the site will lead to constant noise for nearby residents. The application’s Acoustic Design Specification notes this will be at least an ‘adverse impact’ at night – and potentially worse. Long-term exposure to this would undoubtedly cause sleep and mental/emotional health problems. I am aware that developers such as [ORGANIZATION] recommend no closer than 200m to residences – almost three times further than this proposal. The likely negative impact on house values, and on the ability to obtain insurance, would also have knock-on effects on mental and emotional health. 4. Community distrust and developer transparency The beneficiary of this development is London-based [ORGANIZATION] financial investment company. Meanwhile [ORGANIZATION] has several roles: as a landowner, with opportunity to profit from land-leasing, and as a planning authority, with responsibilities to the local community (in addition a statutory role in monitoring of noise and air pollution). These are unacceptable conflicts of interest, and I am aware that the Council has recently refused a Freedom of Information request for the expected annual profit from the leasing arrangement. This land was purchased to create economic development opportunities and create local jobs, but it is my understanding that the BESS will create no jobs. 5. Loss of prime grade 1 arable greenfield land National Planning Framework 4 sets out that greenfield land should only be considered for development where brownfield land is unavailable. That is not the case here, therefore the nearby brownfield site should be preferred. Action requested I request urgent consideration of the following: · There must be clear national guidance developed around the proximity of BESS to residences; no communities should be faced with the risks being proposed at [PLACE]. · There should be a properly independent body to oversee the planning process. The fact that local authorities to act as both landowners and planning authorities is a conflict of interest which needs to be addressed urgently. · BESS sites should never be sited on greenfield land where appropriate brownfield sites exist, and careful consideration must be given to permanent loss of prime agricultural land for a BESS site which may supply the grid only infrequently and at great benefit to its owners. · Communities’ interests and benefits for land next to residences, amenity and community space must be prioritised over financial gain for landowners. I specifically request that you: · raise my concerns directly with [PERSON] MSP, Acting Cabinet Secretary for Net Zero and Energy; · identify opportunities in parliament (such as questions and debates) to raise the case of the proposed BESS at [PLACE] and the concerns of our communities; · work with other MSPs, including through Committees and Cross-Party Groups, to explore how regulation in relation BESS sites could be tightened, and the interests of communities could be better represented, as suggested above.

target_text: I am writing to express support for the planning application [APPLICATION_CODE] for a new Battery Energy Storage System at [PLACE]. As a concerned resident invested in the sustainable development of our community, I firmly believe that this project aligns with our shared goals for a cleaner, more efficient energy future. The need for reliable energy storage has become increasingly evident in today's dynamic energy landscape. The implementation of a battery energy storage facility not only addresses this pressing need but also represents a significant step towards a more resilient and sustainable energy infrastructure. The utilisation of battery energy storage supports the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions by enabling the integration of more renewable energy sources into our grid, ultimately aiding in our collective efforts to combat climate change. Furthermore, it contributes to grid stability, reducing the risk of power outages and enhancing the overall efficiency of our energy distribution system. The facility is very small and will have minimal impact on its surroundings. Also, additional screening has been included to further ensure there is minimal visual impact following concerns raised by residents. In conclusion, I wholeheartedly endorse the approval of planning permission for the battery energy storage facility. This will not only meet our immediate energy needs but also contribute significantly to a more sustainable, resilient, and prosperous future for our community.

retrieved_examples.text: I write to express my concern at the proposals to site a Battery Energy Storage Site (BESS) on prime grade 1 arable land at [PLACE] (Refs [APPLICATION_CODE] and [APPLICATION_CODE]). The proposal would be one of the largest BESS in Scotland and the UK at 342MW in total, more than three times the size of the largest active BESS site. Although smaller than some consented, the specifics of the proposed site at [PLACE] are different and cause concerns about the chosen location’s suitability which I will set out below. The applications were submitted on 30 August 2023 ([APPLICATION_CODE], later amended on 12 November 2024) and 12 November 2024 ([APPLICATION_CODE]) to the Energy Consents Unit by [ORGANIZATION] on behalf of [ORGANIZATION]. I was alerted to these applications when our Community Council received notifications in mid-February 2024 and November 2024. I have concerns that [ORGANIZATION], the parent company of [ORGANIZATION] and [ORGANIZATION], based on comments by [PERSON] of [ORGANIZATION]) and [ORGANIZATION] who during an online question and answer meeting agreed to have questions forwarded and they would answer. They did not provide responses to the questions and were constantly requested to answer and reply. They chose to answer some of the question at the last minute which affected my response to this consultation. Due to my concerns previously listed in my email to you last year at the first BESS proposal and now my additional new concerns after research, I object to this application in its proposed form in the strongest possible way. No matter the BESS size it is not the correct site for a BESS. I understand the need for energy storage within the grid but the proposed site is not suitable for the amended BESS proposed and, given the presence of other, more suitable sites, in the vicinity, risks setting a dangerous precedent. My concerns are: Loss of prime grade 1 arable greenfield land & NPF4 National Planning Framework 4 sets out that greenfield land should only be considered for development where brownfield land is unavailable. That is not the case here, as there is an unused brown field site south of the BESS proposed site, therefore the brownfield site should be preferred. [ORGANIZATION] propose to build the BESS on prime 1 agricultural green land when there is a brown field site to the south of this site. The Brown field site is also owned by [ORGANIZATION] and I would suggest that the BESS is moved to the brownfield site as is recommended in NPFP4. The National Planning Policy Framework guides all development away from the ‘best and most versatile’ agricultural land, that is, good to excellent quality agricultural land. The framework also states that elements of many renewable energy projects are not “appropriate” development for green belt land. National Planning Framework 4 clearly sets out its policy intent as follows. “To encourage, promote and facilitate the reuse of brownfield, vacant and derelict land and empty buildings, and to help reduce the need for greenfield development.” And policy outcomes that “Development is directed to the right locations, maximising the use of existing assets and minimising additional land take.” The proposed BESS site is greenfield grade 1 arable land, sitting as the only such site (approx. 5ha) within a much larger site of approx. 100ha the vast majority of which is brownfield. I suggest the BESS is sited on the Brown field site as advised and recommended in NPF4. In this way the BESS will be more distant from homes, gardens, our primary [PLACE] and grounds and playpark as well as walking and cycling core paths. The site for the Bess does not follow NFP4. Other BESS operators like [ORGANIZATION] have described that they would not select this site. This site could form a precedent for national developments of BESS in proximity to residential and important local assets such as schools and to permit development on greenfield sites even where suitable brownfield sites exist. This cannot be allowed to happen. National Planning Framework 4, Scottish Government, Page 50: [LINK] There are absolutely no economic benefits to the community from this development. Why was no other land considered? Surely this is a requirement? especially when there is a large vacant unused 20 acres or more of brown field site south of the proposed site which would be better suited to a BESS and it would have the protection of Bunds that are in situ. The issue with the proposed location increases the issues of loss of amenity and safety. The decision to site in that location cannot be understood or accepted as the location is unsuitable. There are more suitable sites in the area. We are also losing a network of Core paths which is devastating especially when everyone is trying to promote and encourage active travel as its good for the environment and our mental health. Safety Safety is a primary concern. Despite multiple requests for further assurances since August 2023, and the concerns raised in the community councils original response, [ORGANIZATION] have provided no further information in these new applications to reassure the community. An e-mail sent on 23 December 2024 to the Community Council finally provided confirmation that [ORGANIZATION] proposes to use Lithium-Ion batteries on the site (this information has been requested since August 2023). Lithium-Ion batteries are different to Lithium Iron Phosphate batteries (a specific type) and behave differently in relation to the risk of thermal runaway and in the emergency response. It is ludicrous and unbelievable that we were to comment on a BESS application with no information on the batteries they were intending to use. I also attended the very first meetings with [ORGANIZATION] representatives over a year ago and found they could not answer my questions then either. This seems to be a reoccurring theme from a company we are to trust. The Battery Storage Safety Management Plan prepared by National Fire Safety Services (Ltd) on two occasions states the presence of Lithium-ion Phosphate batteries on the site. Lithium-ion Phosphate is not a recognised technology. It was previously assumed that this was a typographical error for Lithium Iron Phosphate batteries, noted within the report as “relatively safer than other types of batteries”. The report must be discarded as deficient as it does not mention the possibility of the production of Hydrofluoric Acid from Hydrogen Fluoride which is possible in the event of fire. Without this consideration no other safety information contained in the report can be trusted. Where hydrofluoric acid production during an emergency is possible, a Plume Assessment, Evacuation Plan, and Emergency procedures must be considered. Due to the prevailing winds, in the event of a large accident, [PLACE] and the [PLACE] (the community’s primary emergency shelter) would both be down-wind, as would the main evacuation routes out of the village. The National Fire Chiefs Council guidance specifically identifies battery chemistry alongside various other measures which should be contained in an application, allowing Fire and Rescue Services to appropriately respond. I request a proper response from the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service. I have been informed that if there is a fire the only viable course of action would be to allow a fire to burn out over a course of days. It is researched and recommended that water as an extinguishant would not be used due to the risk of environmental contamination as the water would turn into hydrofluoric acid and would contaminate the ground and the water course, drains etc. Hydrofluoric acid is highly corrosive and the toxins produced are dangerous. The site is too close to our children's [PLACE], playpark and houses for this to happen. Why is there no Plume report, no evacuation plan, no warning system for the community as I for one wish to evacuate if there is a fire. I feel the application is not complete as several assessments and reports are missing. With all of these points considered, the current design of the site is unsuitable for the proposed location. Further work should be carried out such as a Plume Assessment, Evacuation Plan, and Emergency Response, involving Community Resilience and the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service, should also be undertaken Until such time there can be no true consideration of the absolute safety of the site, but the risks of this particular site are clearly higher than other possible sites due to their proximity to houses and core amenities of the community the overwhelming conclusion must be drawn that this site is not suitable for a BESS. EIA: Environmental Impact Assessment Examples, Methods & Steps When a project, policy change, or event has a chance of impacting any part of an environment or ecosystem, it’s important to do an environmental impact assessment (EIA). Not only is an EIA screening the responsible way to proceed with a project or plan, but it’s also often required by law to ensure that human interventions won’t cause undue harm or irreversible damage to the environment. An environmental impact assessment example would be the need to assess what a new manufacturing facility in a region means as far as air quality, water quality, noise pollution, ecosystem upset, and more. An environmental impact assessment project will look for effects, both positive and negative, on things like air and climate, land, water, ecology and biodiversity, and human environment. Is it not important that an EIA is carried out so as to ascertain the prevention of the contamination of drinking water for a community. Despite the challenges of environmental impact assessment in developing countries, the results can mean the difference between life or death. For example, in an underdeveloped community with rich natural resources, environmental impact assessment meaning can be the halt of a project that would ruin farmland and thus the community’s ability to thrive. An environmental impact assessment example will generally categorize impacts as: - Air and Climate: This includes things like air quality, health implications, ecosystem impacts, contributions to climate change, etc. - Land: This includes the use of non-renewable resources, changes to land morphology, impacts to historic or cultural sites, etc. - Water: This includes impacts on local drinking water, sustainability, the effect of local use for irrigation and other activities, health implications, etc. - Ecology & Biodiversity: This includes the importance of biodiversity value, both terrestrial and marine, economic use to the community, ecosystem well-being, etc. - Human Environment: This includes things like light and noise pollution, community safety, employment opportunities, community value creation, etc. - designing for location weather – consideration should be given to how weather at the selected battery site may impact operating capabilities or asset degradation. This formal objection is being lodged in response to planning application [APPLICATION_CODE] (Council Ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]) submitted by [ORGANIZATION] for the establishment of a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) near [PLACE], [PLACE], under the jurisdiction of the [ORGANIZATION]. This proposal is deemed unsuitable as it represents an inappropriate industrialisation of a serene rural area rich in heritage, posing risks to landscape, heritage, community safety, and the local environment. It would have an irreversible negative impact on the unique rural and historical character of [PLACE]. Despite claims of "limited visibility," the proposed BESS would be situated on an elevated site with clear views from roads and residences in the area, including significant tourist and heritage sites. Covering 5.5 hectares, its size is not in harmony with the surrounding farmland and coastal views. The application lacks strategic or locational justification for this particular site. There is no evident technical reason why this facility could not be located on brownfield or industrial land. The proximity to the approved [PLACE] appears to be the primary reason for its placement, rather than being based on any evidence-based national or regional planning rationale. Without clear siting criteria, rural communities in Scotland are left vulnerable to unplanned industrial developments that erode landscape quality and cohesion. Concerningly, the potential risks to local residents and the wider community from a fire or other incidents at the site have not been adequately addressed. Of particular concern is the site's proximity to [PLACE], a Category A Listed building, a royal heritage site, and a symbol of [PLACE], located just 1.8km away. The combined visual, symbolic, and reputational impact of a facility of this nature near such a significant landmark would be substantial. Landscape and Visual Impacts The proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) would be situated on open, elevated farmland within the Landscape Character Type (LCT) 143: Farmed Lowland Plain – a landscape cherished for its expansive skies, peaceful ambiance, and agricultural heritage. The visual impact of the project would be substantial, given its large industrial scale featuring more than 200 battery units, fencing, transformers, and the introduction of stark, metallic security infrastructure. This development would be clearly visible from nearby residences, public roads, and popular tourist routes such as the [PLACE]. Superficial landscaping efforts are inadequate in mitigating the long-lasting visual disruption to the landscape. The applicant's assessment significantly underplays both the immediate and cumulative visual impacts. In contravention of NPF4 Policy 11(e)(ii), the proposal neglects to thoroughly evaluate or address the considerable cumulative effects in conjunction with the [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], and [PLACE] infrastructure, all located within close proximity. Community Consultation and Planning Process This proposal was directly submitted to the Energy Consents Unit of the Scottish Government, circumventing local democratic planning oversight. There has been a lack of substantial public consultation with the residents of [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], or [PLACE]. In communities where the implications will be enduring and pervasive, this approach undermines environmental justice and contravenes the place-based policy ethos of NPF4. Consultations for the [ORGANIZATION] BESS were conducted independently of related developments in the area The community affected deserves a fair opportunity to voice their opinions on whether industrial energy infrastructure is suitable for their surroundings. Projects with significant local ramifications should be determined through meaningful local engagement, rather than being marginalized as mere footnotes in energy infrastructure discussions. Cultural Heritage - The [PLACE] The development site is situated within the wider context of [PLACE], a location of national heritage and royal importance. The historical and symbolic significance of the Castle has been carefully maintained over the years. Introducing a modern industrial complex in such a setting would detract from the overall ambiance and vistas of the Castle and its surrounding areas. This development could potentially compromise the experience of the thousands of tourists who visit annually. The proposed facility shows a lack of regard for the royal heritage of the Castle, which is closely linked to HM Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother. Furthermore, it contravenes NPF4 Policy 7(a) and the Historic Environment Policy for Scotland (HEPS), which mandate developers to conserve the character and environment of listed buildings, safeguard the cultural importance of designed landscapes, prevent or mitigate harm to historical assets, and consider the combined effects with nearby developments. None of these obligations have been met in this instance. There has been no comprehensive assessment of the visual environment or cumulative landscape impact from various viewpoints such as approach roads, the [PLACE] setting, and the Castle's vantage points. Visibility from key locations may change with the seasons or could be altered by the removal of trees. The [ORGANIZATION] BESS is not an isolated project but is part of a cluster of energy initiatives in the same vicinity, including the [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], and the extensive [PLACE] marine energy infrastructure. This cluster of projects is significantly reshaping the visual, ecological, and social landscape of the region. Despite the requirements set out in NPF4 Policy 11(e), a comprehensive Cumulative Impact Assessment (CIA) has not been submitted. The current approach of fragmented and piecemeal applications fails to provide a full picture of the combined impact of these developments. This lack of cumulative assessment is misleading decision-makers and the public, potentially allowing significant landscape changes to occur without adequate oversight, evaluation, or mitigation measures in place. Tourism and the Rural Economy The economy of [PLACE] is closely tied to its pristine landscapes, serene natural environment, and rich cultural heritage. Tourism plays a vital role in driving the economy, supporting local businesses, accommodation providers, artisanal industries, and historic sites. The region's allure stems from its rugged beauty, stunning coastal vistas, and historical landmarks, notably [PLACE], a popular destination for thousands of visitors each year. The presence of industrial energy infrastructure, like large-scale battery compounds, poses a threat to this unique charm by introducing visual clutter, noise pollution, and an industrial character that clashes with the rural tourism experience. The close proximity of the [ORGANIZATION] BESS to [PLACE] and the [PLACE] tourist route raises concerns about diminishing the quality of visitor experiences, potentially discouraging future tourism growth, and negatively impacting the delicate rural economy. This development proposal directly contradicts Scotland's objectives for sustainable tourism and the localized aspirations outlined in NPF4. Cumulative Impact The [ORGANIZATION] BESS is part of a larger complex of energy projects in the area that includes the [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], and the extensive [PLACE] marine energy infrastructure. This cluster of projects is significantly reshaping the visual, ecological, and social landscape of the region. Despite the requirements set out in NPF4 Policy 11(e), a comprehensive Cumulative Impact Assessment (CIA) has not been submitted. The current approach of fragmented and piecemeal applications fails to provide a full picture of the combined impact of these developments. This lack of cumulative assessment is misleading decision-makers and the public, potentially allowing significant landscape changes to occur without adequate oversight, evaluation, or mitigation measures in place. Environmental Impact The lack of an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) for a development of this magnitude, complexity, and sensitivity is a matter of great concern. Given the project's proximity to protected habitats, its potential interactions with existing infrastructure, and the possible impacts on water, biodiversity, heritage, landscape, and community well-being, an EIA should have been a mandatory requirement under the Town and Country Planning (Environmental Impact Assessment) (Scotland) Regulations 2017. The absence of an EIA deprives the project of thorough scrutiny, erodes public confidence, and raises doubts about the legality of the application process. This oversight represents a significant procedural deficiency and undermines the validity of any decision made without a comprehensive and transparent environmental assessment. Wildlife, Habitats and Biodiversity The installation of concrete surfacing, fencing, artificial lighting, and vegetation clearance would result in a significant disruption to the local ecosystem, creating a dead zone. This area is hydrologically linked to the [PLACE], which is internationally protected for migratory and overwintering birds. The potential impact on qualifying species, particularly the Greenland white-fronted geese, is being underestimated. The Ecological Impact Assessment (EcIA) falls short in capturing the seasonal presence of wildlife and undervalues important features such as field margins, foraging corridors, and wet habitats. The assessment only conducts minimal site surveys, which goes against the nature-positive principle outlined in NPF4 Policy 3 and the obligations of the EU Habitats Directive. Furthermore, this proposal poses a threat to biodiversity and the landscape under the guise of promoting green initiatives. It lacks evidence of nature restoration, biodiversity net gain, or responsible land use. The EcIA does not provide a measurable or actionable plan to showcase any positive impact on biodiversity. Industrialisation of Prime Agricultural Land The proposed development would result in the permanent sterilisation of 5.5 hectares of productive farmland, which has served as the foundation of rural livelihoods and land stewardship for generations in the area. The installation of hardstand, impermeable surfaces, high-voltage equipment, and fencing would render the land unsuitable for agricultural purposes, grazing, or promoting biodiversity. This directly conflicts with NPF4 Policy 5, which aims to protect prime agricultural land for the development of climate-resilient food systems and sustainable land management practices. Replacing arable land with speculative energy infrastructure undermines local resilience and jeopardises Scotland's objectives for food security. The industrialisation of rural areas through such projects represents a myopic and irreversible decision that fails to strike a balance between national infrastructure demands and local sustainability goals. Disruption to Local Residents and Amenity Noise, lighting, construction traffic, and operational disturbance will have a significant negative impact on the quality of life for local residents. Battery Energy Storage Systems are known to generate continuous operational noise, particularly from cooling fans, HVAC systems, transformers, inverters, and emergency fire suppression systems. Industry experts highlight that these systems can also produce constant background noise and tonal disturbances that can be more disruptive than their measured decibel levels, especially in quiet rural settings. The BS4142:2014([PLACE]:2019) standard acknowledges the increased nuisance of tonal noise in peaceful environments, a factor that has not been adequately addressed in the assessment. Additionally, there is a lack of effective measures to mitigate issues such as nighttime security lighting, disruptions during the construction phase (including dust, traffic, and noise), and the long-term impact on residential quality of life. The serene visual environment of the area is complemented by its peaceful soundscape, a crucial aspect that appears to have been overlooked in the evaluation. Grid Expansion and Landscape Fragmentation This proposal exemplifies a situation of grid-driven development, where infrastructure is chosen based not on strategic spatial planning or environmental compatibility, but solely on its proximity to existing grid assets. The approval of one energy facility sets the stage for further development, a trend often known as infrastructure creep. In [PLACE], this leads to the gradual transformation of open rural landscapes into zones for energy production and storage. These developments cut through and break apart cohesive landscape character areas, disturb natural views, and diminish the unique identity that defines rural communities. The [ORGANIZATION] BESS project would contribute to this incremental industrialisation and hasten the disappearance of regional landscape identity, contradicting the principles of landscape and community-focused planning outlined in NPF4. Road Network and Drainage The site can only be accessed through narrow single-track unclassified rural roads that are not suitable for heavy goods vehicles or construction traffic. The applicant has not provided a comprehensive traffic management plan, nor have they assessed the structural risks to road verges and bridges, or considered the cumulative impact of increased road use due to other local energy developments. The presence of construction traffic, heavy equipment, and future maintenance vehicles poses a risk of congestion, surface damage, and potential danger to local residents and livestock. The Drainage Impact Assessment (DIA) falls short of meeting the requirements set out in NPF4 Policy 22 (f) and [PLACE] LDP Policy 66 concerning sustainable drainage and water quality protection. It neglects to evaluate climate resilience, pollution containment, or runoff modelling. The installation of impermeable infrastructure such as container bases and roads is likely to exacerbate issues related to runoff. Fire and Safety Risks Large lithium-ion battery storage systems pose well-documented fire risks. While rare, these incidents can be severe, challenging to extinguish, and pose a threat to nearby individuals, animals, and emergency responders. The current Outline Battery Safety Management Plan (OBSMP) is deemed inadequate for several reasons. Firstly, it lacks a clear strategy for how emergency services would handle a thermal runaway event or toxic gas release. Furthermore, it does not address the absence of a nearby fire station or water hydrants. The plan also lacks evidence of consultation with the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service, a crucial stakeholder in ensuring effective emergency response. Moreover, the OBSMP fails to adequately address the heightened fire risk posed by the facility's rural location. Lithium-ion battery energy storage systems are particularly susceptible to prolonged and severe fires, which could have catastrophic consequences for life, property, and agricultural land in a low-resource area like this. It is imperative that these deficiencies in the safety management plan are rectified promptly, as the potential risks associated with lithium-ion BESS facilities cannot be ignored or underestimated, especially in remote locations where resources and response capabilities may be limited. Decommissioning and Restoration There is a lack of a legally binding decommissioning strategy or financial guarantee associated with this proposal. Without specific requirements and sufficient financial resources for site restoration, there is a significant risk of prolonged neglect. Once the infrastructure is established and profitability decreases, developers may lack motivation to carry out comprehensive site cleanup, landscape rehabilitation, or environmental remediation. This situation could result in the community being left with abandoned infrastructure, potential hazards of toxic contamination, and irreversible loss of land. NPF4 emphasises the importance of circular economy principles and obligations for post-operational restoration. However, the applicant has not even met the basic criteria for ensuring decommissioning security. Summary This proposal is of an industrial scale, lacking in justification, and fundamentally incompatible with the setting of a protected royal heritage site, local land use, and the planning principles outlined in NPF4 and HEPS. There is no proven national need for this facility at this particular location. The proposal would have significant negative impacts visually, ecologically, and socially. Approving this development would essentially sacrifice a valued rural community to unplanned infrastructure expansion, damaging the integrity of one of Scotland’s most iconic landscapes and undermining national policies on heritage, nature, and rural sustainability. This large-scale project offers no tangible community benefits, such as local employment guarantees, infrastructure improvements, or revenue sharing. There is no community vote, referendum, or meaningful community support in favor of this development. A project that has such a profound impact on daily life, health, heritage, and land should not be imposed without active, positive, and locally driven consent, which this development lacks. It goes against the core values of sustainability, place-based decision-making, heritage protection, and rural equity as outlined in NPF4. Furthermore, in conjunction with other developments in the area, this project would transform the iconic [PLACE] landscape into an extensive industrialized zone, permanently altering the local landscape and the historic rural setting of [PLACE], a site of national and symbolic importance. It is unacceptable to approve an industrial battery installation in such close proximity to a Royal heritage site based on speculation, incomplete evidence, and flawed policy application. This development directly contradicts the key objectives of NPF4, which prioritize rural protection, nature restoration, climate resilience, and community well-being. It also goes against the [PLACE] Council’s goal of preserving the cultural and environmental quality of [PLACE]. Introducing a large-scale battery compound in a rural landscape undermines these planning objectives and contributes to a pattern of rural sacrifice zones for national energy infrastructure. Rather than attempting to address or rectify the shortcomings in the application, I respectfully urge the Reporter and Scottish Ministers to reject consent for the [ORGANIZATION] BESS entirely, in order to uphold the long-term public interest in safeguarding the [PLACE] landscape and cultural environment.
