Poor Design and Materials Despite this being a 4 hectare site this choice of location is a poor choice of site as there is a high powered gas mainline pipe running at the southern tip of the site which is severely impacting on where these units can be sited within the field. There is also overhead pylons to the north. Both of these structures mean there is only a triangle in the centre of the field where the shipping containers can be placed with the larger side running adjacent to [PLACE]. The applicant has asked for ‘micrositing’ up to 25metres. As the current layout plans to put the site as far to the east as possible it means that if they do intend to use ‘micrositing’ the only way they will be able to move is to the west.closer to [PLACE]. The applicant plans to use lithium ion batteries. It should be noted that there are other types of batteries that are infinitely safer to use in grid systems. Vanadium redox batteries can remain discharged indefinity without any damage, they have no noise or emissions, have a longer discharge/charge cycle life so would not need to be replaced as frequently as 7 years like these lithium ion batteries and are non flammable. They are of course more expensive. There is a watercourse running adjacent to the western border of the site. As the applicant has highlighted, on the other side of the road there is a high risk of flooding and it has been known to cause flooding onto [PLACE] road in the past (a retaining wall had to be rebuilt as flooding destroyed this a few years ago). This area drains directly into the water course just before the location where the access road is proposed. The access road will directly run across this watercourse and the applicant has not included as part of the planning application a definitive plan as to how this will be addressed instead proposing some options of what could be done – a ford (impractical with the 5 foot drop from the road to the field directly into the stream) or culverting the water through what would be an approximately 30 metre pipe to cover the width of the access road at that point (risk of blockage and opening up questions as to how this will be maintained). The access road is depicted on the drawings to have a wide mouth opening which starts at the current bus stop and extends to the middle of the driveway at [PLACE] before eventually tapering to the 3 metre wide access road that they state in their plans. This opening is around 25 metres and highlights the difficulty they will have in manoeuvring these large containers around a greater than 90 degree angle (essentially turning back on themselves) onto the site both during construction and every 7 years for the sites 40 year lifespan. The applicant makes very little mention of how they will connect to the [PLACE] within the documents submitted. They informed us at the public consultation events that the plan would be to connect via underground cabling along the main road via [PLACE] to the substation greater than 4 miles away. By having it this far away from the grid there is an approximately 10% loss of transmission each way. This is of no concern to the applicant as they will still make substantial profits from the electricity they do store and sell back to the grid but if Scotland as a nation is going to be sensible about how they manage BESS developments then at this early stage in this technology we should not be locating these installations at the limit of their viability (which is 5 miles) and picking sites which maximise their potential. Visual Impact [PLACE] descends from [PLACE] towards [PLACE]. I have concerns that this means this industrial installation encompassing will be highly visible from the road for every [PLACE] resident that travels down the [PLACE] every day. The units being placed are shipping containers and painting them green or grey is going to have minimal impact on hiding them. The visualisations provided are frankly misleading. The water tank is incorrectly sized – its plan states it is 4 metres tall therefore should be one of the highest buildings on site – yet it is shown on the visualisations as smaller than the BESS units at 2.9 metres. For example a picture taken at [PLACE] at [PLACE] is not representative of the majority of the communities view and has been taken behind a hill. In one case they have specifically stood behind a tree to take a photo (VP01)! The picture at the underpass has been taken through the trees – move 10 metres uphill beyond this point and this creates an entirely different vista – with direct views over the hedgerow onto the installation. There is no picture that demonstrates the vast majority of the communities view point on a daily basis– just above the mid Borland turn off where you descend from [PLACE]. The hedgerows planned are double root stock being planted in two rows. The applicant has stated it will take 15 years for these to reach the height of the perimeter fencing of 2.4metres (no mention of reaching the 2.9m height of ) The plans are for the batteries to be raised up on concrete pads on top of a permeable underlayer and the area needs to be flat and high enough due to the fact that they have admitted that this is waterlogged site (which will be compounded by the heavy plants compacting the soil on the site.) By the time the permeable road and the concrete pads are installed it seems highly likely that a degree of land raising will have occurred. The applicants are not taking into consideration any form of shielding the appearances from the [PLACE] side, relying on the existing tress that are not on the land that they will be leasing. There are two large gaps that view into the field from the [PLACE] in a location where slow/standstill traffic is often present. In the winter the existing trees offer no shielding and even in summer there would be a direct line of sight towards the BESS units and their ancillary structures through the gaps. The applicant plans to put the access road directly opposite a [PLACE] which is so listed because it is an example of a late 18th or early 19th century farmhouse. Part of the charm of any listed building is the setting within which it resides. An access road to an industrial unit directly opposite this markedly changes this setting. The European landscape convention in there document Guidelines for landscape and visual impact assessment (GLVIA3), as quoted in the landscape and visual appraisal report state that “landscape is an area, as perceived by people, whose character is the result of the action and interaction of natural and/or human factors” they go on to say “character is not just about the physical elements and features that make up a landscape, but also embraces the aesthetic, perceptual and experiential aspects of the landscape that make different places distinctive. it concerns more than simply the appearance”. Essentially in applying this statement to the [PLACE] community who pride themselves on being a conservation village, the impact of this very visible development to the community, will be sorely felt. At the second public consultation the attendees were told that there would be 16 BESS units in the form of standardized shipping containers. It is therefore disappointing to note that along with the 16 6.06 x 2.9 m standard shipping containers there will also be 8 larger 12.16 x 2.44m shipping containers marked as ‘PVC’. They have been disingenuous regarding this. The applicant has asked for permission to undertake ‘micrositing’ by up to 25 metres from the original position. This means, because they are limited by the pylons and high pressure gas pipeline that converge on the east border of the site, the realistic position change they can make is to move the containers closer to [PLACE]. Concerns over this Type of Company I have major concerns about allowing a limited company with no liability to construct a BESS. The public consultations were done on behalf of [ORGANIZATION] by [ORGANIZATION] (as detailed in the newspaper article on page 6 of the [ORGANIZATION] public consultation report). All three of these companies have the same director. It concerns me that this current organisation is a limited company. Unless they have personal guarantees they are able to walk away from any venture at any stage with no comeback. Bearing in mind the equipment being placed is potentially dangerous, if they did choose to abandon the site at any stage after the ground was dug who would take responsibility for a now brownfield site that may require decommissioning of hazardous materials, would it be the Scottish government, [ORGANIZATION] themselves or the land owner? NPF4 policy 11 states that project design and mitigation will demonstrate that they can “guarantee availability of finances” around site restoration plans. As this would in 40 years time I would be keen to know how this could be guaranteed with such a volatile group of companies. [ORGANIZATION] has no experience in the installation of BESS developments and neither does [ORGANIZATION]. Excess Noise Levels The applicant states that they are not putting in any noise mitigation. The batteries omit a continual humming noise due to the need for air conditioning units to cool them. [PLACE] is used heavily by people walking between [PLACE] as well as cyclists using the road to head primarily towards the windfarm. These developments will be audible for these area users. When the council are trying to encourage the use of walking and cycling a development that will deter this goes against ERC’s policies. Environmental Considerations The flow of the water run off travels from the middle of the western border of the site directly under the proposed placement of the batteries to the north-eastern most tip and then drains into the [PLACE]. In the event of a fire if any water was applied due to the permeable underlayer the water, now contaminated with hydrofluoric acid, would drain into one of Glasgow’s major rivers causing significant environmental impact. There is a large site of special scientific interest ([PLACE]) of ancient woodland on the eastern side of the river at [PLACE]. Bats roost in the tress in the surrounding area. The ecological report confirms that this is likely in 4 of the trees surrounding the site and residents have confirmed that bats reside within the area. I would have concerns that this project would impact on their habitat as well as the security lights disturbing their natural behaviours. The preliminary ecological appraisal states that the current landscape is of low ecological value but could recommended three measures to enhance the biodiversity. The three recommendations (development of a SUDS pond, creation of a herptile hibernaculum and creation of species rich native grassland that have been suggested) have not been taken on by the applicant and therefore what they are proposing reduces the ecological value of the site rather than adding to it. The access road once the site is operational appears to have no gate planned at [PLACE]. As this is an unmanned site, and with no gate barring access I believe that it will be very easy for fly tipping to occur on this road especially in relation to the ease of access form the [PLACE] and the fact that that design of the access road will allow easy access for large vehicles. Light Pollution The applicant plans to put in put in three 4 metre tall posts that will house CCTV and security lighting. They state that “it will not be illuminated at night time other than by intruder activated security lighting. The ecological report states that a 10cm gap should be left on the perimeter fence so that badgers can get onto the site. This space would allow relatively large sized animal onto the site which could trigger the lights. In addition bats and owls fly in the area and I would be concerned that they would trigger the security lights frequently. Community Benefits In there statement of community involvement the applicant states that a Community Wealth Building Plan accompanies the planning application – I have not seen any attached document to this effect to this planning application. This community has already taken on its fair share of energy related infrastructure in the area with [PLACE], the largest onshore windfarm in Europe, being on our doorstep NPF4 (Scotland’s fourth national planning framework) states that community benefits should be put in place for developments such as this. From the applicant’s proposal they seem to think that offering jobs in the local area is sufficient to say that the community is being benefited. In conclusion, please take the above objection points into consideration, as part of your duty of care responsibility for myself as a local resident to the proposed application site.

Development in a Green Belt location In the planning documents, the applicant listed their selection criteria and reasoning to arrive at the chosen location. It is not clear, how the applicant has justified why the green belt location is essential and why it cannot be located on alternative sites either directly next to existing generation sites or within the confines of [PLACE] Industrial Estates close to the [PLACE] sub-station located in [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE]. The chosen land is good quality agricultural land used for growing arable crops each year and grazing to livestock in the Winter in at least the last decade. Siting the access road, parking area and BESS facility removes that land from its current agricultural use. The surrounding countryside, as shown on the applicant’s planning documents, is an open outlook of gently rolling countryside. The proposal to add an industrial unit generating noise and light pollution with 2.4 metre high security fencing is NOT compatible with the surrounding countryside. Its external appearance and use of metal buildings, metal switchgear and metal fencing is not in harmony with the rolling fields with low boundary walls and hedges Given this is a long term industrial site with a working life of 20+ years, it is reasonable to assume there will be unplanned incidents. Given that the chosen site is less than 50 metres upslope from the [PLACE], and spillage of chemical, fuel, oil, or any failure of the drainage system to collect and treat all liquid run-off is likely to pollute the [PLACE]. This would mean long term damage to the local environment. The chosen site is next to a heronry breeding location on the [PLACE], less than 155 from a badger sett, sited in a Roe Deer, Buzzard and Red Kite feeding zone. The long term (20+ years) noise and light from the BESS will mean harm and disruption to the local wildlife mentioned above. Set a precedent for industrial use in a Green Belt location The chosen site is in a relatively remote undisturbed Green Belt location which is home and feeding ground to much wildlife. It is reached by travelling circa 1.4km down a farm lane. By siting an industrial installation in this remote untouched location sets a precedent that will mean more developments could follow thus eroding away the green belt to nothing. Harmful to nature and biodiversity The area of greenbelt is home to various wildlife and feeding area for many more. The close proximity of a heronry on the [PLACE] bank and a badger sett 150m to the North East of the site means those wildlife will be affected by the construction and operation of a new industrial site. Local honey bee hives are within 300m of the site. Red Kite have only been living and hunting in this area since 2023 and this new industrial unit would be within its feeding area. Visual Impact Objection The surrounding area has low agricultural walls and hedges to divide fields. The adjacent fields are used for arable farming. The security fencing at 2.4m height and battery storage containers at 2.645m height would present an unnatural and imposing visual impact to countryside users and the nearby housing properties, particularly the dwellings [PLACE] Farmhouse and [PLACE], both within 100m of the site. Not in keeping with surroundings The chosen land is good quality agricultural land used for growing arable crops each year and grazing to livestock in the Winter in at least the last decade. Siting the access road, parking area and BESS facility removes that land from its current agricultural use. The surrounding countryside, as shown on the applicant’s planning documents, is an open outlook of gently rolling countryside. The proposal to add an industrial unit generating noise and light pollution with 2.4 metre high security fencing and 2.645m high buildings is NOT compatible with the surrounding countryside. Its external appearance and use of metal buildings, metal switchgear and metal fencing is not in harmony with the rolling fields with low boundary walls and hedges. Prime agricultural land loss The agricultural land on the proposed site and access road is used to grow barley in Spring/Summer and graze livestock in Autumn/Winter months. It is not, as described within the proposers documents, low value land. This development proposal would mean the loss of such valuable land to domestic grain production. The consequence of this would in its widest sense mean that grain would have to be imported from overseas to replace that amount lost. Surely this is not economic and environmental good sense. Noise nuisance In the proposer’s documents noise levels from background noise at [PLACE] Farmhouse are 49 dBA and nighttime 40 dBa. ( section 6.61 of noise assessment document) These are significantly different to the adjacent planning proposal [APPLICATION_CODE]. (section 5.2.4 of the appendix 3 noise assessment) In this noise assessment, the daytime background level for [PLACE] Farmhouse is 45dBa and nightime background level is 33 dBa This discrepancy in noise measurement, an exact science, means the veracity of the results of either, must be questioned. Thus the planning documents proposed for the BESS at this site cannot be relied upon to reliably predict the noise nuisance. The daytime and nighttime background levels are based upon averages of noise which has peaks and troughs. The sound emanating from the BESS is a constant level nuisance. Thus predicting that the site sound is negligible above background levels is misleading. The applicant has tried to equate two noise levels that are NOT equivalent (one continuous from site, one intermittent and variable background). This once again begs the question as to whether the applicant knows what they are doing or are they deliberately trying to confuse the public. Light pollution The chosen site is in the fields, well away from street lamps/industrial lighting and thus the site lighting is introducing an unwanted new source of light pollution for local residents and countryside users. Consultation Process inadequate before reaching planning application stage. The proposal for the BESS site held consultation sessions and zero visitors attended. The first time we knew about this proposal was when [PLACE] Planning notification arrived informing us of a nearby planning application. What was even more of a surprise was that the proposal suggests modifying our garden, trees and garden fence at the end of the farm access lane where it meets [PLACE]. No one from the proposing/applicant company had contacted us to either discuss or ask our permission. This showed that the planning applicant did not use reasonable endeavours to contact us about our owned land! Planning Application process not complied with. The planning applicant did not follow due process, nor common decency, to seek our permission to modify my garden and lower my garden wall in modifying the entrance to the farm access lane off [PLACE] before putting in their planning application. The removal of two mature trees within my garden near that junction may also occur. As such, I withhold my permission to modify any of my property. Within the planning application document, dated 31st Jan 2025, page 6 of 8 is factually incorrect. The applicant states he owns all of the land for the proposed development. The development includes a proposal to modify the access from [PLACE] onto the circa 1.4km farm access lane. We are the owner of that land. Despite this revision to the planning application, the applicant, nor his agents have (still) not contacted us to ask our permission to modify our garden. I reiterate that we withhold permission to modify any of my property. Site Design not following best practice. The site design is shown on drawing number [APPLICATION_CODE], a scaled drawing. The dimensions of each battery storage unit are shown on drawing number TES-HWYLG1118.2KW-0001 REV B, 1.554m width by 7.80m length. Should an maintenance or replacement of batteries individual or a complete storage unit, then there is not sufficient space around the units shown in the site design drawing to access for repair and maintenance purposes. The space between each unit is approximately half of the width of a unit, thus approximately 0.75m on the long (length) side and approximately 0.3m on the short width. If access is needed for emergency response reasons, then a fire appliance cannot fit in the 1.75m space between the battery storage units or in the 0.3m space on the ends. This is not even sufficient for firefighters on foot trying to fight the fire. Note in the fire risk management plan, document number [APPLICATION_CODE], it states in point 4.10 that “building placement is designed in accordance with BRE 187:2014 - External Fire Spread: Building Separation and Boundary Distances”. The scaled drawing of the site design does not reflect this statement. Conservatively calculating the distance for a highly insulated building under the above design code, the separation should be in excess of 2m. The site design shows equipment arranged on one side (NE side) of the compound and vehicular access along the SW length of the compound. If an emergency vehicle attends the site, there is no space to turn around or bring in other vehicles. Thus the design is not fit for emergency response access. The presence of tree planting next to the NE side of the compound for screening purposes is close to the battery containers. If there is a fire, then the tree planting would become another fuel source for that fire because of its close proximity, escalating the spread of the emergency. Construction phase Issues The chosen site is located approximately 1.4km down a 2.5m width farm access lane. This lane is surfaced with compacted hardcore/crumbling layer or tarmac. During periods of regular movement of farm HGV level vehicles (tractor and trailers loaded with grain or bales of straw) the surface quickly gets ripped up and maintenance is required. The construction management plan, document [APPLICATION_CODE] states that an estimated 307 HGV journeys will be undertaken, up to a maximum of 15 in one day. The farmers lane is not constructed of suitably robust materials to withstand this level of use. Over the length of the approximate 1.4km farmers lane, there are no laybys or passing places suitable for HGV (nor LGV vehicles nor vans no cars). In addition, there will be daily movement of site workers for 9 months of up to 20 vehicles per day. One side of the lane is bounded by a stream and the other side has a ditch for part of the way, there are also mature trees on both sides of the lane along the full length, so there is little room for manoeuvre. The construction management plan has not fully considered how to control vehicle movements up and down the lane, not provided for ‘staging points’ at either end of the lane such that the vehicle movements can be adequately controlled to one vehicle at any time moving along the farm lane. This construction management plan is naive in its formulation and shows the applicant has an unrealistic view of the real life situation. The revised application dated 5th February states that passing places will be fabricated. I draw attention to the above facts about ditches, stream and mature trees that it is not feasible to fabricate passing places along most of the farm lane. This revision of the traffic management plan remains naive. The access onto the farmers lane from its junction on Whistestripes road is proposed to be modified by altering our garden and garden wall. The removal of two mature trees within my garden near that junction may also occur. Since no one from the applicant company has contacted us, we have not given our permission for such things to occur. Whitestripes road is a classified unnumbered road with light traffic. The movement of 307 HGV vehicle deliveries plus up to 20 daily construction member transport vehicles represents a significant increase in traffic on that minor road. There is a difficult geometry on the junction of Whitestripes road and the B997 road in both directions to and from site. At that junction, the Whitestripes road narrows and there is not room for two HGV vehicles width. The likelihood of road traffic accidents is thus increased beyond acceptable levels. Operation phase Issues The layout of the equipment on the site is not conducive to repair and replacement. There is not enough room for vehicular access onto the site. For instance, for battery unit replacement or individual battery cell replacement, the necessary vehicles cannot get close to the battery units to deliver the spares/replacements. This then presents a manual handling issue, which is not recognised in any of the planning submission documents. Health, Safety and Environmental Aspects The site construction is inferred to be compacted hardcore. This is not confirmed. There is no mention of an impermeable concrete base. Thus liquid run off will easily reach the [PLACE], a mere 50m away down slope. There is no bunding in place to contain any form of spills. The site pond with a drainage system is not detailed enough to understand how polluted liquid is contained. This level of information is inadequate on which to make a decision about the planning application. It is also inadequate considering what the downside is of getting the drain design wrong and polluting the [PLACE]. Should fire engines be required to attend the site, they would have to drive along farm lane from Whitestripes road down to the site is 2.5m wide and with no passing places. So access would be hindered. When arriving at site, there is no mains water supply, and thus hydrants, in that area, all houses have private well supply. So if a fire engine required additional water, it would have to drive elsewhere to take on water, thus prolonging the emergency. Missing Information in planning application The BESS operates on the principle of importing surplus electricity during night periods and exporting it during peak use times. The details of the import/export cable and routing are not in the planning application. Thus the planning application has insufficient detail on which to make a decision about the planning application. I know that the farm lane has telephone and fibre utilities buried alongside it and has gas transmission line(s) crossing under it. If that is where the import/export cables are proposed to be routed, then careful explanation of how it can be achieved is needed. This is a serious omission from the planning application and once again does not give the people responsible for making a decision enough information. The owner of the land which is proposed to be modified at the entrance to the farm lane from Whitestripes road has been missed of the planning application. That owner is myself and I have not been spoken with nor asked about permission to modify my land.

I am writing to object the Installation of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at land to North East of [PLACE], [APPLICATION_CODE]. Firstly, my objection in general terms is the further industrialisation of rural areas and the impact on an agricultural area that already has significant Energy infrastructure. Currently it is not possible to look in any direction from this area without seeing excessive amounts of windmills and pylons (both at land and at Sea). By approving this BESS within this area it will present a further huge impact on our natural countryside, wildlife, and prime agricultural land. If approved it will be adding more industrial infrastructure to an already industrially congested rural area and potentially setting precedence for even more future industrial development of a rural setting. This is wholly unacceptable to anyone who values our countryside and the well-being of its residents and inhabitants. Below I lay out more pointed reasons that I object this development. Each of these objections has merit individually and collectively. NON-ESSENTIAL INFASTRUCTURE We are already 3x above the 2045 target for net zero in the area so this is not a required facility. Within the [PLACE] catchment area there is currently 102MW of intermittent renewable energy generation online or awaiting construction, that could benefit from energy storage backup. Within the same area code, there is currently 130MW of BESS approved and awaiting construction; that leaves 28MW of excess energy storage capacity already due to come online. This local overcapacity (combined with national capacity well on the way to far exceed 2045 targets), demonstrates that no further BESS sites are necessary and should not be considered as 'essential infrastructure' within this area. As non-essential infrastructure, building this BESS will in fact be in conflict with any Green Agenda or Policy as we will be destroying natural land and expending resource and creating pollution on a scheme that provides Zero benefit due to overcapacity in supply. The environmental impact of manufacturing all items that would be installed at this site must be considered along with the destruction of agricultural land. Also, the civil engineering work utilising plant and equipment, transportation, construction of access roads, installation of foundations, and all building activities associated with the placement of these units which is not required. Where this BESS would connect to the grid, and the distance between this site and the grid connection, also has to be considered in the context of Non-Essential Infrastructure (See INADEQUATE LOCATION below) FLOOD CONCERNS The land is in a flood prone area as advised by SEPA. It has a high likelihood (10%) of annual surface flooding. Severe flooding and run off can regularly be witnessed in the area of the proposed BESS (as anyone who uses this road can confirm). The run off from [PLACE] and its natural reservoirs is significant, especially after periods of sustained rain, significant down pours, or during winter when the ground is frozen and impermeable. It is generally understood and accepted that these conditions will only get worse due to climate change and predicted weather patterns - so we can anticipate that flooding will be worse than historically experienced. When flooding does happen then any contamination will leak into the [PLACE] which will damage our wildlife, pollute the water and cause significant negative effects. Further consideration should also be made of the nearby area that these waters discharge into the sea: [PLACE] is an [ORGANIZATION] [PLACE] and any potential contamination could have a significant detrimental effect on the birdlife. Thermal runaway is a major health risk for our local community and wildlife. Current policies do not permit development in flood risk areas unless for essential infastructure. As previously noted, this is not essential due to the overcapacity of BESS. However, taking this out of the equation, there has been no valid points raised as to why this location is the most appropriate for linking to a substation that is miles away, taking up prime agricultural land, invading an area thriving with wildlife and surrounded by residential properties. There is also no clarity provided for this development on how this BESS would be connected to the substation - several miles of ditches and cabling adding to the Net Positive impact of a site that simply is not required? There are two main areas relating to my flood concerns. The first is natural flooding (which already occurs on a regular basis), and the second is flooding in a fire scenario where, as has been experienced elsewhere, substantial amounts of water have to be used over extended periods of time to control battery fires. INADEQUATE LOCATION It is understood the location of this application is a considerable distance from the substation that it is being connected to. Although nothing in the application states where this is actually being connected to? Therefore, a report should be commissioned into where this is being connected to and how they propose to do this without causing unjustifiable disruption and damage. At the initial consultation it was advised that it is due to be connected to [PLACE] and this location was carefully considered due to the close proximity to [PLACE]. The location of [PLACE] substation, which is now the presumed substation due to initial plans with [PLACE] not going ahead, is between 7.4 miles and 11 miles away depending on the route they take. Therefore, requiring major disruption to our local community during the digging to allow the cables to be placed in the ground. This road is a [PLACE] bus route and if closed is going to impact our children getting to [PLACE], along with locals getting to work and going about their daily routine. This route would need to cross the [PLACE] and would cause significant disruption to place significant quantities of cabling all this way along single track roads. It is hard to justify that this scheme and location has any logical or reasonable benefit in reaching net zero. Common sense determines that if this development is absolutely necessary, then a location near the substation is the right thing to avoid disruption to roads, noise pollution from diggers, air pollution and emissions from construction plant running in excess due to the distance required to be dug up, disruption to countryside digging up verges and therefore disturbing wildlife which may inhabit these areas. There is simply no logic that can reasonably support this as a reasonable chosen location for a BESS. I would request that a report is commissioned into why this is even considered an appropriate location, and seek clarity on the connection point to the grid which appears to be a substantial distance away? ACCESS ROAD CONCERNS Another major concern is that having the stated 21 vehicles and one HGV per day accessing the site on multiple occasions for an extended duration. Plus the cranes etc that will inevitably be involved with construction activity and loading and offloading of battery and associated units. The road is already in very poor condition (probably due to the flooding mentioned above). It has significant pot holes which get very deep very quickly due to wash out. What measures would be taken to ensure the condition of this road is not worsened by the increased volume of traffic during construction, and what will be done to ensure the road is returned to its current condition (or better) after construction There is no slip off from the [PLACE] to turn onto the single carriageway road and this is extremely dangerous for a car, having more and larger vehicles turning off is definitely going to increase the risk of a road traffic accident HGV type vehicles will need to come to an almost complete stop on the duel carriageway before turning off due to the tightness of the turn off. Knowing the behaviours of drivers on this fast stretch of road will most definitely cause accidents. Equally heading North and turning onto the [PLACE], the middle area at the intersection, that does not even fit a car comfortably, will be so dangerous for a HGV. Heading South will be HGVs turning into a Major Road without the benefit of any slip road to gain speed. CLOSE PROXIMITY TO HOMES & NATURAL RESOURCE This proposed area is encircled by properties who will all be directly impacted by the building of this BESS. The noise and light pollution emitted from it will be significant due to how open this area is. If it was to go on fire this would be a major concern for loss of property, loss of woodland, loss of protected wildlife, and health complications. Situated right next to woodland which is currently being replanted, and being in such a windy spot, this could get out of control very quickly. Recent fires of battery storage have proven that they will burn for days. The toxic chemicals leaked from this are a massive health concern for nearby residents and wildlife and these concerns also need to be considered as part of the Planning consideration. FIRE RISK As well established by media reports BESS carry significant risk of substantial fire. The fumes from a thermal runaway can be fatal to anyone present, including first responders. Via the Media we are also advised that such fires burn for at least a few days until it has burnt out. Given the proximity to houses this is not an acceptable scenario. The proposed plan states that there will be a pond, however, this only has enough to provide initial firefighting for 2 hours. The [ORGANIZATION] guidance states that there is no way to extinguish a BESS fire so it is difficult to understand how the pond is deemed adequate and simply increases the concern of local residents of an uncontrolled fire scenario. NOISE IMPACT The noise impact assessment needs to be reviewed and reconsidered as it appears to be inadequate and contains anomalies which are neither explained nor understood. Within the Report itself it states that the findings were considered unusual. It is also understood that the noise surveys were not carried out at all property locations adjacent to the site (i.e. [PLACE]). With these anomalies and omissions it is clear that a proper noise assessment has not been conducted and the proposer has not determined any level of suitability and acceptability. Environmental Considerations The flow of the water run off travels from the middle of the western border of the site directly under the proposed placement of the batteries to the north-eastern most tip and then drains into the [PLACE]. In conclusion, please take the above objection points into consideration, as part of your duty of care responsibility for myself as a local resident to the proposed application site.

This response has been prepared on the premiss that the proposals are unacceptable and the writer objects to the development in the strongest terms. It is acknowledged that renewable energy is essential for maintaining a reliable, ecological source of electricity, which will gradually mitigate the need for other, more polluting, forms of production, such as gas, coal, and nuclear. It is recognised that the physics of producing electricity using, for example, wind energy results in spikes of supply, which do not correspond with demand times and that storage is required to smooth out the availability of electricity for consumers. What is not accepted is the justification for locating such a facility on greenfield land, immediately beside dwellings and land where livestock is being raised. This response looks at the documents compiled by [ORGANIZATION] and their team. It raises concerns, highlights relevant issues and poses questions, to which written responses are required. SUBMITTED DOCUMENTS This response is based on the majority of the documents submitted. Those referred to appear to have most relevance to the arguments being presented. Battery energy storage facility with associated infrastructure, substation, security fencing, CCTV, security lighting and landscaping on land near [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE] (Grid Reference: X 251181, Y 674239) This is an overarching, introductory document and so more general observations of the proposals and questions have been included here. LOCATION The document implies that the site is in a remote location. It does not mention the residential properties that lie immediately adjacent to the development site, which will be severely impacted by the proposals. Why can the facility not be located on brownfield, formerly industrial land where this type of use is established? It is understood the grid infrastructure, located adjacent to the facility, will NOT be used for the distribution of the electricity being stored here; instead, the [PLACE], some 30km to the north east will be used ([ORGANIZATION] Consultants’ website “Why was this Location Chosen?”). So, there is no practical reason why the development needs to be on this particular greenfield site. VISUAL IMPACT The site is located in open countryside, so will be highly visible from near and far views to the detriment of the area. The site is on sloping exposed ground, which ensures the views to the site are maximised. No amount of screening planning will prevent this, in the short to medium term. OTHER DETRIMENTAL IMPACT Sound - Please confirm the source of sound and the sound levels that will be produced from the facility. Local residents would expect a zero-decibel impact at their property, given the rural nature of the setting. Wildlife Habitat - The development will destroy 29 hectares (or 36.2 hectares, according to the [ORGANIZATION] Consultants’ website) of natural habitat and farmland; more if road widening goes ahead. This alone is reason to force the developers to seek out an urban brownfield site for this facility. Global loss of habitat is not being taken seriously enough and the reduction in wild places and biodiversity will have direct consequences for humanity, if this is not halted now. Walking interest - The immediate area of the site is a place of significant walking interest, with the site bounded on three sides by core paths and with many other routes of access to and around the surrounding countryside and the [PLACE] including the long distance route, the [PLACE], which goes along the eastern boundary of the proposed development. Pre-historic rock art - The proposed development impacts on one of the densest and most accessible accumulations of pre-historic rock art in Scotland’s central belt. The proposed development site at [PLACE] has seven cup and ring marked rocks along the boundary, and 9 more within 250m of the boundary. The [PLACE], which is one of the most important and most extensive pieces of prehistoric rock art in Scotland lies only 500m from the boundary of the development. The site dominates the Neolithic landscape of [PLACE] and would significantly impact on the setting of the stones. SCALE The development is of a scale inappropriate to its location. How was the scale of this development established? HEALTH and SAFETY Fire - Any outbreak of fire at the facility will be a significant hazard to health, directly from heat and flame but perhaps more significantly from the dangerous pollutants that will be released should fire take hold. Ground Contamination - Any leakage from the batteries will contaminate the surrounding land. Leaching of leaked chemicals/toxins to adjacent properties will present risk to life/health. Provide written confirmation that there are no such risks from the installation and that the ground can be given back to farming or other natural rural uses once the site is abandoned. Air contamination - Do the batteries issue any fumes or gases in operation. It is assumed that any malfunction of the batteries or damage to their containment will result in the release of toxic chemicals into the airborne environment. COSHH Regulations. Please provide a written report on all chemical substances used within the battery storage units. Any contamination of the environment, as a result of the development, will affect the health and wellbeing of local residents and the flourishing wildlife here. Risks for vandalism/terrorism. - The rural nature of the site means that supervision and security will be difficult to control and any unwanted events will lack the rapid response that could be put in place within a more urban setting. ROADS and ACCESS [PLACE] is a winding, single track road with poor surface and a steep gradient. It is wholly unsuited to this type of development. The traffic generated by both construction works and the operation of the facility will be extremely hazardous for local users. To increase the width of the road would be detrimental to the rural character of the area, would destroy habitat and reduce biodiversity. The gradient and topography will not result in a road which is safe for all users. [PLACE] is a fast commuter route and the access point, where [PLACE] joins this is already hazardous, given its close proximity to the blind corner to the west. Adding large construction vehicles and increased traffic during operation of the site is likely to exacerbate accident rates here, significantly. Historic Environment Desk-based Assessment “The available archaeological records suggest that there is some limited potential for the survival of prehistoric period remains within the study site. The study site is likely to have remained in agricultural use through the medieval and post-medieval periods. It is possible that buried remains relating to medieval or early post-medieval agriculture, such as ploughing or field boundary features, could survive, but these would be considered to be of negligible significance.” The study, which resulted in these conclusions was desk-based, so it cannot be stated, at this stage, that any remains would be of “negligible significance”. The presence of the nearby [PLACE] and Neolithic – Bronze Age Cup and Ring markings alone must raise concerns whether this site is suitable for development. Other historic features and events are noted within the study site. The quantity of notes of historical interest within and surrounding the study site requires that a full scheme of site investigation works be carried out, both at application stage and ongoing during installation. It seems highly probable that further examples of significant heritage value would be destroyed, should the development be allowed to progress to site. Item 5.2.7 makes reference to the views to the site, which will be possible from local landmarks but that “the proposals would have no significant impact upon the setting of this part of the WHS”. This cannot be for the applicant to decide and must be independently and impartially assessed. Even if the battery storage units can be installed without any disruptive excavation being carried out, potential leakage from the batteries will contaminate sub-surface archaeology. NOTE other documents submitted make reference to cut and fill operations, which would destroy any archaeology in the affected area. The conclusion to this report focuses on designated heritage, however it is the undiscovered archaeology that must be identified and protected here. The report highlights human activity across the site, continuously, from the earliest times. Another site with less historic interest should be considered. Photographs - The photos annexed to this document show clearly the site’s elevated and prominent position. It has commanding views out to the city and surrounding countryside, so views to the site will be equally clear. Notice to the Scottish Ministers. to construct and operate a battery energy storage facility. The Notice describes the development as: “.battery energy storage facility with associated infrastructure, substation, security fencing, CCTV, security lighting and landscaping” The visual impact of security fencing surrounding the site will be inappropriate and out of keeping in a rural area. Security lighting cannot be entertained in a rural area. Light pollution will have a detrimental impact on the amenity and wellbeing of local residents. Further, lighting of this type is known to have a detrimental effect on night-flying creatures like bats. The light alters their flight paths and interferes with their feeding patterns. [ORGANIZATION] [ORGANIZATION] has been appointed to act on behalf of the developer, [ORGANIZATION]. Their website contains a section, titled “How will the local community benefit from this proposal?” This goes on to explain “The proposed battery storage facility will benefit UK consumers as a whole by facilitating the supply of low-cost, low carbon electricity on the national grid.” In fact, [ORGANIZATION] are unable to state ANY benefits to the local community from this development. Pre-application Consultation Report - [ORGANIZATION] No comment at this stage. Design and Access Statement (DDA) - [ORGANIZATION] The Introduction (item 1.4) makes reference to: “Policy 14 of the National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4) states how the planning system should “encourage, promote and facilitate well designed development that makes successful places by taking a design-led approach and applying the Place Principle.” Annex D of NPF4 then lays out the ‘Six Qualities of Successful Places’, with quality number 2 ‘Pleasant’ emphasising the importance of creating “attractive and welcoming” places which mitigate against noise, air and light pollution, as well as avoiding undesirable features.” This is indefensible. There is not a single instance, in this development, where “design” can be seen to have been used. The battery facility will be a scar on the landscape; its location and topography will exacerbate its inappropriate scale and the batteries themselves are industrial in nature. The site enclosure and floodlighting will be reminiscent of a high security institution. (item 1.5) Place Principle. Whilst public consultation has taken place, this has only alerted the local community to the blight to the countryside and their lifestyle, which is proposed here. Property values will be destroyed and the rural amenity local people have enjoyed, will be removed. Discussions with local people cannot and will not result in this development becoming acceptable. The very nature of the proposal is so alien to this place that no amount of “tweaking” will resolve concerns. (item 2.1) The Site. The DDA states the facility will connect to the grid via [PLACE] and [PLACE] substations. This is different to the information on AAH’s website (see above) but nevertheless, these substations are remote from this site, reinforcing the suggestion this location is not critically important to the functioning of the grid feed-in. (item 2.3) Flooding. Please confirm if the SEPA records, referred to, factor-in climate change? SEPA is updating their data, currently, to reflect climate change and this often results in a very different picture for sites where a low risk was indicated previously. NPF4 recommends that no development should take place on land at risk of flooding and certainly, where electricity and hazardous chemicals are involved, this must surely be avoided completely. NOTE Raising of equipment to avoid flooding will only increase the visual impact of the proposals. (item 3.4) Sustainability. This development is not sustainable if leakage from batteries renders the land barren and unusable for future generations and these risks have not been explored, fully. (item 3.5) Mitigation. How will the loss of natural habitat be mitigated? Were the development located on brownfield land, this would not be an issue. (item 3.7) Planning. Since this application will be determined by the Scottish Ministers and NOT the local planning authority, please confirm how the planning system will form part of this process? (item 3.8 and 3.0) Planning Policy and Guidelines. Whilst relevant policies are identified, the DDA does not delve into these nor expand on how the proposals comply. With regard to Policy 1, this only considers renewable energy installations to be appropriate “in principle”. It is worth exploring, too, whether the proposals do, in fact, constitute a renewable energy development or rather, is battery storage an adjunct to that industry, which comes with a host of issues, which need to be overcome. Not least of these are the visual impact implications and risks to health and wellbeing. (item 4.4) Temporary development. Please clarify the finite lifespan of the development. (item 5.3) Scale. The size of the development is stated as filling the land available. This is not a calculated justification for the proposals scale. It is noted in 5.7 the scale is required for viability, however the measure of this is not stated. (item 5.11) States the development is of an appropriate scale. This is the opinion of the applicant and therefore cannot be taken at face value. Comparing the proposals with other land uses in the vicinity demonstrates clearly how out-of-scale this development will be in this location, where other structures comprise dispersed single houses and farm buildings. (Image 5.1) Proposed Layout. The proposed site access is too far up [PLACE], meaning construction and then operating vehicles will clash with other road users over a greater length of road than is necessary. Far more information is required on proposed screening, by way of planning and bunding. There is no key provided to accompany the layout. (item 5.15) Access and security. The measures described will be completely out of character here. Widening the road, as described, will destroy natural habitat and is likely to encourage joy-riders in this remote location. There is no description of the boundary fencing proposed in this document but the pole-mounted CCTV cameras and security lighting suggest a grim and hostile appearance, which is unacceptable. (item 5.17/ 5.18) Landscaping. Please explain how the introduction of c. 30 Ha of battery storage along with a high security enclosure and lighting will “preserve and enhance the existing landscape features.” The retention of hedgerows will not compensate for the destruction of a large swath of natural land where ground-dwelling plants and animals reside. (item 5.19) Appearance. The overall appearance of the proposed development will NOT be “.sympathetic and in keeping with the surrounding context”. This is simply not true and it defies understanding how [ORGANIZATION] can promote this view. (items 5.2 – 5.23) Access. The disruption that will be caused to local residents during the 24-month construction phase is unacceptable. (item 6.2) Carbon reduction. This is acknowledged as vital to the future of the planet but if a natural and wild place needs to be destroyed to facilitate this, what’s the point? What are we saving the planet for? Outline Safety Management Plan - [ORGANIZATION] (item 1.5) The battery technology system to be employed has not been chosen yet, so this document is irrelevant, other than it flags up there ARE risks to those, out-with the site, to: - Fire - Explosion - Release of harmful gases The document states that detection and suppression systems will be put in place but by the time an alert is raised, the accident has already happened. All the systems do is attempt to minimise its impact. This is not acceptable to adjacent property owners; indeed, the release of harmful gases could affect those living remotely to the site too. Noise Impact Assessment – Professional Consult As noted previously, local neighbours should expect a zero decibel effect from the development. Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment - [ORGANIZATION] No further comment at this time. Landscape Proposal Drawings - [ORGANIZATION] Drwg No APA-PL-01 Whilst the proposed tree planting is welcomed, the size of tree specimens proposed (6080cm) is inadequate. The mitigating effect of the new woodland will not be established for 15-20 years, which is not acceptable. Heavy standards should be used throughout and a programme of maintenance and replacement put in place from the outset. Consideration should be given to bunding between new planting and the battery storage containers. Transport Statement – [ORGANIZATION] 21,190 two-way vehicle trips during construction is unacceptable. Six-day working week is unacceptable. The impact on other road users during construction is unacceptable. Danger to other road users from construction traffic is too great. Preliminary Ecological Appraisal – [ORGANIZATION] Concerns about impact on ecology noted elsewhere. Access Gate and Fencing (drawing) - [ORGANIZATION] The appearance of this style of fencing is unacceptable in this location. A boundary fence location plan is required. Any fencing required must be located to the inside of any landscape buffer. Appendix B2 Accurate Visual Representation and Methodology Slide Viewpoint 8 – Year 1 demonstrates clearly the extremely adverse visual impact presented by this elevated site. According to the subsequent slide, it will take 15 years for the screening planning to have its proper effect. This is not acceptable. LIDAR data is limited and the visuals produced using LIDAR are not useful representation of actual situations. CONCLUSION Until the advent of NPF4, Development in the countryside came under the utmost scrutiny and an assumption against development was made in most cases. The new guidelines, which seem to favour developments such as this; where a “green” or “sustainability” label can be attached, appear to attract no such attention. Indeed, they are encouraged without the usual means of recourse. However, due care must be exercised by any local authority that supports such a venture. This is unknown and untried territory with both real and perceived levels of risk to health and life, not to mention the impact the development will have on the visual amenity of this beautiful rural area and the lives of the families who live here. The [ORGANIZATION] website tries to justify the use of agricultural land as follows: “The draft National Policy Statement for Renewable Energy (EN-3) confirms that Agricultural Land Classification (ALC) should not be the predominant test in site selection.” This conflicts strongly with the overarching principles of NPF4, which promotes the protection of natural habitat and creation of places where biodiversity can thrive as being of paramount importance in planning decision-making. It appears these sentiments have been lost in our eagerness to embrace renewable energy systems, at all costs.

The proposed site is only 275 metres from the village of [PLACE] (in Fife) and we believe the site isn’t suitable as it’s prone to routine flooding and presents a significant environmental risk should there be a fire. FLOOD RISK 1. The developer flooding report states that the overall flood risk of the site has been found to be ‘low’. This is factually inaccurate. The site is on a narrow strip of land bounded by two water courses, [PLACE] and [PLACE] and both are subject to significant and routine flooding. The report produced by the developer is just a computer model and doesn’t reflect the local reality. The two most recent flooding examples happened on the 18th November 2022 and 30th December 2022 following a normal pattern of winter rain - See photos A-F. 2. The developer is proposing to construct the battery energy storage system and associated infrastructure on 600mm plinths to raise it above any potential flood water, but as seen in the photos, this may not be enough. 3. The regular flooding and drying of the land makes ground stability a concern and unsuitable for surface placed concrete plinths supporting heavy battery storage and electrical equipment that may move and subside as surface conditions change. This may make the site inherently unsafe. The site was also used by ‘Dalgety Skip Hire’ during the late 1970’s and 1980’s, so there’s also the potential that waste was buried onsite, further weakening ground stability. A geotechnical survey may be required. 4. If the developer must construct an entire site on 600mm stilts you know it’s in the wrong place. The site must be resilient and safe. Lithium batteries must not be exposed to water or moisture (Google the consequences!) No reasonable person would deliberately and knowingly construct part of our critical national energy infrastructure on potentially unstable land, in an area that routinely floods and on a site that will be subjected to more extreme flooding events due to climate change. ENVIROMENTAL RISK 1. Most of the time these battery sites in the UK and elsewhere in the world function as designed and deliver as expected. However, all types of Lithium-ion batteries, even the newer versions, have a known weakness of thermal runaway (“battery fire”) and when this occurs at an energy battery storage facility it can result in fire, explosions, toxic run off, and a toxic vapour cloud which, if it reaches an ignition point, will explode as happened at a fire in [PLACE] in 2020. 2. Since 2018, more than 50 fires and explosions have been reported at battery installations such as this - BESS Failure Event Database - EPRI Storage Wiki 3. It is little wonder then that [PERSON] proposed a bill in September 2022 (it is due its second reading in parliament on 24 March 2023), "Lithium-Ion Battery Storage (Fire Safety and Environmental Permits)." Its aim is to ensure that lithium-ion battery storage facilities are correctly categorised as hazardous, so that the Environment Agency, [ORGANIZATION] and Fire and Rescue Service must be statutory consultees when planning applications are considered." (They currently are not). 4. As Dame Miller states, "lithium-ion batteries are innocuous when they function normally, but if they fail, a process called thermal runaway. occurs. The only way to stop a battery fire is to cool it down with a constant stream of water and wait for the fire to go out, which might take days, creating huge quantities of water containing highly corrosive hydrofluoric acid and copper oxide - by-products of battery fires. These toxic chemicals cannot be allowed to seep into watercourses, because they would cause immense environmental damage." 5. Due to the inherent risk of fire and contaminated fire water entering [PLACE] and [PLACE] and therefore the [PLACE] river catchment, there appears to be no mitigation planned such as on-site fire tanks and bunds that would be needed to comply with environmental legislation such as the Water Framework Directive and other environmental legislation. 6. In addition, the field adjacent to the site is in a high-risk area of flooding which potentially further increases toxic run-off risk. 7. The village ([PLACE]) above the site raises questions about the potential for winds blowing a toxic vapor cloud up and around the village.

These developments, although they place demands on resources create intergenerational communities, we suggest this development will put people off moving to the area. -Vernacular of the area- All residential planning applicants have to ensure the proposed property fits in and adds to the vernacular of the area in terms of placement and construction type, sometimes meaning increased expense and time. From the sparse plan of the proposed site we have seen, it looks like a hybrid of a container park and a prisoner of war camp. We challenge the applicant to show another such development in Aberdeenshires' tranquil rural farming areas. There has been no attempt whatsoever to merge it into its setting. An embankment and a few trees is totally inadequate. The site bounds a commercial forest which will be felled at some stage. This would leave the proposed site looking even more out of place. This construction would fit into the vernacular of a business park on a brown field site. Or can't this be done for safety reasons? -Further developments at Bogfern- The previous application was for a windfarm located in a different part of [PLACE]. This proposal is further south. We suspect if this proposal is passed that there would be a further application for the windfarm. Logically this would place the green power source near its storage site. I hope this is not the case.

I am writing to formally object to the proposed development of an industrial-scale battery storage facility in the [PLACE] area. My primary concern is the serious risk posed by lithium-ion battery fires. These types of fires are notoriously difficult to extinguish, highly volatile, and capable of producing large volumes of toxic fumes and potentially hazardous waste. In the event of such a fire, both human and animal life in the surrounding area would be placed at significant risk due to the release of harmful gases and contaminants into the environment. In addition, the infrastructure in this rural area is wholly unsuitable for supporting a rapid emergency response. The narrow access roads are not designed for large emergency vehicles travelling at speed, particularly in high-pressure situations. This, combined with the area's distance from the nearest emergency service hubs, means that any response to an incident would likely fall well outside recommended guideline times. Can this please be investigated? A delayed response in the event of a fire could lead to widespread exposure to toxic fumes and a potentially catastrophic outcome for the local community. For these reasons-specifically the heightened fire risk, environmental hazard, and inadequate emergency access-I strongly urge the planning authority to reject the proposal. The safety of residents, the protection of the environment, and the practical limitations of emergency services in this area must take precedence.

target_text: As Senior Pastor of several Churches in and around [PLACE], I write with my objections about the above proposal. I live about 3 km from the site, but my objections are more far reaching. It sits at the centre of a densely populated area of some 90,000 people. [PLACE] Valley acts as a funnel The site is just north of the [PLACE]. In the event of a fire within the proposed site, having watched on television the huge plumes of toxic poisonous fumes from fires at similar sites, no matter which way the wind blows – as it frequently / constantly does, it will affect people living in at least one area, be it [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE] or [PLACE]. If as happens the wind direction changes, perhaps all of them – anything up to 90,000 people. From previous incidents at similar sites, the fumes dictate that people must stay indoors, for days. Traffic If there is a fire and the wind funnels the toxic / poisonous fumes towards the sea (eastwards) from the site it will affect all three bridges crossing the river, effectively the fumes will close the bridges, stop traffic and cut [PLACE] off from anywhere north of the river without, a very long diversion. However, those bridges are a life line. All emergency services are situated south of the river, the Police, Fire Brigade, Ambulance Service and Hospitals. Environment The site being close to the [PLACE], if a fire breaks out, which produces plumes of smoke, with toxic / poisonous fumes, and the wind takes them across the river, poisonous / toxic material fall out will enter the river, and subsequently make its way downstream and enter the North Sea. Has there been an impact report on the effects ‘toxic fall’ out on maritime / river life and on the effects on the ‘health of the river? This objection is not, ‘a Not in my backyard’ scenario. retrieved_examples.text: I am writing to express my objection with regards to the proposals to site a Battery Energy Storage Site (BESS) on prime grade 1 arable land at [PLACE] (Refs [APPLICATION_CODE] and [APPLICATION_CODE]) both as a local resident and long serving Firefighter. -This is one of the largest active BESS in Scotland and is also much closer to residential buildings than any other existing site in the country (including a doctor's surgery and primary [PLACE]). I feel that this proposal unnecessarily risks the safety and wellbeing of the families in close proximity to the site and the community as a whole. It lowers multiple standards and protections and sets a race to the bottom. After sharing and collating our knowledge as a community, the main concerns of note are as follows: - High grade farmland will needlessly be lost with multiple brownfield sites available in similar proximity. The land in it's current state is a source of homegrown food and supports local wildlife. Current excavation in proximity of the proposed site have already correlated with instances of disrupted deer and fox activity in the area. - After meeting with my community and community council, and following multiple Q&A sessions with planning representatives (the few willing or able to speak to us), there was an alarming lack of key information relation to this development, including Emergency Plans, an Evacuation Plan, and nobody involved in the discussions could confirm the type of battery to be used in the development. It is either the current technology with all of it's documented risks or a new emerging battery technology with a reduced knowledge of real-world performance. Either way, there can be little confidence in a proposal (or the proposers) that doesn't include such a key piece of information. - The noise impact from the completed running BESS runs a high risk of being significantly, and near constantly, adverse. This is totally unacceptable to both close-living residents and the community as a whole. -The proximity to residential houses, [PLACE] and [PLACE] pose a significant risk to a great number of people in the event of a fire situation. It is widely documented that, despite fire detection and suppression systems being in place, BESS sites have suffered thermal runaway, resulting in fires, explosions and the release of toxic gases. Often over a protracted period of time. At present, and to the best of my knowledge, our policy covering BESS fires puts emphasis on defensive firefighting. Due to a number of factors including the environmental impact of contamination from water application, the dangers of explosion and sudden reignition, and where there is no immediate life risk (assuming the successful and confident evacuation of nearby houses), consideration is to be given to defensive firefighting, allowing batteries to burn themselves out. The long duration of a fire event, and given the prevailing westerly wind, could in turn lead to a large-scale evacuation of the aforementioned GP, primary [PLACE] and a significant number of houses. There is little doubt that people will be exposed to the toxic fumes, including hydrofluoric acid, and smoke to varying degrees and that this will lead to both short- and long-term health complications. - Future of the site and impact wider ecosystem Especially in the event of accident what assurances exist that the site can be returned to prime arable land? What drainage exists for emergencies other than dumping contaminated water in [PLACE]? Is there any information about the acoustic impacts on protected species such as bats? None of this is clear from the application and unless these questions are answered the longer term impact of this development on the environment of our community may be tremendous. As will be quite obvious, I do not support these applications by [ORGANIZATION] on behalf of [ORGANIZATION] and [ORGANIZATION]. Please take account of my concerns and objections in your consideration of this application.
