target_text: I would like to strongly object to the [PLACE] BESS S36 project REF [APPLICATION_CODE] being granted planning permission. I am not satisfied with the documentation presented in the application as there is no Module test result showing credible objective testing of the battery units under thermal runaway. (i.e. what happens when they are on fire). There are current standards for this from UL. [LINK] A test protocol and certificate must surely be provided to allow a full assessment of any combustion products that may be formed to be assessed? There will be Inorganic particulates formed during combustion (from lithium and other metals). It is also difficult to put out the fire as only water seems to be being used. The water will only cool the chemical reaction and not put it out. This will lead to contamination of soil and groundwater in the area giving a potential for any chemicals (unknown as they have not been assessed) to leech into the [PLACE], potentially causing damage to the river eco system). Any smoke would surely be both toxic and a respiratory irritant and depending on the wind direction, at the time of any fire, move towards/over the [PLACE]/[PLACE]/or even the [PLACE] area leading to road closure(s) for some time. Battery fires seem to be more common (al beit at recycling centers) where the results are well documented. Even today, Monday 24th June 2024, a fire started in [PLACE] using similar technology that will be employed at the BESS site in [PLACE]. [LINK] I am not convinced of the sound modelling carried out as there are very low frequency sounds which will diffract (travel) over large areas. This diffraction and prominent wind direction does not appear to have been taken into consideration. It is worth noting that the Paper Mill at [PLACE] was also subject to sanctions due to the low frequency noise emissions at night and I see the BESS site at [PLACE] being no different as the fans causing the noise will be subject to random operation over 24hrs as it is dictated by the cooling requirements of the batteries. It is also worth noting that the site appears to be a brownfield one with potential asbestos contamination (from the old piggery roof). I am not sure how the company will deal with this to ensure that any asbestos in the soil is not disturbed and blown outside the area, potentially into the road/[PLACE]. This would certainly lead to a significant health scare if any of the dust were to be inhaled. I would be interested to see a documented method for removing the contaminated soil without disturbing potential asbestos. A site remediation document appears to be missing from the submitted documents. The documentation submitted gives great detail on the current flora/fauna but gives no definitive impacts other than positive and negative. As an experienced industrial/environmental chemist I am very angry that so little thought has been put into the submission of documentation and so little thought on the actual/potential impacts of fire and noise on the surrounding environment and community. This application should be rejected as a matter of urgency.

retrieved_examples.text: I am writing to formally object to the above planning application. I am a long-term resident of the area, having lived at [PLACE] with my family since 1991. My parents, now elderly, continue to live here, and I am deeply concerned about the risks this development poses to their health, safety, and quality of life. This proposal is one of six separate BESS applications currently under consideration within a small area around [PLACE]. Yet there appears to be no assessment of the cumulative effects on our community. That in itself is deeply troubling. My objections are as follows: 1. Fire Risk and Emergency Response Lithium-ion battery fires are notoriously difficult to control, as seen in the recent incidents at [PLACE] and [PLACE]. These fires are capable of reigniting, producing toxic smoke, and burning for days. The proposal fails to explain how such an incident would be managed on this rural site, which lacks the infrastructure and proximity to emergency services. Most importantly, there is no public evacuation plan - yet residents like my elderly parents may have limited mobility. We need clarity on how people in their position would be safely informed, assisted, and protected in an emergency. 2. Water Supply for Firefighting The village of [PLACE] does not have a mains water supply, raising serious concerns over how a fire could be effectively tackled. The application does not provide any detail on water storage volumes, sourcing, or whether boreholes could compromise local private water supplies, which my family relies on. 3. Environmental Pollution from Fire Water Run-Off Fire suppression water is often contaminated with harmful chemicals. Without proper containment, this could easily enter the local water table or the burn that flows into [PLACE], putting both human and environmental health at risk. This is particularly serious for homes with private wells. 4. Noise Impacts Cooling units, inverters, and transformers produce continuous operational noise. As a quiet rural area, any new noise sources must be assessed against baseline levels before the substation was built - and must also factor in the noise from the five other proposed BESS facilities. Living close by, this noise will affect our daily lives and long-term well-being. 5. Construction Traffic and Access Concerns This development would lead to significant disruption during construction, especially from heavy goods vehicles and daily movements of large construction crews. Our roads are narrow and not designed for this level of industrial traffic. As a resident of [PLACE] Avenue, I worry about the safety of my elderly parents and other vulnerable people walking or driving on these single lane roads, especially given limited visibility and lack of pavements. 6. Decommissioning and Land Restoration There are no guarantees in the proposal for how the site will be properly decommissioned after the 25-year operational period. Concrete bases, cables, and other infrastructure may remain unless a fully costed restoration plan and secured fund are in place. Without this, the land could be left permanently damaged. In conclusion, this development is completely unsuitable for a rural residential area. The lack of emergency planning, the risks to water and air quality, and the unacceptable disruption to residents - particularly to vulnerable people like my elderly parents - make this proposal deeply inappropriate. I strongly urge [ORGANIZATION] to reject application [APPLICATION_CODE] in the interest of protecting residents, safeguarding our environment, and preserving the character of our community.

I object to the proposed [PLACE] BESS site at [PLACE]. Health & Safety Risks 1. Fire - explosion - smoke hazard There has already been a fire at a BESS site in this area ([PLACE]). This event is a clear reminder of the inherent fire risk associated with lithium battery units. In the context of a clear fire risk, a full evaluation of the proposed 49.9\mw site at [PLACE] should be undertaken by a fire professional to review the site plan, not only for the site but for the potential impact of a runaway fire on the local population and on local infrastructure. Basic work should include reviewing prevailing wind direction and impact of local topography on how toxic fumes may travel and accumulate. What is the plan for emergency access the site in the event of drifting snow? It is well known to residents that tracks become blocked by snow for weeks at a time. In the event of a fire, would people near the site able to evacuate? Again, if a fire was to occur during drifting snow, how would a house blocked in by the snow get away from the toxic fumes? There are houses to the north of the site that regularly become block in by snow. If the wind was in the right direction, they would become trapped. What is the plan for these people? Proximity to [PLACE]: A fire at this site could affect the operation of the adjacent sub-station and bring down the electricity (it would have the potential to shut down the grid). East of the site: to the east of the proposed site there are a group of houses in a shallow valley a few hundred meters (and further to east [PLACE]). Two important factor to bear in mind are, firstly, that the smoke fumes produced by these sorts of fires are denser than air and will sink down when the smoke cools. Secondly, the terrain between the proposed site and [PLACE] is a valley - if the wind was from the west (one of the principal wind directions) this would have the effect of funnelling the smoke along the valley towards the town, rather than allowing the smoke to dissipate. What's is the emergency response plan to evacuate this nearby town under these circumstances? 2. Environmental & Pollution Impacts Groundwater contamination: runoff from fire-fighting foam or leaked battery electrolytes could more easily migrate in local aquifers. 3. Visual & Landscape Impact "Brownfield first" is one of NPF4's core spatial principles, directing planning authorities to "make the most efficient use of land by prioritising the re-use of vacant, derelict and under-used land ahead of development on greenfield sites." NPF4 goes on to require that Local Development Plans must demonstrate a clear sequential approach-only releasing greenfield land where there is "no reasonable prospect" of meeting needs on appropriate brownfield sites. Placing a BESS next door to the sub-station will create a continuous "industrial ribbon," severely eroding the character of a rural setting. Have the developers demonstrated that there are no alternative brownfield sites that could be used for the battery site? The site appears to be optimised for one thing only to provide a short connection for the developers. 4. Inadequate screening The existing site (associated with [PLACE]) at [PLACE] is an eyesore without proper landscaping or fencing may - it would have been easy to completely hide the site from the road - it represents careless planning - will little to no thought pertaining the natural beauty of the area. What guarantees do the public have that live in the area that this proposed site will not be the same? 5. Overconcentration of infrastructure The proximity of this site to [PLACE] is a clear addition of industrial infrastructure to a greenfield site. As such it has a cumulative and detrimental effect on the character of the area. One industrial site should not be an excuse to allow more development, this is not a policy and should not be an excuse to give planning permission. Proximity to the substation is used as a reason for the site selection of the proposed [PLACE] BESS in the planning documents. The bigger picture needs to be taken into account which includes consideration of not allowing the character of the area to radically change. 6. Policy & Local Plan Inconsistency NPPF "Broader Sustainability" Test Under the National Planning Policy Framework, proposals must consider health, amenity, and environmental quality. The combined proposal should be assessed for overall sustainability and cumulative effects, not just energy storage. 7. Community & Amenity Impacts Loss of tranquillity: noise of construction machinery, lighting and activity can undermine local residents' enjoyment of their homes and gardens. Light pollution: Additional security lighting, especially if high-powered LEDs are in use, can impact nocturnal wildlife and neighbour amenity. Again, the cumulative effects of industrialisation of a green tranquil environment needs to be considered in all aspects of this planning proposal. I appeal the planning regulators not to facilitate stealth industrialisation and not to enable development that are driven by close connection costs that appears to be the prime motivation of the developers.

I am writing to formally raise objections to the Section 36 planning application put forward by [ORGANIZATION] ([ORGANIZATION]) for the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development situated to the north of [PLACE], near [PLACE]. The project aims to establish a 100 MW lithium-ion battery facility on currently unused agricultural land, along with associated transformers, fencing, lighting, fire infrastructure, and drainage. My objection is centred on the significant risks that the development presents to public safety, the local environment, and community welfare. These risks encompass fire and contamination hazards, potential harm to biodiversity, degradation of the landscape, disruption to traffic flow, and inadequate emergency preparedness. The planning documentation provided by the developer lacks the necessary technical specifications, safety measures, and compliance with policies essential for the responsible implementation of an energy project of this magnitude. Each part of this objection articulates specific reasons why the application falls short of meeting the criteria outlined in the National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4) and the [PLACE] Local Development Plan. These reasons include deficiencies in consultation, the absence of ecological protections, a lack of assessment of cumulative impacts, and a failure to address the entire lifecycle of hazardous infrastructure. I strongly recommend that the planning authority rejects this application in its entirety. Environmental and Ecological Impact The development site is located in a rural farmland area surrounded by hedgerows, marshy grassland, and drainage features that provide support to wildlife and contribute to the local ecological network. It is in close proximity to the [PLACE] and encompasses habitats recognised for their biodiversity value, including waterlogged ground and species-rich grass margins. However, the ecological assessments that have been submitted are incomplete and crucial seasonal survey data has been omitted. Key assessments such as bat roost evaluations, dusk or dawn emergence surveys, monitoring of badger activity, and studies on amphibians have not been carried out during the appropriate seasons. These assessments are standard requirements under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 and the Nature Conservation (Scotland) Act 2004 when potential habitats are impacted by development. The absence of this data means that the developer cannot accurately claim to comprehend or address the ecological risks associated with the proposal. The site is set to be significantly covered with containerised battery units, impermeable roads, fencing, firewater tanks, and related infrastructure, leading to the permanent loss of semi-natural grassland and the fragmentation of hedgerow corridors. This will eliminate foraging and commuting paths for protected species like bats and birds. While the planting of replacement hedgerows is presented as a biodiversity enhancement, no Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG) calculation has been provided, and there is no proposed habitat management or monitoring plan. According to National Planning Framework 4 Policy 3, developments must enhance biodiversity and prevent harm to existing natural assets. [PLACE] Local Development Plan Policy PV7 mandates the protection and mitigation of priority habitats and species. Unfortunately, this proposal fails to meet either standard. The lack of comprehensive survey work, habitat destruction, and inadequate mitigation measures render it environmentally unsound. There is a risk of long-term ecological deterioration in an area that supports farmland species and local biodiversity. Cumulative Impact The [PLACE] area has emerged as a significant hub for energy infrastructure projects, encompassing large substations, overhead transmission lines, solar developments, and various proposals for Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS). The addition of a 17-acre BESS to the existing cluster of industrial energy assets is expected to intensify the physical, environmental, and psychological pressures on the local community. Despite the presence of other approved or pending developments within a 1 km radius, the current application lacks a cumulative impact assessment. There is no consideration given to how the simultaneous construction, noise emissions, lighting, fire risk, and traffic volumes from multiple projects will be managed. This fragmented approach to development neglects to address the overall impact of infrastructure saturation on the land, wildlife, and residents of [PLACE]. Concerned residents have highlighted issues regarding the industrialisation of the area and the combined effects of these proposals on mental well-being, safety, and environmental standards. It is imperative for the planning authority to evaluate not only the repercussions of this individual development but also its contribution to a broader trend of encroachment and disruption. Policy 29 of the National Planning Framework 4 stipulates the necessity of considering cumulative effects in decision-making processes. The absence of such an assessment represents a significant oversight. Approving this development without a comprehensive overview would further exacerbate the disproportionate and unsustainable strain on this rural community. Increased Traffic and Infrastructure Strain The construction of the Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) would entail almost 900 Heavy Goods Vehicle (HGV) movements over a 12-month period, with peak daily traffic reaching up to 1 large vehicles. These vehicles will navigate narrow rural roads not originally intended for heavy industrial traffic, such as [PLACE] and the surrounding local road network, which are currently shared by [PLACE] transport, agricultural vehicles, cyclists, and pedestrians. Despite the presence of multiple other energy projects proposed or already in progress in the vicinity, there has been no comprehensive assessment of the cumulative traffic impact. The planning application lacks any proposed mitigation measures, such as road reinforcement, visibility enhancements, or traffic diversion plans. Additionally, there is no specified construction delivery schedule to avoid peak traffic hours, and no road safety assessment has been provided. The proposed BESS construction also poses a threat to [PLACE], a popular walking and cycling route that passes near the site. The establishment of the construction compound and access roads is anticipated to cause disruption, visual obstructions, and potential safety risks for path users. No temporary diversion or strategy to safeguard the path has been outlined. According to NPF4 Policy 13, infrastructure should be designed to minimise impacts on local networks and ensure safety for all users, a criterion that this application fails to meet. Without adequate transport planning, this development could lead to road deterioration, heightened collision risks, and prolonged disruption to the community and local access rights. Community Wellbeing, Mental Health, and EMF Concerns The proposed development in the vicinity of [PLACE] raises significant concerns beyond physical risks and environmental impacts, particularly regarding community wellbeing and mental health. The area is already facing pressure from various energy projects, and the introduction of another large-scale, high-risk facility is causing considerable stress and anxiety among residents. Concerns about potential battery fires, pollution, explosions, and toxic smoke are not merely hypothetical, as similar risks have been observed at comparable sites globally. Local residents have voiced worries about the psychological impact of residing near such infrastructure, especially when it is inadequately understood and regulated. The sense of being surrounded by hazardous industrial developments can lead to enduring fear, disrupted sleep patterns, and diminished trust in public decision-making processes. The absence of a Health Impact Assessment accompanying the application is troubling. There is a failure to acknowledge the psychological strain that prolonged proximity to a high-risk site can impose, particularly in rural areas where quality of life hinges on peace, safety, and environmental stability. This oversight is particularly concerning for families, elderly residents, and individuals already grappling with mental health conditions. Furthermore, concerns have been raised about potential exposure to electromagnetic fields (EMFs) emanating from the site's electrical infrastructure, such as transformers and underground cabling. While EMF levels may comply with accepted thresholds, the lack of transparent monitoring or public information contributes to local unease. Perceived risk can be as detrimental to wellbeing as physical exposure, especially when residents feel excluded from the planning process. National Planning Framework 4 Policy 23 mandates that developments safeguard health, wellbeing, and safety, encompassing mental health and quality of life, not solely physical risk. The absence of any wellbeing assessment or mitigation strategy further highlights the applicant's disregard for the local population. Summary The application is fundamentally flawed as it does not address or mitigate the serious risks linked to large-scale lithium-ion battery storage. The planning documents lack essential information concerning fire safety, pollution control, waste management, biodiversity, and community health. The consultation process was insufficient, and the proposal does not adhere to the standards set out in National Planning Framework 4 or the [PLACE] Local Development Plan. If approved, this development would industrialise a rural landscape, compromise local wellbeing, strain emergency services, and create lasting environmental issues. It does not exemplify responsible energy infrastructure and does not serve the public interest. Therefore, it should be rejected.

The need for battery storage facilities, such as this, results from the inherent intermittency of wind energy. It is not clear whether the further roll out of wind energy infrastructure is needed and many are now projecting that there will be a surplus of wind energy which cannot be used or exported. Battery storage facilities only provide power for one or two hours which is of little use during cold spells when there may be little or no wind for days. The proposal should be considered on its merits, not the perceived generic benefits of renewable energy. There are currently numerous proposals for the area including wind farms, pylons, substations and batteries. When added to the existing wind farms and infrastructure there will be a significant cumulative visual impact. There does not seem to be any overall plan for the siting of BESS facilities but rather it depends on the existence of a willing landowner. Siting a further potentially hazardous industrial plant near [PLACE] and next to the river doesn’t make any sense to me and I wonder whether alternative locations have really been considered. My main concern is in relation to health and safety. The Outline Battery Safety Plan (section 3) only refers to reported fires relating to BESS facilities in the UK whereas there have been many incidents in other parts of the World, including the USA. The major hazard with BESS facilities is the risk of “thermal runaway”, not just “fires”. The applicant refers to the BESS that exploded in [PLACE] in September 2020 but fails to distinguish it from their proposal. In the [PLACE] case the fire took 59 hours to extinguish. In September 2022, a bill was introduced in the House of Commons which sought to categorise lithium-ion battery storage units as “hazardous” and to “ensure that the Environment Agency and the [ORGANIZATION] were consulted during planning applications”. It was noted that “the only way to stop a battery fire is to cool it down with a constant stream of water and wait for the fire to go out, which might take days, creating huge quantities of water containing highly corrosive hydrofluoric acid and copper oxide – by products of battery fires. These toxic chemicals cannot be allowed to seep into watercourses, because they would cause immense environmental damage” (Hansard). In March 2023, the fire chief for Hampshire is reported to have said in respect to a BESS scheme “in the event of a fire, our teams would face an impossible choice between protecting the community from potentially toxic or explosive gas plume or applying water that could pollute the water course for many years”. The proposed site is very close to [PLACE], the river and nearby homes. The Applicant seems to be saying that they would let any fire run its course, with a “controlled burn”, rather than cool it with huge quantities of water which might pollute the river. But what about toxic fumes spreading to nearby towns and homes? Residents of [PLACE] have had a recent reminder of what can happen when fires get out of control. In that case, the cause was a camping stove; not an explosion involving hazardous industrial materials. How is our overstretched rural fire service supposed to cope with huge industrial scale fire and thermal runaway incidents? Furthermore, guidance on these matters seems to be fluid at present; the applicant is dispensing with the current 6m rule for container separation based on new material yet to be approved. I have seen at least one large commercial insurance company recommending concrete walls between battery containers. Like most other people, I use Lithium batteries in various consumer products. However, I have become increasing concerned about the reported human rights abuses associated with the mining of these minerals in developing countries. There is also the issue of pollution caused by chemicals used in the mining process and associated high water consumption in what are usually arid areas. Furthermore, the World Bank predicts that the demand for such minerals will eventually outstrip known reserves. In this case, is battery storage truly sustainable? I would ask you to refuse this application due to the cumulative impact with other similar and related proposals, and because I do not believe the applicant has properly addressed the legitimate health & safety concerns associated with battery technology and battery storage facilities of this type.

target_text: The consultation process undertaken by the applicant was neither inclusive nor constructive in any form with the following occurrences: - The first ‘public’ event was only advertised to residents in the local area who were related to the applicant, all other residents were not informed. This was confirmed by the applicant at the first event and that ‘it didn’t look good’ for their consultation process. - Adverts were placed in non-local newspapers including the [PLACE] Express ([PLACE]) and the [PLACE] Advertiser ([PLACE]) neither of which cover the [PLACE] area. - The second ‘public’ event was again letter dropped to select residents while those with a direct view of the proposed site were again ignored despite being told this was the case for the first event. - Repeated and lengthy attempts to get answers from the applicant on specific questions have never resulted in a suitable response, only ever receiving a copy and paste response from the generic documentation being provided by the applicant when pressed by our local MSP to respond to my queries. - Many local residents were not made aware of the protocol for submitting their views on this application through the complicated and archaic ECU website. There is absolutely no way that this consultation process adheres to the best practice guidelines put in place by the ECU. Suitability of Site Yet more crucial local agricultural land being lost to be replaced by electrical infrastructure can always be rationalised away ‘in the national interest for net zero’ when there are plenty of brownfield sites available for projects like this. Why does more green belt land have to be sacrificed for industrial projects, particularly in this already saturated area. The proposal is nearly twice the size of the area identified by Moray Council (with no chance of representation by local residents) in their [PLACE] Green Energy Zone. Why bother wasting public money producing a document for the first application to ignore the suggested areas suitable for development? Serious questions need to be asked for how this area was deemed suitable as the applicant had already submitted outline proposals for this area before the report was produced, then to no surprise it was deemed a suitable area to develop on. The proposed site is either side of what will become one of the main power lines between [PLACE] and the proposed new sub-station at [PLACE]. Is there precedent for a BESS site being either side of major infrastructure given that in the ‘unlikely’ event that a fire breaks out it will cripple the local energy infrastructure? [ORGANIZATION] should surely be a major consultee on this proposal given its close proximity to the overhead lines. Landscaping Proposals Given the proposed site slopes in two directions (sharply in one towards the [PLACE]) the suitability for the site be hidden by permanent earthworks is not possible, this was undertaken with success at the [PLACE] BESS whereby the impact on the landscape from most viewpoints is minimised by permanent earthworks supplemented by planting. This proposal relies heavily on acoustic fencing and trees to do most of the disguising. Given that trees take many years to grow (if they are maintained at all unlike at the [PLACE] sub-station which looks the same as the day it was fenced off) and only provide screening while in leaf, the site will always look like a field of shipping containers and is why it is not a suitable site for this type of project. The view from the [PLACE] on the approach to [PLACE] will let everyone know that this once rural area of Scotland has been further scarred by this industrialisation. ‘Grangemouth of the North-East’ may be a fitting name rather than the Friendly Toon for [PLACE]. It should be a pre-requisite that any planting used for screening on this project is undertaken at the onset of the project rather than at the end given the construction timescales being put forward. Cumulative Impact At what point can it be decided that the developments at [PLACE] have reached saturation point and the once rural landscape has been completely turned into an industrial landscape? The sub-station at [PLACE] was the first advertised step but at no point was it communicated that two BESS sites, 2 further sub-station extensions, a proposed extension to the [PLACE] quarry, further wind turbines and yet more overhead lines would be part of the landscape. None of the applications around [PLACE] (including this one) have the background noise and light pollution reports produced when the most recent project completed at [PLACE] is online. After all, it will not be the owners of the sites who will deal with any fires/disasters but instead the local volunteer fire brigade will be at the front line. Are they adequately trained/equipped to deal with such an event (given that it is only more likely to happen with the quantity and size of sites such as this BESS) and if not, why aren’t the applicants contributing to the community they so richly wish to integrate into? Traffic Management Proposals The basic and frankly copy and paste natures of the CTMP supplied by the applicant does not address my main concern with the application, that the [PLACE] road at [PLACE] will be used as a shortcut to the site by suppliers, contractors and sub-contractors as has been the case with all other sites at [PLACE] in the past and currently. retrieved_examples.text: The applicant asserts that the BESS would have "limited visibility," however, its location on a ridge would make it clearly visible from various viewpoints, including roads frequented by locals and visitors. This would significantly alter the current tranquil, agricultural, and tourist-oriented character of the area. The proposal lacks a clear local or national strategic framework for the placement of such developments, raising questions about why this specific rural location was chosen over brownfield or industrial alternatives. The absence of strategic siting criteria leaves rural communities in Scotland vulnerable to unplanned industrial proposals that erode landscape quality and cohesion. Furthermore, the potential risks to local residents and the wider community from incidents such as fires at the site have been downplayed. Of particular concern is the threat posed to the setting and experience of [PLACE], a significant heritage asset in Scotland. The Castle, once a cherished retreat of the late Queen Mother, holds symbolic importance across the Commonwealth. Its meticulously preserved setting would be compromised by the proximity of a BESS facility, tarnishing the legacy of this royal site. Approving this development would not only commercialize and diminish the value of [PLACE] but also have far-reaching consequences on Scotland's planning integrity and tourism image. The decision regarding this application carries international visibility and could impact Scotland's long-term reputation. Landscape and Visual Impacts The proposed site is situated in an expansive, unsheltered terrain offering panoramic views of [PLACE]. Even with the addition of vegetation, this location is not conducive to accommodating large-scale energy infrastructure without significantly altering its existing character. The project would introduce rigid boundaries, metal enclosures, and 6-metre tall structures into a tranquil countryside setting, with numerous residents residing just a short distance from the entrance. The resultant impact is neither justified nor effectively mitigated. Precedent For Cumulative Industrial Development Approving the [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in this location could establish a precedent for a series of energy-related projects in a historically undeveloped rural setting. The proposal is situated near the [PLACE] and planned developments at [PLACE] and [PLACE], all sharing the same local road access, grid infrastructure, and potential combined impact on the rural landscape. The fragmented approach to planning raises concerns about transparency and the long- term preservation of the landscape. The lack of a comprehensive assessment of these projects together may indicate a failure to adhere to National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4), particularly in relation to Policies 1, 2, and 6, which focus on climate resilience, nature conservation, and safeguarding cultural heritage. Threat to Local Wildlife and Habitats The area forms a diverse landscape of pasture, hedgerows, and fringe woodland habitats that provide a home to various bird species, small mammals, and invertebrates. A comprehensive ecological evaluation for the BESS project has not been made available. Instead, a simplistic assessment skewed towards the developer's interests has been conducted. The introduction of concrete surfacing, fencing, artificial lighting, and vegetation removal would result in an ecological void within the immediate environment. This goes against the nature-positive planning principle outlined in NPF4. Absence of Environmental Impact Assessment The proposed BESS project, despite its size and scope, has not undergone a comprehensive Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA). Typically, a development of this nature would warrant an EIA due to its potential impacts on the landscape, heritage sites, biodiversity, noise levels, and overall infrastructure. The absence of a formal EIA process is a notable oversight in terms of environmental assessment and compromises the transparency and thoroughness of the planning procedures. No Long Term Decommissioning or Restoration Plan The applicant has not presented a definitive long-term plan for the decommissioning, restoration, or safety measures for the site once the BESS reaches the end of its operational lifespan. Without established restoration requirements and financial security measures in place, there is a potential for the site to be abandoned with deteriorating infrastructure, contamination problems, or ongoing maintenance responsibilities long after the energy benefits have ceased. Summary This project is being situated in close proximity to a small rural village without any discernible public benefit, contravening the principles of environmental justice and democratic planning. The Council's own guidance acknowledges "particular sensitivities in this location" that remain unaddressed. This large-scale industrial endeavor offers no tangible advantages to the community, such as local job opportunities, infrastructure improvements, or revenue sharing, thus falling short of the standards outlined in the Scottish Planning Policy (SPP) and [PLACE] Council's Community Benefit Policy for Renewables. There has been no community referendum, vote, or significant public support for this development. The consultation process has been merely procedural, lacking meaningful engagement with local residents. Despite clear opposition from the community, their concerns have been consistently disregarded. A project with such significant implications for daily life, health, heritage, and the environment should not be imposed without genuine, enthusiastic, and locally driven approval. This project does not align with the core principles of sustainability, place-specific decision-making, heritage preservation, and rural fairness as outlined in the National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4). The proposed development is disproportionate and incongruous with its surroundings. It would irrevocably alter the local scenery and the historical rural backdrop of [PLACE], a site of national significance and symbolism. Approving an industrial battery installation in such close proximity to a Royal heritage site based on conjecture, insufficient evidence, and flawed policy implementation is unacceptable.

Firstly – I would ask if there is a need for this particular BESS - various national reports are highlighting over-subscription of planning applications for such storage units and that the national picture for infrastructure shows that there are many more bids in the system than required. My family members attended all of the public meetings held by [ORGANIZATION] plus those with the Community Council. I feel that information was poorly presented and lack of knowledge of the area by the company undermined confidence in any appropriate approach and research for the siting. I felt that community members were not fully respected for their local knowledge and information. - Areas of specific concern Safety and fire risk Answers to questions at the open meeting around risk from fire, chemicals, smoke and ground leakage were far from detailed or clear leading those present to be very concerned. There remains lack of clarity about management of accident response at the proposed site making me feel the arrangements are not in place. no residents should be subjected to this or expected to support such a development. Impact on value of properties I have undertaken some research and expect properties in the surrounding area of the proposed BESS to suffer considerable devaluation. This is an extremely negative factor which is inescapable for many of us in the area. I assume local elected members are aware of this. Location should always be selected with minimum impact on local households. Impact on the environment The site is right next to a waterway. Local people know that this provides a haven for wildlife and could well be at risk from this development. Has this been taken into consideration adequately? Is there research to create any confidence that disturbance will be very minimal or non-existent. Inappropriate use of good agricultural land One of the arguments against the siting of the [ORGANIZATION] recent proposed large substation was the use of good agricultural land in an area of importance to farming. The same argument stands with this application even though it is smaller in scale. There is land at [PLACE] and in other places which are not designated for agriculture which should be considered before this use of good farmland. Impact on Tourism This area benefits from the tourism created around the history and culture of [PLACE] and in particular the land associated with James Leslie Mitchell – one of Scotland’s best regarded authors. This BESS will endanger the experience of tourists and affect local businesses and the wider world of tourism. This was a huge factor in the consultation with [ORGANIZATION] and many academics, historians, tourist managers and lovers of literature pointed to the danger of undermining the “Sunset Song” story. Impact on culture and heritage Following on from the issue highlighted above – this area has many sites of ancient historic interest which the University of [PLACE] are currently working with. There are neolithic sites, a stone circle and burial cairns overlooking the very area affected by this application, even if not directly. Noise and light pollution No-one from [ORGANIZATION] has been able to reassure residents about potential noise and light pollution. Research shows both of these to be factors affecting local people when such sites are up and running. The impact on wildlife is likely to be a challenge also. Danger of flooding and snow closures of roads impeding access Flooding and snow road closure is an annual issue at [PLACE], This does not seem to have been adequately allowed for. In any health and safety incident there is no mitigation against weather impeding access to the BESS. Those who live here know this. Conflicting underground cabling proposed The BESS proposal does not seem to be planned in conjunction with the likely underground cabling from the coast to [PLACE] which means local residents may be disturbed twice with considerable road closures. This lack of co-ordination does not build confidence in local people. - Final comments I would point out that the recent proposal for the substation by [ORGANIZATION] in the same area as the BESS was withdrawn and an alternative with less impact was eventually selected. I hope for the same here. If Battery Energy Storage Systems are to be agreed by planning authorities then it should be clear that the proposed sitings are appropriate – in the case of [PLACE] BESS there must be better places for such a development than in this location. Other sites should be explored – we were told that this site was not the ideal location but that the landowner concerned was the only one offering up his land. This should not be a prime aspect of any such development – it should surely be about a strategic plan and locations based on more than a single landowner being offered a sum of money. This is a very good way to destroy neighbour relations and community wellbeing. In consultation the community to be affected should be awarded the highest of status in terms of consideration and process – I definitely feel this is not the case here. I personally have felt aggrieved at the way information was shared with the public for this [PLACE] development and in particular I was offended by the declaration that the development would be going ahead as agreement was already in place with [ORGANIZATION] for access to the [PLACE] and there was no going back. This is entirely inappropriate to say at an event which is declared a consultation. This makes me feel that the information sharing and consultation was a waste of time as it was a done deal in the eyes of the developer. The impact of a sense of low status of the community in any process results in disengagement from the public and failure of the developer to build any relationship with those ultimately concerned and lessons seem not to be learned. I very much hope this development is not approved for the reasons shared above. The area is too valuable to be lost to such an inappropriately located piece of infrastructure.

I have lived and worked in this area for nearly 20 years and during that time I have enjoyed the peace, tranquillity and unspoilt countryside in this beautiful part of the Scottish Borders. I have no wish to live next to an industrial site and this development will totally destroy my lifestyle, cause my family and I much stress, worry and anxiety for not only our future health, wellbeing and safety but also for that of our community. National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4), Policy 5 (Soils) makes it clear that development proposals will only be supported if they are designed and constructed in accordance with the mitigation hierarchy by first avoiding and then minimising the amount of disturbance to soils on undeveloped land. It also clearly states that development proposals on prime agricultural land will only be supported where it is for essential infrastructure and there is a specific locational need and no other suitable site. The site at [PLACE] is located on prime agricultural land and as such, specifically goes against the mitigation hierarchy. Its location over 2 miles from the [PLACE] means there is no “specific locational need” for the BESS to be on this site. Location at this site is purely based on landowner speculation for financial gain, and as far away as possible from his own residence and land he owns nearer the [PLACE]. Granting it permission would set a hugely dangerous precedent and would open up the potential for BESS developments outside the immediate vicinity of substations right across Scotland, unnecessarily threatening swathes of prime agricultural land and deeming the guidance within NPF4 Policy 5 to be virtually meaningless. Using the fields in this way will be damaging food production; this is a rural area where the fields are required for food production not BESS sites. This site is prime arable land and should remain so, the applicant states it will be reinstated once the site is not longer required, due to the proposed length of time the site is to operate, and that it will most likely fall to the applicants descendants or subsequent landowner to clear the site, the current landowner should be required to lodge with the Scottish Government a sum of not less than 1 million pounds to enable the site to be reinstated once it is redundant, this should be a condition applied to all applications of this nature by the ECU, so that future generations do not have to pay for any reinstatement costs for these projects. BESS sites should not be sited on prime arable land, but on brownfield sites away from homes. FIRE*** Fire-fighting issues is another great concern. Is the infrastructure for the water supply to the sites adequate for this purpose. Scottish Water should also be consulted as to whether their infrastructure is resilient enough. The lithium batteries have a concerning reputation for combusting into flames and creating uncontrollable fires. The local [PERSON] are not equipped to cope with such fires. There will always be a threat and risk of fire/explosion and vapour cloud within these sites which I find totally unacceptable. I am extremely concerned about the environmental impact as well as the risks due to fire pollution. The applicant has not read the guidance from the fire service stating that there should two points of access to the site, in the application there is only one very restricted access which would make fighting any fire almost impossible. The prevailing wind direction from the site puts properties at risk from the toxic cloud created by any fire including the village of [PLACE], the applicant does not provide any evacuation plan and also accommodation plan for residents during a fire at the site. The light and noise level of the development is also of major concern. Having this development within our local community will detract from the future marketability of our properties. There are already three BESS developments that have been approved within the local community so to accept more BESS sites will change the character and demeanour of this area. With three other BESS developments within the local community having been approved, the generation of construction traffic and associated noise will be vastly increased. This has already been proven with current works to the [PLACE]. I work with in the construction industry and having read the proposed number of vehicle movements stated, it is quite apparent that this vastly understated. Our community should not be paying a higher price in terms of local amenity than other communities across Scotland. There should be no further developments within this locality other than the three BESS developments that have already been approved immediately adjacent to [PLACE] Sub-Station.

One of my major concerns relating to this development is the road access. - The proposed site is along a single-track narrow road with very little opportunity to create suitable passing places. - The developer themselves refer to this road as a “lane” (fig 1). This is wholly inappropriate for any large-scale development. - The road leading to the development “C1S” has been deemed inappropriate for HGV traffic by [ORGANIZATION] who are also proposing a substation in the locality. The road is so unsuitable that [ORGANIZATION] are creating their own access road which avoids using this access route and small bridge. - The small bridge over “[PLACE]” burn is not strong enough to cope with the increased HGV traffic this development will bring. I don’t see in any of the submitted documentation by the applicant that they have conducted any structural survey work to ensure this bridge is strong enough to withstand the increased HGV traffic. - The applicant refers to previous HGV traffic for the forestry operations, but they did not access the site over this small, old and fragile bridge. - Please see Fig 2, Fig 3 & Fig 4 for map and photographs of single-track road and mentioned bridge. A full structural survey is required before any large-scale developer is granted permission to use this road. Additional concern is that the developer has failed to conduct a breeding bird survey due to their rush to submit their application. - Having visited the location in June 2025 I can confirm the presence of Corn Bunting. - The Corn Bunting is a red list species, and this development will be detrimental to the species and its survival in our rural farmland habitat. 1. Location and Land Use Concerns The proposed BESS site is situated in close proximity to residential dwellings, schools, and recreational areas. The selection of this particular site raises several issues: - Proximity to Homes: The planned facility is less than 500 metres from the nearest residential properties, exposing inhabitants to potential risks associated with noise, air pollution, and possible catastrophic failures. - Impact on Community Character: BESS installations are industrial in nature. Their presence in a rural environment fundamentally alters the character of the area, undermining its aesthetic and amenity value. - Future Development Restrictions: The establishment of a large-scale, high- voltage facility may restrict future residential or commercial development in the area. 2. Safety and Fire Risk Battery energy storage systems can pose significant safety hazards, especially in the event of malfunction or fire. Lithium-ion batteries, in particular, are known for their volatility under certain conditions. - Thermal Runaway: Industry records from similar installations globally have recorded incidents of thermal runaway, leading to fires that are extremely difficult to extinguish, sometimes requiring days to fully control. - Lack of Emergency Preparedness: The application does not provide sufficient details regarding emergency response protocols, coordination with local fire services, or the provision of specialised equipment and training necessary to manage BESS incidents. - Public Health and Safety: The proximity to [PLACE] raises significant concern for the wellbeing of children. In the event of a fire or chemical release, evacuation and containment may be challenging. - The location of the fire water tank to the north of the site proposes a serious fire safety risk. In the event of any fire, any emergency vehicles will have to access this tank via the only access route which will be through burning battery compounds on either side to reach the only water source on site. Another flaw in the design which is extremely dangerous to those attending and another reason for this development to be refused planning. 3. Environmental Impact The environmental assessment presented in the application appears insufficient in several respects: - Potential for Soil and Water Contamination: In the event of battery leakage or fire, hazardous substances could seep into the soil or local waterways, posing long- term risks to ecosystems and human health. - Noise and Air Pollution: The operation of cooling fans, inverters, and other ancillary equipment may result in unacceptable noise levels, especially during periods of peak operation or emergency venting events. Chemical off-gassing and emissions during normal operation or, worse, during thermal incidents are also a concern. - Insufficient Mitigation Measures: The application does not provide robust or verifiable measures to mitigate these environmental risks, nor does it propose ongoing monitoring beyond the construction phase. - Potential disruption to private water supplies and water contamination. o [PLACE] and the [PLACE] which originate on or adjacent to [PLACE]. These feed into the [PLACE] priority catchment drinking water area. o “[PLACE]” and “[PLACE]” both run into the [PLACE] area. o Contaminants from this development have the potential to enter both [PLACE] and [PLACE]. o The developer has not referenced the potential of this or any mitigation matters, they seem to have completely ignored these watercourses and omitted any reference of them from their application in its entirety. If they have missed these obvious water courses visible on any map, what else have they omitted in their rushed application? 4. Inadequate Community Consultation A critical aspect of any major infrastructure project is meaningful engagement with the affected community. - Lack of Transparency: Many local residents became aware of the BESS proposal only after the formal application was submitted, signalling a lack of early-stage consultation. - Insufficient Information: Public information sessions, where they have occurred, have not addressed fundamental questions about risk, mitigation, or alternative siting. - 2 Public Consultations were held on 25th February and 18th March 2025. Even though the applicant has held the required 2 consultations these were held extremely close together with very little difference in the 2 sessions. This felt like a very rushed process simply to “tick the box”. 5. Alternatives and Site Selection The application does not adequately demonstrate why this specific location was chosen over others that may present fewer risks to the community. - Lack of Alternatives Analysis: No comprehensive site assessment has been shared that weighs the risks and benefits of this site versus more remote or industrial settings. - Potential for Co-location: Opportunities to co-locate the BESS with existing infrastructure or within industrial zones have not been explored in detail. This site is neighbouring the proposed [ORGANIZATION] [PLACE] 2 substation development. 6. Economic and Property Impacts Beyond the immediate health and safety risks, the presence of a BESS facility may have a profound effect on local property values and the economic well-being of current residents. - Devaluation of Property: Evidence from similar projects suggests that nearby property values may decrease due to perceived risks and reduced desirability of the area. - Lack of Compensation: The application does not identify any plan for compensating affected property owners or for contributing to community benefit funds. - A transparent and meaningful community benefit fund has not been provided by the applicant. 7. Regulatory and Planning Policy Issues The proposal appears to be inconsistent with existing local planning policies that prioritise the welfare of residents, the protection of green spaces, and the sustainable development of infrastructure. - Non-Compliance with Planning Guidelines: Local development frameworks often stipulate the need for buffer zones, robust environmental assessments, and clear justification for siting major infrastructure near sensitive receptors. The BESS application, as it stands, falls short of these requirements. - Precedent Setting: Approval of this application may set a worrying precedent, opening the door for further industrial encroachment into residential and environmentally sensitive areas. Conclusion and Request While the integration of advanced energy storage solutions is a commendable goal, the current application for the BESS facility fails to address, in a satisfactory manner, the considerable risks it poses to health, safety, the environment, and the character of our community. The lack of meaningful consultation, inadequate safety measures, insufficient environmental protection, and disregard for local planning frameworks demand that this application be denied or, at the very least, substantially revised. I respectfully urge the planning authority to reject the current application for the BESS facility at the proposed location. Should the applicant wish to proceed, I request that they be required to undertake a thorough review of alternative sites, perform a detailed risk assessment in collaboration with local emergency services, and enter into sincere and transparent consultation with the community. Only through such a robust and inclusive process can the legitimate concerns of residents be addressed and the best interests of all stakeholders safeguarded.

the proposed site is designated as greenbelt in the council's approved Local Development Plan (LDP). Given that the LDP is an authoritative planning document and it is key for the assessment of planning proposals in [PLACE], I believe it would be counter-intuitive under the council's planning regime to accept this application As the land in [PLACE] has not been allocated for the purposes of a new battery energy storage facility in the council's LDP, and it is marked as a greenfield site, and not for the introduction of a battery plant, I hope that this would represent strong grounds for refusing the planning application. Overshadowing / Overlooking - I am concerned that this planning application will be overlooking the rear of my property ([PLACE], G76 0JJ), which I object to. Road safety issues given that the construction of the site and the day to day usage will incur additional traffic volumes I am concerned about the road safety aspects this site will present through the additional use of heavy and industrial vehicles. Moving the street light, with no disclosed plans as to how far will increase the risk of an accident from cars leaving these exits due to poor lighting. The applicant has stated that there will be 12 months of road disruption while the area is prepared and these units are installed. This not only will impact on [PLACE] residents for a prolonged period of time (the queues at the [PLACE] at rush hour frequently extend up the [PLACE] towards [PLACE]) but due to the access roads vicinity to the [PLACE] is likely to impact on the [PLACE] (where the queues at rush hour can extend back 3⁄4 mile directly along this sites northernmost border). This is likely to lead to increased crashes at an already dangerous roundabout that sees frequent accidents. The large volume of mud that will be deposited during construction, and transported towards the roundabout is also a significant concern. This is likely to make the road slippery in the wet and increase the risk of accidents. The applicant has also stated in their transport statement section 6.8 that “vehicle parking for site workers during all stages of construction and operation will be accommodated on site with no vehicles allowed to park or wait on the adjoining road network during any stage of the development”. However for the first two months, before any groundwork has taken place there will be no on site parking. This raise the question of where these workers are going to park as there is no space for parking in the vicinity surrounding low Borland. Will this mean there are increased cars parking in [PLACE] and [PLACE]? This itself is likely to contribute to road safety issues in the wider community. The proposed access road entrance is just over the brow of the hill on exiting from the [PLACE] and will not be visible to traffic until almost upon the entrance, thus creating a blind summit. Its important to note that a planning application for a church dwelling diagonally opposite this proposed development on the other side of the roundabout was recently declined in part because of concerns over road safety. In that instance the plan for the entrance to the had been moved closer to [PLACE] by not much less than what is proposed here. Poor Design and Materials Despite this being a 4 hectare site this choice of location is a poor choice of site as there is a high powered gas mainline pipe running at the southern tip of the site which is severely impacting on where these units can be sited within the field. There is also overhead pylons to the north. Both of these structures mean there is only a triangle in the centre of the field where the shipping containers can be placed with the larger side running adjacent to [PLACE]. The applicant has asked for ‘micrositing’ up to 25metres. As the current layout plans to put the site as far to the east as possible it means that if they do intend to use ‘micrositing’ the only way they will be able to move is to the west.closer to [PLACE]. The applicant plans to use lithium ion batteries. It should be noted that there are other types of batteries that are infinitely safer to use in grid systems. Vanadium redox batteries can remain discharged indefinity without any damage, they have no noise or emissions, have a longer discharge/charge cycle life so would not need to be replaced as frequently as 7 years like these lithium ion batteries and are non flammable. They are of course more expensive. There is a watercourse running adjacent to the western border of the site. As the applicant has highlighted, on the other side of the road there is a high risk of flooding and it has been known to cause flooding onto [PLACE] road in the past (a retaining wall had to be rebuilt as flooding destroyed this a few years ago). This area drains directly into the water course just before the location where the access road is proposed. The access road will directly run across this watercourse and the applicant has not included as part of the planning application a definitive plan as to how this will be addressed instead proposing some options of what could be done – a ford (impractical with the 5 foot drop from the road to the field directly into the stream) or culverting the water through what would be an approximately 30 metre pipe to cover the width of the access road at that point (risk of blockage and opening up questions as to how this will be maintained). The access road is depicted on the drawings to have a wide mouth opening which starts at the current bus stop and extends to the middle of the driveway at [PLACE] before eventually tapering to the 3 metre wide access road that they state in their plans. This opening is around 25 metres and highlights the difficulty they will have in manoeuvring these large containers around a greater than 90 degree angle (essentially turning back on themselves) onto the site both during construction and every 7 years for the sites 40 year lifespan. The applicant makes very little mention of how they will connect to the [PLACE] within the documents submitted. They informed us at the public consultation events that the plan would be to connect via underground cabling along the main road via [PLACE] to the substation greater than 4 miles away. By having it this far away from the grid there is an approximately 10% loss of transmission each way. This is of no concern to the applicant as they will still make substantial profits from the electricity they do store and sell back to the grid but if Scotland as a nation is going to be sensible about how they manage BESS developments then at this early stage in this technology we should not be locating these installations at the limit of their viability (which is 5 miles) and picking sites which maximise their potential. Visual Impact [PLACE] descends from [PLACE] towards [PLACE]. I have concerns that this means this industrial installation encompassing will be highly visible from the road for every [PLACE] resident that travels down the [PLACE] every day. The units being placed are shipping containers and painting them green or grey is going to have minimal impact on hiding them. The visualisations provided are frankly misleading. The water tank is incorrectly sized – its plan states it is 4 metres tall therefore should be one of the highest buildings on site – yet it is shown on the visualisations as smaller than the BESS units at 2.9 metres. For example a picture taken at [PLACE] at [PLACE] is not representative of the majority of the communities view and has been taken behind a hill. In one case they have specifically stood behind a tree to take a photo (VP01)! The picture at the underpass has been taken through the trees – move 10 metres uphill beyond this point and this creates an entirely different vista – with direct views over the hedgerow onto the installation. There is no picture that demonstrates the vast majority of the communities view point on a daily basis– just above the mid Borland turn off where you descend from [PLACE]. The hedgerows planned are double root stock being planted in two rows. The applicant has stated it will take 15 years for these to reach the height of the perimeter fencing of 2.4metres (no mention of reaching the 2.9m height of ) The plans are for the batteries to be raised up on concrete pads on top of a permeable underlayer and the area needs to be flat and high enough due to the fact that they have admitted that this is waterlogged site (which will be compounded by the heavy plants compacting the soil on the site.) By the time the permeable road and the concrete pads are installed it seems highly likely that a degree of land raising will have occurred. The applicants are not taking into consideration any form of shielding the appearances from the [PLACE] side, relying on the existing tress that are not on the land that they will be leasing. There are two large gaps that view into the field from the [PLACE] in a location where slow/standstill traffic is often present. In the winter the existing trees offer no shielding and even in summer there would be a direct line of sight towards the BESS units and their ancillary structures through the gaps. The applicant plans to put the access road directly opposite a [PLACE] which is so listed because it is an example of a late 18th or early 19th century farmhouse. Please find below a note of my strong objections to the proposal outlined for the land at [PLACE] to erect a battery energy storage system.
