It should be noted and considered that an extremely small number of notification letters appear to have been issued which is in itself a concern and shows a lack of respect for this decision process. There are still a number of huge challenges and unknowns with regard to BESS, with particular concern voiced over the potential fire risk. There are a large number of recorded fires in these storage units which is held up by the fact that a number of insurers have withdrawn from offering coverage for the facilities due to the high risks. The large number and range of safety factors to be considered further highlight the very real safety issues, including layout and construction of the containers, gas detection and venting systems and explosion relief panels. A fire at a BESS site in [PLACE] took 59 hours to extinguish and caused a significant blast. The ability to contain potential explosion in the event of fire cannot be guaranteed and this would be catastrophic in a building which is planned directly to the side of an extremely busy traffic route into [PLACE], less than 50 m from multiple areas of housing and with a primary [PLACE] in very close proximity. The potential fire risks are widely acknowledged and agreed by various sources that can be confirmed in multiple papers on the subject should you care to research this. The planned development is also adjacent to Hutchison scrap yard which is known for being the site of multiple fires started by youths who enter at night to ride their motorbikes around and there have been numerous call outs of both police and fire services. I understand there are no plans for the development to be manned continuously to provide onsite security. c The development would be on a helicopter flight path. When/if a fire does occur in the facility, the release of highly toxic gases would have serious implications on local residents and a highly detrimental effect on the local environment and important infrastructure. Lithium-ion battery expert Professor [PERSON] of Newcastle University has stated that most applications for BESS should be ripped to shreds as there is no outlines provided with regard to fire suppression which is critical. He has stated that fire services need to be involved at design stage to understand the risks and hazards. He has reviewed countless lithium-ion battery fires, some of which have resulted in death and/or injury, and has stated that we cannot ignore the 60 or so BESS that have exploded. Most lithium-ion BESS are designed to have a 40-year lifetime and "Every one of them can expect to have at least one major incident in its lifetime." "Every single one". A report from the Faraday Institution, noted there is a huge volume of legislation in place globally to minimise electric vehicle battery safety risks. But legislation and testing for battery safety in other areas, including stationary storage, is "in its infancy". Apart from the high risks of fire, explosion and toxic pollution, the disruption to vehicles using [PLACE], and to the surrounding area, while cables are put in place to link the structure to the national grid would be prolonged and extensive. There would also be considerable risk to road traffic on this extremely busy road due to vehicles entering and leaving the proposed development. Access tracks to easily access and maintain the modules are documented as an important consideration. This is a 50 mph road but the local houses will attest to the fact that vehicles travel on this road far beyond the speed limit and there have already been numerous accidents, some involving multiple vehicles. Last but by no means least, the unsightly buildings and noise-reducing fencing to be erected 50 m from multiple back gardens, the noise of the vehicles entering and leaving the site and the high risk to the surrounding developments, will no doubt cause a depreciation in local housing values. I doubt the developer or their agents from the [ORGANIZATION] would agree to this development at the end of their garden or wish to buy a house in its vacinity. I sincerely hope the concerns and welfare of the local community will be given serious thought and consideration prior to giving this development further consideration.

I am writing to formally object to the proposed installation of a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) near my residence in [PLACE]. While I support the advancement of renewable energy and sustainable infrastructure, I have serious concerns about the siting of this project so close to a [PLACE], playpark, doctors surgery and residential area. First and foremost, BESS facilities pose well-documented safety risks, including the potential for thermal runaway events, fires, and even explosions. Incidents involving large lithium-ion battery installations in other communities have resulted in hazardous conditions, evacuations, and long-term health and environmental consequences. Locating such a facility near homes, schools, or community centers increases the potential danger to public safety. Additionally, there are concerns about the environmental and health impacts of such a facility. Potential noise pollution, electromagnetic fields, and chemical leakage during operation or in the event of an accident are all issues that must be carefully considered. These factors could significantly degrade the quality of life for residents and potentially impact property values in the area. Furthermore, there appears to be a lack of transparency and community consultation regarding this project. Decisions of this magnitude should involve meaningful input from those most affected, and many residents were either unaware of the proposal or not given an adequate opportunity to voice their concerns. In light of these issues, I strongly urge the relevant authorities and project developers to reconsider the location of the BESS facility. A more appropriate site — at a safe distance from residential neighbourhoods — should be identified to minimize the risks to human health and property.

target_text: 1. Noise. The noise from the air conditioning units for the battery containers, as well as the additional transformers need to be assessed in conjunction with the other cumulative projects in this area. The noise report from the developer specifically states that this has not been done in full. They also state that they have not taken into consideration the existing known noise issue with the Overhead Lines. 2. Fire. It is not possible to extinguish a lithium-ion battery fire. The Scottish Fire & Rescue Service have not been consulted and the National Fire Chiefs Council Guidance regarding BESS has not been followed in full (the battery containers are too close together, there is not a second emergency access, etc.). An emergency response plan is required for the site and for the area as a whole – including evacuation of residential properties and livestock. 3. Water source, for fire containment. There is no mains water on site. The developers propose to install 2 tanks to hold water to be used for cooling in the event of a fire; however there is no maintenance plan submitted for how the water stored on site will be maintained – e.g. against freezing in the winter and against biological growth in the summer. If chemicals are being added to treat this water, then this will need to be tested on a regular basis. Testing the water system works will also be required to ensure that it will work in the event of a fire, this will allow these chemicals to soak into the ground and cause pollutants to the local water table. 4. Fire water run-off and containment. What is the plan to prevent water used going back into the local eco- system after it has been contaminated? The drainage report states there will be a valve from the attenuation pond before the polluted water enters the burn, but does not describe how they will prevent chemicals from seeping through the earth. 5. Infrastructure. During construction, there will be major disruption on single track roads from both the large volume of construction workers arriving and leaving each day, along with the heavy goods vehicle deliveries for all of the concrete and the equipment. The developers report also clearly states that they have not undertaken any cumulative effects of construction into account with the numerous other projects happening adjacent to this site. 6. Rehabilitation. Where are the guarantees that the land will be restored at the end of the project – for example, how is the concrete going to be removed from the ground, and is there a secured fund for the money required to carry out this work? Details need to be made available to the public for this.

retrieved_examples.text: The proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) site raises significant environmental and safety concerns that need to be addressed: 1. Hazardous Substances: The presence of hazardous materials in the batteries, specifically lithium-ion, is a major concern. Have the Control of Major Accident Hazards (COMAH) regulations been consulted to ensure the safety of surrounding residents? 2. Impact on Landscape and Visual Integrity: The planning documents suggest that the site is located in an area with "wooded and diverse valleys" that are "attractive with a high degree of integrity." The proposed change from agricultural land to industrial use will be highly visible to local residents, visitors, and recreational users, impacting the landscape's visual appeal. 3. Noise Pollution: The noise generated by the BESS, which may vary in type and level depending on the time of day, needs to be assessed against pre-substation noise levels, not current elevated levels. Additionally, cumulative noise from all sites, including air conditioning units, must be considered. There is also the unresolved issue of noisy overhead power lines in [PLACE], which already cause stress and anxiety for local residents. 4. Fire Risk: Lithium-ion battery fires burn uncontrollably over extended periods, and the site will be unmanned, making emergency response challenging. No emergency response plan for adjacent residents has been provided, and concerns about snow-blocked access roads further complicate emergency response. What measures will be taken to ensure timely intervention and address risks to nearby woodlands and trees in the event of a fire? 5. Water Contamination: Water used to suppress a fire is likely to be contaminated, posing risks to the local water supply. A Sustainable Urban Drainage System (SUDS) pond is planned, but it is located on top of a hill, with water runoff potentially contaminating local aquifers and springs. The SUDS pond may also overflow during storms or fire suppression, impacting water courses. Has SEPA (Scottish Environment Protection Agency) been consulted on these issues?

Objection to Proposed BESS Development - Site-Specific and Infrastructure Concerns I strongly object to the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development in [PLACE] due to a number of unresolved safety, environmental, and infrastructure concerns: 1. Fire Risk & Emergency Planning Lithium-ion battery fires are extremely difficult to control and cannot be extinguished by conventional means. A detailed and site-specific fire containment and emergency response plan is essential. This must include evacuation procedures for nearby homes and livestock, particularly given the rural setting and limited access for emergency services. Recent incidents at [PLACE] and [PLACE] show that these risks are real and significant. 2. Contaminated Fire Water Run-off If water is used to cool or suppress a battery fire, it will likely be contaminated. There must be robust plans to contain this run-off and prevent pollution of the local environment. Contamination of the water table or nearby watercourses would be unacceptable in an area where residents often rely on private supplies. 3. Noise Pollution The site will introduce continuous noise from cooling units, transformers, and other infrastructure. This noise must be assessed against existing rural baseline levels. The potential long-term disturbance to nearby residents and wildlife should not be underestimated. 4. Construction Disruption Construction will cause major disruption on narrow rural roads, with regular heavy goods vehicle traffic and construction worker commutes. Noise, dust, and light pollution during the build phase will also negatively affect the surrounding area. 5. Decommissioning and Land Restoration At the end of the 40-year lifespan, there must be binding guarantees that all infrastructure, including concrete foundations, will be removed. A secured financial bond should be in place from the start to ensure full decommissioning and land restoration are properly funded.

Please accept this letter as a formal objection to the proposal for a [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE]. This development would contribute to an already disproportionate cluster of BESS proposals in the immediate area - six in total - with no clear assessment of the cumulative impact on the local community, environment, infrastructure, or emergency response capabilities. My specific concerns are outlined below: 1. Noise Pollution: The proposal fails to adequately consider noise generated by the cooling systems (air conditioning units) for the battery containers, as well as transformers and inverters. These noise sources must be measured against pre-substation background levels, and should also be modelled collectively across all six proposed BESS sites, in addition to existing noise from the [PLACE] and Grid Stability Facility. 2. Fire Risk and Emergency Response: Lithium-ion battery fires are extremely difficult - often impossible - to extinguish. The recent incidents at the [PLACE] locally, and more recently at [PLACE] in [PLACE], highlight the catastrophic potential of such fires. This application lacks: A clearly defined containment strategy for fire events on-site. A coordinated emergency response plan, including evacuation routes and procedures for local residents and livestock. Any reference to how emergency services would be supported or equipped to deal with a fire of this nature in a rural area with limited access. The absence of a robust, area-wide emergency framework is deeply concerning. 3. Water Supply for Fire Containment: The village of [PLACE] does not have a mains water connection. It is unclear how water will be sourced or stored in sufficient volume to manage a fire. If boreholes are proposed, this raises serious questions about the impact on private water supplies used by local residents. 4. Contaminated water entering the local ecosystem, particularly the burn that runs into [PLACE], could have devastating effects. This is especially alarming given the high dependency on private water supplies in the area. 5. Construction Impact and Infrastructure Pressure: Construction would create unacceptable disruption to the local area: Single-track rural roads will be overwhelmed by construction traffic and daily travel of over 100 workers. Increased risk to road safety, particularly for pedestrians, [PLACE] transport, and agricultural vehicles. Site Decommissioning and Land Rehabilitation: There is no assurance that the land will be fully restored at the end of the 25-year lifespan of the project. This includes: The removal of underground concrete foundations and infrastructure. A secured decommissioning fund to ensure taxpayers or residents are not burdened with the costs. A detailed rehabilitation plan ensuring the land is returned to agricultural or natural use. This proposal presents unacceptable risks to public safety, water security, environmental quality, and local infrastructure, with insufficient plans for emergency response, community protection, or long-term stewardship. In the absence of meaningful community engagement, a cumulative impact assessment, and robust mitigation strategies, this application should be refused. I respectfully urge [ORGANIZATION] to reject planning application [APPLICATION_CODE] in the best interests of the local community, the environment, and public safety.

This proposal raises significant concerns regarding public safety, environmental protection, and local infrastructure-each of which is a material planning consideration. Fire Risk: Lithium-ion battery fires are known to be extremely difficult to extinguish and can burn for extended periods, producing toxic fumes and runoff. No emergency response plan has been submitted, despite the site being unmanned, remote, and often snowbound in winter months. Access for emergency services is unreliable. There is no evidence that the fire service has been consulted, nor confirmation that the development complies with COMAH (Control of Major Accident Hazards) regulations, despite the hazardous nature of the materials on site. Noise Pollution: The site will introduce continuous and variable noise from cooling systems, inverters, and battery operations-especially during peak energy discharge periods. This will result in low-frequency hums or high-pitched whistles, depending on conditions. Critically, noise assessments appear to be benchmarked against current elevated levels caused by the substation and grid facility. They should instead be measured against pre-development baseline levels to accurately reflect the added impact. There is also no assessment of cumulative noise from multiple facilities operating simultaneously. Noise pollution, especially in a quiet rural area, will significantly harm residential amenity and mental wellbeing. Flooding and Water Contamination: The SUDS pond is located on elevated land and drains directly into natural aquifers and springs that supply local homes with drinking water. During a fire event, suppression water will be contaminated with toxic battery chemicals-posing a major risk to groundwater and private water supplies. Additionally, local burns feeding into [PLACE] are already known to cause flooding, with recent events recorded as recently as 2023. The planning documents do not demonstrate sufficient flood mitigation or show that SEPA has been adequately consulted. Road Safety and Access: Both construction and operational phases would increase heavy goods traffic on single-track roads used frequently by walkers, cyclists, and horse riders. The access point is located next to domestic dwellings. There is no traffic management plan, no road safety impact assessment for [PLACE], [PLACE], or surrounding areas, and no clear responsibility outlined for road repair due to construction damage.

I write to object to the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development on the following grounds: 1. Public Safety and Hazardous Materials The presence of hazardous substances in lithium-ion batteries introduces a significant risk. There is no evidence that COMAH regulations have been consulted, nor any indication of coordination with the [ORGANIZATION]. The absence of an emergency response plan, especially given the site's remote, unmanned status, raises serious safety concerns. 2. Landscape and Character Degradation The area in question is part of a valued rural landscape described by the applicant's own assessment as "well settled, wooded, and attractive." The conversion from agricultural land to an industrial facility will irreversibly change the character of the area. Its proximity to the substation does not justify such a transformation, which will be visibly and experientially intrusive to residents and visitors. 3. Unassessed Noise Impact The noise emissions from this development will be variable and dependent on load and operational conditions. Assessment should consider original baseline levels before the substation was introduced, and should evaluate cumulative noise from all adjacent infrastructure. Residents already report stress due to unresolved powerline noise - further disturbance will compound this issue. 4. Fire Risk and Emergency Preparedness Lithium-ion battery fires are notoriously difficult to manage and cannot be extinguished by conventional means. Given the site will not be permanently staffed, it is unclear how emergency services would respond, particularly in winter when roads are often impassable. Risks to nearby woodland, livestock, and rural homes have not been adequately accounted for. 5. Water Contamination and Flood Risk Fire suppression efforts would introduce contaminated water into an environment where residents rely on private wells and local watercourses. The proposed SUDS pond, situated on an elevated site, increases the risk of pollution entering aquifers and burns. With more frequent extreme weather events, overflow is a real concern. Consultation with SEPA appears absent. 6. Construction and Road Impact Significant disruption is expected during the construction phase, especially to narrow rural roads used daily by residents, walkers, and cyclists. No clear traffic impact assessments or mitigation plans have been shared for [PLACE], [PLACE], or surrounding routes. The impact on domestic properties adjacent to the access point has not been addressed. 7. Biodiversity and Protected Species The proposed site borders sensitive ecological areas such as the [PLACE], where several badger setts and ground-nesting birds have been identified. There is no clear evidence of recent ecological assessments or consultation with relevant conservation bodies such as the Badger Trust or [ORGANIZATION]. The potential impact on bats has also been overlooked. 8. Visual Appearance and Design Control Though the developer claims the battery units will be coloured to suit the landscape, there are no binding conditions to ensure this will be upheld. Past experience with similar developments suggests this may not be enforced, leading to an eyesore in what is currently an unspoiled area. 9. Restoration and Developer Responsibility There is no plan for site rehabilitation, no soil baseline data, and no mechanism to ensure land restoration. Developers of similar projects have sold them post-approval, raising accountability concerns. An ESCROW fund for environmental recovery should be a non-negotiable requirement. 10. Cumulative Impact on Community Wellbeing The local population has already endured years of disruption from adjacent energy infrastructure. This development will only intensify noise, traffic, and stress, further diminishing the health and quality of life of residents. The area is also an important recreational space for nearby communities - its degradation will be widely felt. 11. Absence of Community Benefit It is troubling that no community benefit is proposed, particularly given the long-term impact and scale of the development. This omission highlights a lack of local engagement or responsibility toward the communities affected. Conclusion Given the risks to public safety, environmental harm, disruption to rural life, and lack of community gain, this proposal is fundamentally unsuitable for this location. I urge the Council to reject the application unless all these matters are fully addressed and resolved through meaningful consultation.

This application is not required as part of achieving ‘net zero’ objectives and indeed presents little evidence in support of that aim. Duty of care has not been addressed. Rural residents in particular appear to be treated as a disposable commodity by [ORGANIZATION] and the Scottish Government. The financial objectives of large corporations and businesses and ‘after the event’ attempts at planning by [ORGANIZATION] and others appear to take precedence over basic concerns for the population, landscape and wildlife. Lack of regulation and risk of serious incident A full assessment of the risk associated with this proposal should include risks identified with the post construction phase as well as risks during construction. The proposed industrial development poses a threat to the historic landscape and rural character of the area. Despite the applicant's claim of "limited visibility," the location on a ridge would make it clearly visible from various points, including roads frequented by locals and visitors. The current tranquil, agricultural, and tourist-oriented character of the area would be irreversibly altered by this development. The BESS is being put forward without a clear local or national strategic framework dictating the appropriate siting of such facilities. The lack of justification for selecting this rural location over brownfield or industrial alternatives raises concerns about the potential for ad hoc industrial proposals to erode landscape quality and cohesion in rural communities across Scotland. Furthermore, the inadequate assessment of risks to local residents and the wider community from potential incidents at the site is troubling. Of utmost concern is the impact on the setting and experience of [PLACE], a significant and symbolic heritage asset in Scotland. The [PLACE], formerly a cherished retreat of the late Queen Mother, holds a prominent place in the Commonwealth's heritage. Its carefully preserved setting is integral to its historical significance. Allowing a BESS facility in close proximity risks commercializing and devaluing the legacy of this royal site. This decision carries international visibility and could have long-term reputational implications for Scotland's planning integrity and tourism image. Summary This project is being situated on the outskirts of a small rural village without a clear public benefit, contravening the principles of environmental justice and democratic planning. The Council's own guidance acknowledges "particular sensitivities in this location" that remain unaddressed. This large-scale industrial project offers no discernible community advantages, such as local employment guarantees, infrastructure improvements, or revenue sharing, thus falling short of the requirements outlined in the Scottish Planning Policy (SPP) and [PLACE] Council's Community Benefit Policy for Renewables. There has been no community referendum, vote, or significant public support for this development. Consultation has been merely perfunctory, lacking in effectiveness. Despite clear local opposition, it has been consistently disregarded. A project with such significant implications for daily life, health, heritage, and land should not be imposed without genuine, positive, and locally driven consent. This development lacks such consent. It goes against the core principles of sustainability, place-based decision-making, heritage preservation, and rural fairness as outlined in the National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4). The project is clearly disproportionate and unsuitable for the area. It would irrevocably change the local landscape and the historic rural surroundings of [PLACE], a site of national and symbolic significance. Heritage Impact: Irreparable Harm to [PLACE] and Its Setting The [PLACE] is a unique, irreplaceable asset. Its value lies not just in its architecture, but in its setting: a vast, open, rural coastal landscape with uninterrupted views to the north and west. The proposed BESS, with its 50MW of containerised battery modules, switchgear, access roads, fencing, and substations, will destroy this setting with industrial clutter, noise, and security lighting—24/7. The applicant’s Heritage Impact Assessment is fatally flawed. It grossly underestimates visibility, ignores seasonal variation, and dismisses experiential and cumulative harm. [ORGANIZATION] has failed to defend the setting of this vital heritage asset, despite receiving robust objections and FOI evidence of concerns. 3. Landscape and Visual Impact: Industrialisation of Unspoiled Countryside [PLACE] is under siege. [PLACE] is not an isolated project—it forms part of a coordinated wave of industrialisation, including: - [PLACE] and Switching Station - [PLACE] Tidal Project - [PLACE] - RIGIFA Substation - [PLACE] (proposed turbines and BESS) These projects combine to devastate the open, farmed, coastal landscape. The developer’s Planning Statement Addendum attempts to downplay this cumulative impact, despite clear guidance from NatureScot and NPF4 that such development must not result in significant visual or experiential harm. The “low-lying” claim is misleading. Even at 3–4m height, the BESS containers, substations, palisade fencing, and CCTV masts will break the visual line of the landscape and permanently scar its character. No amount of planting or bunding will mitigate this unnatural industrial form. 4. Public Safety and Fire Risk: A Catastrophic Blind Spot BESS systems are known to pose serious fire and explosion risks. Lithium-ion battery fires are toxic, uncontrollable, and extremely difficult to extinguish. Incidents around the world ([PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE]) have demonstrated the risks of thermal runaway, vapour cloud explosions, and first responder incapacitation. No credible plan has been provided to demonstrate how [PLACE]—with no full-time fire service, no nearby HAZMAT-trained crews, and no large-volume firefighting foam resources—would respond to such an incident. [PLACE] Council’s failure to demand a full Fire Risk Assessment or statutory Fire Safety consultation is negligent. 5. Policy Non-Compliance Across the Board This application fails every relevant test in NPF4 and [PLACE] policy, including: - Policy 1: Tackling the Climate and Nature Crises – No evidence of biodiversity net gain, ecological enhancement, or protection of prime agricultural land. - Policy 2: Climate Mitigation and Adaptation – No life-cycle emissions analysis; the project may worsen rather than reduce emissions. - Policy 4: Natural Places – Total disregard for rural amenity, wildland characteristics, and high-quality farmland. - Policy 6: Design, Quality, and Place – A functional industrial site with no design merit or community benefit. - Policy 16: Quality Homes – Nearby residents will suffer noise, light, and visual pollution, undermining quality of life. 6. Social Injustice and Community Exploitation This development has been imposed on a tiny rural community of fewer than 100 people, with no genuine consultation, no community buy-in, and no benefit-sharing mechanism. Local residents—many elderly—were blindsided by a stealth planning process that relied on a centralised Energy Consents Unit system, bypassing meaningful local scrutiny. The Scottish Government’s much-touted Social Values Charter is exposed as toothless. No health impact assessment, no local socio-economic study, no rural equality analysis. This is extractive development at its worst: profit for developers and investors; risk and loss for residents. 7. The Precedent: If This Is Approved, Nothing Is Safe If [PLACE] is approved—despite proximity to a royal castle, a Category A listed building, open agricultural land, and a fragile community—then no rural area in Scotland is safe from speculative industrialisation. The Reporter must take a stand. The Scottish Ministers must draw the line. This development is not green energy—it is greenwashed infrastructure driven by grid balancing speculation, not public need. It does not serve Scotland’s people. It damages Scotland’s heritage, landscape, and communities. Conclusion: Refuse [PLACE], Defend Rural Scotland I urge the Reporter and Scottish Ministers to reject this application in full. [PLACE] is the wrong development in the wrong place at the wrong time. It fails national policy, threatens lives and landscapes, and tears at the very fabric of rural Scotland. We cannot let this become the model for the future of energy planning. Refuse this application. Defend our heritage. Stand up for [PLACE].

target_text: I write to you to state that I object to this applicant's development of 162 MW BESS in my community. As a resident in the area greatly affected by the growth of renewable energy applicants I cannot agree to this additional development. The applicant has chosen this site due to the proximity of the planned extension and growth of the [PLACE] needed to support energy transmission from renewable energy generated in and around [PLACE] throughout Scotland. Until there is a strong and robust Fire Safety and Chemical Toxicity plan for large scale Lithium-ion battery storage that mitigates all risks of BESS developments from the Scottish Government and [ORGANIZATION] there should be a stop to all BESS development being granted permission in any area of Scotland but in particular remote and rural locations where there are severe limitations on the [PERSON] and Health care. Currently [PLACE] council do not have an emergency safety plan for Lithium-ion fire from BESS or Ecotoxity, this is concerning for residents and communities in [PLACE] when planning is granted in absence of a BESS fire safety plan. There needs to be accountability for the granting of BESS developments. The risk of fire, thermal runway or the release of hazardous material is gravely concerning. This development is planned adjacent to an electric substation and when completed the company acknowledges there is no long-term employment as this development will be remotely managed. This is a significant risk to our remote and rural area alongside the risk to this development's location adjacent to an electricity transmission and station infrastructure. This development should not be looked at as an individual case, this is unfortunately one of several BESS applicants for our small rural community but should instead be taken into context alongside the multiple wind farms already in situ and must also include all the additional renewable energy companies seeking to develop new wind farms or BESS in our small remote and rural area. There needs to be a robust examination of the exploitation of our area for the unprecedented growth of renewable energy in our small community. The cumulative impact of all these renewable projects has severe consequences if not assessed appropriately. This company admits that it will not offer any local long-term employment. [PLACE] is an area with an expected 9.3% depopulation over 10 years’; yet we have had a 60% increase in residents over the age of 75. There is falling [PLACE] roll and births across the county of [PLACE] with limited opportunities for the youth. Over 33% of the highland population is in power poverty, there is a real serious social-economic crisis happening in remote and rural areas. Developments like this do not value our landscape, heritage and nor sadly the residents. Our community is swamped with renewable energy infrastructure and continual applicants for more, we often feel that we are unheard and that we do not have a voice or a choice and that we are clearly insignificant to planners who granted permission out of context of the whole picture of developments. This applicant in their visuals has not disclosed all the other renewable and energy upgrades in their application. The location of this development is unnecessary and inappropriate, causing further destruction. Offering short-term battery storage in the wrong area where it will not be required. This is an opportunist company expecting to be allowed to exploit a small rural area as where there is less of a population to raise concern, an area that has already been allowed to have the landscape sacrificed for renewable energy infrastructure, the mass of industrialisation in our small community is terrifying with no end in sight. There are no positives in this development for the local area or residents, instead additional mass industrialisation, with a significant risk to our community, heritage, and landscape. The only group that benefits from the magnitude of this development is the applicants who are based out with Scotland but happy to profit from and destroy it. I hope that at time of planning that the concerns of the residents and our social-economic imbalance is taken into consideration alongside the cumulative amount of renewable infrastructure in place or seeking permission to be here. Communities across [PLACE] feel that they are being expected to carry the burden of the national energy policy, recently the Community Council Convention has developed across [PLACE] which is seeking a pause to major renewable applications until there is a more joined up approach to this situation. I strongly object to this development.

Fire: It is not possible to extinguish a lithium-ion battery fire. Scottish Fire & Rescue have not been consulted on the plans for this site. Over the last few years the residents of [PLACE] have become increasingly concerned that our rural community is being industrialised without our consent. retrieved_examples.text: Including this application, there are now six proposed BESS sites in this local area, along with multiple renewable projects around [PLACE]. Yet no consideration has been given to the cumulative effects of these developments. Despite [PLACE] Council’s recommendation, no Environmental Impact Assessment has been undertaken to address these impacts. My principal objections are as follows: Landscape and Visual Impact The site covers 16.3 hectares (equivalent to 23 football pitches) with a 25m gradient. The developers propose six terraces to address the slope. The project includes 470 shipping containers (332 battery containers and 138 power converters), 4,608 solar PV panels, three 12m-high Super Grid Transformers, and other associated infrastructure. Even with the proposed 4m fences and 8m earth bunds, this scale of development will remain highly visible on the sloping site. This would create a significant and permanent industrial intrusion into the rural landscape, contrary to National Planning Framework 4 (Policy 11). Noise The noise assessment submitted is inadequate, omitting key details on sound sources, site layout and receptors. Experts have concluded that the development could raise background noise levels to three times their current levels. The sloping nature of the site makes effective noise mitigation unlikely, both during construction and operation. With insufficient detail on equipment specifications and cumulative impact, there is a high risk of significant noise pollution affecting the locality. Fire Risk Lithium-ion battery fires cannot be extinguished by conventional means. Scottish Fire & Rescue have not been consulted, and National Fire Chiefs Council guidance has not been fully followed. A robust emergency response plan is essential, including evacuation procedures for residents and livestock. Alarmingly, some households currently have no evacuation route that avoids the site. Water for Fire Suppression Large volumes of water would be required on site for fire containment. It is unclear where this supply would come from, whether it would be trucked in (increasing traffic), and what chemicals would be added to prevent stagnation or freezing. Drainage, Water Supply and Contamination The terracing of the slope and installation of an impermeable membrane have not been properly modelled in relation to drainage, infiltration, SuDS performance, or the risk of contaminating private water supplies and watercourses. There has been no peer-reviewed assessment of the potential impact on groundwater. Infrastructure and Traffic Construction will cause severe disruption on narrow single-track roads. Over 100 workers will travel to and from the site daily, in addition to heavy goods deliveries of equipment and materials. The developer’s Construction Management and Traffic Plan significantly underestimates vehicle movements, excluding welfare units, fencing, solar infrastructure, water tanks, landscaping, and waste removal. Biodiversity Without an Environmental Impact Assessment, there has been no proper evaluation of the effects on habitats for badgers, bats, ground-nesting birds and other protected species in the adjoining Ancient Woodland. Construction disturbance, extensive earthworks, and kilometres of 4m-high fencing will cause major disruption. In the event of a fire, contaminated run-off could pollute the [PLACE] and the [PLACE] with devastating consequences for local ecology. Decommissioning and Land Restoration There are no clear or enforceable guarantees regarding how the site will be restored after the 25-year lifespan of the project. The removal of impermeable membranes, extensive concrete foundations and 8m-high berms, once matured with trees and shrubs, is not addressed. Community Benefit The “Community Wealth Building Plan” offers no firm commitment to employing a local workforce and provides no direct community benefit. Scottish Government guidance recommends community benefits equivalent to £5,000 per installed megawatt per annum – for this project, £2.5 million annually. The developer has ignored this entirely. Planning Policy National Planning Framework 4 (Policy 11) supports renewable energy projects only where landscape and visual impacts are minimised and where there are demonstrable local and community benefits. This proposal fails on both counts and therefore does not meet the requirements of national policy. Conclusion In summary, the proposed development poses unacceptable risks to the environment, local amenity, and community wellbeing. It does not comply with planning policy and should therefore be refused.

If approved, this development would be one of six large-scale BESS projects in a small, rural area. No assessment has been undertaken to examine the cumulative environmental, safety, and community impacts, despite [PLACE] Council’s clear recommendation for an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA). Proceeding without this is a serious planning failure. Key reasons this proposal must be refused: 1. Landscape and Visual Harm This is an industrial-scale project - 16.3 hectares (23 football pitches) on a steeply sloped site with a 25m height drop. The plan involves six terraces, 470 shipping containers, 4,608 solar PV panels, three 12m-tall transformers, and multiple other large structures. Even with 4m fences and 8m bunds, the site will dominate the landscape, permanently altering rural views and character. 2. Unacceptable Noise Impact Independent experts confirm that background noise could triple. The sloping site will make containment difficult, both during construction and operation. The developer’s own noise report is incomplete, omitting key details on sound sources, layout, and receptor points, and makes no assessment of cumulative noise from other nearby BESS sites. 3. Fire Safety Risk Lithium-ion battery fires cannot be extinguished and can burn for days. Scottish Fire & Rescue has not been consulted. The proposal fails to meet all National Fire Chiefs Council guidance and offers no credible emergency plan. In the event of a fire, some residents would have no safe evacuation route except towards the danger. This is wholly unacceptable. 4. Water Supply for Fire Control The huge water volumes needed for suppression have no confirmed source. Delivery would add further HGV traffic, and chemical treatments to prevent stagnation/freezing could add environmental hazards. 5. Drainage, Water Contamination & Private Supply Risk No robust hydrological assessment has been carried out. The impermeable membrane and terracing could alter natural drainage, contaminate private water supplies, and pollute the [PLACE] and [PLACE] in the event of firewater runoff. This risk has been ignored rather than mitigated. 6. Construction Traffic & Infrastructure Strain Single-track roads cannot safely accommodate the hundreds of daily vehicle movements expected - 100+ construction workers, heavy goods deliveries, water tankers, waste removal, and all other site servicing. The developer’s traffic plan significantly underestimates the real volumes. 7. Biodiversity Damage With no EIA, there is no serious assessment of the impact on protected species - badgers, bats in adjacent Ancient Woodland, and ground-nesting birds. The sheer scale of earthworks, fencing, and human activity will cause lasting habitat loss. Fire incidents would release toxins into waterways, further damaging local ecology. 8. Lack of Restoration Commitment There is no binding plan to remove the impermeable membrane, dismantle 8m bunds, or fully restore the land after the 25-year lifespan. The risk is permanent industrialisation of agricultural land. 9. Zero Meaningful Community Benefit The developer’s “Community Wealth Building Plan” contains no guarantee of using local labour and no financial benefit for the community. Scottish Government guidance recommends £5,000 per MW per year - £2.5 million annually for this project. The developer has chosen to offer nothing. Conflict with National Policy National Planning Framework 4 Policy 11 supports renewable projects only where they minimise landscape harm and deliver genuine local benefit. This application fails both tests. It is environmentally risky, socially negligent, and economically dismissive of the host community. Conclusion This proposal is not simply flawed - it is dangerous, incomplete, and in breach of planning principles designed to protect rural Scotland. Without an Environmental Impact Assessment, proper safety planning, or binding community benefit, it cannot be justified and must be rejected. On a personal level, I am deeply concerned about the potential noise, pollution, risk of contamination to private water supplies, and the sheer volume of traffic this project would bring to an already busy single-track road. My young family regularly walk along the surrounding roads, and I am gravely worried for our safety should construction and operational traffic increase to the extent anticipated. This development poses a direct threat not only to the peace and character of our rural community, but also to the safety of the people who live here.

target_text: I write to object to this proposed development of a very large (500MW) BESS scheme on prime agricultural land in a rural area of [PLACE]. [ORGANIZATION], the nominal developer, is a "paper" company (established in 2022, HQ'd in [PLACE] but with Norwegian principals) and appears to be a spin-off from/subsidiary of another, English-HQ'd "paper" company, [ORGANIZATION] (established in 2019, whose principle activities are listed at Companies House as "PR and communications" and "management consultancy activities"). That is to say, this is business interests with zero demonstrable track record in the UK energy industry, seeking the opportunity to create one of the largest BESS complexes (the size of 21 football pitches) in Europe, utilising a still-emergent technology prone to low- probability but very high-impact consequences in the event of thermal runaway, in an effort to cash in on the weakly-regulated "green energy" Gold Rush in northern Scotland. A government with its wits about it will want to stress-test such a large-scale and potentially impactful application from such an unproven outfit. A government concerned with public accountability and the transparency of its decision- making will pay close heed to the many significant public objections to this proposed development and respond accordingly. The behind-closed-doors opacity of the Energy Consents Unit simply does not cut it. The application itself is a monument to misinformation and missing information, especially in relation to fire-risks, their prevention and mitigation in the event of an incident occurring. The would-be developers are clearly hoping to take advantage of the well-known loopholes in UK health & safety legislation in respect of lithium-ion battery technology in search of an early pay-day. At minimum, such is the scale of this proposed development and its cumulative impact along with the large new electricity sub-station immediately next door (a fact largely and conveniently overlooked by the applicant), this alone should require the application to be remitted to a public inquiry where the information underpinning the application and its full cumulative impacts can be challenged and tested in public. Anything less is weak government abdicating its public safety and well-being responsibilities to the public it is elected to serve. in a world of coherent policy-making, this application would be paused - along all others in the planning pipeline (or trying to enter it) - until such time as the Scottish Government produces an energy/energy security strategy (the current one dates back to 2017) and a Just Transition strategy (promised back in 2023 but still AWOL) so that any further developments could then be bench-marked against them, as well as against the as-yet unpublished National Energy Spatial Plan promised by [ORGANIZATION] and [ORGANIZATION]. Right now the Scottish Government appears rudderless on energy security whilst what is passed off as "policy" involves Ministers being led by the nose by well-resourced developers and their lobbyists. Get a grip.

retrieved_examples.text: I write to strongly object to the above application. I am co-owner of the adjacent fields to the East of this proposed Battery Storage Site - land known as [PLACE]. I have never at any point received neighbour notification regarding this project and was not aware of the public consultations held back in 2024. The first I knew about it, was reading about the planning application in our local newspaper! My grave concerns are that, as there are reports almost on a daily basis of fires breaking out from BESS installations, though the industry wants to play this down, the poisonous smoke and fumes will seriously affect those living close by and depending on the direction and speed of the wind, could be carried for miles! The toxic particles in the smoke will most definably, be detrimental to human health and these particles will also contaminate waterways and fields for miles around. Who will compensate us if we can no longer grow crops in our fields or graze livestock? If these Battery units catch fire, is there provision to contain run off? I can see no mention of this in their website. How can this be classed as environmentally friendly and green energy? Minerals used to construct the batteries is mined in foreign countries, with no regard to pollution caused by their extraction, then shipped half way round the world to get here. A huge carbon footprint has already been created getting the materials into this country! It is of little benefit to our community, as it will not create local jobs. The workforce employed for the construction will be from other parts of the country. I find it very hard to believe, that [ORGANIZATION] have not had to complete an environmental risk assessment given the wildlife that reside in the gully between our land and [PLACE]! How many hours will the BESS hold power for? Is the environmental impact and carbon footprint caused by this project going to be offset by the benefits? There is no mention of any of this on their website! There is also no mention of how the site will be maintained, secured or what measures will be in place to prevent unauthorised access. There is no mention of how long this BESS will be in place. Surely these are all points that should be stated before any planning application is considered! It is criminal what the Scottish Government is allowing to happen to Scotland - desecrating the beautiful countryside with Wind Turbines, BESS, Solar Panels and Power Stations. This formal objection is hereby submitted in response to planning application [APPLICATION_CODE] (Council Ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]) put forth by [ORGANIZATION] for the establishment of a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at [PLACE] within the jurisdiction of the [ORGANIZATION]. The proposed industrial development poses a threat to the historical landscape and rural ambiance of the area. Despite the applicant's assertion of "limited visibility," the BESS's location on a ridge would render it prominently visible from various vantage points, including roads frequented by locals and tourists. The current serene, agricultural, and tourism-focused character of the area stands to be irreversibly disrupted. The lack of a clear local or national strategic framework for the placement of such developments raises concerns. The rationale behind selecting this rural site over available brownfield or industrial alternatives remains unexplained. In the absence of strategic siting guidelines, rural communities in Scotland are left susceptible to arbitrary industrial proposals that erode landscape quality and cohesion. Furthermore, the potential risks to local residents and the wider community from incidents such as fires at the site have been downplayed. Of utmost concern is the impact on the setting and ambiance of [PLACE], a significant and emblematic heritage asset in Scotland. The [PLACE], once a cherished retreat of the late Queen Mother, holds a prominent place in the Commonwealth's landmarks. Its meticulously preserved surroundings have been safeguarded for generations. Allowing a BESS facility in close proximity risks commercializing and devaluing the legacy of this royal site. Such a decision carries international visibility and could have long-term repercussions on Scotland's planning credibility and tourism appeal. Landscape and Visual Impacts The proposed site is situated in a vast, open landscape with expansive views over [PLACE]. Even with the addition of vegetation, this location is ill-suited for accommodating large-scale energy infrastructure without significantly altering its current character. The project would introduce harsh elements such as metal fencing and 6-metre structures into a tranquil rural environment, with many residents residing just a short distance from the entrance. The resulting impact is not adequately justified or mitigated in any substantial manner. Summary This project is being situated in close proximity to a small rural village without demonstrating a clear public benefit, thereby contravening the principles of environmental justice and democratic planning. The Council's own guidance acknowledges "particular sensitivities in this location" that remain unaddressed. Despite its industrial scale, the project does not offer any discernible community advantages such as local employment opportunities, infrastructure enhancements, or revenue sharing. Consequently, it falls short of the criteria outlined in the Scottish Planning Policy (SPP) and [PLACE] Council's Community Benefit Policy for Renewables. There has been no community referendum, vote, or widespread support for this development. Consultation has been superficial, lacking meaningful engagement with local residents. Despite evident opposition from the community, their concerns have been consistently disregarded. A project with significant implications for daily life, health, heritage, and the environment should not be imposed without genuine, positive, and locally-driven consent. This development is incongruent with the core values of sustainability, place-based decision-making, heritage preservation, and rural fairness as outlined in the National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4). Its scale and location are fundamentally inappropriate, posing a threat to the local landscape and the historic rural setting of [PLACE], a site of national significance. Approving an industrial battery installation in such close proximity to a Royal heritage site based on speculation, inadequate evidence, and flawed policy implementation is unacceptable.

Personal Comments FULL OBJECTION TO MEY BESS ([APPLICATION_CODE]) Submitted by [PERSON] 26/05/2025 Introduction I am writing to lodge my strongest and unequivocal objection to the proposed [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development, located just 1.3 km from [PLACE] in [PLACE]. This development is wholly incompatible with the character, values, and future of our rural community. It fails across every relevant policy test, represents a gross abuse of the planning system, and threatens to irreversibly damage the heritage, landscape, safety, and social cohesion of the area. It must be refused. 1. Violation of National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4) NPF4 Policy 11(e)(ii) explicitly states that energy proposals must “not have significant adverse effects on the integrity or special qualities of national or international designations.” The proximity of [PLACE] to [PLACE], a Category A-listed building and internationally significant tourist destination, violates this requirement. The applicant’s attempt to sidestep this is disingenuous. The Castle is not merely a visual asset—it is a cultural anchor for [PLACE], attracting thousands of visitors annually and forming part of Scotland’s Royal and historic identity. Any development that industrialises the surrounding countryside irrevocably damages the integrity of this national treasure. 2. Heritage Impact: Irreparable Harm to [PLACE] and Its Setting The [PLACE] is a unique, irreplaceable asset. Its value lies not just in its architecture, but in its setting: a vast, open, rural coastal landscape with uninterrupted views to the north and west. The proposed BESS, with its 50MW of containerised battery modules, switchgear, access roads, fencing, and substations, will destroy this setting with industrial clutter, noise, and security lighting—24/7. The applicant’s Heritage Impact Assessment is fatally flawed. It grossly underestimates visibility, ignores seasonal variation, and dismisses experiential and cumulative harm. [ORGANIZATION] has failed to defend the setting of this vital heritage asset, despite receiving robust objections and FOI evidence of concerns. 3. Landscape and Visual Impact: Industrialisation of Unspoiled Countryside [PLACE] is under siege. [PLACE] is not an isolated project—it forms part of a coordinated wave of industrialisation, including: - [PLACE] and Switching Station - [PLACE] Tidal Project - [PLACE] - RIGIFA Substation - [PLACE] (proposed turbines and BESS) These projects combine to devastate the open, farmed, coastal landscape. The developer’s Planning Statement Addendum attempts to downplay this cumulative impact, despite clear guidance from NatureScot and NPF4 that such development must not result in significant visual or experiential harm. The “low-lying” claim is misleading. Even at 3–4m height, the BESS containers, substations, palisade fencing, and CCTV masts will break the visual line of the landscape and permanently scar its character. No amount of planting or bunding will mitigate this unnatural industrial form. 4. Public Safety and Fire Risk: A Catastrophic Blind Spot BESS systems are known to pose serious fire and explosion risks. Lithium-ion battery fires are toxic, uncontrollable, and extremely difficult to extinguish. Incidents around the world ([PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE]) have demonstrated the risks of thermal runaway, vapour cloud explosions, and first responder incapacitation. No credible plan has been provided to demonstrate how [PLACE]—with no full-time fire service, no nearby HAZMAT-trained crews, and no large-volume firefighting foam resources—would respond to such an incident. [PLACE] Council’s failure to demand a full Fire Risk Assessment or statutory Fire Safety consultation is negligent. 5. Policy Non-Compliance Across the Board This application fails every relevant test in NPF4 and [PLACE] policy, including: - Policy 1: Tackling the Climate and Nature Crises – No evidence of biodiversity net gain, ecological enhancement, or protection of prime agricultural land. - Policy 2: Climate Mitigation and Adaptation – No life-cycle emissions analysis; the project may worsen rather than reduce emissions. - Policy 4: Natural Places – Total disregard for rural amenity, wildland characteristics, and high-quality farmland. - Policy 6: Design, Quality, and Place – A functional industrial site with no design merit or community benefit. - Policy 16: Quality Homes – Nearby residents will suffer noise, light, and visual pollution, undermining quality of life. 6. Social Injustice and Community Exploitation This development has been imposed on a tiny rural community of fewer than 100 people, with no genuine consultation, no community buy-in, and no benefit-sharing mechanism. Local residents—many elderly—were blindsided by a stealth planning process that relied on a centralised Energy Consents Unit system, bypassing meaningful local scrutiny. The Scottish Government’s much-touted Social Values Charter is exposed as toothless. No health impact assessment, no local socio-economic study, no rural equality analysis. This is extractive development at its worst: profit for developers and investors; risk and loss for residents. 7. The Precedent: If This Is Approved, Nothing Is Safe If [PLACE] is approved—despite proximity to a royal castle, a Category A listed building, open agricultural land, and a fragile community—then no rural area in Scotland is safe from speculative industrialisation. The Reporter must take a stand. The Scottish Ministers must draw the line. This development is not green energy—it is greenwashed infrastructure driven by grid balancing speculation, not public need. It does not serve Scotland’s people. It damages Scotland’s heritage, landscape, and communities. Conclusion: Refuse [PLACE], Defend Rural Scotland I urge the Reporter and Scottish Ministers to reject this application in full. [PLACE] is the wrong development in the wrong place at the wrong time. It fails national policy, threatens lives and landscapes, and tears at the very fabric of rural Scotland. We cannot let this become the model for the future of energy planning. Refuse this application. Defend our heritage. Stand up for [PLACE].

I wish to strongly object to this, the 4th application for a Battery Storage System linked to the National Grid via [PLACE], which in its self, has recently undergone a considerable increase capacity. The first two applications have received approval there is a 50 MW BESS site already under construction, by [ORGANIZATION], adjacent to the substation. The second is a 500MW BESS construction by [ORGANIZATION], just south of the substation. The third for a further 400MW BESS by the [ORGANIZATION], formally [ORGANIZATION] is still under consideration. All are being built on Prime Agricultural Land (BMV) alongside or opposite the Substation. This fourth application from [PLACE] BESS for 340MW storage is also on land classed as ‘Arable Agriculture’ by the LCA Scotland as capable of producing a wide range of crops. The NPF4 Policy 5, SOILS, states that prime agricultural land will only be supported in limited circumstances including for energy generation from renewable sources. “This application does NOT represent a form of electrical generation infrastructure rather it draws power from the grid stores this and releases it back as required”. (Quote from application for [PLACE] BESS by Energy Workshops) The NPF4 Policy 5 SOILS, also makes it clear that development proposals will only be supported if they are designed and constructed in accordance with mitigation hierarchy by first avoiding and then minimising the amount of disturbance to soils on undeveloped land. It also clearly states that development proposals WILL ONLY be supported where it is for essential infrastructure AND there is a specific location need and NO other suitable site. This Application by [PLACE] BESS is, over 2 miles from the Substation. This indicates there is NO “specific location need” for the BESS to be on this site. If A BESS can be 2 miles distant, it can be 5 miles or further distant or better still built to utilise ‘Brown Field’ sites close to the Wind or Solar energy generators. As the Energy Workshops state in their application the [PLACE] will buy energy cheaply from the grid when there is surplus store it for a very short period before selling it back at a profit to the grid when required. Therefore making a considerable profit for the owners and shareholders and at a cost to the consumer. Location of the site is purely based on the landowners speculation for financial gain. Granting permission will set a highly dangerous precedent and would open up the potential for BESS developments outside the immediate vicinity of Substations across Scotland. Unnecessarily threatening swathes of Prime Agricultural land and deeming the guidance within NPF4 to be meaningless. NPF4 also states that the impacts on communities, nature and other receptors, including the cumulative impact, should be important considerations on decision making. However, the impact on the daily lives of communities is not obvious until after permission is granted. The impact on the village of [PLACE] during the current development of the 50 MW site recently under construction has seen numerous journeys by 10 tonne trucks per day through our village Main Street. This is only one of two or three routes used daily during this early earth moving stage. The actual construction of the concrete plinths and storage containers and connection of the batteries hasn’t yet commenced. [ORGANIZATION], have stated that during construction of their 500MW BESS they estimate 80 HGV movements per day. This is only a small example of the current and future impact and, of course, it is not just transport affecting this small village of 40 homes and the 2 other villages in close proximity to the Sub Station. Or to the surrounding countryside, wildlife, nature and other receptors. There is always the possibility of battery fire from any Lithium Battery. This must be a consideration and not ignored. Adjacent to [PLACE] is the [PLACE], a tributary of the [PLACE] which is, with it’s tributaries, a Site of Special Scientific Interest ([PLACE]). Vast amounts of water are needed to extinguish a battery fire which will be contaminated and enter the water table and courses. By 2050 the National Grid ESO, the electricity system operator for Great Britain, is forecasting that the UK as a whole will need at least 50 GW of energy storage power capacity. Three small villages in this glorious area of the Scottish Borders are already committed to 1 GW. Which is more than our fair share. Please call a halt, by refusing this application, to any further BESS in this area before any further fields are turned into an industrial wasteland and our crops covered in concrete.
